nodes.label: Creatine
nodes.description: Sarcopenia is an age-related condition marked by declining muscle mass, strength, and functional capacity. Creatine supplementation combined with resistance training is an effective countermeasure: studies in older adults (>65 years) taking 5 g/day during heavy resistance training promoted greater gains in muscle mass and isometric strength, and meta-analyses confirm that older individuals doing resistance training gain more muscle mass, strength, and functional capacity when supplementing creatine. Creatine also preserves muscle mass and promotes fat loss during energy-restricted diets, helping manage adult-onset obesity while preventing the muscle loss that commonly accompanies weight loss in older individuals.

nodes.label: Sarcopenia
nodes.description: Sarcopenia is an age-related condition marked by declining muscle mass, strength, and functional capacity. Creatine supplementation combined with resistance training is an effective countermeasure: studies in older adults (>65 years) taking 5 g/day during heavy resistance training promoted greater gains in muscle mass and isometric strength, and meta-analyses confirm that older individuals doing resistance training gain more muscle mass, strength, and functional capacity when supplementing creatine. Creatine also preserves muscle mass and promotes fat loss during energy-restricted diets, helping manage adult-onset obesity while preventing the muscle loss that commonly accompanies weight loss in older individuals.

nodes.label: Homocysteine
nodes.description: Creatine supplementation has been reported to lower plasma homocysteine, an effect that may reduce cardiovascular disease risk. Because homocysteine is methylated back to methionine by enzymes that require the same methyl-donor pool (S-adenosyl methionine) used for creatine synthesis, supplying exogenous creatine spares methyl groups that would otherwise be consumed in endogenous creatine formation, thereby lowering homocysteine production. Studies in individuals adhering to vegan diets (who tend to have elevated homocysteine) reported that creatine supplementation reduced homocysteine levels and improved systemic microvascular endothelial function, supporting creatine's role in cardiovascular health beyond its direct effects on muscle bioenergetics.

nodes.label: Toll-like Receptor
nodes.description: Creatine down-regulates the expression of toll-like receptors, including TLR-2, TLR-3, TLR-4, and TLR-7, in a mouse macrophage cell line (RAW 254.7). This downregulation could reduce the ability to sense some infections in immunocompromised individuals, but TLR-4 downregulation may also alter Parkinson's disease pathology and inhibit neuronal death as the disease progresses. Creatine's influence on toll-like receptors is one component of its broader immunomodulatory effects, which also include altering cytokine production, possibly through the NF-kB signaling pathway, thereby affecting cytokines, receptors, and growth factors that shape immune responses and inflammation.

nodes.label: Cognition
nodes.description: Creatine supplementation increases brain phosphocreatine content by 5-15% and enhances brain bioenergetics, which is thought to underlie its cognitive benefits. Studies report that creatine attenuates mental fatigue and improves cognition, executive function, working memory, and processing speed, especially in older adults and during sleep deprivation. Examples include improved working memory and processing speed after 5 g/day for 6 weeks, better maintenance of mood, balance, and reaction time after sleep deprivation, and improved long-term memory and random number generation in elderly participants. While not all studies show benefit, the evidence supports creatine as a modest cognitive enhancer, particularly under metabolic or cognitive stress.

nodes.label: Exercise
nodes.description: Creatine supplementation is one of the most studied and effective ergogenic aids for athletes. It increases muscle creatine and phosphocreatine levels, enhances acute exercise capacity, and improves training adaptations, yielding roughly 10-20% improvements in high-intensity exercise tasks across fitness activities, golf, volleyball, soccer, softball, ice hockey, running, and swimming. The International Society of Sports Nutrition concludes creatine is the most effective ergogenic supplement available for increasing high-intensity exercise capacity and lean body mass during training. Ergogenic benefits are seen in men and women across ages from children to the elderly, although most studies have been conducted in men.

nodes.label: Methylglyoxal (MG)
nodes.description: Creatine augments the anticancer efficacy of the metabolite methylglyoxal (MG). Creatine content and energy availability are low in several types of malignant cells and in the T cells that mediate immune responses against cancer, and the creatine transporter SLC6A8 is markedly increased in tumor-infiltrating immune cells. Patra et al. reported that MG efficacy is significantly augmented in the presence of creatine, and combined administration of creatine, methylglyoxal, and ascorbic acid provided greater efficacy and eliminated visible signs of tumor growth. Creatine and creatine kinase, very low in sarcoma tissue, were significantly elevated with concomitant regression of tumor cells.

nodes.label: Antioxidant Properties
nodes.description: Creatine is reported to exert antioxidant effects, scavenging reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and stabilizing membranes, effects that are proposed to protect tissues from oxidative damage. Some studies suggest creatine supplementation reduces markers of oxidative stress and muscle damage after intense exercise, and experimental work indicates creatine can directly scavenge superoxide and peroxynitrite in vitro. Because oxidative stress contributes to DNA damage and tumor promotion, creatine's antioxidant capacity is cited in the trace as one possible mechanism for an anti-cancer effect, although direct evidence linking creatine's antioxidant action to cancer prevention in humans is lacking.

nodes.label: Exercise Performance
nodes.description: Creatine supplementation is one of the most effective and best-documented ergogenic aids for improving performance in high-intensity, short-duration activities. By increasing muscle phosphocreatine stores, creatine enhances the capacity to regenerate ATP during repeated bouts of maximal exercise, increasing power output, strength gains during resistance training, and work performed in repeated sprint protocols. Meta-analyses consistently show moderate improvements in measures such as maximal strength, sprint performance, and lean body mass, with benefit most pronounced in activities relying on the phosphocreatine energy system. These well-established performance effects are the context in which the trace asks whether creatine also influences cancer outcomes.

nodes.label: Glycemic Control
nodes.description: Creatine supplementation supports healthy glucose management by enhancing glucose uptake and insulin sensitivity. Mechanistically, creatine prevents the decline of GLUT4 during muscle disuse, increases GLUT4 during rehabilitation, and co-ingestion with carbohydrate or protein augments muscle creatine and glycogen. In individuals with type 2 diabetes, creatine supplementation during exercise training improved glucose tolerance to a standard meal, increased GLUT4 translocation, and lowered HbA1c, with AMPK signaling implicated in these effects. Creatine uptake into tissue is itself influenced by glucose and insulin, establishing a bidirectional relationship between creatine status and glycemic physiology that supports creatine as an adjunct for metabolic health.

nodes.label: GLUT4
nodes.description: Creatine supplementation influences glucose handling in skeletal muscle, in part by upregulating the GLUT4 glucose transporter. Creatine prevents declines in GLUT4 during immobilization and increases GLUT4 by about 40% during rehabilitation after atrophy, and co-ingestion with carbohydrate and protein enhances creatine uptake and muscle glycogen. In type 2 diabetic patients, 12 weeks of creatine supplementation during training improved glucose tolerance, increased GLUT4 translocation, and significantly reduced HbA1c, with changes in AMPK signaling related to GLUT4 translocation and HbA1c. These findings indicate creatine enhances glucose uptake and supports glucose management, especially when combined with exercise.

nodes.label: Muscle Mass
nodes.description: Creatine supplementation increases muscle creatine and phosphocreatine stores and, particularly when combined with resistance training, promotes gains in lean tissue mass and strength. Randomized trials in older adults show greater gains in muscle mass and isometric strength with creatine plus heavy resistance training compared to training alone, and meta-analyses confirm larger gains in muscle mass and upper-body strength in older individuals supplementing creatine during resistance exercise. Creatine also decreases protein breakdown and can preserve muscle mass during energy-restricted weight loss, making it a broadly useful strategy for maintaining muscle across the lifespan and in clinical rehabilitation populations.

nodes.label: Nutraceuticals
nodes.description: Creatine is a naturally occurring nitrogen-containing compound that is synthesized endogenously in the liver, kidney, and pancreas and is also obtained from dietary sources, particularly red meat and fish. Around 95 percent of the body's creatine is stored in skeletal muscle, approximately one-third of it in the phosphorylated form creatine phosphate. In the muscle it is converted to creatine phosphate, which donates its high-energy phosphate group to regenerate ATP from ADP, supporting short-duration, high-intensity exercise. Because of its role in ATP regeneration, creatine is one of the most widely used sports supplements and is increasingly examined for additional therapeutic effects, including possible anti-cancer properties.

nodes.label: Red Meat
nodes.description: Dietary creatine is obtained almost exclusively from animal-derived foods, with red meat and fish being the richest sources. Cooking does not destroy creatine, and an omnivorous diet typically supplies one to two grams of creatine per day, which complements the roughly one gram synthesized endogenously per day. Vegetarians have lower muscle creatine stores and show larger increases in response to supplementation than meat-eaters, reflecting the lower baseline intake. This dietary origin is relevant to epidemiologic questions about meat consumption and cancer risk, because creatine is often discussed alongside other meat-derived compounds when considering diet-cancer associations.

nodes.label: Creatine Phosphate
nodes.description: Within cells, creatine is phosphorylated by the enzyme creatine kinase to form creatine phosphate (phosphocreatine), which serves as a rapidly mobilizable reserve of high-energy phosphate. The reaction creatine plus ATP yields creatine phosphate plus ADP, and the reverse reaction regenerates ATP during bursts of high energy demand, such as muscle contraction. The phosphocreatine pool is the immediate energy buffer that sustains ATP levels for the first several seconds of maximal effort, before glycolysis and oxidative metabolism fully contribute. This conversion of creatine to creatine phosphate is the mechanistic heart of the creatine-phosphocreatine energy system.

nodes.label: Phosphocreatine (PCr)
nodes.description: Roughly two-thirds of the body's creatine pool is phosphorylated and stored as phosphocreatine (PCr), with the remainder held as free creatine. The creatine kinase (CK) reaction interconverts creatine and PCr, and the energy liberated by breaking PCr down into phosphate and creatine (about 10.3 kcal) is used to resynthesize ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. This PCr/CK system is the rapid, phosphagen-based buffer that maintains ATP availability during intense exercise, ischemia, hypoxia, and high metabolic demand. Creatine supplementation raises muscle creatine and PCr stores, expanding this reserve and thereby enhancing high-intensity exercise capacity and training adaptations.

nodes.label: Dietary Supplement
nodes.description: Creatine monohydrate is among the most extensively studied dietary supplements and is generally regarded as safe when used at recommended doses over periods of many years. Long-term supplementation studies report no consistent adverse effects on renal, hepatic, or cardiovascular function in healthy individuals, and creatine is approved for use by many sports organizations. Common minor side effects include water retention and occasional gastrointestinal discomfort. This favorable safety profile is noted in the trace as relevant to the potential evaluation of creatine as an adjunct in oncology settings, where tolerability is a central concern.

nodes.label: Skeletal Muscle
nodes.description: Approximately 95 percent of the body's creatine is stored in skeletal muscle, where it exists partly as free creatine and partly as creatine phosphate. The muscle creatine pool is maintained by both endogenous synthesis and dietary intake, and it is depleted by high-intensity activity and resynthesized during recovery. Muscle total creatine concentrations can be increased by supplementation, typically by 10-20 percent, and this elevated store extends the time for which high-intensity exercise can be sustained. The predominance of skeletal muscle as a creatine depot explains why most creatine research has focused on muscle function, strength, and performance.

nodes.label: Amino Acids
nodes.description: Creatine is synthesized endogenously from the amino acids arginine, glycine, and methionine in a two-step pathway. The first step, catalyzed by arginine:glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT), takes place primarily in the kidney and pancreas and produces guanidinoacetate; the second step, catalyzed by guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase (GAMT), transfers a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to guanidinoacetate in the liver, producing creatine. This biosynthetic origin connects creatine metabolism to the methylation cycle and one-carbon metabolism, a connection relevant to hypotheses linking creatine status to epigenetic regulation and cancer risk.

nodes.label: Arginine
nodes.description: Creatine is a naturally occurring nitrogen-containing compound synthesized endogenously in the body. The first step of its biosynthesis condenses arginine and glycine into guanidinoacetate (GAA), a reaction catalyzed by arginine glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT), which is expressed in the kidney, pancreas, liver, and certain brain regions. Endogenous synthesis supplies roughly half of the daily creatine requirement; the remainder must come from the diet, primarily red meat and fish, or from supplements. Deficiencies in the enzymes of this pathway (AGAT, GAMT) or the creatine transporter produce creatine synthesis deficiency syndromes marked by low brain creatine and neurodevelopmental impairment.

nodes.label: Glycine
nodes.description: Glycine serves as the second amino acid substrate for endogenous creatine synthesis. Arginine glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT) condenses arginine with glycine to produce guanidinoacetate (GAA), which is then methylated by guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase (GAMT) using S-adenosyl methionine to yield creatine. Because glycine and arginine are the committed substrates for creatine biosynthesis, their availability influences the rate of endogenous creatine production, which normally covers about half of daily needs. The rest is obtained from dietary red meat, fish, or supplements, and total body creatine stores are typically around 120 mmol/kg of dry muscle mass.

nodes.label: DNA Methylation
nodes.description: Because endogenous creatine synthesis is the major consumer of methyl groups donated by S-adenosylmethionine, creatine status may influence DNA methylation reactions that govern gene expression, including the expression of oncogenes and tumor suppressors. Supplemental creatine, by reducing the requirement for de novo creatine synthesis, could preserve methyl groups for DNA methyltransferases and thereby modulate global DNA methylation patterns. The trace notes that this is an emerging and largely hypothesis-driven area: creatine's effects on DNA methylation and on one-carbon metabolism have been examined mainly in animal and small human studies, and any causal link to cancer prevention remains to be firmly established.

nodes.label: Cancer Metabolism
nodes.description: Creatine and the creatine kinase system are increasingly studied in the context of cancer metabolism. Some cancer types, particularly those with a poor prognosis, upregulate creatine kinase isoenzymes, and creatine metabolism has been reported to support the growth and invasiveness of certain tumors, whereas in other contexts creatine appears to restrain tumor growth, possibly through effects on energy homeostasis and AMPK. The trace explicitly notes that creatine's relationship to cancer is context-dependent and that current evidence is insufficient to recommend creatine as an anti-cancer intervention, underscoring the need for direct experimental studies.

nodes.label: Tumorigenesis
nodes.description: Emerging evidence reviewed in the source trace suggests creatine may exert direct anti-cancer effects, inhibiting tumorigenesis rather than only supporting athletic performance. Mechanistic studies indicate that creatine supplementation can raise cellular phosphocreatine and creatine kinase activity, and the resulting change in the cellular energy state, together with creatine-mediated effects on AMPK and anabolic signaling, may suppress cancer cell proliferation and transformation. Because cancer cells depend on high glycolytic flux and altered energy metabolism, interventions that perturb the creatine-phosphocreatine system are hypothesized to restrain tumor growth, although the trace stresses that much of this evidence is preliminary and requires confirmation in well-powered clinical studies.

nodes.label: AMPK
nodes.description: Creatine supplementation can alter the cellular energy status in ways that modulate AMPK, the central sensor of cellular energy charge. High phosphocreatine and low AMP levels generally suppress AMPK activation, while creatine depletion or energetic stress activates it. Because AMPK regulates anabolic processes, including protein synthesis and cell growth, and influences pathways relevant to cancer metabolism, creatine-induced changes in AMPK signaling are proposed to be one mechanism by which creatine could affect tumor cell proliferation. The trace presents this as a plausible but incompletely validated mechanistic link, noting that AMPK-dependent effects of creatine have been shown mainly in skeletal muscle and liver.

nodes.label: Muscle Wasting
nodes.description: Creatine supplementation has been investigated for its ability to attenuate muscle wasting in conditions of disuse, catabolism, and disease. In healthy subjects it amplifies the muscle gains from resistance training, and in some clinical populations, including elderly individuals and people with neuromuscular or catabolic diseases, creatine supplementation preserves lean mass and strength. Because cancer and its treatments frequently cause sarcopenia and cachexia, creatine's potential to blunt muscle loss is proposed as a supportive-care role for creatine in oncology, even if any direct anti-tumor effect remains unproven.

nodes.label: Ischemia-reperfusion Injury
nodes.description: Creatine and phosphocreatine play an important role in maintaining myocardial bioenergetics during ischemic events, reducing arrhythmias, ischemia-related damage, and improving heart function. Intravenous phosphocreatine prevented accumulation of arrhythmogenic lysophosphoglycerides in the ischemic zone of canine hearts, and adding phosphocreatine to cardioplegic solutions improved myocardial energy availability and reduced arrhythmias. Creatine supplementation also maintains energy availability during brain ischemia and reduces stroke-related damage. Several studies report benefits of oral creatine in chronic heart failure patients in rehabilitation, and phosphocreatine administration is considered a protective strategy for the heart during acute myocardial ischemia.

nodes.label: Spinal Cord Injury (SCI)
nodes.description: Preclinical studies suggest creatine supplementation can reduce the severity of spinal cord injury. Rats fed creatine before and after moderate spinal cord contusion developed less scar tissue and performed better on locomotor function tests than controls, and rats fed a 2% creatine diet before and after injury experienced less loss of gray matter. In humans with cervical spinal cord injury, creatine supplementation enhanced aerobic exercise capacity, ventilatory anaerobic threshold, and, combined with vitamin D and resistance training, improved arm muscle area, strength, and functional capacity. These findings support creatine as an adjunct that may reduce injury severity and enhance rehabilitation outcomes after spinal cord injury.

nodes.label: Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)
nodes.description: Creatine supplementation has shown neuroprotective potential in traumatic brain injury. In animal models, providing creatine in the diet for 5 days prior to TBI decreased cortical brain damage by 36% in rats and 50% in mice, an effect attributed to improved energy availability in the injured brain. Creatine also reduces the severity of mild concussions and ischemic brain damage and improves learning and memory during recovery in neonatal mice. While these preclinical studies cannot be replicated in humans, they support the contention that creatine supplementation may reduce the severity of TBI and serve as an adjunctive strategy in individuals at risk of head injury, complementing its established role in muscle and rehabilitation settings.

nodes.label: Neuroprotection
nodes.description: Creatine supplementation elevates brain creatine and phosphocreatine, improves brain bioenergetics, and has documented neuroprotective benefits, particularly in response to injury and ischemia. Animal studies show creatine feeding reduces cerebral ischemic brain damage volume by 25-40%, decreases infarct size, and attenuates neuronal death, while human studies report increased brain creatine (9.2% after 7 days), improved corticomotor excitability, and preserved attention during hypoxia. These findings suggest prophylactic creatine may reduce the severity of brain ischemia and stroke-related damage, and it has been investigated as a neuroprotective strategy in pregnancy to improve neonatal outcomes following birth asphyxia.

nodes.label: ADP
nodes.description: Creatine provides the immediate phosphate group needed to recycle ADP back into ATP, the cellular energy currency, keeping cellular energy pools saturated and reducing metabolic stress, which protects HRV from plunging during hard training. It is recommended daily at 3-5 grams, ideally post-workout or with the largest carbohydrate meal, because creatine uptake is enhanced by insulin. Pairing creatine with carbohydrates and protein helps drive it into muscle and brain cells more efficiently, with consistency mattering more than exact timing.

nodes.label: Pro-inflammatory Cytokines
nodes.description: Creatine has immunomodulatory effects that include reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and other inflammatory markers like TNF-alpha and PGE2. A creatine-induced reduction of these inflammatory mediators may help explain some of the neuroprotective benefits observed in patients with central nervous system diseases and the attenuation of inflammatory and muscle damage markers after intense exercise. Creatine also down-regulates expression of toll-like receptors (TLR-2, TLR-3, TLR-4, TLR-7) in a mouse macrophage cell line and may influence cytokines through the NF-kB signaling pathway, with potential consequences for immune response and, notably, for TLR-4-mediated pathology in Parkinson's disease progression.

nodes.label: ATP
nodes.description: The primary biochemical function of creatine is to buffer cellular ATP levels through the creatine-phosphocreatine system. Creatine kinase reversibly catalyzes the transfer of a phosphoryl group from phosphocreatine to ADP, regenerating ATP at rates far exceeding mitochondrial or glycolytic ATP production, which is essential for short bursts of intense activity. The creatine kinase reaction therefore acts as a rapid temporal energy buffer, maintaining ATP:ADP ratios during muscle contraction and other energy-demanding processes. This ATP-regenerating capacity is the basis for creatine's ergogenic effects and is also central to hypotheses about its influence on cancer cell metabolism.

nodes.label: Creatine Kinase
nodes.description: The biological actions of creatine are mediated by the creatine kinase enzyme family, which catalyzes the reversible phosphorylation of creatine by ATP. Tissue-specific creatine kinase isoforms are expressed in muscle, brain, and other tissues, and the enzyme couples the phosphocreatine pool to cellular ATP demand. In tissues with high and fluctuating energy requirements, the creatine kinase reaction buffers ATP levels and transports high-energy phosphate between sites of production and consumption. Because creatine kinase is also expressed in several tumors, the enzyme is a candidate interface through which creatine supplementation could influence cancer cell energy metabolism.

nodes.label: Creatine Synthesis Deficiency
nodes.description: High-dose, long-term creatine supplementation is a nutritional strategy for creatine synthesis deficiencies caused by mutations in AGAT, GAMT, or the creatine transporter (SLC6A8), which reduce endogenous creatine synthesis or cellular uptake and result in low brain creatine and phosphocreatine. Supplementation at 0.3-0.8 g/kg/day increases brain creatine and PCr levels and improves or stabilizes clinical symptoms including intellectual disability, epilepsy, and movement disorders. Patients with GAMT or AGAT deficiency treated early (e.g., starting at four months of age) can experience normal psychomotor development, and such therapy is well tolerated and may also benefit ornithine aminotransferase deficiency causing gyrate atrophy.

nodes.label: Methyl groups
nodes.description: Creatine synthesis is the single largest consumer of S-adenosylmethionine-derived methyl groups in the body, using approximately 70 percent of available methyl donor flux. Guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase transfers a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to guanidinoacetate to form creatine, thereby competing with DNA methylation and other methylation reactions for the methyl pool. Because exogenous creatine supplementation reduces the demand for endogenous creatine synthesis, it can spare methyl groups and shift the balance of methylation reactions. This creatine-methionine interaction forms the mechanistic basis for the hypothesis that creatine could influence epigenetic processes relevant to cancer.

nodes.label: Creatine Kinase (CK)
nodes.description: Creatine kinase (CK) is the enzyme at the core of the creatine/phosphocreatine energy system. It catalyzes the reversible transfer of a phosphate group between creatine and ADP, using the free energy released from phosphocreatine breakdown (approximately 10.3 kcal) to resynthesize ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. This provides a rapid means of replenishing depleted ATP during high-energy-demand states such as intense exercise or conditions where energy production is impaired (ischemia, hypoxia) or insufficient due to increased demand (mental fatigue, disease states). Cytosolic, glycolytic, and mitochondrial CK isoforms cooperate to buffer ATP/ADP ratios and shuttle high-energy phosphate from mitochondria to sites of ATP consumption.

nodes.label: Adenosine Triphosphate
nodes.description: Creatine kinase (CK) is the enzyme at the core of the creatine/phosphocreatine energy system. It catalyzes the reversible transfer of a phosphate group between creatine and ADP, using the free energy released from phosphocreatine breakdown (approximately 10.3 kcal) to resynthesize ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. This provides a rapid means of replenishing depleted ATP during high-energy-demand states such as intense exercise or conditions where energy production is impaired (ischemia, hypoxia) or insufficient due to increased demand (mental fatigue, disease states). Cytosolic, glycolytic, and mitochondrial CK isoforms cooperate to buffer ATP/ADP ratios and shuttle high-energy phosphate from mitochondria to sites of ATP consumption.

nodes.label: CTPI2
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md
nodes.description: CTPI2, a third-generation SLC25A1 inhibitor, delays the onset of frailty in aged mice as measured by a validated 31-parameter frailty index, alongside improvements in fur condition, coordination, balance and grip strength. In aged tissues, CTPI2 suppresses SASP-associated inflammatory gene expression across skeletal muscle, liver and heart while leaving p16 and p21 unchanged, and circulating inflammatory cytokines are reduced, indicating a systemic attenuation of inflammatory burden. These benefits arise without broad metabolic reprogramming: body weight, composition, metabolic rate, respiratory exchange ratio, activity and lipid metabolic pathways are largely unaffected.

nodes.label: Healthspan
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md
nodes.description: Aged (19-month-old) C57BL/6 mice gavaged with CTPI2 (50 mg/kg three times weekly for 3 months) exhibited more lustrous fur, reduced alopecia and greying, and delayed onset of frailty as measured by a 31-parameter frailty index. Functional assessment revealed enhanced neuromuscular performance: improved coordination and balance (tightrope test), increased strength (hanging and grip strength tests) and preservation of muscle integrity. CTPI2 reduced SASP gene expression in skeletal muscle, liver and heart without altering p16 or p21, indicating that suppressing the mitochondrial citrate-acetyl-CoA axis improves healthspan through SASP modulation rather than senescent cell clearance.

nodes.label: SLC25A1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md
nodes.description: CTPI2 is a third-generation inhibitor of the mitochondrial citrate carrier SLC25A1 with high binding affinity and specificity. CTPI2 treatment results in dose-dependent suppression of SASP components at transcript and protein levels without altering cell cycle regulators, HMGB1 localization, DNA damage foci or proliferation markers. It reduces global nuclear acetylation and H3K27ac at SASP loci and abolishes incorporation of glucose-derived carbon into histone acetylation, yet does not broadly impair mitochondrial function: OXPHOS gene expression, ATP production, coupling efficiency, mitochondrial ROS and morphology remain largely unchanged.

nodes.label: DELE1
nodes.description: DELE1, previously identified as a poorly characterized mitochondrial protein from a yeast two-hybrid screen, was converged upon by two independent CRISPR-based screens as the mediator of mitochondrial stress signaling to the ISR. Under mitochondrial stress, the cleaved cytosolic fragment DELE1-S directly binds and activates the heme-regulated kinase HRI. Importantly, HRI activation by DELE1 was shown to be heme-independent, ruling out the classical heme-depletion mechanism. HRI activation in turn leads to eIF2alpha phosphorylation and downstream ATF4 induction, linking mitochondrial dysfunction to the integrated stress response.

nodes.label: HRI

nodes.label: Diabetes Mellitus
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Aminoguanidine An AGE Product Inhibitor  Antiaging Systems Articles.md
nodes.description: Diabetes mellitus is often seen as a form of accelerated aging, and the levels of cross-linking products in diabetics are two to three times those of their equivalent normal non-diabetics. Advanced glycation end products are increased in diabetes and play an important role in the development of diabetic complications. Aminoguanidine acts to bind to sugars, preventing them from binding to the lysine groups of proteins, and diabetic clinical trials with humans have highlighted its ability to prevent oxidative modification of LDL, inhibit atherosclerotic plaque formation, reduce albuminuria and delay end-stage renal disease.

nodes.label: DRP1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of mitochondrial dynamics in disease.md
nodes.description: Cytosolic DRP1 monomers are recruited to the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) to initiate fission, where they are anchored by four main adaptor proteins: mitochondrial fission factor (MFF), mitochondrial fission 1 protein (FIS1), and mitochondrial dynamics proteins MID49 and MID51. These adaptors physically interact within a DRP1 complex to coordinate fission, and MFF, MID49 and MID51 are directly associated with mitochondrial division; their absence leads to significant mitochondrial elongation. The endoplasmic reticulum and ER-mitochondria contact sites (MAMs) provide a platform for DRP1 oligomerization and constriction of the OMM.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial Fission
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of mitochondrial dynamics in disease.md
nodes.description: Cytosolic DRP1 monomers are recruited to the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) to initiate fission, where they are anchored by four main adaptor proteins: mitochondrial fission factor (MFF), mitochondrial fission 1 protein (FIS1), and mitochondrial dynamics proteins MID49 and MID51. These adaptors physically interact within a DRP1 complex to coordinate fission, and MFF, MID49 and MID51 are directly associated with mitochondrial division; their absence leads to significant mitochondrial elongation. The endoplasmic reticulum and ER-mitochondria contact sites (MAMs) provide a platform for DRP1 oligomerization and constriction of the OMM.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial Fission Sites
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial Fusion and Fission The fine-tune balance for cellular homeostasis.md
nodes.description: DRP1 is recruited from the cytosol to defined sites on the mitochondrial outer membrane, where division occurs. Its adaptor proteins, including MFF, FIS1, MID49, and MID51, serve as receptors that concentrate DRP1 at prospective fission sites, often at positions where mitochondria are already constricted or associated with the endoplasmic reticulum. In cultured cells, MFF recruits DRP1 to the majority of fission events, while MID49 and MID51 recruit DRP1 to mitochondria independently of MFF in certain conditions. Once concentrated, DRP1 oligomerizes into spirals that wrap around the tubule, and GTP hydrolysis drives the membrane constriction required for complete scission.

nodes.label: Alzheimer's Disease
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of mitochondrial dynamics in disease.md
nodes.description: Biochemical evaluation of Alzheimer's disease (AD) brains demonstrates significantly increased DRP1 and FIS1 and reduced MFN1, MFN2 and OPA1 mRNA and protein levels, correlating with mitochondrial fragmentation and compromised neuronal energy production. Excessive mitochondrial fission interferes with OXPHOS complex assembly and cristae integrity, and S-nitrosylation of DRP1 induced by amyloid beta triggers mitochondrial fission and neuronal damage. Significantly increased DRP1 phosphorylation at Ser616 stimulates DRP1 translocation to mitochondria and fission activity in AD brain, and impaired axonal transport and reduced mitophagy accompany AD progression.

nodes.label: Epacadostat
nodes.description: Epacadostat is a small-molecule inhibitor of IDO1 tested in clinical trials as an immuno-oncology strategy, often in combination with checkpoint inhibitors targeting PD-1/PD-L1. These combinations aim to relieve IDO1-mediated immunosuppression in the tumor microenvironment by blocking tryptophan depletion and kynurenine production, thereby restoring effector T cell function. However, results from such trials have been mixed, and challenges including isoform selectivity, compensatory pathways (TDO, IDO2), and context-specific effects have limited clinical success.

nodes.label: IDO1
nodes.description: Epacadostat is a small-molecule inhibitor of IDO1 tested in clinical trials as an immuno-oncology strategy, often in combination with checkpoint inhibitors targeting PD-1/PD-L1. nodes.label: Everolimus
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Pathway as a Target of Anti-aging Therapies The Role of Rapamycin and Its Analogs in the Regulation of Cellular Processes and Their Impact on Longevity.md
nodes.description: Two randomized placebo-controlled clinical trials tested rapalogs among the elderly for immunomodulation. Treatment with everolimus monotherapy or everolimus in combination with RTB101 for six weeks resulted in a better response to influenza vaccine and fewer infections over the next year compared to placebo. The proposed mechanism is an increase in autophagy through inhibition of mTOR along with increased expression of antiviral proteins. The observation that immune function improves after a single six-week period of mTORC1 inhibition has important clinical implications, since elderly patients are particularly at risk of dying from influenza.

nodes.label: Immune System
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Pathway as a Target of Anti-aging Therapies The Role of Rapamycin and Its Analogs in the Regulation of Cellular Processes and Their Impact on Longevity.md
