nodes.label: Glyoxalase System
nodes.description: The glyoxalase system, composed of GLO1 and GLO2, is the primary defense system against dicarbonyl stress. Methylglyoxal, glyoxal, and 3-deoxyglucosone are highly reactive dicarbonyl intermediates generated during glycolysis and lipid peroxidation, and if left unchecked they form irreversible AGE crosslinks on cysteine, lysine, and arginine residues. The glyoxalase system neutralizes these precursors, and maintaining GLO1 activity is a primary target for reducing endogenous AGE accumulation. Dysfunction of this system is therefore linked to increased dicarbonyl stress and accelerated protein glycation, with consequences for aging, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease.

nodes.label: Methylglyoxal
nodes.description: The glyoxalase system, composed of GLO1 and GLO2, is the primary defense system against dicarbonyl stress. Methylglyoxal, glyoxal, and 3-deoxyglucosone are highly reactive dicarbonyl intermediates generated during glycolysis and lipid peroxidation, and if left unchecked they form irreversible AGE crosslinks on cysteine, lysine, and arginine residues. The glyoxalase system neutralizes these precursors, and maintaining GLO1 activity is a primary target for reducing endogenous AGE accumulation. Dysfunction of this system is therefore linked to increased dicarbonyl stress and accelerated protein glycation, with consequences for aging, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease.

nodes.label: GLO1
nodes.description: GLO1 (glyoxalase I) is the rate-limiting enzyme of the glyoxalase system. It catalyzes the conversion of hemithioacetals, formed spontaneously from methylglyoxal and glutathione, into S-D-lactoylglutathione. Because methylglyoxal is one of the most reactive dicarbonyl precursors of advanced glycation end products, GLO1 activity is critical for preventing dicarbonyl stress from damaging proteins. Enhancing or maintaining GLO1 function is considered a primary target for reducing endogenous AGE accumulation and for protecting against age-related pathologies in which glycation plays a role.

nodes.label: S-D-lactoylglutathione
nodes.description: GLO1 (glyoxalase I) is the rate-limiting enzyme of the glyoxalase system. It catalyzes the conversion of hemithioacetals, formed spontaneously from methylglyoxal and glutathione, into S-D-lactoylglutathione. Because methylglyoxal is one of the most reactive dicarbonyl precursors of advanced glycation end products, GLO1 activity is critical for preventing dicarbonyl stress from damaging proteins. Enhancing or maintaining GLO1 function is considered a primary target for reducing endogenous AGE accumulation and for protecting against age-related pathologies in which glycation plays a role.

nodes.label: GLO2
nodes.description: GLO2 (glyoxalase II) is the second enzyme of the glyoxalase system. It converts S-D-lactoylglutathione into D-lactate, regenerating glutathione in the process. Because glutathione is both the cofactor for GLO1 and a major cellular antioxidant, GLO2 activity sustains the capacity of the glyoxalase system to detoxify methylglyoxal and other dicarbonyls. The conversion of reactive dicarbonyl intermediates into lactate thereby prevents them from forming irreversible AGE crosslinks on proteins, making GLO2 an integral component of the body's defense against glycation stress.

nodes.label: D-lactate
nodes.description: GLO2 (glyoxalase II) is the second enzyme of the glyoxalase system. It converts S-D-lactoylglutathione into D-lactate, regenerating glutathione in the process. Because glutathione is both the cofactor for GLO1 and a major cellular antioxidant, GLO2 activity sustains the capacity of the glyoxalase system to detoxify methylglyoxal and other dicarbonyls. The conversion of reactive dicarbonyl intermediates into lactate thereby prevents them from forming irreversible AGE crosslinks on proteins, making GLO2 an integral component of the body's defense against glycation stress.

nodes.label: PARK7
nodes.description: PARK7 (DJ-1), historically characterized as a protein deglycase, is now understood from biochemical evidence to function primarily as a glutathione-independent glyoxalase. It stereospecifically detoxifies free methylglyoxal and glyoxal directly into L-lactate and glycolic acid, preventing these reactive species from forming irreversible AGE crosslinks on cysteine, lysine, and arginine residues. Mutations or loss of PARK7 lead to significant tissue-specific accumulation of novel AGEs. PARK7 therefore provides a second, glutathione-independent layer of protection against dicarbonyl stress in addition to the classical glyoxalase system.

nodes.label: Glycolic acid
nodes.description: PARK7 (DJ-1) detoxifies the reactive dicarbonyl species glyoxal and methylglyoxal in a glutathione-independent manner, converting glyoxal into glycolic acid and methylglyoxal into L-lactate. This stereospecific conversion removes dicarbonyls before they can form irreversible AGE crosslinks on protein residues. Because glyoxal is a major product of glucose and lipid oxidation, PARK7-dependent conversion of glyoxal to glycolic acid is an important route for limiting dicarbonyl stress. Loss of PARK7 activity is associated with tissue-specific accumulation of novel AGEs and, in humans, is linked to early-onset Parkinson's disease.

nodes.label: Aldo-Keto Reductases
nodes.description: Aldo-keto reductases (AKRs) and aldehyde dehydrogenases (ALDHs) are enzyme families that assist in reducing or oxidizing reactive aldehydes and dicarbonyls, such as 3-deoxyglucosone and methylglyoxal, into less toxic alcohols or carboxylic acids. By converting these reactive species into less harmful products, AKRs prevent them from participating in glycation cascades that form advanced glycation end products. This enzymatic detoxification is one of the three lines of defense against AGE accumulation, operating alongside the glyoxalase system and PARK7. Impaired AKR or ALDH function would be expected to increase dicarbonyl burden and accelerate protein glycation.

nodes.label: Aldehyde Dehydrogenases
nodes.description: Aldehyde dehydrogenases (ALDHs), together with aldo-keto reductases, help neutralize reactive aldehydes and dicarbonyls such as 3-deoxyglucosone and methylglyoxal by oxidizing them into less toxic carboxylic acids. This prevents these highly reactive species from participating in glycation cascades that form advanced glycation end products. ALDH activity therefore contributes to the body's first line of enzymatic defense against dicarbonyl stress, operating alongside the glyoxalase system and PARK7. Reduced ALDH function would be expected to increase the pool of reactive dicarbonyls available to damage proteins, promoting AGE accumulation.

nodes.label: Fructosamine-3-kinase
nodes.description: Fructosamine-3-kinase (FN3K) is an intracellular enzyme that initiates protein deglycation by phosphorylating fructosamine, the Amadori residues on glycated proteins, converting them into fructosamine-3-phosphate. This phosphorylated compound is highly unstable and spontaneously decomposes, regenerating the original, undamaged amino acid and releasing 3-deoxyglucosone, which is then neutralized by detoxifying enzymes. By repairing early glycation intermediates before they progress to irreversible AGEs, FN3K provides the repair arm of the enzymatic defense against AGE accumulation, complementary to prevention by dicarbonyl detoxification.

nodes.label: Fructosamine
nodes.description: Fructosamine-3-kinase (FN3K) is an intracellular enzyme that initiates protein deglycation by phosphorylating fructosamine, the Amadori residues on glycated proteins, converting them into fructosamine-3-phosphate. This phosphorylated compound is highly unstable and spontaneously decomposes, regenerating the original, undamaged amino acid and releasing 3-deoxyglucosone, which is then neutralized by detoxifying enzymes. By repairing early glycation intermediates before they progress to irreversible AGEs, FN3K provides the repair arm of the enzymatic defense against AGE accumulation, complementary to prevention by dicarbonyl detoxification.

nodes.label: 3-deoxyglucosone
nodes.description: Fructosamine-3-kinase (FN3K) phosphorylates Amadori (fructosamine) residues on glycated proteins to form fructosamine-3-phosphate, a highly unstable compound that spontaneously decomposes. The decomposition regenerates the original amino acid, repairing the glycated protein, and releases 3-deoxyglucosone, a reactive dicarbonyl that is then neutralized by detoxifying enzymes such as the glyoxalase system. FN3K therefore reverses early-stage glycation but generates a dicarbonyl byproduct that must be cleared, illustrating how the prevention and repair arms of AGE defense work together to limit the accumulation of advanced glycation end products.

nodes.label: Fructosyl-Amino Acid Oxidases
nodes.description: Fructosyl-amino acid oxidases (FAOD), also known as amadoriases, are enzymes found primarily in fungi and bacteria, such as Aspergillus species, that catalyze the oxidation of Amadori products. The reaction yields an unmodified amino acid, a glucosone, and hydrogen peroxide. Because they deglycate early glycation intermediates, FAOD are actively researched for therapeutic and cosmetic applications, and some research explores pairing FAOD with fructosamine-3-kinase to synergistically deglycate damaged structural proteins such as skin collagen. These enzymes represent a repair-based strategy for reducing AGE accumulation.

nodes.label: Cathepsin D
nodes.description: Lysosomal proteases are responsible for degrading glycated proteins intracellularly. Cathepsin D, an aspartic protease, and Cathepsin B, a cysteine protease, are major enzymes that break down AGE-modified proteins after they are directed to lysosomes for degradation. A decrease in Cathepsin D expression or activity, which occurs during aging and UV exposure, directly correlates with the accumulation of AGEs such as N-epsilon-carboxymethyl-lysine (CML). Cathepsin-dependent lysosomal degradation therefore represents the third line of defense against AGE accumulation, removing established glycated proteins that prevention and repair enzymes cannot handle.

nodes.label: AGE-modified proteins
nodes.description: Lysosomal proteases are responsible for degrading glycated proteins intracellularly. Cathepsin D, an aspartic protease, and Cathepsin B, a cysteine protease, are major enzymes that break down AGE-modified proteins after they are directed to lysosomes for degradation. A decrease in Cathepsin D expression or activity, which occurs during aging and UV exposure, directly correlates with the accumulation of AGEs such as N-epsilon-carboxymethyl-lysine (CML). Cathepsin-dependent lysosomal degradation therefore represents the third line of defense against AGE accumulation, removing established glycated proteins that prevention and repair enzymes cannot handle.

nodes.label: Cathepsin B
nodes.description: Cathepsin B is a lysosomal cysteine protease that, together with cathepsin D, is a major enzyme responsible for breaking down AGE-modified proteins. Glycated proteins are directed to lysosomes for degradation, and these cathepsins ensure that proteins damaged by non-enzymatic glycation are cleared rather than allowed to accumulate. The activity of such lysosomal proteases declines with age and under UV exposure, which correlates with accumulation of AGEs such as N-epsilon-carboxymethyl-lysine (CML). Maintaining lysosomal cathepsin function is therefore important for proteolytic clearance of glycated material and limiting AGE burden.

nodes.label: N-(carboxymethyl)-lysine
nodes.description: A decrease in Cathepsin D expression or activity, which occurs during aging and UV exposure, directly correlates with the accumulation of advanced glycation end products like N-epsilon-carboxymethyl-lysine (CML). As a major lysosomal aspartic protease responsible for breaking down AGE-modified proteins, Cathepsin D degrades glycated proteins that are directed to lysosomes, preventing their accumulation in cells. Loss of Cathepsin D function therefore promotes CML buildup and glycation-associated cellular dysfunction. Supporting lysosomal cathepsin activity is a plausible strategy to limit tissue AGE accumulation during aging.

nodes.label: Matrix Metalloproteinases
nodes.description: In the extracellular matrix, matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) such as MMP-1 and MMP-2 are involved in remodeling collagen and elastin that have been stiffened by glycation. Because AGE crosslinks make these long-lived structural proteins resistant to normal turnover, MMP-mediated remodeling helps manage matrix that has accumulated glycation damage, though MMP activity can become dysregulated under high-AGE conditions. MMPs thereby act as a degradative countermeasure to AGE-induced matrix stiffening, balancing crosslink formation and matrix turnover in vascular and connective tissue, although excessive or dysregulated MMP activity contributes to matrix destruction.

nodes.label: Glucosepane
nodes.description: Glucosepane is the most abundant and stubborn protein-protein AGE crosslink in human structural tissues, driving the systemic stiffening associated with aging and diabetes. Humans lack endogenous enzymes capable of directly breaking the glucosepane ring without destroying the surrounding collagen. Because of its abundance and stability, glucosepane is considered a major molecular target for anti-glycation therapies. Its crosslinks accumulate in long-lived proteins such as collagen and elastin, and are a principal cause of the extracellular matrix stiffening that contributes to arterial stiffening and age-related loss of tissue compliance.

nodes.label: HemF-like
nodes.description: Through functional metagenomics, researchers identified soil bacteria enzymes capable of utilizing synthetic glucosepane as a nutrient source, including the biocatalysts HemF-like (coproporphyrinogen III oxidase-like), BluB-like (5,6-dimethylbenzimidazole synthase-like), and QueE-like (7-carboxy-7-deazaguanine synthase-like). Remarkably, the human homolog of HemF, alongside homologous bacterial proteins found in the human microbiome, was shown to catalyze the cleavage of glucosepane in vitro, releasing citrulline as a byproduct. These glucosepane-cleaving enzymes represent a promising frontier for therapeutic interventions against age-related vascular stiffness and diabetic complications.

nodes.label: Adrenochrome monoaminoguanidine
nodes.description: Adrenochrome monoaminoguanidine (AMM), historically known as S-Adchnon or adrenochrome guanylhydrazone, is formed by reacting adrenochrome, an oxidation product of epinephrine containing an indoline-5,6-dione core, with aminoguanidine, a nucleophilic hydrazine derivative. The reaction forms a stable guanylhydrazone linkage at one of the carbonyl groups of the dione structure. AMM therefore combines a redox-active indoline core with an established anti-glycation agent, providing a dual-action glyco-oxidative modulator designed to simultaneously target oxidative stress and protein crosslinking by advanced glycation end products.

nodes.label: Guanylhydrazone
nodes.description: Adrenochrome monoaminoguanidine (AMM), historically known as S-Adchnon or adrenochrome guanylhydrazone, is formed by reacting adrenochrome, an oxidation product of epinephrine containing an indoline-5,6-dione core, with aminoguanidine, a nucleophilic hydrazine derivative. The reaction forms a stable guanylhydrazone linkage at one of the carbonyl groups of the dione structure. AMM therefore combines a redox-active indoline core with an established anti-glycation agent, providing a dual-action glyco-oxidative modulator designed to simultaneously target oxidative stress and protein crosslinking by advanced glycation end products.

nodes.label: indoline-5,6-dione
nodes.description: Adrenochrome is an oxidation product of epinephrine built around an indoline-dione core. Indoline-dione and isatin-like structures are recognized privileged scaffolds in medicinal chemistry, often showing antioxidant, neuroprotective, and enzymatic inhibitory activities. This redox-active core provides the oxidative-modulation arm of adrenochrome monoaminoguanidine, while free adrenochrome is unstable and cardiotoxic through redox cycling that generates reactive oxygen species. The scaffold therefore underpins both the potential therapeutic utility and the inherent toxicity of adrenochrome-based compounds, motivating conjugation strategies that stabilize the reactive dione.

nodes.label: Hemostatics
nodes.description: Adrenochrome monoaminoguanidine was historically developed and used clinically, primarily in Japan, as a hemostatic capillary stabilizer and a radioprotective agent. Its hemostatic action reflects its ability to stabilize capillaries and reduce bleeding, and its radioprotective effects are believed to stem from protection of cell membranes and hematopoietic progenitor cells from radiation-induced oxidative damage. This historical clinical use demonstrates that the guanylhydrazone conjugate is stable and tolerated in vivo, in contrast to free adrenochrome. It also indicates that systematic evaluation of AMM in modern long-term aging and glycation models is currently lacking.

nodes.label: Hematopoietic Stem Cell
nodes.description: Adrenochrome monoaminoguanidine's radioprotective effects are believed to stem from its ability to protect cell membranes and hematopoietic progenitor cells from radiation-induced oxidative damage. The compound was historically developed and used clinically, primarily in Japan, as a hemostatic capillary stabilizer and radioprotective agent. Protection of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells by an aminoguanidine-conjugated, redox-active indoline molecule illustrates the potential for such scaffolds to shield proliferative tissues from oxidative insult, a property relevant to both radioprotection and, potentially, anti-aging applications.

nodes.label: Prodrug
nodes.description: For adrenochrome monoaminoguanidine to act as an active AGE inhibitor despite its hydrazine group being locked in a hydrazone bond, it must either retain sufficient nucleophilicity through its remaining guanidine nitrogens, act as a prodrug that undergoes controlled in vivo hydrolysis to slowly release free aminoguanidine, or work via alternative pathways such as chelating transition metals that catalyze glycoxidation. The prodrug hypothesis is plausible because the conjugate is stable for clinical use yet could hydrolyze to release aminoguanidine over time. Whether the bound aminoguanidine retains dicarbonyl-scavenging activity remains unresolved.

nodes.label: oxidation product of epinephrine
nodes.description: Adrenochrome is a chemical compound formed by the oxidation of epinephrine (adrenaline), a catecholamine stress hormone. In humans it arises as a minor oxidative metabolite or byproduct rather than through a dedicated biosynthetic pathway. Oxidation converts the catechol ring of adrenaline to an o-quinone followed by internal cyclization to an indoline-5,6-dione structure. This process occurs in vivo, driven by reactive oxygen species such as superoxide anion and hydrogen peroxide, and in vitro. Because the reaction competes with the primary COMT and MAO degradation routes, adrenochrome formation becomes more prominent under oxidative stress, inflammation, and conditions where adrenaline levels are high, and it is considered a marker of failed homeostasis rather than a normal abundant product.

nodes.label: Adrenochrome formation
nodes.description: Myeloperoxidase is a heme enzyme released by activated neutrophils during inflammation and the respiratory burst. It catalyzes the oxidation of adrenaline into adrenochrome, contributing to adrenochrome formation at inflammatory sites. This enzyme-assisted route operates alongside purely radical-driven oxidation by superoxide and hydroxyl radicals, and it is one reason the adrenochrome pathway is a feature of neutrophil-mediated oxidative stress in inflamed or infected tissues rather than normal metabolism. Myeloperoxidase-derived oxidants can also generate additional reactive oxygen species, further favoring catecholamine oxidation and the generation of aminochromes including adrenochrome.

nodes.label: Liver microsomes
nodes.description: Liver microsomes are subcellular fractions of hepatic endoplasmic reticulum enriched in oxidative enzymes. In the presence of NADPH and oxygen, hepatic microsomal enzymes can oxidize epinephrine to adrenochrome, and the rate is modulated by high oxygen tension or inhibitors such as cyanide. This demonstrates that hepatic microsomal oxidases contribute to adrenaline oxidation alongside the well-known neutrophil and myocardial routes. The microsomal pathway represents an enzymatic or semi-enzymatic route of catecholamine oxidation that may be more relevant when oxidative stress or drug-induced enzyme activity is elevated, though it remains a minor pathway relative to COMT- and MAO-mediated metabolism.

nodes.label: Metanephrine
nodes.description: Metanephrine is the principal COMT-derived metabolite of epinephrine, formed when catechol-O-methyltransferase methylates one of the catechol hydroxyl groups of adrenaline using S-adenosylmethionine as the methyl donor. Together with MAO-mediated oxidative deamination, this conversion is the primary route of adrenaline breakdown in the body. Because COMT and MAO clear adrenaline rapidly, the alternative oxidative pathway that yields adrenochrome is normally a minor side route. Metanephrine measurements are also clinically useful as markers of catecholamine production, and elevated levels reflect increased release of epinephrine from the adrenal medulla.

nodes.label: COMT Inhibitors
nodes.description: COMT inhibitors such as entacapone, tolcapone, and opicapone block catechol-O-methyltransferase, one of the principal enzymes that degrades catecholamines by methylation. Inhibiting COMT therefore increases synaptic and circulating levels of dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine, and this is exploited clinically in Parkinson's disease, often combined with MAO inhibitors and levodopa, to prolong dopaminergic effects and reduce off time. The resulting higher catecholamine levels, together with inhibition of MAO-mediated clearance, provide more substrate for oxidative conversion to adrenochrome, though this effect is mostly theoretical in clinical use and benefits are generally judged to outweigh risks.

nodes.label: Catecholamines
nodes.description: COMT inhibitors such as entacapone, tolcapone, and opicapone block catechol-O-methyltransferase, one of the principal enzymes that degrades catecholamines by methylation. Inhibiting COMT therefore increases synaptic and circulating levels of dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine, and this is exploited clinically in Parkinson's disease, often combined with MAO inhibitors and levodopa, to prolong dopaminergic effects and reduce off time. The resulting higher catecholamine levels, together with inhibition of MAO-mediated clearance, provide more substrate for oxidative conversion to adrenochrome, though this effect is mostly theoretical in clinical use and benefits are generally judged to outweigh risks.

nodes.label: Smoking
nodes.description: Cigarette, cigar, and wood smoke contain enormous amounts of free radicals and oxidants (cigarette smoke alone carries on the order of 10^17 oxidant molecules per puff). These external oxidants directly increase reactive oxygen species, deplete antioxidants such as vitamin C and glutathione, and cause systemic oxidative stress. Smoke also activates sympathetic nervous system responses and inflammation, further raising endogenous ROS production. This oxidative environment promotes the oxidation of adrenaline to adrenochrome and supports the redox cycle by which adrenochrome generates more superoxide, linking smoking to increased catecholamine oxidation and oxidative damage.

nodes.label: Neuromelanin formation
nodes.description: Adrenochrome and related aminochromes serve as intermediates in the synthesis of neuromelanin, the dark pigment that accumulates in catecholaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra and locus coeruleus. When catecholamines such as dopamine, norepinephrine, and adrenaline are oxidized, they generate reactive quinones and aminochromes that polymerize into melanin-like pigments. In the brain, this process is tied to iron- and metal-catalyzed autoxidation, and the oxidative metabolism of catecholamines into quinone compounds contributes to the age-dependent buildup of neuromelanin. Adrenochrome-like structures are thus chemically upstream of neuromelanin formation, with neuromelanin granules accumulating progressively from birth to middle-to-late adulthood.

nodes.label: Dopamine
nodes.description: Dopamine, like epinephrine, undergoes oxidation to an aminochrome: dopamine is converted through an o-quinone intermediate to dopaminochrome, the dopamine analog of adrenochrome. These aminochromes are unstable reactive intermediates that can polymerize into melanins, including neuromelanin in dopaminergic neurons. This oxidation pathway is relevant to the brain, where oxidative metabolism of catecholamines into quinone-like compounds contributes to the age-dependent buildup of neuromelanin pigments in the substantia nigra. The reactivity of dopaminochrome and related aminochromes underlies their potential neurotoxicity and their sequestration by neuromelanin.

nodes.label: Carbazochrome
nodes.description: Carbazochrome is a stabilized derivative of adrenochrome used in some parts of the world as a hemostatic agent that promotes blood clotting and helps manage hemorrhaging. Whereas adrenochrome itself is too unstable for practical medical use, derivatives such as carbazochrome and its sulfonate and monosemicarbazone forms are much more stable and have been developed pharmaceutically as hemostatics. Carbazochrome's hemostatic action reflects the pharmacological repurposing of the adrenochrome scaffold, in contrast to the lack of any proven medical use for adrenochrome itself as a drug.

nodes.label: Low pH
nodes.description: Acidic conditions strongly slow or prevent the cyclization step of adrenochrome formation, because at low pH the side-chain amine of the oxidized epinephrine intermediate is protonated and reduced in nucleophilicity, so it cannot easily attack the quinone ring. In highly acidic solutions the open-chain quinone form is favored and more stable, while neutral-to-alkaline pH accelerates cyclization and oxidation. This pH dependence explains why pharmaceutical epinephrine solutions are kept acidic (pH 3-5) with antioxidants to minimize oxidation and adrenochrome formation, and it is the most important factor in controlling the reaction rate.

nodes.label: Bisulfite
nodes.description: Bisulfite (sodium bisulfite or metabisulfite) is a reducing agent added to pharmaceutical epinephrine injections to prevent oxidation of the catechol and thereby inhibit adrenochrome formation. By scavenging oxygen and reactive oxygen species and reducing oxidized intermediates, bisulfite keeps adrenaline solutions stable and usable for extended periods, preventing the pink-to-red discoloration that signals adrenochrome accumulation. This practical application reflects the general principle that the epinephrine-to-adrenochrome oxidation can be slowed by antioxidants, acidic pH, low temperature, and protection from light. Without such stabilizers, adrenaline auto-oxidizes visibly within days to weeks.

nodes.label: Elastin
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: Advanced glycation end products accumulate within the extracellular matrix and cross-link elastic fibers as well as collagen. This cross-linking of extracellular proteins reduces the elasticity of connective tissues such as blood vessels, skin, and tendons, affecting especially vascular function. Glycated modifications alter the balance between ECM synthesis and degradation, accelerating skin aging and increasing skin stiffness. AGE-elastin cross-linking is one of the three major mechanisms by which AGEs injure tissues, alongside intracellular glycation and RAGE-mediated inflammatory signaling.

nodes.label: protein function
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: Glycation is a spontaneous non-enzymatic reaction of reducing sugars with free amino groups of proteins, DNA, and lipids that leads to loss of protein function and impaired elasticity of tissues such as blood vessels, skin, and tendons. The process is highly accelerated in the presence of hyperglycemia and tissue oxidative stress, implicating it in diabetic complications and aging. Intracellular AGE modification of signaling molecules can impair cellular functions and gene expression, and glycation of antioxidant enzymes such as catalase, glutathione peroxidase, and glutathione reductase reduces their activity, further increasing cellular oxidative stress.

nodes.label: diabetic complications
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: Advanced glycation end products accumulate in tissues and organs during diabetes and contribute to the pathogenesis of diabetic complications. AGE formation and accumulation in diabetic patients results in vascular alterations leading to diabetic vasculopathy, and glycation is implicated in diabetic renal, retinal, and neural complications. Because the glycation reaction is accelerated by hyperglycemia and oxidative stress, poor glycemic control exacerbates AGE burden. AGE inhibitors such as aminoguanidine were shown to prevent diabetic complications by inhibiting AGE formation, supporting the causal role of glycation in diabetic pathology.

nodes.label: Reactive Oxygen Species generation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: RAGE is the receptor for advanced glycation end products that regulates cell processes including inflammation, apoptosis, ROS signaling, proliferation, autophagy, and aging. Activation of RAGE by AGEs leads to ROS generation and downstream inflammatory signaling, providing a receptor-mediated route by which glycated proteins damage cells. This ROS generation contributes to oxidative stress in diabetes, renal failure, and aging. The AGE-RAGE axis is therefore a key molecular link between glycation and oxidative damage, and blocking RAGE signaling is a potential therapeutic strategy against AGE-mediated pathology.

nodes.label: ECM
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: Advanced glycation end products accumulate within the extracellular matrix (ECM), such as in collagen and elastic fibers, and cross-link with ECM components. This accumulation and cross-linking cause a decrease in connective tissue elasticity, alter ECM structure and function, and impair vascular function, facilitating plaque formation and basement membrane hyperplasia. AGE accumulation in the ECM is one of the three major mechanisms by which AGEs contribute to aging, alongside intracellular glycation and RAGE-mediated signaling. ECM glycation is strongly implicated in arterial stiffening, skin aging, and age-related stiffness of tendons and cartilage.

nodes.label: Glycated proteins
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: Glycated proteins are normally removed from cells via ubiquitin-dependent 20S proteasome-mediated proteolysis, an important quality control pathway for damaged proteins. AGE modifications can disturb this proteolytic degradation, contributing to a further increase in the cellular content of glycated proteins. The resulting accumulation of glycated proteins is a hallmark of aging and is associated with loss of cellular function. Proteasomal degradation of glycated proteins is thus a key cellular defense against glycation stress, and its impairment creates a feed-forward loop of AGE accumulation.

nodes.label: Ubiquitin-dependent 20S proteasome
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: Glycated proteins are normally removed from cells via ubiquitin-dependent 20S proteasome-mediated proteolysis, an important quality control pathway for damaged proteins. AGE modifications can disturb this proteolytic degradation, contributing to a further increase in the cellular content of glycated proteins. The resulting accumulation of glycated proteins is a hallmark of aging and is associated with loss of cellular function. Proteasomal degradation of glycated proteins is thus a key cellular defense against glycation stress, and its impairment creates a feed-forward loop of AGE accumulation.

nodes.label: Arterial Stiffening
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: N-(carboxymethyl)-lysine (CML) is a prominent advanced glycation end product formed from glycated proteins. There is a marked correlation between the serum concentration of CML and vessel stiffness in elderly individuals, reflecting the role of AGE accumulation and ECM cross-linking in arterial stiffening. CML also accumulates in heart tissue with age, and dietary CML-enriched protein induces functional arterial aging in a RAGE-dependent manner in mice. Serum CML is therefore used as a biomarker of glycation burden and age-related vascular pathology.

nodes.label: Pentosidine
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: Pentosidine is a cross-linking advanced glycation end product that accumulates in skin with age, together with argpyrimidine. It is also found to increase with age in the lamina cribrosa, lung collagen, patellar tendon, vitreous body, oocytes, intervertebral disk, and cartilage. Pentosidine is formed from the reaction of sugars with lysine and arginine residues and functions as a fluorescent AGE marker of cumulative glycation. Its age-dependent accumulation in skin and other connective tissues reflects the progressive cross-linking and stiffening of the extracellular matrix during aging.

nodes.label: Skin
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: Pentosidine is a cross-linking advanced glycation end product that accumulates in skin with age, together with argpyrimidine. It is also found to increase with age in the lamina cribrosa, lung collagen, patellar tendon, vitreous body, oocytes, intervertebral disk, and cartilage. Pentosidine is formed from the reaction of sugars with lysine and arginine residues and functions as a fluorescent AGE marker of cumulative glycation. Its age-dependent accumulation in skin and other connective tissues reflects the progressive cross-linking and stiffening of the extracellular matrix during aging.

nodes.label: Heart
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: N-(carboxymethyl)-lysine (CML) is an advanced glycation end product that increases with age in heart tissue. It is one of the most abundant AGEs and is also a biomarker of glycation burden, with serum CML correlating with vessel stiffness in elderly individuals. CML accumulation results from the non-enzymatic glycation of proteins by glucose and other carbonyls, and it contributes to the cross-linking and functional impairment of extracellular matrix proteins. Heart CML accumulation is part of the broader age-related AGE buildup that affects cardiovascular tissues.

nodes.label: Dietary Advanced Glycation End Products
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: Food is an important source of exogenous advanced glycation end products, since significant AGE generation occurs when sugars are cooked with proteins via the Maillard reaction. In a mouse model, feeding an AGE-rich diet for 16 weeks promoted a 53% increase in serum AGE levels. In renal failure patients, an AGE-rich diet produced a 29% increase in blood CML, while a low-AGE diet produced a 34% reduction. These findings suggest that a diet restricting AGEs is an effective way to reduce the AGE burden in the human body.

nodes.label: serum AGE levels
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md

In renal failure patients, an AGE-rich diet produced a 29% increase in blood CML, while a low-AGE diet produced a 34% reduction. These findings suggest that a diet restricting AGEs is an effective way to reduce the AGE burden in the human body.

nodes.label: Endothelial dysfunction
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: Exogenous advanced glycation end products from the diet contribute to vascular aging. A 9-month dietary exposure to CML in mice accelerated endothelial dysfunction and arterial aging, and dietary CML-enriched protein induces functional arterial aging in a RAGE-dependent manner. These effects link dietary glycotoxins to cardiovascular aging through AGE-RAGE signaling and ECM cross-linking. Because modern diets cooked at high heat are rich in dietary AGEs, restricting dietary AGE intake is proposed as an effective way to reduce the AGE burden and protect vascular function.

nodes.label: Advanced Glycation End Products formation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: Aminoguanidine was the first agent introduced as an AGE inhibitor. It and related inhibitors such as pyridoxamine prevent AGE accumulation by interacting with highly reactive carbonyl species and acting as carbonyl traps. Aminoguanidine prevented diabetic renal, retinal, and neural complications through the inhibition of AGE formation in animal models. However, it cannot be used clinically due to safety concerns including pro-oxidant activities and inhibition of nitric oxide synthase, so its role is now primarily as a research tool and reference compound.

nodes.label: Pyridoxamine
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: Pyridoxamine is a synthetic AGE inhibitor that prevents AGE accumulation by interacting with highly reactive carbonyl species and acting as a carbonyl trap, similar to aminoguanidine. By scavenging carbonyl intermediates, pyridoxamine blocks the formation of advanced glycation end products and is considered a candidate for preventing glycation-mediated pathology. Unlike aminoguanidine, pyridoxamine (a vitamin B6 derivative) has a more favorable safety profile. AGE inhibitors and carbonyl-trapping agents remain an active area of research for reducing AGE burden in diabetes and aging.

nodes.label: Epicatechin
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: Epicatechin, a flavanol, demonstrates potent AGE-breaking properties in vitro and in vivo. It destroyed preformed glycated serum albumin in vitro and decreased AGE accumulation in retinal tissues of rats injected with exogenous AGE. Mechanistically, side chains attached to the pyrrole ring carbons of AGE structures are susceptible to nucleophilic attack, and because C6 and C8 on the A-ring of epicatechin are nucleophilic, epicatechin can attack and destroy AGE cross-links. These findings position epicatechin as a naturally occurring AGE breaker with potential for preventing AGE-mediated tissue damage.

nodes.label: glycated serum albumin
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md

It destroyed preformed glycated serum albumin in vitro and decreased AGE accumulation in retinal tissues of rats injected with exogenous AGE. Mechanistically, side chains attached to the pyrrole ring carbons of AGE structures are susceptible to nucleophilic attack, and because C6 and C8 on the A-ring of epicatechin are nucleophilic, epicatechin can attack and destroy AGE cross-links. These findings position epicatechin as a naturally occurring AGE breaker with potential for preventing AGE-mediated tissue damage.

nodes.label: Kaempferol
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: Kaempferol is a flavonoid polyphenol reported to possess anti-glycation properties. Along with other flavonoids such as genistein, quercitrin, and quercetin, kaempferol inhibits the glycation process in vitro, and several herbal polyphenols have anti-glycation activities similar to or stronger than aminoguanidine. These compounds act partly through their antioxidant capacity, which reduces the ROS-driven acceleration of protein glycation. Flavonoid-rich herbs and dietary plants are therefore considered promising, relatively safe agents for the prevention of glycation and AGE formation during aging.

nodes.label: Quercetin
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: Quercetin is a flavonoid polyphenol with reported anti-glycation properties. Along with kaempferol, genistein, and quercitrin, quercetin inhibits the glycation process in vitro, and the anti-glycation activities of several polyphenols are similar to or even stronger than the reference inhibitor aminoguanidine. These flavonoids act partly through high antioxidant capacity, which counteracts the ROS that accelerate glycation. Because naturally occurring phytochemicals are relatively safe and available in oral forms, flavonoid-rich herbs are promising agents for the prevention of glycation and AGE formation.

nodes.label: Genistein
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: Genistein is an isoflavone flavonoid reported to possess anti-glycation properties. Together with other flavonoids such as kaempferol, quercitrin, and quercetin, genistein inhibits the glycation process in vitro. The anti-glycation activities of these polyphenols are similar to or even stronger than aminoguanidine, and they act in part through trapping reactive carbonyl species and antioxidant capacity. Herbal products and dietary plants containing these flavonoids are therefore considered promising, relatively safe agents for preventing glycation and AGE accumulation during aging.

nodes.label: antioxidant enzyme expression
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: Moderate physical exercise induces the expression of antioxidant enzymes, leading to the reduction of oxidative stress. Exercise effectively inhibits ROS generation and improves the activities of antioxidant enzymes, and because the protein glycation reaction is driven and accelerated by ROS, the inhibition of AGE formation by regular exercise is attributed mainly to exercise-associated antioxidant activity. Physical exercise also decreases oxidative stress in rodent models and is reported to improve systemic antioxidant activity in humans. These antioxidant effects link exercise to reduced AGE accumulation and healthier aging.

nodes.label: AGE inhibition
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: The inhibition of AGE formation and accumulation in tissues can lead to an increase in lifespan, as concluded from extensive evidence that AGE accumulation accompanies aging and age-related diseases. Because there are no enzymes to remove glycated products, AGEs accumulate as metabolic waste and contribute to tissue senescence. Inhibiting the glycation process and removing existing glycation products may prolong lifespan, and dietary herbal supplements or physiological exercise are advantageous in reducing the AGE burden in the body.

nodes.label: AGE-restricted diet
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: A diet restricting advanced glycation end products can effectively reduce the AGE burden in the human body. In renal failure patients, a low-AGE diet produced a 34% reduction in blood CML levels, while an AGE-rich diet increased CML by 29%. Because significant AGE generation occurs when sugars are cooked with proteins, dietary intake is an important exogenous source of glycotoxins. Restricting dietary AGEs is therefore proposed as an effective way to reduce circulating AGE levels and protect against AGE-related organ dysfunction and tissue aging.

nodes.label: AGE burden
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
nodes.description: A diet restricting advanced glycation end products can effectively reduce the AGE burden in the human body. In renal failure patients, a low-AGE diet produced a 34% reduction in blood CML levels, while an AGE-rich diet increased CML by 29%. Because significant AGE generation occurs when sugars are cooked with proteins, dietary intake is an important exogenous source of glycotoxins. nodes.label: Nicotinamide Mononucleotide
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is a pyridine nucleotide consisting of a nicotinamide riboside molecule bound to a phosphate group. It is an intermediate of the NAD+ salvage pathway and, when administered orally or intraperitoneally, is rapidly converted into NAD+ in major metabolic tissues such as the liver and skeletal muscle. In healthy subjects, oral NMN at 250 mg/day for 12 weeks elevated NAD+ levels in whole blood, and a 300 mg dose for 60 days raised serum NAD+/NADH levels by about 38%. In mice, oral NMN was absorbed from the intestine within minutes and produced a consistent increase in hepatic NAD+ at 15 to 30 minutes, showing that NMN acts as a direct biosynthetic precursor that replenishes the cellular NAD+ pool.

nodes.label: CD73
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: CD73 is an ecto-5'-nucleotidase that sustains NAD+ synthesis by processing extracellular nucleotide precursors. It dephosphorylates nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) into nicotinamide riboside (NR), which can then be taken up by cells, and it also degrades NAD+ into nicotinamide. In cell studies where NAMPT was inhibited, CD73 activity allowed cell viability by maintaining NAD+ synthesis through this extracellular conversion of NMN to NR. This CD73-mediated dephosphorylation is considered a route by which NMN becomes bioavailable for cellular uptake and salvage into NAD+, complementing the direct transporter pathway and highlighting the importance of ecto-enzymes in precursor metabolism.

nodes.label: CD157
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: CD157, also called bone marrow stromal cell antigen 1 (BST1), is a glycohydrolase that participates in NAD+ precursor metabolism. It hydrolyzes nicotinamide riboside (NR) into nicotinamide (NAM), which is then further metabolized by gut microbiota into nicotinic acid and routed through the Preiss-Handler pathway to NAD+. In addition, CD157 displays base-exchange activity against both NR and niacin riboside (NAR), interconverting amidated and deamidated precursor pathways. This dual activity means CD157 not only diverts NR toward the deamidated route but also links the two branches of NAD+ biosynthesis, providing alternative substrates that maintain intracellular NAD+ levels depending on tissue and dietary context.

nodes.label: Gut Microbiome
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: The gut microbiome participates in host NAD+ metabolism because intestinal bacteria possess enzymes that convert nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) into nicotinic acid mononucleotide (NAMN) through deamidation, after which NAMN proceeds through the Preiss-Handler pathway toward NAD+ synthesis. Isotope-labeled NMN given orally to rats was partially deamidated by the intestinal microbiota before absorption, and nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide levels rose in the liver, as also seen after NR supplementation. Shats and colleagues reported that NAD+ enhancement by nicotinamide and NR occurred mostly through this microbiota-dependent deamidated pathway, establishing gut bacteria as active metabolic partners that boost mammalian host NAD+ metabolism rather than simple bystanders.

nodes.label: NAD+ Salvage Pathway
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: The NAD+ salvage pathway is the main recycling system for the oxidized coenzyme, and its principal substrates are the amidated precursors nicotinamide (NAM), nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), and nicotinamide riboside (NR). NR taken up directly from the diet enters cells and is phosphorylated to NMN and adenylated back into NAD+, restoring intracellular levels that fall with aging, overnutrition, and disease. The reduced forms dihydronicotinamide riboside (NRH) and dihydronicotinamide mononucleotide (NMNH) have also been shown to promote synthesis. Together with the de novo route from tryptophan and the Preiss-Handler pathway from nicotinic acid, this redundancy lets multiple dietary precursors maintain NAD+ homeostasis across tissues.

nodes.label: PARP
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs) are NAD+-consuming enzymes that transfer ADP-ribose units onto proteins and nucleic acids, playing critical roles in DNA repair and antiviral immunity. During aging, accumulated DNA damage activates PARPs, which depletes NAD+ and reduces SIRT1 activity. In SARS-CoV-2 infection, PARPs inhibit viral transcript translation through ADP-ribosylation, but viral macrodomain proteins hydrolyze these ADPR units, and the compensatory hyperactivation of PARPs consumes NAD+; restoring NAD+ may therefore support the antiviral functions of PARPs. PARPs also consume NAD+ during diabetes-associated DNA repair, contributing to the NAD+/NADH redox imbalance that drives diabetic complications.

nodes.label: SARM1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: SARM1 is a NAD+-consuming enzyme, grouped with CD38 and CD157 as an NAD+ glycohydrolase that degrades the coenzyme in signaling and stress pathways. Alongside ADP-ribosyl transferases, poly-ADP polymerases, and sirtuins, SARM1 mediates essential NAD+-dependent processes such as DNA repair, apoptosis, cell survival, lifespan regulation, and metabolic adjustments. Its NAD+ consumption contributes to the constant synthesis-catabolism-recycling cycle that sustains NAD+ levels, and disturbances that shift this balance, such as aging or infection, can reduce NAD+ availability. Dietary precursors like NMN and NR counter this by replenishing the NAD+ pool consumed by these signaling enzymes.

nodes.label: NAMPT
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: NAMPT (nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase) is the rate-limiting enzyme that converts nicotinamide into nicotinamide mononucleotide in the NAD+ salvage pathway. A significant cause of age-associated NAD+ decline is the decrease in NAMPT-mediated biosynthesis: NAMPT protein and NAD+ levels fall in white adipose tissue and skeletal muscle of old mice, reducing the activity of NAD+-dependent enzymes such as sirtuins. Inhibiting NAMPT decreases cell growth and increases susceptibility to oxidative stress, a concept being explored for cancer therapy, whereas NMN and NR bypass NAMPT to reverse the cell death it induces, underscoring NAMPT as the central control point of endogenous NAD+ production.

nodes.label: NAD+ Biosynthesis
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: NAMPT (nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase) is the rate-limiting enzyme that converts nicotinamide into nicotinamide mononucleotide in the NAD+ salvage pathway. A significant cause of age-associated NAD+ decline is the decrease in NAMPT-mediated biosynthesis: NAMPT protein and NAD+ levels fall in white adipose tissue and skeletal muscle of old mice, reducing the activity of NAD+-dependent enzymes such as sirtuins. Inhibiting NAMPT decreases cell growth and increases susceptibility to oxidative stress, a concept being explored for cancer therapy, whereas NMN and NR bypass NAMPT to reverse the cell death it induces, underscoring NAMPT as the central control point of endogenous NAD+ production.

nodes.label: Telomere
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) promoted telomere lengthening in aged mice, pre-aging mice, and humans. In one study, treating generation-4 mice with NMN in drinking water for 8 weeks lengthened telomeres, dampened the DNA damage response and p53 activation, functionally rescued liver fibrosis, and improved mitochondrial biogenesis and function in a partially SIRT1-dependent manner. The increased NAD+ levels in the liver of NMN-treated mice reversed hyperacetylation of several sirtuin targets, reinforcing sirtuin activity. These effects counteract the telomere shortening and sirtuin repression that accompany DNA damage accumulation, positioning NMN as a nutraceutical candidate to prevent age-related physiological decline.

nodes.label: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is an effective intervention against the pathophysiology of type 2 diabetes in both diet-induced and age-induced mouse models. Intraperitoneal administration at 500 mg/kg body weight per day for 11 days substantially ameliorated impaired glucose tolerance and enhanced hepatic insulin sensitivity, with the reversal of gene expression changes related to oxidative stress, inflammatory response, and circadian rhythm partly resulting from SIRT1 activation. NMN also restored glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in aged beta-cell-specific SIRT1-overexpressing (BESTO) mice and aged wild-type mice, and in postmenopausal women with prediabetes, 250 mg/day for 10 weeks increased NAD+ in PBMCs and improved insulin signaling and sensitivity in skeletal muscle.

nodes.label: Insulin Secretion
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) restores insulin secretion that is impaired by inflammation and metabolic stress. In islets cultured with the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1beta and TNF-alpha, NMN administration at 100 umol/L restored insulin secretion in a partially SIRT1-dependent manner and corrected inflammation-induced islet dysfunction by reversing changes in genes encoding islet markers essential for glucose sensing and beta-cell differentiation. In mice fed a fructose-rich diet, NMN improved glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, indicating protection against beta-cell failure through an anti-inflammatory mechanism. This action supports NMN's anti-diabetic effects and its capacity to preserve pancreatic beta-cell function under cytokine-driven stress.

nodes.label: Neurogenesis
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) enhances neurogenesis while reducing neurodegenerative pathology in Alzheimer's disease models. NR treatment increased neurogenesis by almost 20% and simultaneously reduced neuroinflammation, apoptosis of hippocampal neurons, phosphorylated Tau, and DNA damage. These effects protect cognitive function, synaptic plasticity, learning, memory, and motor function in animal models. The mechanisms are attributed to NR raising NAD+ levels, which sustains sirtuin activity and mitochondrial gene expression, and reducing the beta-amyloid burden. This positions NR as a promising NAD+ precursor for counteracting the neuronal loss and cognitive decline associated with aging and Alzheimer's disease.

nodes.label: Neuroinflammation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) reduces neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease models and in alcohol-induced depression models. In AD models, NR significantly reduced neuroinflammation, apoptosis of hippocampal neurons, phosphorylated Tau, and DNA damage while increasing neurogenesis. In mice with alcohol-induced depression, dietary NR for 10 weeks reduced both pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokine levels and inhibited microglial activation, with the protective effect attributed to NR upregulating brain-derived neurotrophic factor by altering gut microbiota composition. These findings connect NR's NAD+-boosting action to suppression of neuroinflammation, microglial reactivity, and preservation of cognitive and emotional function.

nodes.label: Obesity
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) prevents and improves metabolic disorders such as high-fat diet-induced obesity. NR supplementation promoted metabolic flexibility by enhancing energy expenditure, significantly attenuating high-fat diet-induced body weight gain and decreasing fat mass, particularly in the liver where triglyceride levels dropped by 40%. NR also protected against hyperinsulinemia and elevated total and LDL cholesterol caused by a high-fat diet, while having no effect on body weight when given with a normal chow diet. Additionally, NR-conditioned gut microbiota conferred protection against high-fat diet weight gain through fecal transfer, linking the gut microbiome to its anti-obesity effects.

nodes.label: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) protects against non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and its metabolic sequelae by increasing NAD+ and stimulating sirtuins. NR supplementation increased hepatic beta-oxidation and mitochondrial content, reversing glucose intolerance, insulin resistance, liver lipid accumulation, and hepatic fibrosis in mouse models. In high-fat diet studies, NR reduced liver fat mass and decreased hepatic triglyceride levels by 40%. These benefits arise from NR elevating NAD+ in liver and muscle, which stimulates SIRT1 and SIRT3 activity to enhance oxidative metabolism and mitochondrial function, counteracting the fatty liver and metabolic inflexibility driven by overnutrition.

nodes.label: SOD2
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: SIRT3 is the primary mitochondrial NAD+-dependent deacetylase, and among its targets is SOD2 (manganese superoxide dismutase). When NR raises NAD+ and activates SIRT3, the acetylation of SOD2 is reduced, increasing mitochondrial SOD2 activity and thereby lowering mitochondrial reactive oxygen species. SIRT3 also deacetylates isocitrate dehydrogenase 2, enhancing mitochondrial antioxidant capacity and quality control. This SIRT3-SOD2 axis is central to NR's protective effects against oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and it also mediates the benefit of gut-microbiota-derived NMN in acute pancreatitis, where the SIRT3-PRDX5 pathway is engaged.

nodes.label: NLRP3 Inflammasome
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: SIRT3, along with SIRT1 and SIRT2, suppresses the activity of NF-kB and the NLRP3 inflammasome through multiple mechanisms. Because sirtuins are NAD+-dependent, raising NAD+ with precursors such as NR enhances this suppression. In human peripheral blood mononuclear cells, 24-hour NR administration recapitulated the fasting effect of blunting NLRP3 inflammasome activation and enhancing mitochondrial quality control in a SIRT3-dependent manner, reducing secretion of IL-1beta and TNF-alpha. This sirtuin-mediated restraint of the NLRP3 inflammasome helps prevent cytokine storm in severe infections and mitigates the chronic inflammation associated with aging and metabolic disease.

nodes.label: IL-1β
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) decreases secretion of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-1beta in human immune cells. In healthy volunteers, 24-hour NR administration reduced IL-1beta secretion in monocytes by over 50% (from approximately 22,000 to 10,000 pg/mL) and in macrophages by around 20% (from above 300 to less than 250 pg/mL). This effect is mediated by SIRT3-dependent blunting of NLRP3 inflammasome activation and enhanced mitochondrial quality control. By reducing IL-1beta and TNF-alpha production, NR demonstrates systemic anti-inflammatory activity consistent with its NAD+-boosting and sirtuin-activating mechanism.

nodes.label: Acute Pancreatitis
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) derived from the gut microbiota ameliorates acute pancreatitis injury. In acute pancreatitis mouse models, NMN increased NAD+ levels and activated the SIRT3-PRDX5 pathway, mitigating pancreatic mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative damage, and inflammation in a partially SIRT3-dependent manner. Acute pancreatitis is exacerbated by gut microbiota dysbiosis, and normobiotic fecal microbiota transplantation induced higher serum NMN levels, enhancing NAD+ biosynthesis in the pancreas. This makes NMN an important mediator of the protective effects of fecal microbiota transplantation and highlights the role of gut microbiota-produced NAD+ precursors in pathological outcomes of the host.

nodes.label: Lactobacillus
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) can selectively stimulate the growth of beneficial gut bacteria such as Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus. These bacteria are associated with improved gut health, including prevention of diarrhea, improved gut barrier function, reduced inflammation, and immune support. NR also modulates gut microbiota in ways protective against high-fat diet-induced weight gain: mice fed 60% HFD with 0.4% NR for 168 days had nearly 16% less weight gain and lower fasting blood glucose, and fecal transfer from NR-treated donors reproduced the protective effect with a microbiota enriched in butyrate-producing Firmicutes. NR thus reshapes the microbiome to favor metabolically beneficial bacteria.

nodes.label: Faecalibacterium
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Long-term nicotinamide riboside (NR) supplementation modulates gut microbiota composition in humans, increasing the abundance of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii. In a twin study, NR at 250-1000 mg/day for 5 months raised F. prausnitzii abundance, and association analysis suggested this bacterium contributes to regulation of NAD+, inflammation, amino acid, and lipid metabolism. Faecalibacterium prausnitzii is a butyrate-producing commensal that promotes metabolic health and anti-inflammatory responses, and its decline characterizes dysbiosis in inflammatory bowel disease. NR's ability to enrich this beneficial organism supports its role in improving gut and systemic health through microbiota modulation.

nodes.label: Gut Dysbiosis
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) reverses gut dysbiosis and protects the intestinal tract. In an experimental mouse model of colitis induced by dextran sodium sulfate, NMN given by gavage at 1 mg/g body weight increased microbial abundance and diversity, improved mucus secretion and tight-junction protein expression, and attenuated intestinal mucosal permeability, protecting against inflammatory bowel disease. Long-term NMN treatment modulated gut microbiota diversity and composition, increasing butyric acid-producing bacteria such as Ruminococcaceae UCG-014 and Prevotellaceae NK3B31 as well as Akkermansia muciniphila, while decreasing harmful bacteria like Bilophila and Oscillibacter. NMN thereby restores intestinal homeostasis and barrier integrity through microbiota remodeling.

nodes.label: Intestinal Barrier
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) improves intestinal barrier function, which is important for preventing translocation of harmful bacteria and toxins from the gut into the bloodstream. In colitis models, NMN increased the expression of tight-junction proteins and improved mucus secretion, attenuating intestinal mucosal permeability. Long-term NMN treatment also increased the number of goblet cells, mucus thickness, and tight junction protein expression, maintaining the integrity of the intestinal epithelium. NMN and NR share this gut-protective property alongside selective stimulation of beneficial bacteria, and NAD+-precursor-activated sirtuins also protect intestinal endothelial cells against oxidative injury, collectively reinforcing the gut barrier.

nodes.label: Alcohol-Induced Depression
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) protects against alcohol-induced depression-like behaviors in mice by altering gut microbiota composition. Dietary supplementation with NR for 10 weeks at 400 mg/kg daily reduced both pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokine levels, inhibited microglial activation, and provided protection against alcohol-induced depression-like behaviors. The effect was attributed to NR's ability to upregulate brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) through microbiota changes: brain BDNF levels correlated positively with bacteria enriched in the NR group such as Barnesiella, Alloprevotella, Prevotella, Alistipes, and Mucispirillum. Fecal microbiota transplantation from NR-treated donors reproduced the protective features in germ-free recipients, demonstrating a gut-microbiota-gut-brain axis mechanism.

nodes.label: BDNF
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) upregulates brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) by altering gut microbiota composition. In a mouse model of alcohol-induced depression, 10 weeks of NR supplementation reduced pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines, inhibited microglial activation, and protected against depression-like behaviors, with the protective effect attributed to NR-driven increases in BDNF. Brain BDNF levels were positively correlated with bacteria abundant in NR-treated mice, such as Barnesiella and Alloprevotella, whereas brain inflammatory cytokines correlated with bacteria enriched in the depression model group. This BDNF upregulation via microbiota remodeling links NR intake to improved emotional behavior and neural plasticity.

nodes.label: Butyrate
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Butyrate, a short-chain fatty acid produced by gut bacteria such as Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Eubacterium rectale, and Roseburia, reduces adiposity by inhibiting intestinal cholesterol biosynthesis and promoting beneficial metabolic effects including insulin secretion, insulin sensitivity, and energy expenditure. Butyrate can also increase satiety and gut motility by upregulating the expression of peptide YY and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1). In studies where NR supplementation enriched butyrate-producing Firmicutes, these metabolic benefits contributed to protection against high-fat diet-induced weight gain, and fecal transfer reproduced the effect, underscoring butyrate as a key mediator of microbiota-driven metabolic health.

nodes.label: Edamame
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is found in a range of foods including edamame beans, avocado, broccoli, cucumber, cabbage, and tomato, according to the first evidence published by Mills et al. (2016). Among the investigated sources, the highest NMN content was found in edamame at 0.47-1.88 mg/100 g and avocado at 0.36-1.60 mg/100 g, with smaller amounts in seafood and raw meats (0.06-0.42 mg/100 g). Milk also contains NMN, with human milk the richest source at 2.1-9.8 uM. These natural occurrences support the idea that a normal diet can contribute to NAD+ precursor intake, though optimal sources remain to be established.

nodes.label: Bovine Milk
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) was first discovered in milk and, until recently, had only been measured there. Bovine milk contains the highest NR content among milk sources at 0.5-3.6 uM, while human milk is the richest source of nicotinamide mononucleotide at 2.1-9.8 uM. NR and NMN are also determined in different species of milk and beer. The niacin quantified by microbiological assay (AOAC Method 944.13) actually includes NR and NMN, because hot acid or alkaline extraction hydrolyzes these molecules into nicotinic acid, meaning NR and NMN contribute to the measured niacin content of milk and other foods.

nodes.label: Saccharomyces cerevisiae
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Yeast-mediated production of nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) was demonstrated in craft beers, with hop indicating a role in enhancing NR levels during fermentation. This finding opens new perspectives for enriched sources of NAD+ precursors through fermented foods and beverages. Additionally, fructophilic lactic acid bacteria have been investigated for biotechnological production of NMN and NR for functional probiotic products and supplements. These microbial routes complement natural dietary sources such as vegetables, meat, milk, and mushrooms, and could enable the development of new functional foods and biotechnological strategies to maintain and enhance the physiological benefits of NAD+ precursors.

nodes.label: 900 mg per day
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: A sub-chronic 90-day toxicity study in rats established that repeated oral administration of synthetic NMN at doses up to 1500 mg/kg/day appears safe and did not promote toxic effects on body weight, food and water consumption, feed conversion efficiency, or biochemical and blood parameters, although higher doses increased kidney, liver, and adrenal gland weights and elevated hepatic enzymes such as alkaline phosphatase, alanine aminotransferase, and aspartate aminotransferase. Based on these findings, the established upper intake level of NMN for a 60 kg individual was set at 900 mg per day. Human studies at 100-500 mg single doses and 250-300 mg/day over weeks to months reported no adverse effects.

nodes.label: Blood
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is unstable in blood, degrading very rapidly even at -80 degrees Celsius. In the first clinical trial of single oral NMN doses (100-500 mg) in healthy subjects, NMN was not detected in plasma, most likely because sample freezing before extraction caused NMN degradation. This rapid degradation complicates accurate measurement of circulating NMN and may explain why plasma NMN levels are kept low and constant, presumably due to balanced NMN distribution from plasma to tissues. In mice, orally administered NMN was quickly absorbed from the intestine, eliminated from circulation within 15 minutes, and rapidly converted into NAD+ in tissues such as the liver and soleus muscle.

nodes.label: Nicotinamide
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: Although nicotinamide (NAM) effectively increases NAD+ in tissues, it also exerts an inhibitory effect on sirtuins and PARP activity, a property that distinguishes it from the other precursors NMN and NR. At high doses, NAM is methylated by nicotinamide N-methyltransferase to generate N1-methylnicotinamide for elimination in urine, which can lower the cellular methyl pool over time. This depletion could reduce DNA and protein methylation and alter gene expression patterns and protein activity, since DNA methylation in gene promoter regions is typically associated with transcriptional repression. These effects may explain why NR administration raises NAD+ levels more than NAM treatment in some studies.

nodes.label: NRH
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: NRH (dihydronicotinamide riboside) is the reduced form of nicotinamide riboside and has recently been shown to promote NAD+ synthesis. Alongside NMNH (dihydronicotinamide mononucleotide), the reduced form of nicotinamide mononucleotide, NRH expands the repertoire of NAD+ precursors beyond the amidated molecules nicotinamide, NMN, and NR. These reduced precursors are additional substrates for the salvage pathway and are considered orally bioavailable NAD+ precursors. Their discovery illustrates the redundancy of NAD+ biosynthetic routes and suggests that multiple dietary and pharmacological compounds can contribute to maintaining intracellular NAD+ levels across tissues.

nodes.label: NMNH
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: NMNH (dihydronicotinamide mononucleotide) is the reduced form of nicotinamide mononucleotide and has been shown to promote NAD+ synthesis. Together with NRH, the reduced form of nicotinamide riboside, NMNH adds to the set of NAD+ precursors available for cellular salvage and NAD+ replenishment. These reduced precursors demonstrate that the NAD+ metabolic cycle is more flexible than initially recognized, providing alternative routes to boost NAD+ levels beyond the classic precursors tryptophan, nicotinamide, nicotinic acid, NMN, and NR, and supporting efforts to develop effective strategies for preventing NAD+ decline in aging and disease.

nodes.label: SLC12A8
nodes.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
nodes.description: SLC12A8 is a transporter encoded by the gene SLC12A8 that has been proposed to mediate cellular uptake of nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), in addition to the CD73-mediated dephosphorylation route in which NMN is converted extracellularly to nicotinamide riboside for uptake. The expression of a gut transporter reinforces that NMN could be made bioavailable through oral delivery, and the presence of such a transporter in the intestine supports the idea that dietary NMN can enter the circulation.
