nodes.label: Catalase downregulation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Oxidative Stress Harms and Benefits for Human Health.md
nodes.description: Catalase downregulation contributes to cancer because reduced H2O2 clearance permits sustained oxidative stress that can drive DNA damage, genomic instability, and altered redox signaling favoring proliferation. Catalase is frequently downregulated in breast, prostate, and hepatocellular carcinomas relative to normal tissue. The directionality is loss-of-defense promoting tumorigenic oxidative damage. A caveat is that many tumors also exploit moderate ROS for survival signaling, so catalase levels represent a context-dependent balance rather than a simple tumor suppressor.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial catalase overexpression
nodes.description: Mitochondrial catalase overexpression extends lifespan, as demonstrated by MCAT (mitochondrial catalase transgenic) mice showing roughly 20 percent increased median lifespan and delayed age-related pathology. By concentrating catalase in the mitochondrial matrix, H2O2 from Complex I or III leak is removed before it propagates damage. The directionality is targeted detoxification promoting longevity. A caveat is that lifespan extension is modest and tissue-specific, and overexpression does not abolish all aging phenotypes, indicating multiple parallel aging mechanisms.

nodes.label: Selenium
nodes.description: Glutathione peroxidase requires selenium in the form of a catalytic selenocysteine residue at its active site, which is essential for the redox chemistry of peroxide reduction. Dietary selenium deficiency lowers GPx activity and leaves cells more vulnerable to oxidative injury. The directionality is nutrient to enzyme function. A caveat is that excess selenium is toxic and does not further increase activity, so there is a narrow optimal range for antioxidant benefit. Selenocysteine is incorporated into GPx during translation at a recoded UGA codon, and selenium status tracks circulating GPx activity closely, making the enzyme a sensitive functional marker of selenium nutrition.

nodes.label: Selenium deficiency
nodes.description: Selenium deficiency causes Keshan disease, an endemic cardiomyopathy found in selenium-poor regions, driven by insufficient cardiac glutathione peroxidase activity and consequent oxidant damage to myocardium. Affected hearts show necrosis and fibrosis with reduced antiviral and antioxidant defenses. The directionality is nutrient lack to enzyme failure to tissue injury. A caveat is that coxsackievirus infection interacts with the deficiency, so Keshan disease is not purely a selenium-deficiency disorder.

nodes.label: Keshan disease
nodes.description: Selenium deficiency causes Keshan disease, an endemic cardiomyopathy found in selenium-poor regions, driven by insufficient cardiac glutathione peroxidase activity and consequent oxidant damage to myocardium. Affected hearts show necrosis and fibrosis with reduced antiviral and antioxidant defenses. The directionality is nutrient lack to enzyme failure to tissue injury. A caveat is that coxsackievirus infection interacts with the deficiency, so Keshan disease is not purely a selenium-deficiency disorder.

nodes.label: Malondialdehyde
nodes.description: Lipid peroxidation produces malondialdehyde (MDA), a three-carbon dialdehyde arising from cyclization and fragmentation of peroxidized polyunsaturated fatty acids such as arachidonic acid. MDA is reactive and forms adducts with proteins and DNA, contributing to downstream toxicity. The directionality is membrane damage yielding a diffusible, immunogenic byproduct. A caveat is that MDA is one of many aldehyde products, so its measurement captures only part of the peroxidation burden. MDA forms under both physiological and pathological conditions and is the most commonly measured TBARS-based endpoint in redox research.

nodes.label: 4-Hydroxynonenal
nodes.description: Lipid peroxidation produces 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), a highly reactive alpha,beta-unsaturated aldehyde generated mainly from n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids. 4-HNE forms Michael adducts with protein cysteine, histidine, and lysine residues, altering enzyme function and signaling. The directionality is membrane oxidation yielding a potent endogenous electrophile. A caveat is that at low concentrations 4-HNE can act as a signaling molecule inducing adaptive responses, blurring the line between damage and signal.

nodes.label: Cholesterol
nodes.description: Malondialdehyde modifies cholesterol by forming MDA-lysine adducts on LDL apolipoproteins, creating MDA-LDL that is recognized by macrophage scavenger receptors. This modification enhances unregulated uptake and foam-cell formation in the arterial wall. The directionality is peroxidation product to LDL modification to atherogenic uptake. A caveat is that other aldehydes (4-HNE, acrolein) modify LDL similarly, so MDA-LDL is a representative but not exclusive epitope. MDA-modified LDL is pro-inflammatory and immunogenic, and its accumulation in plaques is used as a marker of oxidative modification of lipoproteins.

nodes.label: 8-oxo-2'-deoxyguanosine
nodes.description: 8-oxo-2'-deoxyguanosine is a biomarker for oxidative stress, representing the major product of DNA oxidation and one of the most widely used indicators of oxidative DNA damage in urine and tissue. Its steady-state level integrates the rate of formation by ROS and the efficiency of repair and sanitization. The directionality is DNA oxidation to measurable lesion. A caveat is that sample handling and artifactual oxidation during extraction can inflate measurements, requiring careful standardized assays.

nodes.label: OGG1
nodes.description: OGG1 repairs 8-oxo-2'-deoxyguanosine as a bifunctional DNA glycosylase that excises the damaged base and cleaves the backbone, initiating base-excision repair that liberates free 8-oxodG. This prevents the lesion from mispairing with adenine during replication. The directionality is lesion to repair pathway. A caveat is that OGG1's role in processing 8-oxodG is most critical in nuclear DNA, while mitochondrial isoforms handle mtDNA damage with somewhat different kinetics. OGG1 also releases the free 8-oxodG into urine, which is why urinary levels of the lesion report both damage and active repair.

nodes.label: G→T transversions
nodes.description: 8-oxo-2'-deoxyguanosine causes G to T transversions because the oxidized base pairs promiscuously with adenine during replication, so a G:C pair becomes an A:T pair after a round of replication and repair. These transversions are signature mutations in many cancers. The directionality is miscoding lesion to mutagenic outcome. A caveat is that accurate repair by OGG1 before replication averts most mutations, so only unrepaired lesions are mutagenic. G to T transversions are among the most frequent mutations found in oncogenes and tumor suppressors in human cancers, underscoring the relevance of this lesion.

nodes.label: MTH1
nodes.description: MTH1 prevents 8-oxo-dGTP incorporation by hydrolyzing the oxidized nucleotide triphosphate to 8-oxo-dGMP, sanitizing the dNTP pool before DNA polymerase can insert it. This provides a front-line defense that complements OGG1's post-replicative repair. The directionality is sanitization to mutation prevention. A caveat is that MTH1 knockout is tolerated in many contexts because backup repair exists, though cancer cells can become dependent on it (synthetic lethal vulnerability). Because DNA polymerases preferentially misinsert the oxidized nucleotide opposite adenine, MTH1 action is essential for maintaining replication fidelity in oxidatively stressed cells.

nodes.label: 8-oxo-dGTP incorporation
nodes.description: MTH1 prevents 8-oxo-dGTP incorporation by hydrolyzing the oxidized nucleotide triphosphate to 8-oxo-dGMP, sanitizing the dNTP pool before DNA polymerase can insert it. This provides a front-line defense that complements OGG1's post-replicative repair. The directionality is sanitization to mutation prevention. A caveat is that MTH1 knockout is tolerated in many contexts because backup repair exists, though cancer cells can become dependent on it (synthetic lethal vulnerability). Because DNA polymerases preferentially misinsert the oxidized nucleotide opposite adenine, MTH1 action is essential for maintaining replication fidelity in oxidatively stressed cells.

nodes.label: Elevated 8-oxodG
nodes.description: Elevated 8-oxodG is associated with cancer, being increased in lung, breast, bladder, and colorectal cancers where it marks heightened oxidative DNA damage and genomic instability. Persistent oxidative lesions increase mutation burden that can drive oncogenesis. The directionality is oxidative damage to cancer risk or marker. A caveat is that elevated 8-oxodG may be a consequence of the tumor's metabolic and inflammatory state as much as a cause. Urinary and tissue 8-oxodG are frequently elevated in cancer patients and have been proposed as markers of exposure and disease burden.

nodes.label: NOX4
nodes.description: NOX4 produces hydrogen peroxide rather than superoxide because it is constitutively active and dismutates its product internally, releasing H2O2 as the main extracellular and matrix signaling oxidant. This makes NOX4 a major source of the diffusible second messenger in fibroblasts and the kidney. The directionality is enzyme activity to H2O2 signaling. A caveat is that NOX4's H2O2 output is context-dependent and can be both profibrotic via TGF-beta signaling and protective depending on tissue. NOX4 is unique among NOX isoforms in being constitutively active and regulated primarily at the transcriptional level, for instance by TGF-beta and hypoxia.

nodes.label: NOX2
nodes.description: NOX2 deficiency causes chronic granulomatous disease, a group of genetic defects in NOX2 (gp91phox) subunits that abolish the phagocyte respiratory burst. Patients suffer recurrent, life-threatening bacterial and fungal infections due to failure to generate microbicidal ROS. The directionality is enzyme defect to immunodeficiency. A caveat is that the disease severity varies with the specific mutation and residual oxidase activity, and some organisms evade even normal ROS killing. X-linked CGD from CYBB mutations is most common, and patients show granuloma formation, colitis-like inflammation, and susceptibility to catalase-positive organisms.

nodes.label: Chronic granulomatous disease
nodes.description: NOX2 deficiency causes chronic granulomatous disease, a group of genetic defects in NOX2 (gp91phox) subunits that abolish the phagocyte respiratory burst. Patients suffer recurrent, life-threatening bacterial and fungal infections due to failure to generate microbicidal ROS. The directionality is enzyme defect to immunodeficiency. A caveat is that the disease severity varies with the specific mutation and residual oxidase activity, and some organisms evade even normal ROS killing. X-linked CGD from CYBB mutations is most common, and patients show granuloma formation, colitis-like inflammation, and susceptibility to catalase-positive organisms.

nodes.label: Angiotensin II
nodes.description: NADPH oxidase is activated by angiotensin II via the AT1 receptor, which triggers assembly of NOX isoforms (especially NOX1) in vascular smooth muscle and endothelial cells. This couples the renin-angiotensin system to vascular oxidative stress and hypertension. The directionality is hormone to enzyme activation. A caveat is that AT1 signaling also activates other ROS sources and inflammatory pathways, so NOX is a major but not sole mediator of angiotensin-II effects. Angiotensin-II-driven NOX activation is a well-established mechanism in hypertension, contributing to vascular remodeling and target-organ damage.

nodes.label: Nitrative Stress
nodes.description: Peroxynitrite causes nitrative stress by oxidizing and nitrating biomolecules, most characteristically forming 3-nitrotyrosine on proteins, an irreversible modification that can inactivate enzymes. It also nitrates nucleic acids and lipids, broadening its toxic footprint. The directionality is hybrid oxidant to nitrative modification. A caveat is that 3-nitrotyrosine can also arise from other nitrating species such as myeloperoxidase-derived species, so it is not exclusively peroxynitrite-specific.

nodes.label: MnSOD
nodes.description: Peroxynitrite inactivates MnSOD by nitrating Tyr34 in the mitochondrial matrix enzyme, impairing its ability to dismutate superoxide. This creates a vicious cycle in which peroxynitrite both consumes NO and disables a key superoxide-scavenging enzyme. The directionality is nitration to loss of antioxidant defense. A caveat is that the magnitude of MnSOD inactivation depends on local peroxynitrite concentration and the availability of peroxynitrite scavengers such as uric acid. Because MnSOD is a first-line mitochondrial defense, its inactivation amplifies superoxide levels and further feeds peroxynitrite production in a self-sustaining loop.

nodes.label: 3-Nitrotyrosine
nodes.description: 3-nitrotyrosine is a biomarker for nitrative stress, reflecting peroxynitrite- or myeloperoxidase-mediated nitration of protein tyrosines. It is elevated across many inflammatory and neurodegenerative conditions. The directionality is nitrative insult to stable protein modification. A caveat is that 3-nitrotyrosine can arise from multiple nitrating pathways and can be repaired or degraded, so it indicates historical rather than instantaneous nitrative load. Quantification in plasma, CSF, and tissue by mass spectrometry or immunoassay has made 3-NT a standard endpoint in redox biomarker studies.

nodes.label: Uric Acid
nodes.description: Uric acid scavenges peroxynitrite, acting as a physiologic antioxidant in humans (who lack the uricase that degrades it) at the high plasma concentrations typical of the species. It reacts with peroxynitrite to limit tyrosine nitration and lipid oxidation. The directionality is scavenger to oxidant neutralization. A caveat is that urate is also pro-oxidant and pro-inflammatory at high levels and contributes to gout, so its net effect is concentration- and context-dependent. Because humans and great apes lost uricase, urate circulates at near-saturating concentrations, providing a constitutive antioxidant buffer in plasma.

nodes.label: Reactive Nitrogen Species
nodes.description: Reactive nitrogen species are derived from nitric oxide, which combines with superoxide or other radicals to yield peroxynitrite, nitrogen dioxide, and related species. Thus NO is the nitrogenous precursor of the broader RNS family. The directionality is NO to RNS expansion. A caveat is that RNS also include species from myeloperoxidase and other enzymatic pathways, so RNS origin is not exclusively nitric-oxide-derived. Because NO is itself a free radical with signaling functions, RNS can be viewed as both downstream products and, under excess, pathological mediators of nitrative stress.

nodes.label: Alpha-Lipoic Acid
nodes.description: Alpha-lipoic acid recycles glutathione by providing the reduced dihydrolipoic acid (DHLA) form, which directly reduces oxidized glutathione and also regenerates vitamins C and E. This restores the cellular thiol redox buffer and amplifies other antioxidants. The directionality is lipoate redox cycling to antioxidant network support. A caveat is that exogenous lipoic acid's in vivo recycling efficiency depends on tissue uptake and the endogenous reductase capacity. By maintaining the GSH pool, lipoic acid indirectly supports glutathione peroxidase, glutaredoxin, and glutathione S-transferase activity throughout the cell.

nodes.label: Coenzyme Q10
nodes.description: Coenzyme Q10 transfers electrons between mitochondrial Complex I (or II) and Complex III as a mobile lipophilic carrier in the inner membrane, shuttling single electrons and buffering the pool. In its reduced form (ubiquinol) it also acts as an antioxidant. The directionality is electron transport coupled to redox buffering. A caveat is that CoQ10's electron-transfer role is distinct from its antioxidant role, and statin-mediated depletion can affect both. CoQ10 is synthesized endogenously via the mevalonate pathway and is also a potent lipophilic antioxidant in both its ubiquinol and ubiquinone forms.

nodes.label: Statins
nodes.description: Statins reduce synthesis of Coenzyme Q10 because they inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the upstream enzyme shared by the mevalonate pathway that produces both cholesterol and the isoprenoid side chain of CoQ10. This can lower tissue CoQ10 levels, particularly with high-dose or lipophilic statins. The directionality is enzyme inhibition to CoQ10 depletion. A caveat is that the clinical significance of statin-associated CoQ10 reduction is debated, with most patients not developing myopathy attributable to it.

nodes.label: Tetrahydrobiopterin
nodes.description: Peroxynitrite oxidizes tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) to BH2, depriving eNOS of its essential cofactor and thereby promoting eNOS uncoupling and superoxide production. This establishes a feed-forward loop of vascular oxidative stress. The directionality is nitration of cofactor to enzyme dysfunction. A caveat is that BH4 can be regenerated by dihydrofolate reductase, partially buffering peroxynitrite-driven loss. Restoring BH4 by supplementation or by dihydrofolate reductase-dependent recycling re-couples eNOS and improves endothelial function in experimental studies.

nodes.label: Uncoupled eNOS
nodes.description: Uncoupled eNOS produces superoxide radicals when BH4 or L-arginine becomes limiting, causing the enzyme to redirect electron flow from NO synthesis to oxygen reduction. This converts the principal vascular protective enzyme into a ROS source. The directionality is cofactor deficiency to superoxide generation. A caveat is that partial uncoupling may still yield some NO, and the transition is graded rather than binary. This uncoupling is a central mechanism of endothelial dysfunction in hypertension, diabetes, and atherosclerosis, and therapies that restore BH4 or arginine aim to re-couple the enzyme.

nodes.label: ADMA
nodes.description: ADMA inhibits eNOS by competitively occupying the L-arginine binding site of all NOS isoforms, reducing NO production and promoting uncoupling. Elevated ADMA (from reduced catabolism by dimethylarginine dimethylaminohydrolase) is a marker of endothelial risk. The directionality is endogenous inhibitor to NO deficiency. A caveat is that ADMA also inhibits other NOS isoforms and its effects are modulated by L-arginine availability and methyltransferase activity. Because ADMA is primarily cleared by DDAH, oxidative inactivation of DDAH raises ADMA and further suppresses NO, a self-reinforcing cycle in endothelial disease.

nodes.label: Phagocytes
nodes.description: Phagocytes use the respiratory burst to produce high concentrations of ROS and RNS via NOX2 and inducible NOS, creating an antimicrobial environment in the phagosome and extracellular space. This oxidant surge kills engulfed pathogens but also risks collateral tissue damage. The directionality is immune activation to oxidant deployment. A caveat is that the burst is tightly compartmentalized and regulated; failure (CGD) causes infection, while excess causes inflammatory injury. The burst is also coordinated with phagosome maturation, degranulation, and acidification, ensuring oxidants act where pathogens are contained.

nodes.label: Respiratory Burst
nodes.description: Phagocytes use the respiratory burst to produce high concentrations of ROS and RNS via NOX2 and inducible NOS, creating an antimicrobial environment in the phagosome and extracellular space. This oxidant surge kills engulfed pathogens but also risks collateral tissue damage. The directionality is immune activation to oxidant deployment. A caveat is that the burst is tightly compartmentalized and regulated; failure (CGD) causes infection, while excess causes inflammatory injury. The burst is also coordinated with phagosome maturation, degranulation, and acidification, ensuring oxidants act where pathogens are contained.

nodes.label: T cell polarization
nodes.description: Glutathione determines T cell polarization because the GSH/GSSG redox state tunes the balance between pro-inflammatory Th1/Th17 and anti-inflammatory Th2/Treg responses. Oxidized extracellular glutathione can itself act as a danger signal influencing differentiation. The directionality is thiol redox to immune phenotype. A caveat is that glutathione is one of several metabolic and cytokine inputs to T-cell fate, so it biases rather than dictates polarization. Redox modulation of T cells is therefore being investigated as an adjunctive target in autoimmunity and chronic inflammation.

nodes.label: A20
nodes.description: A20 terminates NF-kappaB signaling by removing K63-linked ubiquitin chains from RIP1 and TRAF6, thereby shutting down IKK activation and the downstream cascade. As a feedback inhibitor, A20 limits excessive inflammation and tissue damage. The directionality is deubiquitination to signal termination. A caveat is that A20 mutations or insufficiency are linked to chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, showing its role is non-redundant in some tissues. Mice lacking A20 in specific tissues develop severe spontaneous inflammation, confirming its role as an essential inflammatory brake.

nodes.label: NF-kappa B signaling
nodes.description: A20 terminates NF-kappaB signaling by removing K63-linked ubiquitin chains from RIP1 and TRAF6, thereby shutting down IKK activation and the downstream cascade. As a feedback inhibitor, A20 limits excessive inflammation and tissue damage. The directionality is deubiquitination to signal termination. A caveat is that A20 mutations or insufficiency are linked to chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, showing its role is non-redundant in some tissues. Mice lacking A20 in specific tissues develop severe spontaneous inflammation, confirming its role as an essential inflammatory brake.

nodes.label: S-Nitrosylation
nodes.description: S-nitrosylation inhibits NF-kappaB when NO-derived S-nitrosothiols modify key cysteines (p50 Cys-62 and RelA Cys-38), disrupting DNA binding and transcriptional activity. This provides a redox-based brake on inflammatory signaling. The directionality is NO-mediated modification to transcriptional repression. A caveat is that the effect is reversible and concentration-dependent, and high NO can also paradoxically promote NF-kappaB under some conditions. This mechanism contributes to NO's ability to restrain inflammatory gene expression and may explain some anti-inflammatory actions of nitrosating agents.

nodes.label: Bortezomib
nodes.description: Bortezomib blocks NF-kappaB by inhibiting the proteasome, preventing degradation of IkappaB and thus trapping NF-kappaB in the cytoplasm. This therapeutic strategy exploits the dependence of many cancers on NF-kappaB survival signaling. The directionality is proteasome inhibition to transcriptional blockade. A caveat is that bortezomib also inhibits degradation of many other proteins, causing toxicity such as peripheral neuropathy. The drug is used in multiple myeloma and mantle-cell lymphoma, where its NF-kappaB blockade and proteotoxic stress together induce myeloma cell death.

nodes.label: Aconitase
nodes.description: Peroxynitrite inactivates aconitase by disrupting its [4Fe-4S] cluster, impairing the TCA-cycle enzyme and diverting citrate metabolism. This links nitrative stress to mitochondrial metabolic dysfunction. The directionality is cluster destruction to enzyme inactivation. A caveat is that aconitase is also sensitive to superoxide and other oxidants, so its inhibition is not uniquely peroxynitrite-driven. Because aconitase also acts as iron regulatory protein 1 when its cluster is lost, oxidative inactivation links metabolic and iron-regulatory responses.

nodes.label: Nitrated lipids
nodes.description: Nitrated lipids activate PPARgamma, as electrophilic nitrated fatty acids such as nitrolinoleic acid act as ligands that promote the receptor's transcriptional program. This redirects metabolism and induces anti-inflammatory and antioxidant genes. The directionality is lipid nitration product to nuclear receptor activation. A caveat is that nitrated lipids can also signal through PPARalpha and other targets, so PPARgamma is a major but not exclusive node. This pathway represents a feedback mechanism in which nitrative stress generates endogenous ligands that dampen inflammation.

nodes.label: Redox-Active Metals
nodes.description: Amyloid-beta binds redox-active metals (Cu2+ and Fe3+), forming complexes that generate superoxide and H2O2 via Fenton-like chemistry at the metal site. This positions Abeta as a localized source of ROS in the Alzheimer brain. The directionality is metal binding to radical generation. A caveat is that metal-free Abeta aggregation also drives pathology, so redox activity is one of several toxic functions. Abeta is proposed to act as a redox-active metal chaperone, and metal chelators have been tested as candidate therapies to limit this pro-oxidant activity.

nodes.label: Autoxidation
nodes.description: Dopamine undergoes autoxidation, a spontaneous oxidation in which dopamine quinones, superoxide, H2O2, and 6-hydroxydopamine are produced, especially at physiological pH. This creates ROS in dopaminergic neurons independent of external insults. The directionality is catecholamine oxidation to oxidant and quinone formation. A caveat is that autoxidation is accelerated by metal ions and pH, and the quinones also form adducts that may be more directly toxic than the radicals. In Parkinson's disease, the resulting oxidant and quinone stress is thought to contribute to the selective vulnerability of dopaminergic substantia nigra neurons.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial Complex I
nodes.description: Mitochondrial Complex I activity is reduced (about 30 to 40 percent) in the substantia nigra of Parkinson's disease patients, contributing to electron leak and superoxide generation. This localized respiratory defect is among the earliest bioenergetic abnormalities described in PD. The directionality is enzyme deficiency to increased mitochondrial ROS. A caveat is that Complex I inhibition can be both a cause and a consequence of oxidative damage, and not all PD cases show the same magnitude of defect.

nodes.label: MitoQ
nodes.description: MitoQ reduces mitochondrial ROS as a mitochondria-targeted ubiquinone derivative that accumulates in the matrix and chain-breaks peroxyl radicals at their source. By concentrating antioxidant capacity inside mitochondria, it limits the downstream damage from leaked electrons. The directionality is targeted antioxidant to lowered mitochondrial oxidant burden. A caveat is that high doses of MitoQ can accumulate and potentially act as a pro-oxidant by virtue of its redox-cycling quinone structure. MitoQ has shown benefit in models of ischemia-reperfusion, neurodegeneration, and age-related vascular dysfunction.

nodes.label: Signaling Molecules
nodes.description: Hydrogen peroxide acts as a signaling molecule, functioning as a second messenger in insulin signaling, growth-factor pathways, and immune responses. Its relatively long half-life and membrane permeability allow it to diffuse and oxidize specific targets reversibly. The directionality is H2O2 from enzyme or leak to signal propagation. A caveat is that the same molecule is toxic at higher concentrations, so concentration and compartmentalization determine whether H2O2 signals or damages. Reversible oxidation of target cysteines, such as those in PTP1B and PTEN, allows H2O2 to propagate kinase-dependent responses.

nodes.label: Cysteine Thiols
nodes.description: Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes cysteine thiols, transducing signals through reversible oxidation to sulfenic acid, disulfide, or higher oxides that alter protein activity. This post-translational modification is a core mechanism by which oxidants regulate phosphatases, kinases, and transcription factors. The directionality is oxidant to thiol modification to functional change. A caveat is that excessive or irreversible over-oxidation (sulfinic/sulfonic acid) leads to loss of function and damage rather than signaling.

nodes.label: Protein Tyrosine Phosphatases
nodes.description: Protein tyrosine phosphatases are inactivated by hydrogen peroxide because their catalytic cysteines (e.g., PTP1B Cys-215) are oxidized to sulfenic acid, blocking substrate dephosphorylation. This shifts the phosphorylation balance toward active kinase signaling, notably in insulin and growth-factor pathways. The directionality is H2O2 to reversible PTP inhibition to enhanced phosphorylation. A caveat is that sustained oxidation can progress to irreversible inactivation and that some phosphatases are less redox-sensitive, adding specificity.

nodes.label: Xanthine Oxidase
nodes.description: Xanthine oxidase catalyzes the conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid, using molecular oxygen as the electron acceptor. This enzyme thus sits at the junction of purine catabolism and ROS production. The directionality is purine oxidation to urate plus superoxide generation. A caveat is that the enzyme exists in an NAD+-dependent dehydrogenase form (XDH) that, when converted to the oxidase form (XO), becomes the prominent ROS-producing variant. The reaction also generates superoxide and hydrogen peroxide when oxygen serves as the electron acceptor, coupling urate production to oxidant release.

nodes.label: Allopurinol
nodes.description: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, as allopurinol and its active metabolite oxypurinol competitively bind the molybdenum center and block purine oxidation. Clinically this lowers uric acid and also curbs XO-derived superoxide. The directionality is competitive inhibition to reduced urate and ROS. A caveat is that allopurinol inhibits the dehydrogenase and oxidase forms differently and can cause hypersensitivity in some patients, notably those with HLA-B*58:01. Beyond gout, allopurinol has been studied for cardiovascular protection, chronic kidney disease progression, and prevention of tumor lysis syndrome.

nodes.label: Febuxostat
nodes.description: Febuxostat inhibits xanthine oxidase as a non-purine, selective inhibitor that blocks both the oxidized and reduced forms of the enzyme. Compared with allopurinol it achieves more complete suppression of urate production. The directionality is enzyme inhibition to lower urate and less XO-derived ROS. A caveat is that febuxostat carries cardiovascular black-box warnings in some populations and, like allopurinol, does not address pre-existing urate crystal deposits immediately. Febuxostat is primarily metabolized by the liver, allowing use in some renally impaired patients, although cardiovascular safety warnings limit broad adoption.

nodes.label: ABCA1
nodes.description: ABCA1 regulates cholesterol homeostasis by mediating the efflux of cellular cholesterol and phospholipids to lipid-poor apolipoproteins such as apoA-I. This is the first step in reverse cholesterol transport and HDL biogenesis. The directionality is transporter activity to lipid export. A caveat is that ABCA1 also influences phospholipid trafficking and immune cell function, so its role extends beyond pure cholesterol handling. Loss of ABCA1 function underlies Tangier disease, and its deficiency in macrophages promotes foam-cell formation and accelerated atherosclerosis.

nodes.label: Cholesterol Homeostasis
nodes.description: ABCA1 regulates cholesterol homeostasis by mediating the efflux of cellular cholesterol and phospholipids to lipid-poor apolipoproteins such as apoA-I. This is the first step in reverse cholesterol transport and HDL biogenesis. The directionality is transporter activity to lipid export. A caveat is that ABCA1 also influences phospholipid trafficking and immune cell function, so its role extends beyond pure cholesterol handling. Loss of ABCA1 function underlies Tangier disease, and its deficiency in macrophages promotes foam-cell formation and accelerated atherosclerosis.

nodes.label: LXRα
nodes.description: ABCA1 is regulated by LXRalpha, as the nuclear receptor directly drives ABCA1 transcription in response to oxysterol ligands, coordinating cholesterol efflux. This places ABCA1 downstream of LXR-controlled reverse-cholesterol-transport programs. The directionality is LXRalpha activation to ABCA1 expression. A caveat is that PPARgamma and other transcription factors also regulate ABCA1, so LXRalpha is a major but not exclusive controller. This LXR-ABCA1 axis is also redox-responsive, since oxidative modifications of LDL generate LXR ligands that upregulate the transporter as a protective response.

nodes.label: ABCA1 mutations
nodes.description: ABCA1 mutations cause Tangier disease, a rare disorder in which loss-of-function ABCA1 alleles lead to extremely low HDL and accumulation of cholesteryl esters in macrophages and other tissues. The defect blocks cholesterol efflux, producing enlarged orange tonsils and neuropathy. The directionality is transporter loss to lipid accumulation. A caveat is that incomplete versus complete loss of function yields a spectrum of severity, and modifier genes influence phenotype. Heterozygotes show intermediate HDL reduction, illustrating a gene-dosage effect and the clinical spectrum between Tangier disease and familial HDL deficiency.

nodes.label: Tangier disease
nodes.description: ABCA1 mutations cause Tangier disease, a rare disorder in which loss-of-function ABCA1 alleles lead to extremely low HDL and accumulation of cholesteryl esters in macrophages and other tissues. The defect blocks cholesterol efflux, producing enlarged orange tonsils and neuropathy. The directionality is transporter loss to lipid accumulation. A caveat is that incomplete versus complete loss of function yields a spectrum of severity, and modifier genes influence phenotype. Heterozygotes show intermediate HDL reduction, illustrating a gene-dosage effect and the clinical spectrum between Tangier disease and familial HDL deficiency.

nodes.label: Pro-oxidants
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Oxidative Stress Harms and Benefits for Human Health.md
nodes.description: Flavonoids can act as pro-oxidants at high concentrations because, in the presence of transition metals, they undergo autoxidation that generates semiquinone radicals and subsequently superoxide and H2O2. This biphasic behavior underlies their hormetic profile. The directionality is high-dose flavonoid to radical generation. A caveat is that pro-oxidant effects are favored by metal abundance and high dose, whereas low doses are generally antioxidant. This pro-oxidant behavior is implicated in their anticancer effects, where selective ROS generation can drive apoptosis in malignant cells.

nodes.label: Nitric Oxide bioavailability
nodes.description: Genistein enhances nitric oxide bioavailability by upregulating eNOS expression and scavenging superoxide that would otherwise consume NO. The combined effect improves endothelial NO signaling. The directionality is isoflavone to increased bioavailable NO. A caveat is that genistein can also bind estrogen receptors, so part of its vascular benefit may be receptor-mediated rather than purely redox-based. Clinical studies report improved flow-mediated dilation after soy isoflavone intake, consistent with enhanced NO-dependent vasorelaxation in vivo.

nodes.label: Alpha-1 Antitrypsin
nodes.description: Hypochlorous acid inactivates alpha-1 antitrypsin by oxidizing critical residues, especially methionine, abolishing its ability to inhibit neutrophil elastase. In COPD and similar conditions this unleashes unopposed proteolysis that destroys lung matrix. The directionality is HOCl to serpin inactivation to tissue damage. A caveat is that cigarette smoke and other oxidants also inactivate alpha-1 antitrypsin, so HOCl is one of several mechanisms. The same oxidative inactivation contributes to emphysema in cigarette smokers, where neutrophil-derived HOCl meets a poorly protected lung interstitium.

nodes.label: 3-Chlorotyrosine
nodes.description: Hypochlorous acid chlorinates tyrosine to form 3-chlorotyrosine, a stable adduct that is a specific biomarker of myeloperoxidase activity in vivo. Its presence marks HOCl exposure in inflamed tissues. The directionality is HOCl to chlorinated protein residue. A caveat is that 3-chlorotyrosine reflects historical MPO activity and can be turned over with protein degradation, so it is an integrative rather than instantaneous marker. 3-chlorotyrosine levels rise in atherosclerotic plaques, pneumonia, and other inflammatory conditions, supporting its use as a clinical research biomarker.

nodes.label: L-arginine
nodes.description: L-arginine is a precursor for nitric oxide, as the guanidino nitrogen of arginine is converted to NO and L-citrulline by nitric oxide synthase. This makes arginine availability a determinant of NO production. The directionality is substrate to product in NOS catalysis. A caveat is that arginine availability rarely limits basal eNOS because intracellular arginine is usually sufficient, though competition with arginase can matter. The arginine paradox, in which supplemental arginine raises NO despite saturating intracellular concentrations, points to compartmentalized arginine pools and competition with arginase.

nodes.label: Arginase
nodes.description: Arginase competes with NOS for L-arginine, hydrolyzing arginine to ornithine and urea and thereby lowering substrate available for NO synthesis. In vascular and immune contexts this shifts the arginine pool away from NO toward polyamine and proline synthesis. The directionality is metabolic competition to reduced NO. A caveat is that arginase and NOS also compete for the same intracellular compartment, so local colocalization strongly influences the outcome. Arginase is induced by inflammatory cytokines and oxidants, so vascular arginase upregulation is a recognized mechanism of endothelial dysfunction.

nodes.label: L-arginine:ADMA ratio
nodes.description: The L-arginine to ADMA ratio is a biomarker of cardiovascular risk because it reflects the balance between NOS substrate and the endogenous inhibitor ADMA. A low ratio predicts impaired NO bioavailability and endothelial dysfunction. The directionality is substrate-inhibitor balance to vascular risk. A caveat is that the ratio is one of several endothelial markers and is influenced by renal function and inflammation, which regulate ADMA clearance. The ratio has been proposed as a clinically accessible biomarker for monitoring NO-related vascular health in at-risk populations.

nodes.label: Cardiovascular Risk
nodes.description: The L-arginine to ADMA ratio is a biomarker of cardiovascular risk because it reflects the balance between NOS substrate and the endogenous inhibitor ADMA. A low ratio predicts impaired NO bioavailability and endothelial dysfunction. The directionality is substrate-inhibitor balance to vascular risk. A caveat is that the ratio is one of several endothelial markers and is influenced by renal function and inflammation, which regulate ADMA clearance. The ratio has been proposed as a clinically accessible biomarker for monitoring NO-related vascular health in at-risk populations.

nodes.label: iNOS
nodes.description: iNOS produces high-output NO for innate immune defense, generating micromolar NO in activated macrophages and other innate cells to kill intracellular pathogens. This sustained output is transcriptionally induced by cytokines and microbial products. The directionality is immune activation to bactericidal NO burst. A caveat is that the same high NO combines with superoxide to form peroxynitrite, causing collateral nitrative tissue damage. Because its expression is transcriptionally controlled, iNOS is absent from resting cells but appears within hours of cytokine or pathogen exposure.

nodes.label: Innate Immune Defense
nodes.description: iNOS produces high-output NO for innate immune defense, generating micromolar NO in activated macrophages and other innate cells to kill intracellular pathogens. This sustained output is transcriptionally induced by cytokines and microbial products. The directionality is immune activation to bactericidal NO burst. A caveat is that the same high NO combines with superoxide to form peroxynitrite, causing collateral nitrative tissue damage. Because its expression is transcriptionally controlled, iNOS is absent from resting cells but appears within hours of cytokine or pathogen exposure.

nodes.label: Polyphenols
nodes.description: Polyphenols activate NRF2 by modifying KEAP1 cysteine residues, releasing NRF2 to induce more than 200 cytoprotective and antioxidant genes. This harnesses the cell's own defense program rather than only direct scavenging. The directionality is electrophilic polyphenol to NRF2-dependent transcription. A caveat is that the specific cysteines and magnitude of activation differ among polyphenol structures and depend on metabolism. Examples include resveratrol, curcumin, and EGCG, whose electrophilic moieties and metabolites trigger NRF2 stabilization.

nodes.label: Nucleic Acids
nodes.description: Nucleic acids are prone to damage by reactive oxygen species, particularly hydroxyl radicals, which attack both the sugar-phosphate backbone and nucleobases. Guanine is the most readily oxidized base, yielding 8-oxo-dG and strand lesions. The directionality is ROS to nucleic-acid modification. A caveat is that DNA is partly protected by histones, repair enzymes, and metal sequestration, so damage is non-uniform across the genome. Oxidative lesions accumulate with age and in numerous diseases, and their levels are widely used as biomarkers of oxidative exposure and damage.

nodes.label: Base Excision Repair
nodes.description: Base excision repair is the primary repair pathway for oxidative DNA damage, initiated by lesion-specific DNA glycosylases such as OGG1 that excise oxidized bases and hand the intermediate to downstream nucleases, polymerases, and ligases. This pathway restores genome integrity after ROS exposure. The directionality is lesion recognition to excision and resynthesis. A caveat is that BER can be overwhelmed or error-prone under heavy damage, and backup pathways (MMR, NER) handle subsets of lesions.

nodes.label: Proteins
nodes.description: Proteins are major targets of oxidative stress, sustaining side-chain oxidation, backbone fragmentation, and cross-linking that alter enzyme activity, signaling, and turnover. Because proteins are abundant and long-lived, they integrate oxidative exposure over time. The directionality is oxidant to protein modification. A caveat is that some oxidative modifications are reversible (e.g., methionine sulfoxide) and can serve signaling roles rather than purely damage. Protein oxidation markers such as carbonylation and 3-nitrotyrosine are therefore widely used to estimate the severity of oxidative burden in disease.

nodes.label: Carbonylated proteins
nodes.description: Carbonylated proteins are degraded by the 20S proteasome, which recognizes their unfolded, oxidized structure and degrades them independently of ubiquitin. This removes damaged proteins before they aggregate or lose function. The directionality is oxidized protein to proteasomal clearance. A caveat is that severe oxidation can form cross-links that resist degradation and instead promote aggregates, especially in aging and neurodegeneration. Because 20S degradation is ATP- and ubiquitin-independent, it provides a rapid, energy-sparing route for clearing mildly oxidized proteins.

nodes.label: 20S Proteasome
nodes.description: Carbonylated proteins are degraded by the 20S proteasome, which recognizes their unfolded, oxidized structure and degrades them independently of ubiquitin. This removes damaged proteins before they aggregate or lose function. The directionality is oxidized protein to proteasomal clearance. A caveat is that severe oxidation can form cross-links that resist degradation and instead promote aggregates, especially in aging and neurodegeneration. Because 20S degradation is ATP- and ubiquitin-independent, it provides a rapid, energy-sparing route for clearing mildly oxidized proteins.

nodes.label: Methionine sulfoxide reductases
nodes.description: Methionine sulfoxide reductases repair oxidized methionine by reducing methionine sulfoxide back to methionine using the thioredoxin system. This restores protein function and acts as an antioxidant defense because methionine oxidation can be a benign, reversible sink for oxidants. The directionality is MsrA/MsrB-catalyzed reduction to repaired protein. A caveat is that repeated oxidation and repair of the same residue has a kinetic cost and is not unlimited, so chronic stress still accrues damage.

nodes.label: Oxidized Methionine
nodes.description: Methionine sulfoxide reductases repair oxidized methionine by reducing methionine sulfoxide back to methionine using the thioredoxin system. This restores protein function and acts as an antioxidant defense because methionine oxidation can be a benign, reversible sink for oxidants. The directionality is MsrA/MsrB-catalyzed reduction to repaired protein. A caveat is that repeated oxidation and repair of the same residue has a kinetic cost and is not unlimited, so chronic stress still accrues damage.

nodes.label: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
nodes.description: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is characterized by persistent airway inflammation and poorly reversible airflow limitation driven by neutrophilic and macrophage inflammation. Oxidant-antioxidant imbalance in the lungs fuels this chronic inflammatory state. The directionality is inflammatory airway disease to oxidative burden. A caveat is that COPD heterogeneity means not all patients show the same oxidant signature, and smoking-independent forms exist. This inflammation is sustained by an oxidant-antioxidant imbalance that inactivates antiproteases and perpetuates tissue destruction.

nodes.label: Airway Inflammation
nodes.description: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is characterized by persistent airway inflammation and poorly reversible airflow limitation driven by neutrophilic and macrophage inflammation. Oxidant-antioxidant imbalance in the lungs fuels this chronic inflammatory state. The directionality is inflammatory airway disease to oxidative burden. A caveat is that COPD heterogeneity means not all patients show the same oxidant signature, and smoking-independent forms exist. This inflammation is sustained by an oxidant-antioxidant imbalance that inactivates antiproteases and perpetuates tissue destruction.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial Complex IV
nodes.description: Amyloid-beta impairs mitochondrial Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) after accumulating in mitochondria, depressing respiration and increasing electron leak. This links protein misfolding to bioenergetic failure and ROS. The directionality is Abeta mitochondrial localization to respiratory inhibition. A caveat is that Complex IV inhibition can be both a cause and consequence of oxidative damage in a feed-forward loop. The resulting energetic deficit may precede overt neurodegeneration and contributes to synaptic failure in Alzheimer's disease.

nodes.label: Asthma
nodes.description: Asthma is associated with glutathione depletion, as the GSH/GSSG ratio is markedly decreased in asthmatic airways, weakening local antioxidant defense. This sensitizes the airway to oxidant triggers and allergen-induced inflammation. The directionality is disease to lowered thiol buffer. A caveat is that glutathione changes vary by asthma phenotype and severity, and some patients show different redox patterns. Replenishing airway GSH with N-acetylcysteine has been explored as an adjunctive strategy to restore antioxidant capacity in asthmatic airways.

nodes.label: Glutathione Depletion
nodes.description: Asthma is associated with glutathione depletion, as the GSH/GSSG ratio is markedly decreased in asthmatic airways, weakening local antioxidant defense. This sensitizes the airway to oxidant triggers and allergen-induced inflammation. The directionality is disease to lowered thiol buffer. A caveat is that glutathione changes vary by asthma phenotype and severity, and some patients show different redox patterns. Replenishing airway GSH with N-acetylcysteine has been explored as an adjunctive strategy to restore antioxidant capacity in asthmatic airways.

nodes.label: Asthma severity
nodes.description: Oxidative stress correlates with asthma severity, with greater oxidant burden tracking with worse symptoms and higher exacerbation frequency. Biomarkers of lipid and protein oxidation rise during acute attacks. The directionality is oxidant load to clinical severity. A caveat is that correlation does not establish direction; severe asthma may also generate more ROS via eosinophil and NOX activity. These observations support the use of redox biomarkers in monitoring asthma control and evaluating antioxidant-based therapies.

nodes.label: Eosinophil Peroxidase
nodes.description: Eosinophil peroxidase produces hypobromous acid (HOBr) by using bromide and H2O2 to generate the brominating oxidant in eosinophilic inflammation such as allergic asthma. HOBr is the eosinophil analog of neutrophil HOCl. The directionality is EPO catalysis to HOBr formation. A caveat is that HOBr is less studied than HOCl, and bromination biomarkers are less established, though it is similarly reactive toward proteins. Bromotyrosine adducts are elevated in allergic airway disease and serve as specific markers of eosinophil-mediated oxidant damage.

nodes.label: Hypobromous Acid
nodes.description: Eosinophil peroxidase produces hypobromous acid (HOBr) by using bromide and H2O2 to generate the brominating oxidant in eosinophilic inflammation such as allergic asthma. HOBr is the eosinophil analog of neutrophil HOCl. The directionality is EPO catalysis to HOBr formation. A caveat is that HOBr is less studied than HOCl, and bromination biomarkers are less established, though it is similarly reactive toward proteins. Bromotyrosine adducts are elevated in allergic airway disease and serve as specific markers of eosinophil-mediated oxidant damage.

nodes.label: CD36 Receptor
nodes.description: CD36 receptor mediates uptake of oxidized LDL as the principal scavenger receptor on macrophages, delivering oxLDL-derived lipid to form foam cells. This non-downregulated pathway drives cholesterol accumulation in the artery wall. The directionality is receptor to pathological lipid internalization. A caveat is that CD36 also handles fatty acids and other ligands, and other scavenger receptors (SR-A, LOX-1) contribute to oxLDL uptake. CD36 also recognizes oxidized phospholipids on oxLDL and, in combination with TLR signaling, links lipid uptake to sterile inflammation.

nodes.label: Oxidized LDL
nodes.description: CD36 receptor mediates uptake of oxidized LDL as the principal scavenger receptor on macrophages, delivering oxLDL-derived lipid to form foam cells. This non-downregulated pathway drives cholesterol accumulation in the artery wall. The directionality is receptor to pathological lipid internalization. A caveat is that CD36 also handles fatty acids and other ligands, and other scavenger receptors (SR-A, LOX-1) contribute to oxLDL uptake. CD36 also recognizes oxidized phospholipids on oxLDL and, in combination with TLR signaling, links lipid uptake to sterile inflammation.

nodes.label: Thrombospondin-1
nodes.description: CD36 receptor binds thrombospondin-1, and this interaction activates Fyn kinase and p38 MAPK signaling that influences cell adhesion, survival, and inflammation. Thrombospondin-1 thus acts as a CD36 ligand that shapes macrophage behavior. The directionality is ligand binding to intracellular signaling. A caveat is that thrombospondin-1 has many other receptors (e.g., integrins, CD47), so CD36 is one node in a broader network. This signaling can influence macrophage phagocytosis, angiogenesis, and platelet function, expanding CD36's role beyond lipid uptake.

nodes.label: TLR2/6
nodes.description: CD36 receptor acts as a co-receptor for TLR2/6, enabling recognition of oxidized LDL, amyloid-beta, and microbial products to trigger sterile and innate inflammatory signaling. This bridges lipid sensing to innate immunity. The directionality is co-receptor to inflammasome and NF-kappaB activation. A caveat is that CD36 is not the sole TLR2/6 partner, and its contribution varies by ligand and cell type. This cooperation allows CD36 to bridge lipid sensing and innate immunity, promoting inflammatory responses to oxidized self-ligands.

nodes.label: CD36 expression
nodes.description: CD36 expression is induced by PPARgamma, which transcriptionally upregulates the receptor in macrophages, creating a feed-forward loop that amplifies oxLDL scavenging. ROS can further enhance this PPARgamma-dependent induction. The directionality is nuclear receptor to receptor upregulation. A caveat is that excessive CD36 induction promotes foam-cell formation, so the loop is maladaptive under chronic lipid stress. The PPARgamma-CD36 axis is also central to adipocyte lipid storage and to foam-cell pathology in atherosclerosis.

nodes.label: Oxysterols
nodes.description: Oxysterols regulate LXRalpha as endogenous ligands that activate the nuclear receptor and its target genes controlling cholesterol efflux and transport. This links sterol sensing to reverse cholesterol transport. The directionality is oxysterol to LXRalpha activation. A caveat is that oxysterol structure determines agonist versus antagonist activity at LXR, and some oxysterols also signal through other receptors. LXR activation in turn drives cholesterol efflux and limits inflammation, coupling oxysterol sensing to systemic lipid homeostasis.

nodes.label: 7-Ketocholesterol
nodes.description: 7-ketocholesterol induces apoptosis through ROS-dependent mitochondrial permeabilization and activation of caspase-3, contributing to death of macrophage foam cells in plaques. As a major oxysterol in oxidized LDL, it is implicated in plaque necrosis. The directionality is oxysterol to programmed cell death. A caveat is that 7-ketocholesterol effects are concentration-dependent and can also trigger inflammatory and autophagic responses before death. Plasma and lesion 7-KC levels correlate with plaque vulnerability, and its toxicity to vascular cells is a recognized contributor to plaque necrosis.

nodes.label: PON1
nodes.description: PON1 hydrolyzes oxidized phospholipids on HDL, preventing their transfer to LDL and thereby protecting against lipoprotein oxidation. This paraoxonase activity is a key anti-atherogenic function of HDL. The directionality is enzyme to lipid-peroxide detoxification. A caveat is that PON1 activity is highly polymorphic in humans and is also reduced by oxidative stress, creating a variable defensive capacity. PON1 also hydrolyzes lactones and specific organophosphates, and its activity is used as an index of HDL antioxidant capacity.

nodes.label: Oxidized Phospholipids
nodes.description: PON1 hydrolyzes oxidized phospholipids on HDL, preventing their transfer to LDL and thereby protecting against lipoprotein oxidation. nodes.label: NLRP3 inflammasome assembly
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Oxidative Stress Harms and Benefits for Human Health.md
nodes.description: ROS trigger NLRP3 inflammasome assembly by promoting the conformational changes and ASC speck formation needed for caspase-1 activation. Mitochondrial ROS and oxidized mitochondrial DNA are particularly implicated as upstream signals. The directionality is oxidant to inflammasome activation. A caveat is that NLRP3 is also activated by non-ROS stimuli (ATP, nigericin, crystals), so ROS is a common but not exclusive trigger. ROS derived from both NOX enzymes and mitochondria converge on NLRP3, linking metabolic and inflammatory stress to IL-1beta production.

nodes.label: TXNIP
nodes.description: TXNIP binds NLRP3 after dissociating from thioredoxin when the latter is oxidized by ROS, providing a direct molecular link between the redox state and inflammasome activation. This positions thioredoxin oxidation as the sensor. The directionality is oxidized thioredoxin to TXNIP-NLRP3 engagement. A caveat is that additional adaptors and post-translational steps are required for full caspase-1 activation. This mechanism connects metabolic stress, particularly hyperglycemia, to inflammasome activation in pancreatic beta-cells and other tissues.

nodes.label: IL-1beta
nodes.description: IL-1beta activates NF-kappaB via MyD88-dependent signaling upon binding its receptor IL-1R1, amplifying expression of inflammatory genes. This places IL-1beta upstream of a central inflammatory transcription factor. The directionality is cytokine to NF-kappaB activation. A caveat is that IL-1beta itself is an NF-kappaB target, so the loop is reinforcing rather than linear, and IL-1ra can dampen it. The resulting amplification loop is a target of anti-inflammatory biologics and explains the broad effects of IL-1 blockade in chronic disease.

nodes.label: IL-1beta inhibition (Canakinumab)
nodes.description: IL-1beta inhibition with canakinumab reduces cardiovascular events, as the CANTOS trial showed fewer recurrent myocardial infarction, stroke, and cardiovascular death independent of lipid lowering. This validated inflammation (not just LDL) as a treatment target. The directionality is IL-1beta blockade to lower CVD events. A caveat is that the trial also showed increased infection risk and that not all patients benefited, indicating a selected responder population. The results of CANTOS established the inflammatory hypothesis of atherosclerosis and opened the door to targeted immunomodulation for CVD.

nodes.label: Ionizing Radiation
nodes.description: Ionizing radiation produces hydroxyl radicals through radiolysis of water, generating OH*, hydrated electrons, and hydrogen atoms within picoseconds of energy deposition. These radicals initiate the bulk of radiation-induced biomolecular damage. The directionality is photon/particle energy to water radiolysis to radicals. A caveat is that direct ionization of DNA also occurs, so radicals are the major but not sole mechanism of radiation injury. Because water constitutes most of cellular mass, radiolysis-generated hydroxyl radicals account for roughly two-thirds of radiation-induced DNA damage.

nodes.label: Clustered DNA Damage
nodes.description: Ionizing radiation causes clustered DNA damage, defined as two or more lesions within one or two helical turns, a signature pattern that overwhelms repair and drives lethal or mutagenic breaks. This clustering distinguishes radiation from many chemical genotoxins. The directionality is radiation to locally concentrated lesions. A caveat is that clustering severity depends on radiation quality (LET) and oxygen enhancement, so not all exposures produce identical patterns. Clustered lesions are a hallmark of high-LET radiation and are repaired inefficiently, increasing the probability of mutation and cell death.

nodes.label: ATM Kinase
nodes.description: Ionizing radiation activates ATM kinase by causing DNA double-strand breaks that recruit and autophosphorylate ATM, which then phosphorylates Chk2, p53, and BRCA1 to coordinate the damage response. This initiates cell-cycle arrest and repair. The directionality is DNA break to kinase signaling cascade. A caveat is that ATM also responds to oxidative stress and replication stress, so its activation is not uniquely radiation-driven. ATM is considered the master coordinator of the DNA-damage response to double-strand breaks, integrating cell-cycle arrest, repair, and apoptosis decisions.

nodes.label: Amifostine
nodes.description: Amifostine scavenges hydroxyl radicals as a prodrug that is dephosphorylated to the active thiol WR-1065, which protects normal tissues during radiotherapy. By quenching OH* it spares DNA and proteins from radiation-induced damage. The directionality is radioprotectant to radical neutralization. A caveat is that amifostine preferentially protects some normal tissues over tumors, but it carries side effects (hypotension, nausea) that limit use. Selective uptake by normal tissues gives amifostine its cytoprotective profile during radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

nodes.label: Polyunsaturated fatty acids
nodes.description: Polyunsaturated fatty acids are susceptible to oxidative stress because their bis-allylic methylene groups have relatively weak C-H bonds that are easily abstracted by radicals, seeding lipid peroxidation. The more double bonds, the higher the peroxidation index. The directionality is PUFA structure to peroxidation propensity. A caveat is that some PUFAs (e.g., omega-3) are beneficial despite higher oxidizability, as their oxidation products can be anti-inflammatory, so susceptibility is not uniformly harmful.

nodes.label: F2-Isoprostanes
nodes.description: F2-isoprostanes are the gold-standard biomarker for oxidative stress, formed non-enzymatically by free-radical peroxidation of arachidonic acid into prostaglandin-like compounds. They are measured in urine and plasma and are remarkably stable. The directionality is lipid peroxidation to isoprostane formation. A caveat is that isoprostanes can also arise from cyclooxygenase-independent enzymatic routes in rare cases, and levels are influenced by diet and renal function. Their measurement has become the reference standard for evaluating antioxidant efficacy in human intervention trials.

nodes.label: Reverse Cholesterol Transport
nodes.description: LXRalpha promotes reverse cholesterol transport by upregulating ABCA1, ABCG1, ABCG5/ABCG8, and ApoE, which together mobilize cholesterol from peripheral cells to HDL and the liver. This is a central anti-atherogenic function. The directionality is receptor activation to cholesterol efflux. A caveat is that LXRalpha also induces lipogenic genes (SREBP-1c, FASN), so full activation can raise triglycerides, limiting therapeutic use. Pharmacological LXR activation replicates this program but is limited by concomitant lipogenesis, motivating development of isoform-selective and partial agonists.

nodes.label: Inflammatory Gene Expression
nodes.description: LXRalpha suppresses inflammatory gene expression, as SUMOylated LXRalpha recruits corepressors such as NCoR to NF-kappaB target promoters, dampening cytokine responses. This links cholesterol sensing to immune moderation. The directionality is LXRalpha to transcriptional repression of inflammation. A caveat is that the anti-inflammatory effect is gene- and context-specific and can be overshadowed by pro-lipogenic actions at high activation. This transrepression is SUMO-dependent and independent of DNA binding, distinguishing it from classic LXR agonist responses.

nodes.label: SREBP-1c
nodes.description: LXRalpha induces SREBP-1c and its lipogenic targets (FASN, SCD1, ACC), increasing fatty-acid synthesis when activated. This reflects the receptor's role in coordinating lipid metabolism. The directionality is LXRalpha to lipogenesis program. A caveat is that this same induction causes hepatic steatosis with synthetic LXR agonists, so the metabolic consequence is a double-edged sword. Because SREBP-1c induction underlies the hypertriglyceridemia and hepatic steatosis seen with synthetic LXR agonists, it represents a key liability in LXR-targeted drug development.

nodes.label: Complex I and Complex IV
nodes.description: Complex I and Complex IV have reduced activity in multiple sclerosis, and the resulting electron leakage increases superoxide generation in affected CNS tissue. This bioenergetic defect is observed in lesions and normal-appearing white matter. The directionality is enzyme deficiency to increased mitochondrial ROS. A caveat is that reduced activity may be secondary to inflammation and demyelination as well as a primary driver, so causality is bidirectional. These defects are most pronounced in chronically demyelinated tissue and correlate with axonal loss and disability progression.

nodes.label: Multiple Sclerosis
nodes.description: Complex I and Complex IV have reduced activity in multiple sclerosis, and the resulting electron leakage increases superoxide generation in affected CNS tissue. This bioenergetic defect is observed in lesions and normal-appearing white matter. The directionality is enzyme deficiency to increased mitochondrial ROS. A caveat is that reduced activity may be secondary to inflammation and demyelination as well as a primary driver, so causality is bidirectional. These defects are most pronounced in chronically demyelinated tissue and correlate with axonal loss and disability progression.

nodes.label: Dimethyl fumarate (Tecfidera)
nodes.description: Dimethyl fumarate (Tecfidera) activates the NRF2 pathway in MS therapy by modifying KEAP1 cysteines, inducing HO-1, NQO1, and GPx to bolster antioxidant defense in glia and neurons. This is a registered disease-modifying treatment for relapsing MS. The directionality is fumarate to NRF2-dependent cytoprotection. A caveat is that dimethyl fumarate also shifts lymphocyte subsets and can cause flushing and GI effects, so NRF2 activation is one of several mechanisms. Clinical trials show reduced relapses and disability progression, though the precise contribution of NRF2 versus other fumarate actions remains debated.

nodes.label: NRF2 pathway in MS therapy
nodes.description: Dimethyl fumarate (Tecfidera) activates the NRF2 pathway in MS therapy by modifying KEAP1 cysteines, inducing HO-1, NQO1, and GPx to bolster antioxidant defense in glia and neurons. This is a registered disease-modifying treatment for relapsing MS. The directionality is fumarate to NRF2-dependent cytoprotection. A caveat is that dimethyl fumarate also shifts lymphocyte subsets and can cause flushing and GI effects, so NRF2 activation is one of several mechanisms. Clinical trials show reduced relapses and disability progression, though the precise contribution of NRF2 versus other fumarate actions remains debated.

nodes.label: Oligodendrocytes
nodes.description: Oligodendrocytes are vulnerable to oxidative stress because they contain high iron, relatively low glutathione, and high ATP demand to support myelination, making them sensitive to ROS. Their damage contributes to demyelination in MS and other disorders. The directionality is oxidant burden to oligodendrocyte injury. A caveat is that oxidative vulnerability interacts with metabolic, inflammatory, and energetic stresses, so it is a contributor rather than the sole determinant of oligodendrocyte loss.

nodes.label: Hypoxia-reoxygenation
nodes.description: Hypoxia-reoxygenation produces a ROS burst in rheumatoid arthritis synovium analogous to ischemia-reperfusion, as restored oxygen fuels mitochondrial and enzymatic ROS after hypoxic epochs. This oxidant surge perpetuates synovial inflammation and joint damage. The directionality is reoxygenation to ROS burst in joint tissue. A caveat is that RA synovium is also hypoxic because of high metabolic and infiltrating-cell demand, so the cycle is sustained rather than episodic. This mechanism may explain the vulnerability of the inflamed joint to intermittent blood flow and oxidative injury.

nodes.label: ROS burst in RA synovium
nodes.description: Hypoxia-reoxygenation produces a ROS burst in rheumatoid arthritis synovium analogous to ischemia-reperfusion, as restored oxygen fuels mitochondrial and enzymatic ROS after hypoxic epochs. This oxidant surge perpetuates synovial inflammation and joint damage. The directionality is reoxygenation to ROS burst in joint tissue. A caveat is that RA synovium is also hypoxic because of high metabolic and infiltrating-cell demand, so the cycle is sustained rather than episodic. This mechanism may explain the vulnerability of the inflamed joint to intermittent blood flow and oxidative injury.

nodes.label: Protein Citrullination
nodes.description: Oxidative stress promotes protein citrullination by increasing intracellular calcium, which activates peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD) enzymes that convert arginine to citrulline. Citrullinated proteins become autoantigens in rheumatoid arthritis. The directionality is oxidant to calcium influx to PAD activation. A caveat is that PAD enzymes are also regulated by other factors (pH, NO), so ROS is a contributor rather than the only trigger of citrullination. Citrullinated peptides are recognized by anti-citrullinated protein antibodies, a hallmark of rheumatoid arthritis, linking oxidative stress to autoimmunity.

nodes.label: Anti-TNF therapy
nodes.description: Anti-TNF therapy reduces oxidative stress markers by breaking the TNF-alpha to ROS feed-forward loop, lowering serum MDA and raising glutathione in treated patients. This reflects successful suppression of inflammasome and NOX-driven oxidants. The directionality is TNF blockade to lowered oxidant burden. A caveat is that the magnitude of biomarker change varies among patients and that anti-TNF also has immunosuppressive trade-offs. These biomarker improvements parallel clinical response and support the idea that TNF blockade restores redox balance in chronic inflammation.

nodes.label: Oxidative Stress Markers
nodes.description: Anti-TNF therapy reduces oxidative stress markers by breaking the TNF-alpha to ROS feed-forward loop, lowering serum MDA and raising glutathione in treated patients. This reflects successful suppression of inflammasome and NOX-driven oxidants. The directionality is TNF blockade to lowered oxidant burden. A caveat is that the magnitude of biomarker change varies among patients and that anti-TNF also has immunosuppressive trade-offs. These biomarker improvements parallel clinical response and support the idea that TNF blockade restores redox balance in chronic inflammation.

nodes.label: GSK-3beta
nodes.description: Oxidative stress activates GSK-3beta among other kinases, and the resulting hyperphosphorylation of tau promotes its dissociation from microtubules and aggregation. GSK-3beta is normally restrained by Akt but is released under oxidative and inflammatory conditions. The directionality is oxidant to kinase activation to tau modification. A caveat is that GSK-3beta has many substrates beyond tau, and its activity is regulated by phosphorylation independent of ROS. Because GSK-3beta is a central node in tau pathology, redox-driven kinase activation is considered an early event in Alzheimer's disease progression.

nodes.label: Tau oligomerization
nodes.description: 4-hydroxynonenal promotes tau oligomerization by forming covalent Michael adducts with tau cysteine and lysine residues, altering its conformation and seeding oligomers. As a major lipid-peroxidation aldehyde, 4-HNE thus couples membrane oxidation to protein misfolding. The directionality is aldehyde adduct to tau aggregation propensity. A caveat is that 4-HNE at low levels can also induce adaptive responses, and other aldehydes (MDA, acrolein) modify tau similarly. Elevated 4-HNE and tau adducts colocalize in Alzheimer's disease brain, linking lipid peroxidation to neurofibrillary pathology.

nodes.label: Tau protein
nodes.description: Peroxynitrite nitrates tau protein at tyrosine residues, impairing tau-microtubule interaction and enhancing formation of paired helical filaments. Nitration adds to the spectrum of oxidative modifications that destabilize tau. The directionality is nitrative modification to tau dysfunction. A caveat is that tau is targeted by many oxidative and kinase modifications, so nitration is one of several converging insults. Elevated nitrotyrosine is detected on tau in neurofibrillary tangles, supporting nitration as a contributor to tau pathology in vivo.

nodes.label: Tau acetylation
nodes.description: SIRT1 removes tau acetylation as a deacetylase that normally limits tau aggregation, but SIRT1 activity falls under oxidative conditions, permitting acetylated, aggregation-prone tau to accumulate. This links redox state to tau post-translational control. The directionality is SIRT1 deacetylation to reduced tau aggregation. A caveat is that SIRT1 also deacetylates many other substrates, and its net effect on tau depends on cellular NAD+ availability. The NAD+-dependence of SIRT1 ties tau acetylation to cellular energetics and explains interest in NAD+-boosting strategies for tauopathies.

nodes.label: TGF-beta
nodes.description: TGF-beta induces NOX4 expression, increasing a steady source of H2O2 that acts as a second messenger for TGF-beta's pro-fibrotic program. This couples the cytokine to redox signaling in fibroblasts and epithelium. The directionality is TGF-beta to NOX4 upregulation to H2O2. A caveat is that TGF-beta also signals through Smad and MAPK pathways, so NOX4-derived H2O2 is a contributor, not the sole mediator. NOX4-derived H2O2 is required for TGF-beta-induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition and contributes to fibrosis in kidney, lung, and heart.

nodes.label: Nox4-derived H2O2
nodes.description: Nox4-derived H2O2 is required for TGF-beta-induced EMT, as Nox4 knockout blocks mesenchymal marker expression and cell migration during epithelial-mesenchymal transition. The oxidant thus serves as a necessary signal rather than mere byproduct. The directionality is Nox4 H2O2 to EMT execution. A caveat is that complete EMT also needs Smad and transcription-factor reprogramming, so H2O2 is necessary but not sufficient alone. Nox4 inhibitors are being evaluated as anti-fibrotic agents, underscoring the therapeutic relevance of this redox pathway.

nodes.label: TGF-beta-induced EMT
nodes.description: Nox4-derived H2O2 is required for TGF-beta-induced EMT, as Nox4 knockout blocks mesenchymal marker expression and cell migration during epithelial-mesenchymal transition. The oxidant thus serves as a necessary signal rather than mere byproduct. The directionality is Nox4 H2O2 to EMT execution. A caveat is that complete EMT also needs Smad and transcription-factor reprogramming, so H2O2 is necessary but not sufficient alone. Nox4 inhibitors are being evaluated as anti-fibrotic agents, underscoring the therapeutic relevance of this redox pathway.

nodes.label: PGC-1alpha
nodes.description: TGF-beta suppresses PGC-1alpha, shifting the redox balance toward a pro-oxidant state by lowering mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant gene expression. This reinforces TGF-beta-driven fibrotic and senescence phenotypes. The directionality is TGF-beta to reduced PGC-1alpha to oxidative tilt. A caveat is that the suppression is context-specific and can be opposed by exercise and other PGC-1alpha inducers. Restoring PGC-1alpha, for example through exercise or pharmacological activation, may counteract TGF-beta-driven oxidative and fibrotic stress.

nodes.label: SMAD7 downregulation in TGF-beta signaling
nodes.description: Mitochondrial ROS are required for SMAD7 downregulation in TGF-beta signaling, as mtROS promote removal of this negative feedback inhibitor, permitting full Smad2/3 activation. This embeds mitochondria within the TGF-beta pathway. The directionality is mtROS to loss of SMAD7 restraint. A caveat is that SMAD7 is also regulated by ubiquitination and other mechanisms, so ROS modulates rather than exclusively controls it. This places mitochondria as regulators of TGF-beta signaling strength and explains why mitochondrial antioxidants blunt fibrosis in some models.

nodes.label: TNFR1 signaling
nodes.description: TNFR1 signaling generates mitochondrial ROS when TRAF2 recruits TRIM21, causing electron leak at Complex I and raising mtROS. These ROS then propagate the TNFR1 pro-inflammatory and pro-death program. The directionality is receptor signaling to mitochondrial oxidant production. A caveat is that TNFR1 also engages cytosolic NOX and other ROS sources, so mitochondria are one node in the oxidative response. This mitochondrial ROS signal contributes to necroptosis and inflammatory gene induction downstream of TNF-alpha, and can be suppressed by mitochondrial-targeted antioxidants.

nodes.label: JNK Activation
nodes.description: Mitochondrial ROS are required for JNK activation downstream of TNFR1, representing an obligatory event in sustained JNK signaling that drives apoptosis and inflammation. The oxidants act as upstream amplifiers of the kinase cascade. The directionality is mtROS to JNK activation. A caveat is that JNK can also be activated by non-mitochondrial ROS and by MAPKKK upstream of mitochondria, so the requirement is context-dependent. Persistent JNK activation downstream of mitochondrial ROS promotes apoptosis and is implicated in stress-induced tissue injury.

nodes.label: Antioxidant Gene Program
nodes.description: NF-kappaB upregulates an antioxidant gene program as a negative feedback that limits TNF-alpha-induced tissue damage, inducing enzymes such as MnSOD, ferritin, and heme oxygenase. This self-limiting loop tempers the oxidative consequences of inflammatory signaling. The directionality is NF-kappaB to adaptive antioxidant transcription. A caveat is that the same factor also drives pro-oxidant enzymes (NOX, iNOS), so the net redox outcome depends on stimulus and cell type. This protective arm tempers the tissue damage caused by TNF and other inflammatory mediators.

nodes.label: TNF-alpha with blocked NF-kappaB
nodes.description: TNF-alpha with blocked NF-kappaB shifts signaling to necroptosis, as loss of NF-kappaB-dependent survival genes leaves RIPK1 free to engage RIPK3 and MLKL in lytic, pro-inflammatory cell death. This explains toxicity when NF-kappaB is inhibited in TNF-exposed cells. The directionality is NF-kappaB blockade to necroptotic switch. A caveat is that caspase-8 can still divert cells to apoptosis, so the outcome depends on the full death-receptor complex composition. Necroptosis is highly inflammatory because lysed cells release damage-associated molecular patterns, amplifying tissue injury.

nodes.label: Necroptosis
nodes.description: TNF-alpha with blocked NF-kappaB shifts signaling to necroptosis, as loss of NF-kappaB-dependent survival genes leaves RIPK1 free to engage RIPK3 and MLKL in lytic, pro-inflammatory cell death. This explains toxicity when NF-kappaB is inhibited in TNF-exposed cells. The directionality is NF-kappaB blockade to necroptotic switch. A caveat is that caspase-8 can still divert cells to apoptosis, so the outcome depends on the full death-receptor complex composition. Necroptosis is highly inflammatory because lysed cells release damage-associated molecular patterns, amplifying tissue injury.

nodes.label: NF-kappaB enhancing VCAM-1 transcription
nodes.description: Oxidative stress activates NF-kappaB enhancing VCAM-1 transcription, as ROS activate the transcription factor to bind kappaB response elements in the VCAM-1 promoter. Elevated VCAM-1 then promotes leukocyte adhesion to endothelium. The directionality is oxidant to NF-kappaB to adhesion-molecule expression. A caveat is that many cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta) also induce VCAM-1, so ROS is one of several upstream activators. VCAM-1 upregulation is a key early step in atherogenesis, and its redox-sensitive induction links oxidative stress to leukocyte infiltration.

nodes.label: VCAM-1
nodes.description: VCAM-1 binds VLA-4 (alpha4beta1 integrin) on leukocytes, mediating firm adhesion and transendothelial migration during inflammation.
