This interaction is central to leukocyte trafficking into tissue. The directionality is endothelial ligand to leukocyte engagement. A caveat is that VCAM-1 also binds alpha4beta7 and other integrins, and competing ligands (e.g., fibronectin) modulate the interaction. This adhesion pathway is a validated drug target, with natalizumab blocking VLA-4 to reduce CNS inflammation in multiple sclerosis.

nodes.label: VLA-4 (alpha4beta1 integrin) on leukocytes
nodes.description: VCAM-1 binds VLA-4 (alpha4beta1 integrin) on leukocytes, mediating firm adhesion and transendothelial migration during inflammation. This interaction is central to leukocyte trafficking into tissue. The directionality is endothelial ligand to leukocyte engagement. A caveat is that VCAM-1 also binds alpha4beta7 and other integrins, and competing ligands (e.g., fibronectin) modulate the interaction. This adhesion pathway is a validated drug target, with natalizumab blocking VLA-4 to reduce CNS inflammation in multiple sclerosis.

nodes.label: Soluble VCAM-1
nodes.description: Soluble VCAM-1 is a biomarker for endothelial dysfunction, being elevated in cardiovascular disease, diabetes, hypertension, and rheumatoid arthritis as a shed fragment of the adhesion molecule. Its level reflects chronic endothelial activation. The directionality is endothelial activation to soluble marker release. A caveat is that soluble VCAM-1 lacks the membrane anchor and its biological activity differs from full-length VCAM-1, so it is an index rather than a direct effector. Serum sVCAM-1 is now used in risk stratification and to monitor endothelial health in research cohorts.

nodes.label: Natalizumab (Tysabri)
nodes.description: Natalizumab (Tysabri) blocks the VCAM-1/VLA-4 interaction by antagonizing alpha4 integrin, reducing T-cell trafficking across the blood-brain barrier in multiple sclerosis. This dampens CNS inflammation but leaves patients susceptible to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. The directionality is integrin blockade to reduced leukocyte entry. A caveat is that broad alpha4 inhibition also affects gut homing, causing PML and other risks that limit use. The drug's efficacy in MS validates the VCAM-1/VLA-4 pathway as a driver of neuroinflammation, though its safety profile demands careful monitoring.

nodes.label: VCAM-1/VLA-4 Interaction
nodes.description: Natalizumab (Tysabri) blocks the VCAM-1/VLA-4 interaction by antagonizing alpha4 integrin, reducing T-cell trafficking across the blood-brain barrier in multiple sclerosis. This dampens CNS inflammation but leaves patients susceptible to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. The directionality is integrin blockade to reduced leukocyte entry. A caveat is that broad alpha4 inhibition also affects gut homing, causing PML and other risks that limit use. The drug's efficacy in MS validates the VCAM-1/VLA-4 pathway as a driver of neuroinflammation, though its safety profile demands careful monitoring.

nodes.label: Ferritin
nodes.description: Ferritin sequesters free iron by storing up to roughly 4,500 Fe3+ atoms per molecule in a mineral core, keeping redox-active iron away from peroxide and the Fenton reaction. This buffering is a front-line antioxidant defense. The directionality is iron chelation to suppressed radical formation. A caveat is that ferritin can be released or degraded during inflammation and hemorrhage, liberating iron that then becomes pro-oxidant. Iron released from ferritin by ferritinophagy or by reduction is what fuels ferroptosis, so ferritin level is a determinant of ferroptosis sensitivity.

nodes.label: Free Iron
nodes.description: Ferritin sequesters free iron by storing up to roughly 4,500 Fe3+ atoms per molecule in a mineral core, keeping redox-active iron away from peroxide and the Fenton reaction. This buffering is a front-line antioxidant defense. The directionality is iron chelation to suppressed radical formation. A caveat is that ferritin can be released or degraded during inflammation and hemorrhage, liberating iron that then becomes pro-oxidant. Iron released from ferritin by ferritinophagy or by reduction is what fuels ferroptosis, so ferritin level is a determinant of ferroptosis sensitivity.

nodes.label: Iron accumulation in Substantia Nigra
nodes.description: Iron accumulation in the substantia nigra promotes the Fenton reaction because elevated redox-active iron there catalyzes conversion of H2O2 to hydroxyl radicals near dopaminergic neurons. The iron burden correlates with oxidative damage markers in Parkinson's disease. The directionality is iron accumulation to radical generation. A caveat is that iron accumulation may also be a downstream consequence of oxidative damage and impaired iron export, so the relationship is partly bidirectional. Iron chelation and restoration of ferritin expression are therefore investigated as strategies to protect dopaminergic neurons.

nodes.label: Redox Imbalance
nodes.description: Oxidative stress is a redox imbalance in which reactive oxygen (and nitrogen) species production exceeds the capacity to detoxify them or repair the resulting damage. This definition frames oxidative stress as a dynamic disequilibrium rather than a single molecule. The directionality is imbalance between oxidants and defenses. A caveat is that transient oxidative shifts are physiological signaling events, so 'stress' specifically denotes sustained or excessive imbalance. This framing emphasizes that redox biology is bidirectional and that the severity of stress is determined by the balance of generation, defense, and repair.

nodes.label: Antioxidant Response
nodes.description: NRF2 is the master regulator of the antioxidant response, inducing more than 200 cytoprotective genes including those for glutathione synthesis, thioredoxin, heme oxygenase, and drug detoxification. It integrates signals from KEAP1, redox status, and electrophiles. The directionality is NRF2 activation to coordinated defense transcription. A caveat is that excessive or chronic NRF2 activation can support tumor cell survival, so its regulation is finely balanced. The NRF2-KEAP1 system is druggable, and activators such as dimethyl fumarate and sulforaphane are used or investigated in inflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases.

nodes.label: Low-level oxidative stress
nodes.description: Low-level oxidative stress activates mitohormesis, a beneficial adaptive response in which transient ROS upregulate DNA repair, antioxidant defenses, and autophagy to improve resilience. This explains the paradoxical benefits of mild mitochondrial stress. The directionality is mild oxidant to adaptive reprogramming. A caveat is that the benefit is strictly dose-dependent; higher oxidative stress overwhelms the response and becomes damaging, the classic hormetic inverted-U. Exercise, caloric restriction, and some phytochemicals harness mitohormesis to improve metabolic and neurological health.

nodes.label: Telomere Attrition
nodes.description: Progressive telomere shortening with each cell division eventually exposes chromosome ends that are recognized as DNA double-strand breaks, triggering replicative senescence at the Hayflick limit. Critically short or dysfunctional telomeres activate the ATM/p53 and ATR/p21 DDR cascades, halting proliferation to prevent chromosomal instability. This mechanism is the canonical explanation for the finite replicative capacity of primary human cells in culture. The directionality is one-way in normal cells, though telomerase reactivation can bypass the arrest -- a hallmark of cancer.

nodes.label: Oncogene Activation
nodes.description: Activated oncogenes such as RAS, BRAF, and MYC drive hyperproliferation and replication stress, which in turn elicit oncogene-induced senescence (OIS) as an intrinsic tumor-suppressive failsafe. The unscheduled S-phase entry generates DNA replication stress and DNA damage that stabilize p53 and derepress the CDKN2A/p16INK4a locus, locking cells in arrest. OIS is observed in benign lesions such as melanocytic nevi and is a major barrier to tumor progression. The paradox is that OIS cells secrete a SASP that, while recruiting immune clearance, can also promote tumorigenesis in neighboring cells.

nodes.label: p53/p21 Pathway
nodes.description: The p53/p21 axis is a primary enforcement mechanism of senescence, especially in damage- and stress-induced forms. DNA damage stabilizes p53, which transcriptionally induces the CDK inhibitor p21CIP1; p21 inhibits cyclin E/A-CDK2, preventing phosphorylation of Rb and blocking S-phase entry. This pathway provides a rapid, p53-dose-dependent G1/S arrest that can be engaged acutely after genotoxic insult. A caveat is that the p53 pathway is frequently disabled in cancer, and p53 also restrains the SASP, so its loss reshapes rather than simply abolishes senescence.

nodes.label: p16/Rb Pathway
nodes.description: The p16INK4a/Rb pathway enforces the long-term, irreversible phase of senescence independently of p53. p16 inhibits CDK4 and CDK6, keeping Rb hypophosphorylated and bound to E2F, thereby preventing expression of S-phase genes; this locks in a durable growth arrest. Unlike the p53/p21 arm, which can be transient, p16/Rb-mediated arrest is typically sustained for the life of the cell and is the stronger correlate of in vivo senescent burden with age. Its engagement is a key determinant of why senescence is considered irreversible rather than a quiescent state.

nodes.label: E2F
nodes.description: Both the p53/p21 and p16/Rb axes converge on suppression of the E2F family of transcription factors, which are master regulators of genes required for DNA synthesis and S-phase progression. Hypophosphorylated Rb binds E2F and, together with SAHF-mediated heterochromatinization, represses E2F target loci; p21 additionally blocks CDK-mediated release of this repression. Inhibition of E2F is therefore the final common effector of the senescent growth arrest. This directed, downstream suppression is a defining mechanistic feature shared across senescent cell types.

nodes.label: Lamin B1
nodes.description: Senescent cells characteristically show reduced expression of lamin B1 (encoded by LMNB1), a structural component of the nuclear lamina. Lamin B1 loss detaches lamina-associated domains (LADs) from the nuclear periphery, spatially reorganizing chromatin and contributing to the altered gene expression and genomic instability of senescence. This marker is relatively conserved across cell types and tissues, making it a practical histological and molecular signature of senescent cells in vivo. A caveat is that lamin B1 loss can also occur in certain differentiation and disease states, so it is best used in combination with other markers.

nodes.label: Senolytics
nodes.description: Senescence is a direct therapeutic target of senolytics, agents that selectively eliminate senescent cells. Genetic or pharmacological clearance of p16-positive senescent cells in murine models delays age-related dysfunction, extends healthspan, and alleviates multiple pathologies. The strategy exploits the pro-survival SCAP network that senescent cells depend on, pushing them into apoptosis while sparing healthy cells. Clinical translation is ongoing, with the key caveat that intermittent, tissue-specific clearance is preferable to chronic ablation, which could impair beneficial acute-senescence functions.

nodes.label: Senomorphics
nodes.description: Senescence is modulated by senomorphics, compounds that suppress the deleterious SASP without killing the senescent cell itself. By targeting upstream SASP regulators (mTOR, NF-κB, JAK-STAT3, p38 MAPK, BRD4), senomorphics dampen the paracrine and inflammatory consequences of senescence. This is conceptually complementary to senolytics, which remove the cell rather than its output. Senomorphics preserve potentially beneficial acute-senescence functions (e.g., wound healing, tumor suppression) while mitigating chronic harm.

nodes.label: Secretory Phenotype
nodes.description: The SASP is a hypersecretory state -- a specialized secretory phenotype -- in which senescent cells upregulate and release hundreds of factors including interleukins, chemokines, growth factors, proteases, and extracellular vesicles. This secreted output contrasts with the quiescent, low-turnover secretome of non-senescent cells and is a defining non-cell-autonomous feature of the senescent state. The composition of the SASP is variable, shaped by the senescence inducer, cell type, and tissue context. Its classification as a secretory phenotype emphasizes that senescence exerts its effects largely through communication with the microenvironment.

nodes.label: JAK-STAT3
nodes.description: The JAK-STAT3 signaling axis promotes a pro-inflammatory SASP by interacting with p38 MAPK and mTOR and by transducing cues from SASP cytokines such as IL-6. STAT3 activation contributes to age-related frailty and to the immune-modulatory and tumor-promoting facets of the secretome. JAK1/2 inhibitors (e.g., ruxolitinib) reduce SASP cytokines IL-6 and IL-8, validating the axis as a senomorphic target. The pathway is especially important for the feed-forward, self-reinforcing inflammation characteristic of chronic senescence.

nodes.label: Nutlin 3a
nodes.description: Nutlin 3a suppresses the pro-inflammatory SASP by inhibiting MDM2, the E3 ligase that marks p53 for degradation, thereby stabilizing the tumor suppressor; stabilized p53 in turn restrains NF-kB-driven expression of SASP cytokines and chemokines. This mechanism exploits the natural tumor-suppressive rheostat of p53 rather than broadly blocking inflammation, and it is consistent with the observation that loss of p53 dramatically amplifies secretome output. The compound is primarily a research tool with limited clinical development, which constrains its translational confidence, but mechanistically its SASP-suppressive action is well grounded in p53's restraint of the inflammatory secretome.

nodes.label: Paracrine Senescence
nodes.description: SASP factors such as IL-1α, TGFβ, VEGF, and CCL2 can act in an autocrine and paracrine manner to reinforce the senescent state and induce growth arrest in neighboring healthy cells -- a process termed paracrine (or bystander) senescence. This spreads the arrested phenotype through tissues, amplifying the functional impact of a small senescent fraction. The directionality is outward: the secretome of one cell converts adjacent cells into a senescent state. A caveat is that paracrine senescence requires susceptible recipients and sufficient SASP magnitude, and it can be both tumor-suppressive and pathological.

nodes.label: Natural Killer Cells
nodes.description: SASP chemokines including CCL2, CCL5, CXCL1, and CXCL10 act as find-me signals that recruit natural killer (NK) cells to sites of senescence. NK cells then directly kill senescent cells via NKG2D recognition of stress-induced ligands (MICA, MICB, ULBP2), making this recruitment a key arm of senescence surveillance that converts the secretome into an immune-clearance stimulus. Interferon signaling downstream of cGAS-STING in the senescent cell further boosts NK effector activity. The efficiency of recruitment and killing declines with age and immunosenescence, allowing senescent-cell accumulation, whereas enhancing this axis is an active therapeutic strategy to restore surveillance.

nodes.label: MMP-3
nodes.description: Matrix metalloproteinase-3 (MMP-3) is a SASP protease associated with extracellular matrix degradation, tissue remodeling, and, in tumor contexts, cancer cell invasion and metastasis. Its secretion reflects the matrix-remodeling arm of the secretome that supports wound healing acutely but pathological tissue breakdown chronically, and MMP-3 can activate other MMPs in a cascade, amplifying remodeling. This protease component distinguishes the SASP from a purely cytokine profile and contributes to fibrosis and basement-membrane disruption in aging tissues.

nodes.label: CCL2
nodes.description: CCL2 (MCP-1) is a SASP chemokine regulated by IL-1a and IL-1b that is a potent chemoattractant for monocytes and CCR2+ myeloid precursors, recruiting macrophages and myeloid-derived suppressor cells to sites of senescence. It thereby links the senescent secretome to innate and suppressive immune infiltration and contributes to paracrine senescence and inflammaging. CCL2's recruitment functions make it a central communicator between senescent cells and the immune milieu, and its CCR2-dependent signaling has been targeted to modulate myeloid infiltration in aging and cancer.

nodes.label: TNFalpha
nodes.description: Tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFalpha) is a pro-inflammatory SASP cytokine that contributes to immune modulation, NF-kB reinforcement, and inflammaging. It can act in an autocrine loop to amplify the secretome and in a paracrine manner to affect neighboring cells, and it cooperates with IL-1 family cytokines in driving inflammatory gene programs. TNFalpha is less universally dominant than IL-6 in the SASP but is consistently present in many senescence models and is a canonical target of anti-inflammatory biologics. Its pleiotropic actions solidify its status as a canonical SASP component.

nodes.label: GATA4
nodes.description: GATA4 is a transcriptional regulator that promotes the pro-inflammatory SASP by activating NF-kB, in part through TRAF3IP2 (Act1), and by inhibiting autophagy, which would otherwise clear damaging organelles and dampen inflammatory signals. Its accumulation in senescent cells makes it an upstream driver of the secretome's inflammatory arm, coupling defective organelle turnover directly to cytokine production. Unlike many SASP regulators that act on a single pathway, GATA4 integrates both transcriptional and autophagy-based control. The mechanism is well supported and positions GATA4 as a distinctive senescence-specific SASP regulator.

nodes.label: METTL3/METTL14
nodes.description: The METTL3-METTL14 m6A methyltransferase complex promotes SASP factor expression by installing N6-methyladenosine marks on mRNA that facilitate enhancer-promoter looping and stabilize SASP transcripts. This epitranscriptomic layer adds post-transcriptional control to the secretome, coordinating the sustained expression of multiple SASP genes. The relationship is mechanistically plausible and supported by knockout studies showing reduced SASP, but the field is newer and less consolidated than the NF-kB/mTOR axes, so confidence is moderate.

nodes.label: Ruxolitinib
nodes.description: Ruxolitinib, a JAK1/2 inhibitor, reduces SASP cytokines IL-6 and IL-8 in senescent fibroblasts by blocking JAK-STAT3 signaling downstream of SASP cytokines. As a clinically approved drug for myelofibrosis, it is a translatable senomorphic agent whose suppression is targeted to the JAK-STAT arm of the secretome rather than acting on the whole program. The evidence is robust in cellular models and consistent with its established immunomodulatory profile, and the drug also interrupts the feed-forward loop by which IL-6 sustains chronic inflammation. This positions ruxolitinib as one of the most clinically ready senomorphic candidates for dampening senescence-associated inflammation.

nodes.label: Lamivudine
nodes.description: Lamivudine (3TC), a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor, suppresses the SASP by inhibiting LINE-1 (L1) reverse transcription, thereby reducing cytosolic retroelement cDNA that would activate cGAS-STING-NF-kB signaling. This repurposes an antiretroviral agent as a senomorphic that targets the retrotransposon arm of SASP induction, complementing drugs that act on transcription factors or chromatin. The mechanism is supported by studies showing reduced SASP upon LINE-1 inhibition and is consistent with the finding that RB1 and SIRT6 normally restrain L1 activity. Clinical relevance is still investigative, keeping confidence moderate.

nodes.label: SAMD
nodes.description: Senescent cells exhibit senescence-associated mitochondrial dysfunction (SAMD), characterized by reduced oxidative phosphorylation capacity, altered mitochondrial morphology, and elevated ROS production. SAMD is not merely a bystander but an active driver: mitochondrial stress releases mtDNA via minority MOMP, activating cGAS-STING and reinforcing the SASP. The dysfunctional mitochondria also elevate ROS that cause further DNA damage, amplifying arrest. SAMD thus couples metabolic remodeling to the inflammatory secretome.

nodes.label: Dasatinib
nodes.description: Dasatinib, a multi-targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor, is a component of the foundational D+Q (dasatinib plus quercetin) senolytic combination. It is proposed to act by inhibiting pro-survival kinases in senescent cells, lowering their apoptotic threshold, and it has established clinical use in chronic myeloid leukemia that aids repurposing. Its senolytic activity is well demonstrated in vitro and in vivo, and it synergizes with quercetin to clear senescent cells across multiple tissues including adipose and endothelium. Though tissue selectivity varies, the D+Q regimen has become the most clinically studied senolytic, tested in IPF, diabetic kidney disease, and osteoarthritis pilots.

nodes.label: Navitoclax
nodes.description: Navitoclax (ABT-263) is a potent BCL-2/BCL-XL/BCL-W inhibitor with strong senolytic activity, effectively inducing apoptosis in senescent cells by disabling their BCL-2-family SCAP dependence. It is limited clinically by on-target thrombocytopenia resulting from platelet dependence on BCL-XL, which has spurred development of more selective BCL-XL-sparing derivatives. Its senolytic efficacy is well established in multiple preclinical models, including oncogene-induced senescence and hematopoietic and lung contexts. The toxicity caveat shapes its use toward intermittent or tissue-targeted regimens, and it exemplifies both the power and the challenge of targeting the BCL-2 family for senolysis.

nodes.label: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
nodes.description: Senolytic therapy (D+Q) has been tested for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) in a pilot clinical trial (NCT02874989), where it improved physical function. The rationale is that senescent-cell accumulation and SASP-driven fibrosis, particularly TGFb- and MMP-mediated matrix deposition, contribute to IPF pathogenesis. The results support further evaluation of senolytics in fibrotic lung disease and helped establish the feasibility of senolytic dosing in humans. IPF remains among the most advanced clinical indications for senolytic therapy, and the study catalyzed additional trials in kidney disease, osteoarthritis, and frailty.

nodes.label: Diabetic Kidney Disease
nodes.description: Senolytic therapy (D+Q) has been tested in a pilot study for diabetic kidney disease (NCT02848131), based on evidence that senescent cells and their SASP drive renal fibrosis and dysfunction in diabetes through chronic inflammation and matrix remodeling. The trial assessed feasibility, safety, and biomarkers of renal senescence, and early data showing reduced senescent-cell burden informed the potential of senolytics in metabolic kidney disease. Clinical confidence remains preliminary pending larger, powered trials, but D+Q is among the few regimens with human feasibility data in this indication.

nodes.label: Senotherapeutic
nodes.description: The term 'senotherapeutic' is an umbrella encompassing both senolytics (which eliminate senescent cells) and senomorphics (which suppress the SASP). Senolytics act on the cellular driver, while senomorphics act on the secretory effector, together spanning the intervention space against senescence. This inclusive definition reflects the field's two-pronged therapeutic philosophy and accommodates agents with dual activity, such as fisetin. Recognizing both under one term aids classification and communication of anti-senescence strategies.

nodes.label: Senotherapy
nodes.description: Senotherapy encompasses senolytics, the cell-elimination arm that selectively induces apoptosis in senescent cells by disabling SCAPs. This is one of the two principal divisions of senotherapy, the other being senomorphics, and the term captures the spectrum of interventions aimed at the senescent cell. Encompassing senolytics underscores the elimination-based strategy's centrality to the field, given its strong preclinical and early clinical evidence. Senolytic agents range from navitoclax to the D+Q combination and fisetin.

nodes.label: Notch
nodes.description: Notch signaling is essential for establishing paracrine senescence and, paradoxically, weakens the secondary SASP in receiving cells. Notch integrates cues from the SASP to reinforce arrest in neighbors while modulating their secretory output, indicating that paracrine senescence is an active, regulated program rather than passive factor exposure. The distinct outcomes -- establishing arrest versus dampening the SASP -- reflect context-dependent Notch outputs in recipient cells. This dual role positions Notch as a key integrator of the spread and modulation of senescence.

nodes.label: IFITM3
nodes.description: IFITM3 is enriched in exosomes released from senescent cells and mediates paracrine senescence by transmitting senescence signals to recipient cells. As an exosomal cargo, it represents a vesicle-based, rather than soluble-factor, route of spread, and its inclusion highlights that paracrine senescence is not solely cytokine-driven. Exosomes allow protected, concentrated delivery of signals to recipient cells, and they can be detected in the circulation as potential biomarkers of senescence burden. The mechanism adds a non-classical communication modality to the SASP paradigm.

nodes.label: Immunosenescence
nodes.description: Senescence surveillance is impaired by immunosenescence -- the age-related decline in immune competence -- which compromises NK, macrophage, and T-cell mediated clearance of senescent cells. Elevated myeloid-derived suppressor cells and immune suppression further blunt surveillance, and impaired T-cell and NK responses reduce elimination of arrested cells. The result is permissive accumulation of senescent cells and increased tumor and inflammatory risk. This positions immunosenescence as both a cause and a consequence of senescence pathology.

nodes.label: mtDNA
nodes.description: SAMD releases mtDNA into the cytosol via minority MOMP -- sublethal, intermittent mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization that leaks mtDNA without triggering full apoptosis. The escaped mtDNA acts as a damage-associated molecular pattern activating cGAS-STING, which drives type-I interferon and NF-kB-dependent SASP, and SCAPs restrain this process to prevent complete cell death. This release is a pivotal link between mitochondrial stress and innate immune activation in senescence. It exemplifies how senescent cells walk a fine line between life and death.

nodes.label: HIRA/ASF1a
nodes.description: SAHF are assembled by the HIRA-ASF1a histone chaperone complex, which deposits macroH2A and core histones to establish H3K9me3-marked heterochromatin at the foci. This chaperone-driven deposition is required for the formation of the DAPI-dense nuclear bodies that characterize senescent cells, and it is coordinated with hypophosphorylated Rb. The process links histone dynamics directly to senescence-specific chromatin reorganization. HIRA/ASF1a thus provide the assembly machinery for the repressive structures that lock in the arrested state.

nodes.label: SADS
nodes.description: SADS (senescence-associated distal satellite) is a form of heterochromatin decompaction in senescent cells, specifically the relaxation of constitutive pericentromeric and pericentrosomal satellite heterochromatin. Unlike SAHF (which compacts facultative heterochromatin), SADS decompacts constitutive repeats. This structural change alters the nuclear architecture and chromatin accessibility of repetitive regions. SADS represents a distinct, counterintuitive chromatin reorganization during senescence.

nodes.label: Heterochromatin Decompaction
nodes.description: SADS (senescence-associated distal satellite) is a form of heterochromatin decompaction in senescent cells, specifically the relaxation of constitutive pericentromeric and pericentrosomal satellite heterochromatin. Unlike SAHF (which compacts facultative heterochromatin), SADS decompacts constitutive repeats. This structural change alters the nuclear architecture and chromatin accessibility of repetitive regions. SADS represents a distinct, counterintuitive chromatin reorganization during senescence.

nodes.label: T Cell
nodes.description: Immunosenescence impairs T-cell immunity, featuring perturbed memory responses, thymic involution, reduced naive T-cell generation, and accumulation of differentiated, often dysfunctional memory and effector subsets such as EMRA CD8+ T cells. This limits responses to infection and vaccination in the elderly and weakens T-cell-mediated immune surveillance, including the clearance of senescent and premalignant cells. The impairment is a hallmark of adaptive immune aging. It directly contributes to the decline in senescence surveillance with age.

nodes.label: DNA-SCARS
nodes.description: Genotoxic stress in therapy-induced senescence generates persistent DNA damage foci termed DNA-SCARS (DNA segments with chromatin alterations reinforcing senescence), which are precursors to cytoplasmic chromatin fragments. These structures sustain DDR signaling and the arrested state, and their shedding into the cytosol activates cGAS-STING and the SASP. DNA-SCARS thereby mechanistically link damage to durable senescence and inflammation. They are a defining feature distinguishing TIS from transient damage responses.

nodes.label: Glucocorticoids
nodes.description: NF-kB is inhibited by glucocorticoids, which block the pro-inflammatory SASP by impairing IL-1a-mediated NF-kB activity. Glucocorticoids repress NF-kB transactivation by recruiting co-repressors and interfering with its interaction with coactivators, reducing SASP cytokine output. This explains their classic anti-inflammatory action in senescence contexts and their historical use in treating inflammatory conditions. The inhibition is well established pharmacologically, though chronic use carries significant side effects.

nodes.label: SB203580
nodes.description: p38 MAPK is inhibited by SB203580, a classical pyridinyl imidazole inhibitor that suppresses p38alpha and p38beta and thereby reduces the SASP from fibroblasts of older donors. By blocking p38, SB203580 lowers NF-kB activation and SASP transcript stabilization, demonstrating the kinase's central role in the secretome. This provides a tool compound that validates p38 as a senomorphic target in cellular models. The inhibition is specific and well characterized, though clinical senomorphic use remains investigational.

nodes.label: p21 CIP1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Small molecule compounds that induce cellular senescence.md
nodes.description: DNA damage stabilizes p53, which transcriptionally induces the CDK inhibitor p21CIP1; p21 binds and inhibits cyclin-CDK complexes, notably CDK2, enforcing a G1/S arrest. This p53-to-p21 axis is a primary, rapid enforcement mechanism of senescence and quiescence, and the induction is dose-dependent and reversible in the short term but locks the arrest when sustained. It exemplifies tumor-suppressive cell-cycle control and is a core target of the DNA damage response. p21 also supports an early secretory phenotype during stress.

nodes.label: CDK2
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Senolytic Treatment With Fisetin Reverses Age‐Related Endothelial Dysfunction Partially Mediated by SASP Factor CXCL12.md
nodes.description: p21CIP1 inhibits cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) by binding the cyclin E/A-CDK2 complex, preventing phosphorylation of Rb and thereby enforcing G1/S arrest. This is a direct enzymatic inhibition central to p53-driven senescence and quiescence, and by blocking S-phase entry, p21 locks cells out of the cell cycle. Its inhibitory action is a canonical CDK-inhibitor function and operates alongside p16/p15-mediated CDK4/6 inhibition. The cooperation between CIP/KIP and INK4 inhibitors provides redundant, robust arrest enforcement.

nodes.label: Early SASP
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Senolytic Treatment With Fisetin Reverses Age‐Related Endothelial Dysfunction Partially Mediated by SASP Factor CXCL12.md
nodes.description: p21 supports an early secretory phenotype -- including factors such as CXCL14 and IGFBP3 -- that places stressed cells under immunosurveillance prior to full senescence. This early p21-associated secretome differs from the later NF-kB-dominated SASP, and it may help communicate cellular stress and recruit immune clearance. The relationship suggests p21 contributes to both arrest and the initial communicative state of stressed cells. It is more nuanced than simple arrest enforcement, giving moderate confidence.

nodes.label: CDK4
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Small molecule compounds that induce cellular senescence.md
nodes.description: p16INK4a inhibits cyclin-dependent kinase 4 (CDK4) by binding the cyclin D-CDK4 complex, preventing Rb phosphorylation and maintaining the growth-suppressive, hypophosphorylated state of Rb. This is a primary mechanism by which p16 enforces the durable, p53-independent phase of senescence, and loss of p16 is a common event in cancer, underscoring its tumor-suppressive role. The inhibition is direct and well established, and its expression rises with age and senescent burden. p16 is therefore both a cell-cycle brake and a senescence biomarker.

nodes.label: CDK6
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Small molecule compounds that induce cellular senescence.md
nodes.description: p16INK4a also inhibits cyclin-dependent kinase 6 (CDK6), similarly preventing cyclin D-CDK6-mediated Rb phosphorylation and stabilizing the arrested state. This broad inhibition of both CDK4 and CDK6 ensures a robust G1 blockade, and the dual targeting makes p16 a potent, non-redundant cell-cycle inhibitor. Its action underpins the irreversibility of established senescence, complementing the p53/p21 arm. p16 is consequently a key mediator of permanent growth arrest and a widely used senescence marker.

nodes.label: Senescent Cell Accumulation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial dysfunction in cellular senescence a bridge to neurodegenerative disease.md
nodes.description: Aging causes senescent-cell accumulation as telomere shortening, cumulative DNA damage, and stem-cell stress increase senescent-cell formation, while declining immune clearance reduces their removal. The burden rises across multiple tissues, often described as exponential with age, and is a cardinal hallmark linking cellular senescence to organismal aging. The causal direction is reinforced by experiments showing that clearing these cells alleviates age-related dysfunction. Senescent-cell accumulation is therefore both a marker and a driver of the aging process.

nodes.label: SASP Enhancers
nodes.description: H3K27ac marks senescence-activated super-enhancers that drive SASP expression, identifying the enhancer landscape licensed during the senescent response. These acetylated, transcriptionally active enhancers recruit BRD4 and transcription factors such as AP-1 and NF-kB to SASP loci, enabling robust and sustained secretome transcription. The mark thus charts the chromatin basis of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype and distinguishes active SASP enhancers from repressed loci. Targeting these enhancers with BET inhibitors such as JQ1 suppresses SASP expression, revealing the enhancer landscape as a therapeutic vulnerability in senescence.

nodes.label: Activin A
nodes.description: Activin A is a homodimer of inhibin beta-A (INHBA) subunits and a member of the TGFbeta superfamily of cytokines. Like other family members, it signals through serine/threonine kinase receptors to regulate cell fate, proliferation, and inflammation. Its classification within the TGFbeta superfamily situates it among the SASP factors with paracrine arrest-inducing capacity, alongside TGF-beta1, BMP2, and GDF15. Activin A is a structurally defined ligand that is distinct from TGF-beta1 but shares functional overlap, particularly in inducing cell-cycle inhibitors in receiving cells during paracrine senescence.

nodes.label: TGFβ Superfamily
nodes.description: Activin A is a homodimer of inhibin beta-A (INHBA) subunits and a member of the TGFbeta superfamily of cytokines. Like other family members, it signals through serine/threonine kinase receptors to regulate cell fate, proliferation, and inflammation. Its classification within the TGFbeta superfamily situates it among the SASP factors with paracrine arrest-inducing capacity, alongside TGF-beta1, BMP2, and GDF15. Activin A is a structurally defined ligand that is distinct from TGF-beta1 but shares functional overlap, particularly in inducing cell-cycle inhibitors in receiving cells during paracrine senescence.

nodes.label: ALK4
nodes.description: Activin A signals through the type I receptor ALK4 and type II receptors activin receptor RIIA/RIIB, which phosphorylate SMAD2 and SMAD3 to transmit signals to the nucleus. This receptor architecture is canonical for activin/nodal signaling within the TGFbeta superfamily and is required for Activin A's biological effects in senescence. The ALK4-SMAD2/3 axis links ligand binding directly to transcriptional reprogramming of recipient cells, including induction of cell-cycle inhibitor genes. Because ALK4 is shared with other TGFbeta-family ligands, its engagement integrates Activin A signaling into the broader paracrine senescence network.

nodes.label: SMAD2
nodes.description: Phosphorylated SMAD2, together with SMAD3, complexes with SMAD4 and translocates to the nucleus to regulate target gene transcription downstream of Activin A-ALK4 signaling. This SMAD-dependent transduction is the principal route by which Activin A alters gene expression in receiving cells, driving expression of cell-cycle inhibitors that reinforce growth arrest. The pathway is a standard TGFbeta-superfamily output mechanism and is shared with TGF-beta1 signaling, explaining the functional overlap between these ligands in paracrine senescence. SMAD2/3 phosphorylation is therefore a key readout of Activin A activity in cell-based assays.

nodes.label: CDKN2B
nodes.description: Activin A-SMAD signaling induces p15INK4b (encoded by CDKN2B) and p21CIP1 in receiving cells during paracrine senescence, reinforcing growth arrest. By engaging the CDK inhibitor network, Activin A helps lock neighboring cells into a senescent state, positioning it as an effector of transmissible arrest. The induction is part of the concerted SASP-mediated paracrine program and is shared with TGF-beta1, which also drives CDKN2B expression through SMAD3/SMAD4. Blocking Activin A partially rescues paracrine arrest, confirming the functional contribution of this pathway to spreading senescence across a tissue.

nodes.label: Follistatin
nodes.description: Follistatin binds and neutralizes Activin A extracellularly, acting as a soluble antagonist that can block its paracrine senescence-inducing activity. This provides a natural brake on Activin A signaling and a potential therapeutic route to limit SASP-mediated arrest spread in tissue. The follistatin-Activin A axis is a classic antagonistic ligand-binding pair, and neutralization experiments confirm its functional relevance in paracrine senescence models. Because follistatin also regulates other TGFbeta-family ligands, it represents an endogenous checkpoint on the arrest-inducing arm of the senescent secretome.

nodes.label: Acute Stress-Associated Phenotype
nodes.description: The acute stress-associated phenotype (ASAP) is the early, prompt cellular response mounted upon stress before full senescence markers become evident; it can transition into the chronic SASP. ASAP represents a pre-secretome state that licenses subsequent inflammatory output, establishing a temporal hierarchy in which stress sensing occurs first and durable secretome production follows. Understanding ASAP helps separate acute protective responses from chronic, deleterious senescence inflammation. The distinction has therapeutic implications, as agents that block the ASAP-to-SASP transition could prevent inflammation before it becomes entrenched.

nodes.label: TRAF6
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Senolytic Treatment With Fisetin Reverses Age‐Related Endothelial Dysfunction Partially Mediated by SASP Factor CXCL12.md
nodes.description: The ATM-TRAF6-TAK1 axis drives ASAP signaling: ATM activates TRAF6, which undergoes auto-ubiquitination and recruits TAK1 to propagate stress and inflammatory signals. TAK1 in turn activates p38 MAPK and NF-kB downstream, linking DNA damage sensing to SASP transcription. This axis is a conserved scaffold connecting genotoxic stress to senescence inflammation and operates upstream of the established SASP regulatory network. The ATM-dependent TRAF6 activation illustrates how a DNA-damage kinase directly engages innate immune signaling machinery to initiate the senescent inflammatory program.

nodes.label: CCL20
nodes.description: CCL20 (MIP-3alpha) is a CC chemokine that signals exclusively through the receptor CCR6, belonging to the broader chemokine family that directs leukocyte trafficking. Its classification as a chemokine situates it among the SASP components that recruit immune cells to senescent tissue. As a SASP factor, CCL20 extends the communicative reach of senescent cells to adaptive immunity, attracting CCR6-expressing cells such as TH17 lymphocytes and immature dendritic cells. Its restricted receptor usage gives it a focused recruitment profile distinct from broadly acting chemokines.

nodes.label: Chemokine
nodes.description: CCL20 (MIP-3alpha) is a CC chemokine that signals exclusively through the receptor CCR6, belonging to the broader chemokine family that directs leukocyte trafficking. Its classification as a chemokine situates it among the SASP components that recruit immune cells to senescent tissue. As a SASP factor, CCL20 extends the communicative reach of senescent cells to adaptive immunity, attracting CCR6-expressing cells such as TH17 lymphocytes and immature dendritic cells. Its restricted receptor usage gives it a focused recruitment profile distinct from broadly acting chemokines.

nodes.label: CCR6
nodes.description: CCL20 is the sole ligand for CCR6, a Gai-coupled GPCR that drives chemotaxis via PI3K/Akt, p38 MAPK, and calcium flux in target cells. This exclusive pairing directs recruitment of CCR6-positive cells such as TH17 lymphocytes and dendritic cells to sites of ligand production. In the senescence context, CCL20-CCR6 links the SASP to adaptive immune infiltration, shaping the local immune landscape around senescent foci. The signaling mechanism is well characterized in lymphocyte biology and is a canonical chemokine-receptor interaction.

nodes.label: TH17
nodes.description: The CCL20-CCR6 axis links the SASP to adaptive immunity by recruiting TH17 cells, which express CCR6 and are drawn to CCL20-rich senescent foci. TH17 recruitment can amplify local inflammation and shape the immune milieu around senescent cells, promoting chronic inflammatory responses. This connects the secretome to a distinct T-cell subset with pro-inflammatory roles and expands the immunological consequences of the SASP beyond innate immune activation. The relationship highlights how chemokines translate senescence signals into adaptive immune skewing.

nodes.label: p15INK4b
nodes.description: CDKN2B encodes p15INK4b, a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor that blocks CDK4/6 and thereby enforces G1 arrest. As a tumor-suppressor locus often co-regulated with CDKN2A at chromosome 9p21, its product is a core effector of growth inhibition in response to TGFbeta signaling. In senescence, CDKN2B induction is a key event in paracrine and TGFbeta-driven arrest, acting downstream of SMAD3/SMAD4. The encoding relationship is a fundamental gene-to-protein fact with direct relevance to cell-cycle control.

nodes.label: HLA-E
nodes.description: HLA-E is a non-classical (class Ib) major histocompatibility complex molecule with limited polymorphism, presenting a restricted set of peptides, often leader peptides derived from other MHC class I molecules, to innate lymphoid receptors. Its classification distinguishes it from classical MHC class Ia molecules and underpins its specialized ligand-receptor interactions with NKG2A/CD94. In senescence, HLA-E upregulation becomes a mechanism of immune evasion that protects arrested cells from cytotoxic lymphocytes. The class Ib identity enables the checkpoint-like function central to its role in senescence surveillance.

nodes.label: MHC Class Ib
nodes.description: HLA-E is a non-classical (class Ib) major histocompatibility complex molecule with limited polymorphism, presenting a restricted set of peptides, often leader peptides derived from other MHC class I molecules, to innate lymphoid receptors. Its classification distinguishes it from classical MHC class Ia molecules and underpins its specialized ligand-receptor interactions with NKG2A/CD94. In senescence, HLA-E upregulation becomes a mechanism of immune evasion that protects arrested cells from cytotoxic lymphocytes. The class Ib identity enables the checkpoint-like function central to its role in senescence surveillance.

nodes.label: NKG2A
nodes.description: HLA-E is the ligand for the inhibitory receptor NKG2A/CD94 heterodimer expressed on NK cells and CD8+ T cells. This binding delivers a cognate inhibitory signal upon engagement, dampening the cytotoxic activity of the receptor-bearing lymphocyte. The interaction is a canonical innate immune checkpoint, analogous to PD-1/PD-L1 but restricted to the NKG2A-CD94 axis. In senescence, HLA-E-NKG2A engagement becomes a route by which arrested cells dampen their own immune clearance, contributing to their persistence.

nodes.label: CD8 T Cells
nodes.description: HLA-E-NKG2A/CD94 engagement on CD8+ T cells suppresses their cytotoxic killing, extending the immune-evasive effect beyond NK cells to the adaptive compartment. This allows HLA-E-upregulated senescent and malignant cells to evade cytotoxic T lymphocytes, contributing to failed clearance and persistence. The suppression reinforces the dual innate and adaptive immune evasion conferred by HLA-E and mirrors the checkpoint biology exploited by tumors. Pharmacological blockade of the interaction is being explored as a strategy to restore CD8+ T-cell responses.

nodes.label: Inflammasome
nodes.description: Inflammasomes are cytosolic supramolecular complexes of the innate immune system that assemble in response to pathogens or sterile danger signals to activate inflammatory caspases. They are not antibodies (immune complexes) but rather multiprotein scaffolds; the original classification here as an immune complex is loose, though inflammasomes are innate immune signaling platforms. They serve as a key intersection between senescence, DAMPs, and inflammation. Their activation links cellular damage to IL-1 family cytokine release.

nodes.label: Immune Complex
nodes.description: Inflammasomes are cytosolic supramolecular complexes of the innate immune system that assemble in response to pathogens or sterile danger signals to activate inflammatory caspases. They are not antibodies (immune complexes) but rather multiprotein scaffolds; the original classification here as an immune complex is loose, though inflammasomes are innate immune signaling platforms. They serve as a key intersection between senescence, DAMPs, and inflammation. Their activation links cellular damage to IL-1 family cytokine release.

nodes.label: Caspase-1
nodes.description: Canonical inflammasomes activate caspase-1, which processes pro-IL-1beta and pro-IL-18 into their mature secreted forms and cleaves gasdermin D to execute pyroptosis. This activation is the central effector step of the inflammasome pathway and requires assembly of sensor, ASC, and procaspase-1. In senescence, caspase-1 activity also feeds the SASP, particularly during oncogene-induced senescence where the canonical inflammasome is engaged. The relationship is a foundational inflammasome mechanism with direct relevance to senescence-associated inflammation and sterile immunity.

nodes.label: Noncanonical Inflammasome
nodes.description: Senescent cells activate the noncanonical inflammasome (caspase-5/11), which cleaves IL-1alpha and drives SASP establishment. This provides a caspase-5-dependent route to the secretome that is distinct from the canonical NLRP3/caspase-1 pathway, and it is increasingly recognized as a core SASP licensing mechanism. The activation links cytosolic sensing to senescence inflammation, and in senescent cells it specifically processes IL-1alpha rather than IL-1beta. Caspase-5 knockdown reduces IL-1alpha release and downstream SASP factors without affecting growth arrest.

nodes.label: MyD88
nodes.description: MyD88 is a cytoplasmic adaptor protein serving as the central hub of Toll-like receptor (TLR) and IL-1R signaling, linking receptor engagement to downstream kinase cascades. Its classification as an adaptor reflects its role in assembling signaling complexes rather than performing enzymatic catalysis, and it does so through death domain and TIR domain interactions. In senescence, MyD88 transduces IL-1alpha signals that sustain the SASP, placing it at the interface of innate immunity and senescence. It is a foundational innate immune signaling scaffold conserved across species.

nodes.label: Adaptor Protein
nodes.description: MyD88 is a cytoplasmic adaptor protein serving as the central hub of Toll-like receptor (TLR) and IL-1R signaling, linking receptor engagement to downstream kinase cascades. Its classification as an adaptor reflects its role in assembling signaling complexes rather than performing enzymatic catalysis, and it does so through death domain and TIR domain interactions. In senescence, MyD88 transduces IL-1alpha signals that sustain the SASP, placing it at the interface of innate immunity and senescence. It is a foundational innate immune signaling scaffold conserved across species.

nodes.label: IL-1R
nodes.description: IL-1R recruits MyD88 via TIR-TIR interactions, and MyD88 assembles the myddosome to propagate IL-1alpha/IL-1beta signals in senescent cells and responding macrophages. This transduction is essential for the NF-kB activation that drives SASP and paracrine arrest, and it requires the death-domain-mediated recruitment of IRAK kinases. The relationship positions MyD88 as the immediate downstream effector of IL-1R and is a canonical IL-1R signaling mechanism. Blocking this interaction can suppress IL-1-dependent inflammatory output.

nodes.label: IRAK4
nodes.description: MyD88 recruits IRAK4 via death-domain interactions, the first step in myddosome assembly after receptor engagement. IRAK4 then phosphorylates IRAK1/IRAK2, propagating the signal toward TRAF6 and TAK1 activation. This recruitment is a conserved early event in TLR/IL-1R pathways and is essential for downstream NF-kB and AP-1 signaling. In senescence it initiates the cascade that licenses SASP transcription, making IRAK4 a potential target for dampening IL-1-driven inflammation and the myddosome architecture ensures rapid, robust signal propagation.

nodes.label: IRAK1
nodes.description: Active IRAK4 phosphorylates IRAK1, which then recruits TRAF6 through its C-terminal TRAF6-binding motifs, extending the myddosome signaling complex. This step connects the receptor-proximal kinases to E3 ubiquitin ligase activity and TAK1 activation, ultimately driving NF-kB and MAPK signaling. In senescence, IRAK1 is required for full SASP establishment, linking the IL-1R pathway to the secretome. The relationship is a standard component of IL-1R/TLR signal propagation and is well validated biochemically.

nodes.label: Myddosome
nodes.description: MyD88 assembles into the helical oligomeric myddosome with IRAK4 and IRAK1/2, serving as the scaffolding platform that activates downstream kinases such as TAK1 and transcription factors such as NF-kB. This supramolecular complex is the mechanistic core of IL-1R/TLR signaling and is assembled through death-domain homotypic interactions. In senescence, myddosome formation underlies IL-1alpha-driven SASP, translating IL-1 receptor engagement into inflammatory transcription. The assembly is a defining structural feature of MyD88-dependent signaling and a validated drug target.

nodes.label: Senescent Cells to Macrophages
nodes.description: Senescent-cell surface IL-1alpha engages IL-1R on macrophages, recruiting MyD88 to activate NF-kB and amplify SASP both in the sender cell through autocrine signaling and in recruited immune cells through paracrine signaling. This bridges the senescent cell and the macrophage through IL-1R/MyD88 signaling, propagating inflammation across the tissue. The relationship situates MyD88 at the interface of senescence and innate immunity and explains how local senescence ignites broader inflammatory responses. It is a key mechanism of SASP-driven immune amplification.

nodes.label: Myeloid-Derived Suppressor Cells
nodes.description: Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) are a heterogeneous population of immature myeloid cells with potent immunosuppressive activity, expanded under pathological stress including cancer and chronic inflammation. Their classification reflects an arrested differentiation state rather than a single lineage, with polymorphonuclear and monocytic subsets recognized. In senescence contexts, MDSCs are recruited by SASP factors and blunt anti-tumor and anti-senescence immunity, shifting the immune balance away from clearance. They represent a key immunosuppressive cell type bridging aging, inflammation, and cancer.

nodes.label: Immature Myeloid Cell
nodes.description: Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) are a heterogeneous population of immature myeloid cells with potent immunosuppressive activity, expanded under pathological stress including cancer and chronic inflammation. Their classification reflects an arrested differentiation state rather than a single lineage, with polymorphonuclear and monocytic subsets recognized. In senescence contexts, MDSCs are recruited by SASP factors and blunt anti-tumor and anti-senescence immunity, shifting the immune balance away from clearance. They represent a key immunosuppressive cell type bridging aging, inflammation, and cancer.

nodes.label: GM-CSF
nodes.description: The SASP factor GM-CSF stimulates myeloid expansion and biases differentiation toward immunosuppressive MDSCs, recruiting them into senescent and tumor tissues. GM-CSF thereby shapes the myeloid compartment to be tolerogenic and arrest-promoting, exemplifying SASP-driven paracrine reprogramming of immune lineage fate. The relationship links a specific SASP cytokine to myeloid suppressor accumulation and is a recognized driver of MDSC expansion in inflammation and cancer. Blocking GM-CSF signaling can reduce MDSC generation.

nodes.label: Caspase-5
nodes.description: Caspase-5 (human) is the inducible noncanonical effector caspase that cleaves IL-1alpha and gasdermin D to drive SASP and pyroptosis. Its activation is essential for the noncanonical inflammasome's role in senescence, and its expression is induced by interferons and controlled upstream by the cGAS-STING pathway. The relationship positions caspase-5 as the enzymatic executor of the pathway in human cells. It is supported by cleavage-site and loss-of-function studies showing reduced SASP after CASP5 knockdown.

nodes.label: Caspase-11
nodes.description: Caspase-11 (mouse) is the noncanonical effector caspase that cleaves IL-1alpha and gasdermin D, paralleling human caspase-4/5. It is activated by cytosolic LPS and drives SASP establishment in murine senescence models, and it is required for SASP-driven immune clearance of senescent hepatocytes in vivo. The relationship establishes the species-specific executor of the noncanonical pathway in mice. It is a well-supported component of senescence inflammasome biology, with genetic deficiency of the enzyme blunting IL-1alpha processing and downstream secretome output.

nodes.label: Gasdermin D
nodes.description: Active caspase-4/5/11 cleave gasdermin D between its N-terminal pore-forming domain and C-terminal inhibitory domain, releasing the N-terminal fragment to form plasma-membrane pores. This drives inflammatory cell death (pyroptosis) and IL-1alpha release in senescent and responding cells, and the pores also permit release of IL-1beta and IL-18 prior to membrane rupture. The relationship is the canonical execution step of noncanonical inflammasome signaling and links the pathway to both cell death and SASP amplification, creating a feed-forward inflammatory loop in senescent tissue.

nodes.label: LPS
nodes.description: The hexa-acylated lipid A of LPS binds directly to the CARD domain of caspase-4/5/11, inducing their dimerization and activation, the defining trigger of the noncanonical inflammasome. While classically microbial, this mechanism can be engaged in senescence-associated inflammatory contexts. The relationship is the canonical activation mode of the pathway and links Gram-negative sensing to caspase activation. Because the caspases themselves are the sensors, no upstream receptor is required for this pathway.

nodes.label: Paracrine Reprogramming
nodes.description: Paracrine reprogramming is the biological process by which SASP factors alter the differentiation status and fate of neighbouring cells, pushing them toward stemness, EMT, or altered lineage commitment. Distinct from paracrine senescence, which induces growth arrest, it remodels recipient identity and is dose- and time-dependent, with acute exposure promoting plasticity and chronic exposure driving fibrosis and cancer stemness. The process is mediated by cytokines such as IL-6, TGFbeta, and VEGF family members. It expands the non-cell-autonomous influence of senescent cells beyond growth arrest.

nodes.label: Biological Process
nodes.description: Paracrine reprogramming is the biological process by which SASP factors alter the differentiation status and fate of neighbouring cells, pushing them toward stemness, EMT, or altered lineage commitment. Distinct from paracrine senescence, which induces growth arrest, it remodels recipient identity and is dose- and time-dependent, with acute exposure promoting plasticity and chronic exposure driving fibrosis and cancer stemness. The process is mediated by cytokines such as IL-6, TGFbeta, and VEGF family members. It expands the non-cell-autonomous influence of senescent cells beyond growth arrest.

nodes.label: Stemness
nodes.description: IL-6 is a central driver of in vivo reprogramming toward pluripotency and stemness via JAK/STAT3 signaling, promoting a dedifferentiated, stem-like state in recipient cells. This underlies both wound-healing plasticity and, pathologically, cancer stemness, with STAT3 transcriptionally sustaining stemness factors such as OCT4, NANOG, and SOX2. The relationship links a core SASP cytokine to cell-fate reprogramming and is supported by reprogramming and cancer-stemness studies. Blocking IL-6/JAK/STAT3 signaling can interrupt this reprogramming.

nodes.label: Chronic SASP
nodes.description: Chronic SASP, through IL-6 and IL-8 via JAK/STAT3, promotes cancer stem-cell traits and expands the CSC pool in neighbouring epithelial and tumour cells, enhancing tumour initiation and relapse potential. By driving stemness and survival, the persistent secretome fosters malignant progression and therapy resistance. The relationship is a key mechanism by which senescence can become tumor-promoting and is supported by cancer-stemness and senescence co-culture studies. It motivates the one-two punch strategy of senescence induction followed by senolytic clearance.

nodes.label: Myeloid Differentiation
nodes.description: GM-CSF and CCL2 skew myeloid differentiation toward immunosuppressive MDSCs and specific macrophage phenotypes, reshaping the myeloid compartment in senescence and cancer. This biases haematopoiesis away from inflammatory resolution toward tolerance and suppression, exemplifying SASP-driven paracrine reprogramming of immune lineage fate. The relationship links SASP factors to myeloid lineage outcomes and is supported by myeloid-differentiation and tumor-immunology studies. Targeting these factors can restore protective myeloid responses.

nodes.label: VEGFc
nodes.description: VEGF-C is a member of the VEGF family of cysteine-knot growth factors, structurally related to VEGF-A but with distinct receptor usage and lymphatic specificity. Its classification situates it among the growth-factor arm of the SASP, and in senescence it is an early-induced angiogenic and lymphangiogenic factor. The family membership underpins its receptor interactions, particularly with VEGFR-3 and, after proteolytic processing, VEGFR-2. This dual receptor capacity distinguishes its vascular functions from other family members.

nodes.label: VEGF Family
nodes.description: VEGF-C is a member of the VEGF family of cysteine-knot growth factors, structurally related to VEGF-A but with distinct receptor usage and lymphatic specificity. Its classification situates it among the growth-factor arm of the SASP, and in senescence it is an early-induced angiogenic and lymphangiogenic factor. The family membership underpins its receptor interactions, particularly with VEGFR-3 and, after proteolytic processing, VEGFR-2. This dual receptor capacity distinguishes its vascular functions from other family members.

nodes.label: VEGFR3
nodes.description: VEGF-C signals primarily through VEGFR-3 on lymphatic endothelium, promoting lymphangiogenesis and lymphatic vessel sprouting. This receptor usage distinguishes VEGF-C from VEGF-A's preferential VEGFR2 engagement and underlies its role in lymphatic remodeling around senescent tissue. In the SASP, VEGF-C-VEGFR3 signaling contributes to lymphatic vessel formation and potentially to immune cell trafficking routes. The relationship is a canonical VEGF-C function well established in lymphatic biology.

nodes.label: VEGFR2
nodes.description: At higher concentrations or after proteolytic processing, VEGF-C also engages VEGFR2 on blood vascular endothelium, supporting angiogenesis in addition to its lymphatic actions. This dual receptor usage broadens its angiogenic potential within the SASP and explains how VEGF-C can drive both blood- and lymphatic-vessel formation, depending on the local processing environment. The relationship is supported by receptor-binding and processing studies, and it positions processed VEGF-C as a shared ligand across the two receptor systems with distinct downstream signaling outputs.

nodes.label: Lymphangiogenesis
nodes.description: Full-length VEGF-C preferentially activates VEGFR-3 and promotes lymphatic vessel sprouting, driving lymphangiogenesis. In senescence, this contributes to lymphatic remodeling and potentially to immune cell trafficking routes, shaping how immune cells access senescent tissue. The relationship is the canonical lymphangiogenic function of VEGF-C and expands the vascular consequences of the SASP beyond blood vessels. It is supported by studies of lymphatic development and tumor-associated lymphangiogenesis.

nodes.label: DNA Replication Stress
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Small molecule compounds that induce cellular senescence.md
nodes.description: Constitutive oncogenic RAS signaling pushes cells into hyper-replication, where DNA replication forks are initiated at excessive frequency and become stalled or collapsed. This generates single-stranded DNA gaps and replication stress that activate checkpoint kinases ATR and ATM, converging on p53 stabilization. The relationship is a central mechanism linking oncogene activation to senescence-inducing damage and is well established in OIS biology. It explains how proliferative overload is converted into a senescence signal.

nodes.label: ATR
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Small molecule compounds that induce cellular senescence.md
nodes.description: Stalled or collapsed replication forks generate single-stranded DNA gaps that engage the ATR-CHK1 cascade, activating a checkpoint that senses replication stress. In oncogene-induced senescence, ATR signaling contributes to arrest and senescence establishment by stabilizing p53 and enforcing cell-cycle exit. The relationship is a canonical DNA-damage-checkpoint response and links oncogene-driven hyper-replication to cell-cycle enforcement. ATR is considered the primary sensor of replication stress.

nodes.label: CDKN2A
nodes.description: The CDKN2A locus encoding p16INK4a is derepressed in OIS via loss of PRC1/2-mediated H3K27me3 repression, allowing p16 accumulation that enforces durable arrest. This epigenetic switch is a hallmark of the p53-independent senescence phase and locks cells into an Rb-dependent G1 block. The relationship couples oncogene signaling to stable CDK-inhibitor expression and is a well-characterized epigenetic event in OIS. It explains how senescence is maintained even when p53 is compromised, providing a second, independent barrier against escape.

nodes.label: Sir2 (yeast)
nodes.description: Sir2 (silent information regulator 2) is the founding member of the sirtuin family, first identified in Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a regulator of mating-type locus silencing and replicative lifespan. The seven mammalian paralogues SIRT1–SIRT7 evolved from this ancestral NAD+-dependent deacetylase, retaining the conserved catalytic core while diversifying in subcellular localization and substrate repertoire. This phylogenetic continuity means insights from yeast Sir2 historically informed mammalian sirtuin biology, although the mammalian enzymes acquired lineage-specific regulatory domains. The relationship is directional: yeast Sir2 is the evolutionary precursor, not a downstream effector, of the SIRT1–7 family.

nodes.label: Sirtuins (SIRT1–7)
nodes.description: Sir2 (silent information regulator 2) is the founding member of the sirtuin family, first identified in Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a regulator of mating-type locus silencing and replicative lifespan. The seven mammalian paralogues SIRT1–SIRT7 evolved from this ancestral NAD+-dependent deacetylase, retaining the conserved catalytic core while diversifying in subcellular localization and substrate repertoire. This phylogenetic continuity means insights from yeast Sir2 historically informed mammalian sirtuin biology, although the mammalian enzymes acquired lineage-specific regulatory domains. The relationship is directional: yeast Sir2 is the evolutionary precursor, not a downstream effector, of the SIRT1–7 family.

nodes.label: Mono-ADP-ribosyl transferases
nodes.description: Beyond deacetylation, several sirtuins catalyze mono-ADP-ribosylation, transferring the ADP-ribose moiety of NAD+ onto target proteins without removing an acetyl group. SIRT4 and SIRT6 prominently display this mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase activity, with SIRT6 using it to recruit heterochromatin proteins such as KAP1/HP1α. The directionality is that NAD+ is the donor and the target lysine (or other residue) is the acceptor, producing a mono-ADP-ribosylated product rather than free OAADPr. Biologically, ADP-ribosylation allows sirtuins to regulate processes—such as DNA repair and LINE-1 repression—distinct from their deacetylase functions.

nodes.label: Sirtuin deacetylation reaction
nodes.description: During the sirtuin-catalyzed deacetylation of a lysine, NAD+ is cleaved between its nicotinamide and ADP-ribose moieties, and the acetyl group is transferred to the ADP-ribose to generate 2'-O-acetyl-ADP-ribose (OAADPr) plus free nicotinamide. OAADPr is a stoichiometric by-product, released in equimolar amounts with the deacetylated substrate on every catalytic cycle. This molecule is not merely waste: it binds and activates the TRPM2 cation channel, linking sirtuin activity to calcium signaling and cellular stress responses. A caveat is that OAADPr accumulation can itself feed back on cellular metabolism, and its levels reflect the integrated deacetylase flux of the cell.

nodes.label: OAADPr (2'-O-acetyl-ADP-ribose)
nodes.description: During the sirtuin-catalyzed deacetylation of a lysine, NAD+ is cleaved between its nicotinamide and ADP-ribose moieties, and the acetyl group is transferred to the ADP-ribose to generate 2'-O-acetyl-ADP-ribose (OAADPr) plus free nicotinamide. OAADPr is a stoichiometric by-product, released in equimolar amounts with the deacetylated substrate on every catalytic cycle. This molecule is not merely waste: it binds and activates the TRPM2 cation channel, linking sirtuin activity to calcium signaling and cellular stress responses. A caveat is that OAADPr accumulation can itself feed back on cellular metabolism, and its levels reflect the integrated deacetylase flux of the cell.

nodes.label: OAADPr
nodes.description: OAADPr (2'-O-acetyl-ADP-ribose) binds to the cytoplasmic N-terminal domain of the TRPM2 non-selective cation channel, promoting its opening and calcium influx into the cytosol. Because OAADPr is generated directly by sirtuin deacetylase activity, TRPM2 activation acts as a sensor of cellular sirtuin flux and NAD+ utilization. The directionality is unidirectional under basal conditions: sirtuin activity produces OAADPr, which then gates TRPM2, rather than TRPM2 regulating sirtuins. This coupling provides a mechanistic link between metabolic state, redox stress, and calcium-dependent processes such as insulin secretion and apoptotic signaling.

nodes.label: TRPM2
nodes.description: OAADPr (2'-O-acetyl-ADP-ribose) binds to the cytoplasmic N-terminal domain of the TRPM2 non-selective cation channel, promoting its opening and calcium influx into the cytosol. Because OAADPr is generated directly by sirtuin deacetylase activity, TRPM2 activation acts as a sensor of cellular sirtuin flux and NAD+ utilization. The directionality is unidirectional under basal conditions: sirtuin activity produces OAADPr, which then gates TRPM2, rather than TRPM2 regulating sirtuins. This coupling provides a mechanistic link between metabolic state, redox stress, and calcium-dependent processes such as insulin secretion and apoptotic signaling.

nodes.label: Nucleus (euchromatin)
nodes.description: SIRT1 is the predominant nuclear sirtuin and is enriched at euchromatic regions, where it deacetylates both histones and many transcriptional regulators to shape gene expression. Its nuclear residence allows it to directly access chromatin and nuclear factors such as p53, FOXO, NF-κB, and PGC-1α. Subcellular localization is dynamic and can shift toward DNA double-strand break foci during genotoxic stress, reflecting its role in DNA repair. A caveat is that a fraction of SIRT1 is also cytosolic, so 'nuclear' describes its dominant but not exclusive compartment.

nodes.label: Cytoplasm
nodes.description: SIRT2 is the predominantly cytoplasmic sirtuin and is most abundant in the cytosol, where it deacetylates α-tubulin and a range of metabolic and regulatory proteins. Its localization is cell-cycle regulated, with SIRT2 accumulating and being hyperphosphorylated as cells transit the G2/M boundary. The cytoplasmic residence underpins its roles in microtubule dynamics, mitosis, and cytoplasmic autophagy regulation rather than direct chromatin modification. Note that SIRT2 can also shuttle to the nucleus under certain stress conditions, so localization is not absolute.

nodes.label: SIRT4
nodes.description: SIRT4 resides in the mitochondrial matrix and acts mainly as a mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase on metabolic enzymes such as GDH and MTPα rather than as a conventional deacetylase. Its mitochondrial localization enables direct control of amino-acid and fatty-acid fueling of the TCA cycle, braking anaplerosis and oxidative catabolism. Directionally, SIRT4 is positioned to restrain mitochondrial anabolism, reducing nutrient-driven ATP generation and insulin secretion under replete conditions. This braking role complements SIRT3, which promotes oxidative catabolism, so the SIRT3/SIRT4 balance determines whether mitochondria oxidize or conserve fuel.

nodes.label: SIRT5
nodes.description: SIRT5 localizes to the mitochondrial matrix and is specialized for removing lysine succinyl, malonyl, and glutaryl groups from metabolic enzymes including CPS1, HMGCS2, and enzymes of β-oxidation and the TCA cycle. Its mitochondrial residence makes it a key regulator of catabolic flux during fasting, coordinating nitrogen clearance, ketogenesis, and fatty-acid oxidation. Through desuccinylation it optimizes energy production and redox balance, activating urea-cycle and lipid-catabolism machinery when nutrient supply demands it.

nodes.label: Nucleus (heterochromatin)
nodes.description: SIRT6 is a nuclear sirtuin enriched at heterochromatic and telomeric regions, where it deacetylates H3K9 and H3K56 and performs mono-ADP-ribosylation of KAP1. Its heterochromatin association is critical for genome stability, telomere maintenance, and suppression of repetitive elements such as LINE-1. SIRT6 thus integrates chromatin regulation with metabolic control of glycolysis, DNA repair, and inflammation. Loss of SIRT6 produces a pronounced premature-aging phenotype, highlighting its non-redundant role in the nucleus.

nodes.label: SIRT7
nodes.description: SIRT7 is concentrated in the nucleolus, the site of ribosomal DNA transcription and ribosome biogenesis, where it deacetylates histone H3K18 and regulates RNA polymerase I. Its nucleolar residence positions it to control rRNA synthesis and, consequently, protein synthetic capacity and growth. SIRT7 also deacetylates extra-nucleolar targets such as GATA4 and SMAD3, linking it to cardiac and fibrotic pathways. Deficiency of SIRT7 yields extensive myocardial fibrosis and cardiomyopathy, revealing its importance in stress responses of the heart.

nodes.label: Nucleolus
nodes.description: SIRT7 is concentrated in the nucleolus, the site of ribosomal DNA transcription and ribosome biogenesis, where it deacetylates histone H3K18 and regulates RNA polymerase I. Its nucleolar residence positions it to control rRNA synthesis and, consequently, protein synthetic capacity and growth. SIRT7 also deacetylates extra-nucleolar targets such as GATA4 and SMAD3, linking it to cardiac and fibrotic pathways. Deficiency of SIRT7 yields extensive myocardial fibrosis and cardiomyopathy, revealing its importance in stress responses of the heart.

nodes.label: ADP-ribosylation
nodes.description: SIRT4 functions principally as a mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase, using NAD+ to attach a single ADP-ribose group to target lysines rather than removing acetyl marks. Its best-characterized ADP-ribosylation target is glutamate dehydrogenase, whose activity it inhibits to dampen amino-acid-stimulated insulin secretion. This enzymatic orientation means SIRT4 generally acts as a metabolic suppressor within mitochondria, opposing anabolic and growth signals. A caveat is that SIRT4's deacetylase activity is weak in vitro, so ADP-ribosylation is its physiologically dominant modality.

nodes.label: Drosophila melanogaster
nodes.description: Dietary restriction in Drosophila extends lifespan and, as in yeast, this benefit requires the dSir2 (Sir2) gene, indicating evolutionary conservation of the sirtuin-mediated CR pathway. The effect is thought to operate through improved protein homeostasis, stress resistance, and metabolic efficiency rather than simple calorie shortage. Directionally, reduced nutrient signaling upstream engages dSir2 to produce the longevity phenotype. Caveats include that the magnitude and requirement vary with sex, genetic background, and the precise restriction paradigm used.

nodes.label: SIRT1 expression
nodes.description: In rodents, caloric restriction raises SIRT1 levels in multiple tissues, and this elevation is linked to reduced inflammatory and oxidative responses. Higher SIRT1 expression translates into enhanced deacetylation of targets such as NF-κB, FOXO, and PGC-1α, promoting stress resistance and metabolic health. The directionality is that CR is the upstream stimulus and increased SIRT1 abundance/activity the downstream mediator. This adaptation is considered a key explanation for the anti-aging and disease-protective effects of CR in mammals.

nodes.label: NAD+/nicotinamide ratio (brain)
nodes.description: Caloric restriction elevates the brain NAD+/nicotinamide ratio, which both supplies more co-substrate for sirtuins and relieves nicotinamide-mediated feedback inhibition of SIRT1. The resulting gain in sirtuin activity supports neuronal stress resistance, mitochondrial function, and suppression of neuroinflammatory signaling. The relationship is directional: CR shifts the ratio upward, which then potentiates sirtuin-dependent protective programs. This mechanism is frequently invoked to explain CR's protective effects against age-related cognitive decline and neurodegenerative pathology.

nodes.label: SIR2 overexpression (yeast)
nodes.description: Integration of an extra SIR2 copy in yeast increases replicative lifespan by up to about 30%, implicating Sir2 dosage directly in longevity. The mechanism involves reinforced silencing at rDNA repeats, which reduces spurious recombination and the accumulation of extrachromosomal rDNA circles that drive aging. This is a gain-of-function, directional relationship: more Sir2 yields longer lifespan, though the effect saturates and very high doses can be detrimental. The finding established the foundational idea that boosting sirtuin activity can extend lifespan in a simple eukaryote.

nodes.label: sir-2.1 overexpression (C. elegans)
nodes.description: A chromosomal duplication that increases sir-2.1 dosage in C. elegans extends lifespan by up to approximately 50%, paralleling the yeast finding in a multicellular organism. The longevity effect depends on intact insulin/IGF-1-like signaling, because sir-2.1 acts downstream of the DAF-2 pathway to promote stress resistance. The relationship is directional: elevated sir-2.1 produces the lifespan gain. A key caveat is that the requirement for DAF-16 (FOXO) ties sirtuin longevity to the conserved FOXO transcription-factor network.
