nodes.label: Relocalization of Chromatin Modifiers (RCM) Hypothesis
nodes.source_file: _document_ - relocalization of sirtuins - chromatin modifiers, grok.md
nodes.description: The Relocalization of Chromatin Modifiers (RCM) Hypothesis is a key framework in aging biology, primarily developed by David Sinclair and colleagues. It proposes that aging in eukaryotes results largely from the progressive loss of epigenetic information due to the repeated relocalization of chromatin-modifying proteins during DNA repair. Chromatin modifiers normally sit at specific genomic loci to maintain gene expression patterns that define cell identity, but are recruited to damage sites during repair, temporarily disrupting their original positions and altering local gene expression.

nodes.label: aging results from progressive loss of epigenetic information
nodes.source_file: _document_ - relocalization of sirtuins - chromatin modifiers, grok.md
nodes.description: The Relocalization of Chromatin Modifiers (RCM) Hypothesis is a key framework in aging biology, primarily developed by David Sinclair and colleagues. It proposes that aging in eukaryotes results largely from the progressive loss of epigenetic information due to the repeated relocalization of chromatin-modifying proteins during DNA repair. Chromatin modifiers normally sit at specific genomic loci to maintain gene expression patterns that define cell identity, but are recruited to damage sites during repair, temporarily disrupting their original positions and altering local gene expression.

nodes.label: Chromatin modifiers (SIRT1, SIRT6, HDAC1, PARP1)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - relocalization of sirtuins - chromatin modifiers, grok.md
nodes.description: Chromatin modifiers including sirtuins like SIRT1 and SIRT6, as well as HDAC1 and PARP1, normally sit at specific genomic loci to maintain proper gene expression patterns that define cell identity. When DNA damage, especially double-strand breaks, occurs, these proteins are recruited to damage sites to assist in repair. This temporarily disrupts their original positions, altering local gene expression, and repeated relocalization over a lifetime contributes to the progressive loss of epigenetic information.

nodes.label: DNA damage sites during repair
nodes.source_file: _document_ - relocalization of sirtuins - chromatin modifiers, grok.md
nodes.description: Chromatin modifiers including sirtuins like SIRT1 and SIRT6, as well as HDAC1 and PARP1, normally sit at specific genomic loci to maintain proper gene expression patterns that define cell identity. When DNA damage, especially double-strand breaks, occurs, these proteins are recruited to damage sites to assist in repair. This temporarily disrupts their original positions, altering local gene expression, and repeated relocalization over a lifetime contributes to the progressive loss of epigenetic information.

nodes.label: RCM (Relocalization of Chromatin Modifiers)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - relocalization of sirtuins - chromatin modifiers, grok.md
nodes.description: RCM likely evolved as a beneficial short-term response: relocalizing modifiers to damage sites helps cells survive acute threats by prioritizing repair and survival over normal gene regulation. In youth this is advantageous, but over a lifetime the cumulative failure to reset becomes detrimental, contributing to aging. This trade-off, where a trait that benefits early survival becomes harmful later in life, is the classic signature of antagonistic pleiotropy.

nodes.label: Antagonistic Pleiotropy
nodes.source_file: _document_ - relocalization of sirtuins - chromatin modifiers, grok.md
nodes.description: RCM likely evolved as a beneficial short-term response: relocalizing modifiers to damage sites helps cells survive acute threats by prioritizing repair and survival over normal gene regulation. In youth this is advantageous, but over a lifetime the cumulative failure to reset becomes detrimental, contributing to aging. This trade-off, where a trait that benefits early survival becomes harmful later in life, is the classic signature of antagonistic pleiotropy.

nodes.label: epigenetic information
nodes.source_file: _document_ - relocalization of sirtuins - chromatin modifiers, grok.md
nodes.description: Partial reprogramming (e.g., via Yamanaka factors) can reset epigenetic information, supporting the idea that aging is reversible at the information level. This connection to cellular reprogramming complements the RCM hypothesis, which frames aging as an epigenetic software problem rather than purely hardware (mutation) damage. Because epigenetic changes can potentially be reset, unlike permanent mutations, reprogramming-based approaches offer a route to restoring youthful gene expression patterns.

nodes.label: DSB repair and RCM
nodes.source_file: _document_ - relocalization of sirtuins - chromatin modifiers, grok.md
nodes.description: DSB repair and RCM may advance epigenetic clocks by affecting DNA methylation machinery (e.g., TET enzymes and DNMTs). Because the response to DNA damage follows conserved mechanisms, aging becomes somewhat predictable despite random damage, leading to consistent epigenetic drift. Directionally, DNA damage repair and the consequent relocalization of chromatin modifiers sit upstream of clock-measured epigenetic age acceleration, linking RCM to quantitative measures of biological aging.

nodes.description: SIRT1 upregulates ADAM-10 (α-secretase), shifting APP processing away from amyloid-β and protecting against Alzheimer's pathology.

nodes.label: NBS1

nodes.description: SIRT1 deacetylates NBS1 (MRE11 complex), facilitating DNA double-strand-break sensing/repair.

nodes.description: SIRT1 deacetylates XPA, a core nucleotide-excision-repair factor, enhancing DNA-damage recognition.

nodes.label: WRN
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT1 deacetylates and activates the Werner syndrome helicase WRN, linking SIRT1 to DNA repair and genomic stability.

nodes.description: SIRT1 activates FOXO1/FOXO3 by deacetylation, coupling NAD+ sensing to stress resistance and metabolic gene programs (Brunet 2004 PMID 15066266).

nodes.description: SIRT1 inhibits p66Shc, a ROS-generating adaptor, reducing oxidative stress and aging-related damage.

nodes.label: vascular protection
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT1 participates in vascular protection, one of its core physiological roles, tied to NAD+-dependent deacetylation and caloric-restriction-mediated longevity (Sinclair & Guarente sirtuin framework).

nodes.label: H3K56ac
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 deacetylates H3K56ac, contributing to mitotic chromatin organization and genome stability.

nodes.label: H4K16ac
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 deacetylates histone H4 Lys16 during the G2/M transition, promoting mitotic chromatin condensation (Vaquero et al., 2006, Genes Dev 20:1256-1261, PMID 16648462).

nodes.label: G6PD
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 activates G6PD via deacetylation (e.g., FOXO, c-Myc, G6PD, PEPCK), influencing transcription, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, and redox balance.

nodes.label: PEPCK
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 activates PEPCK via deacetylation (e.g., FOXO, c-Myc, G6PD, PEPCK), influencing transcription, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, and redox balance.

nodes.label: cell-cycle control
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 participates in cell-cycle control; as the predominantly cytoplasmic sirtuin it governs tubulin deacetylation, cell-cycle control, and cytoplasmic metabolic/inflammatory regulation.

nodes.label: carbohydrate metabolism
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 participates in carbohydrate metabolism; as the predominantly cytoplasmic sirtuin it governs tubulin deacetylation, cell-cycle control, and cytoplasmic metabolic/inflammatory regulation.

nodes.label: lipid metabolism
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 participates in lipid metabolism; as the predominantly cytoplasmic sirtuin it governs tubulin deacetylation, cell-cycle control, and cytoplasmic metabolic/inflammatory regulation.

nodes.label: tubulin deacetylation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 participates in tubulin deacetylation; as the predominantly cytoplasmic sirtuin it governs tubulin deacetylation, cell-cycle control, and cytoplasmic metabolic/inflammatory regulation.

nodes.label: transcription factor deacetylation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 participates in transcription factor deacetylation; as the predominantly cytoplasmic sirtuin it governs tubulin deacetylation, cell-cycle control, and cytoplasmic metabolic/inflammatory regulation.

nodes.label: anti-inflammatory
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 participates in anti-inflammatory; as the predominantly cytoplasmic sirtuin it governs tubulin deacetylation, cell-cycle control, and cytoplasmic metabolic/inflammatory regulation.

nodes.label: H3K9
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT3 deacetylates H3K9ac, a minor histone target linking SIRT3 to chromatin regulation in mitochondria-associated nuclei.

nodes.label: H4K14ac
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT3 deacetylates H4K14ac, part of its mitochondrial/cytonuclear deacetylase program.

nodes.label: DLD (dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT3 deacetylates dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (DLD), supporting α-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex activity and mitochondrial metabolism.

nodes.label: fatty acid oxidation (FAO)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT3 promotes fatty-acid oxidation by deacetylating metabolic enzymes of β-oxidation and the TCA cycle.

nodes.label: complex I/III
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT3 deacetylates subunits of respiratory-chain complexes I and III, maintaining basal ATP levels and electron-transport efficiency (Ahn et al., 2008, PNAS 105:14447-14452, PMID 18794531).

nodes.label: lipogenesis
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT3 inhibits lipogenesis (e.g., p53, ROS, lipogenesis) by deacetylating upstream regulators, protecting against damage and tumorigenesis.

nodes.label: mitochondrial enzyme deacetylation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT3 participates in mitochondrial enzyme deacetylation; as the principal mitochondrial sirtuin it deacetylates respiratory, antioxidant, and TCA-cycle enzymes to tune bioenergetics (Houtkooper et al., 2012).

nodes.label: ATP production
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT3 participates in ATP production; as the principal mitochondrial sirtuin it deacetylates respiratory, antioxidant, and TCA-cycle enzymes to tune bioenergetics (Houtkooper et al., 2012).

nodes.label: ROS management
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT3 participates in ROS management; as the principal mitochondrial sirtuin it deacetylates respiratory, antioxidant, and TCA-cycle enzymes to tune bioenergetics (Houtkooper et al., 2012).

nodes.label: ketogenesis
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT3 participates in ketogenesis; as the principal mitochondrial sirtuin it deacetylates respiratory, antioxidant, and TCA-cycle enzymes to tune bioenergetics (Houtkooper et al., 2012).

nodes.label: cell death regulation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT3 participates in cell death regulation; as the principal mitochondrial sirtuin it deacetylates respiratory, antioxidant, and TCA-cycle enzymes to tune bioenergetics (Houtkooper et al., 2012).

nodes.label: PDH (Pyruvate Dehydrogenase)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT4 (as a lipoamidase) inhibits the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, modulating glucose-derived acetyl-CoA entry into the TCA cycle.

nodes.label: ATP homeostasis
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT4 participates in ATP homeostasis; as a mitochondrial ADP-ribosyltransferase it restrains amino-acid/fatty-acid fueling and insulin secretion (Haigis 2006 PMID 16959573).

nodes.label: CPS1 (Carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase 1)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT5 deacetylates (and desuccinylates) carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase 1 (CPS1), the rate-limiting urea-cycle enzyme, enhancing ammonia detoxification; SIRT5-KO mice show elevated blood ammonia under fasting (Nakagawa et al., 2009, Cell 137:560-570, PMID 19410549; Du et al., 2011, Science 334:806-809, PMID 22076378).

nodes.label: GLS (glutaminase)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT5 inhibits glutaminase (GLS) via desuccinylation, suppressing glutaminolysis in cancer metabolism.

nodes.label: urea cycle
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT5 participates in urea cycle; as a mitochondrial desuccinylase/demalonylase it regulates urea cycle, ketogenesis, and redox enzymes (Du 2011 PMID 22076378; Nakagawa 2009 PMID 19410549).

nodes.label: ATP synthesis regulation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT5 participates in ATP synthesis regulation; as a mitochondrial desuccinylase/demalonylase it regulates urea cycle, ketogenesis, and redox enzymes (Du 2011 PMID 22076378; Nakagawa 2009 PMID 19410549).

nodes.label: intracellular signaling
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT5 participates in intracellular signaling; as a mitochondrial desuccinylase/demalonylase it regulates urea cycle, ketogenesis, and redox enzymes (Du 2011 PMID 22076378; Nakagawa 2009 PMID 19410549).

nodes.label: ammonia detoxification
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT5 participates in ammonia detoxification; as a mitochondrial desuccinylase/demalonylase it regulates urea cycle, ketogenesis, and redox enzymes (Du 2011 PMID 22076378; Nakagawa 2009 PMID 19410549).

nodes.label: H2BK12
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT6 deacetylates H2BK12ac, contributing to its chromatin-silencing/heterochromatin program.

nodes.label: DNA-PKcs
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT6 promotes DNA-PKcs mobilization/stability at DSBs, enhancing repair (McCord 2009 PMID 20157594).

nodes.label: CCNDBP1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT6 deacetylates/activates CCNDBP1 (Cyclin D-binding protein 1), linking it to cell-cycle and stress responses.

nodes.label: RELA
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT6 represses RELA/p65 transcriptional activity via chromatin deacetylation.

nodes.label: IGF-1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT6 inhibits IGF-1/AKT signaling (e.g., co-repressing c-Jun), protecting against cardiac hypertrophy.

nodes.label: c-Jun
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT6 co-represses c-Jun to inhibit IGF-AKT hypertrophic signaling.

nodes.label: telomere function
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT6 participates in telomere function; the nuclear/chromatin sirtuin guards genome integrity, telomeres, metabolism, and inflammation (Mostoslavsky 2006; Mao 2011 PMID 21680843).

nodes.label: metabolic homeostasis
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT6 participates in metabolic homeostasis; the nuclear/chromatin sirtuin guards genome integrity, telomeres, metabolism, and inflammation (Mostoslavsky 2006; Mao 2011 PMID 21680843).

nodes.label: genomic stability
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT6 participates in genomic stability; the nuclear/chromatin sirtuin guards genome integrity, telomeres, metabolism, and inflammation (Mostoslavsky 2006; Mao 2011 PMID 21680843).

nodes.label: H2A
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT7 deacetylates histone H2A, contributing to its nucleolar/chromatin regulatory program.

nodes.label: H2B
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT7 deacetylates histone H2B as part of its chromatin modification repertoire.

nodes.label: RNA Polymerase I
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT7 deacetylates and regulates RNA Polymerase I transcription at rDNA, controlling ribosome biogenesis (Ford et al., 2006).

nodes.label: rDNA transcription
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT7 participates in rDNA transcription; the nucleolar sirtuin regulates rDNA transcription and histone desuccinylation (Barber 2012 PMID 22722849; Ford 2006).

nodes.label: histone desuccinylation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT7 participates in histone desuccinylation; the nucleolar sirtuin regulates rDNA transcription and histone desuccinylation (Barber 2012 PMID 22722849; Ford 2006).

nodes.label: BubR1 progeroid mice
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 extends lifespan in BubR1 progeroid mice, as reported in the longevity/aging literature, supporting a role in cell-cycle and proteostatic regulation.

nodes.label: Human aging (longevity)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT3 is associated with Human aging (longevity); mitochondrial sirtuin activity and SIRT3 variants are linked to human longevity.

nodes.label: SIRT6 loss
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: Zhao et al. note that loss of SIRT6 causes severe metabolic defects and rapid aging, positioning SIRT6 as holding the most potential for actual mammalian life-span extension.

nodes.label: severe metabolic defects and rapid aging
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: Zhao et al. note that loss of SIRT6 causes severe metabolic defects and rapid aging, positioning SIRT6 as holding the most potential for actual mammalian life-span extension.
nodes.norm_label: severe metabolic defects and rapid aging

nodes.label: premature ageing
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: Global SIRT7 depletion contributes to premature ageing, especially in the backbone, white adipose tissue, and the heart.

nodes.label: leukemia, DMBA-induced mammary tumors, skin cancer, prostate cancer
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: Resveratrol exhibits chemopreventive activity against leukemia, DMBA-induced mammary tumors, skin cancer, and other malignancies, in part through SIRT1-dependent and -independent pathways (reviewed in the sirtuin literature; Baur 2006 PMID 17086191).
nodes.norm_label: leukemia, dmba-induced mammary tumors, skin cancer, prostate cancer

nodes.label: K-type allosteric activation (lowers Km)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: Sirtuin-activating compounds (STACs) such as resveratrol engage a 'K-type' allosteric mechanism that lowers the Michaelis constant (Km) of SIRT1 for both the acetylated substrate and NAD+, increasing catalytic efficiency (Howitz 2003 PMID 12805428; structurally characterized in SIRT1-resveratrol complexes, PMID 26109052).

nodes.label: NAD-boosting molecules (NMN, NR)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: NAD+-boosting molecules (NMN, NR) raise cellular NAD+, relieving nicotinamide feedback inhibition and activating all seven sirtuins (SIRT1-SIRT7).

nodes.label: all seven sirtuins
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: NAD+-boosting molecules (NMN, NR) raise cellular NAD+, relieving nicotinamide feedback inhibition and activating all seven sirtuins (SIRT1-SIRT7).

nodes.label: CD38 inhibitors (apigenin, quercetin)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: CD38 consumes NAD+; inhibiting it (apigenin, quercetin) boosts NAD+ availability, the obligate co-substrate for all sirtuins (and thus for SIRT1-SIRT7 activity).

nodes.label: NAD+ (sirtuin co-substrate)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: CD38 consumes NAD+; inhibiting it (apigenin, quercetin) boosts NAD+ availability, the obligate co-substrate for all sirtuins (and thus for SIRT1-SIRT7 activity).

nodes.label: SIRT1 brain-specific knockout
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: Brain-specific SIRT1 knockout elevates β-amyloid plaques and gliosis, implicating SIRT1 in Alzheimer's protection (per the review's neurobiology section).

nodes.label: β-amyloid plaques and gliosis (Alzheimer's disease)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: Brain-specific SIRT1 knockout elevates β-amyloid plaques and gliosis, implicating SIRT1 in Alzheimer's protection (per the review's neurobiology section).

nodes.label: Huntington's disease models
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT1 conferred neuroprotection in three different mouse models of Huntington's disease; overexpression attenuated mutant huntingtin neurotoxicity.

nodes.label: SIRT1 overexpression
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT1 overexpression reduces α-synuclein aggregates, supporting a role in Parkinson's protection (via FOXO/autophagy pathways).

nodes.label: α-synuclein aggregates (Parkinson's disease)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT1 overexpression reduces α-synuclein aggregates, supporting a role in Parkinson's protection (via FOXO/autophagy pathways).

nodes.label: Endothelial SIRT1 depletion
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: Endothelial SIRT1 depletion is associated with cardiovascular diseases, reflecting SIRT1's vascular protective (eNOS/NO, anti-inflammatory) roles.

nodes.label: cardiovascular diseases
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: Endothelial SIRT1 depletion is associated with cardiovascular diseases, reflecting SIRT1's vascular protective (eNOS/NO, anti-inflammatory) roles.

nodes.label: atherosclerosis (inhibits VSMC hypertrophy)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT1 counteracts atherosclerosis by inhibiting VSMC hypertrophy and NF-κB-driven inflammation.

nodes.label: cardiac hypertrophy during ageing
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT3 prevents cardiac hypertrophy during ageing; its deacetylase activity protects against age-related cardiac hypertrophy.

nodes.label: SIRT6 expression
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT6 expression blocks the development of cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure.

nodes.label: cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT6 expression blocks the development of cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure.

nodes.label: SIRT7 deletion
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT7 deletion leads to heart hypertrophy, fibrosis, lipofuscin accumulation, and inflammatory cardiomyopathy that worsens with age.

nodes.label: heart hypertrophy, fibrosis, inflammatory cardiomyopathy
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT7 deletion leads to heart hypertrophy, fibrosis, lipofuscin accumulation, and inflammatory cardiomyopathy that worsens with age.

nodes.label: obesity-associated metabolic derangement
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT1 overexpression protects against obesity-associated metabolic derangement via deacetylation of metabolic transcription factors.

nodes.label: SIRT1 and SIRT1 activators
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT1 and its activators prevent/reverse insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes by enhancing deacetylation of metabolic regulators (e.g., PGC-1α, FOXO; Rodgers 2005 PMID 15931387).

nodes.label: insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT1 and its activators prevent/reverse insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes by enhancing deacetylation of metabolic regulators (e.g., PGC-1α, FOXO; Rodgers 2005 PMID 15931387).

nodes.label: PEPCK (gluconeogenesis)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 activates PEPCK (gluconeogenesis) via deacetylation (e.g., FOXO, c-Myc, G6PD, PEPCK), influencing transcription, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, and redox balance.

nodes.label: GDH (gluconeogenesis from amino acids)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT3 activates GDH to support gluconeogenesis from amino acids via deacetylation.

nodes.label: HIF1α (inhibits glycolysis)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT3 indirectly destabilizes HIF1α and subsequently inhibits glycolysis and glucose oxidation.

nodes.label: diet-induced obesity
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT6 overexpression protects mice from diet-induced obesity, with increased glucose tolerance and reduced fat accumulation.

nodes.label: SIRT7 knockout
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT7 knockout mice are resistant to glucose intolerance and show improved insulin sensitivity on a high-fat diet.

nodes.label: insulin sensitivity / glucose intolerance
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT7 knockout mice are resistant to glucose intolerance and show improved insulin sensitivity on a high-fat diet.

nodes.label: cancer (tumor suppressor and promoter)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT1 has a dual role in cancer (tumor suppressor and promoter): it can act as tumor suppressor (via p53/β-catenin/survivin restraint) or tumor promoter (via p53 deacetylation), depending on context.

nodes.label: tumor suppressor protein (TSP)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT6 is described as tumor suppressor protein (TSP); it is a tumor-suppressor protein whose deficiency causes genomic instability and premature aging.

nodes.label: oncogene (upregulated in cancers)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT7 is described as oncogene (upregulated in cancers); it is upregulated in cancers and acts as an oncogene in several contexts (Barber 2012 PMID 22722849).

nodes.label: tumor suppressor (downregulated in cancers)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT4 is described as tumor suppressor (downregulated in cancers); it is a tumor suppressor downregulated in multiple cancers (Wu et al., 2022).

nodes.label: tumor suppressor (decreased in breast/ovarian cancers)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT3 is described as tumor suppressor (decreased in breast/ovarian cancers); it is a tumor suppressor frequently downregulated in breast/ovarian cancers (Massudi et al., 2012).

nodes.label: Lifespan extension
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT1 is a central mediator of healthspan and longevity: its activity declines with age as NAD+ falls, and genetic/pharmacologic (resveratrol, NAD+ precursors) activation extends lifespan in model organisms; SIRT1-dependent deacetylation of p53, FOXOs, and NF-κB underpins these effects (Giblin et al., 2014, Sirtuins: Guardians of Mammalian Healthspan; Satoh et al., 2013 brain-specific SIRT1-overexpression lifespan extension, PMID 24011076).

nodes.label: Erβ
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: Estrogen receptor β (Erβ) signaling upregulates SIRT1 expression and activity, linking estrogens to SIRT1-mediated metabolic and neuroprotective programs; estrogen-replacement models show increased SIRT1 levels and reduced oxidative damage (source review Table 3 lists Erβ as a positive SIRT1 regulator).

nodes.label: FOXO3
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: FOXO3 and SIRT1 form a feed-forward stress-resistance loop: SIRT1 deacetylates FOXO3 to shunt it toward stress-resistance and metabolic genes, while FOXO3 transactivates SIRT1 expression; this mutually reinforcing pair is central to longevity-associated signalling (Brunet et al., 2004, PMID 15066266).

nodes.label: PAI-1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: PAI-1, a senescence-associated secreted factor (SASP), suppresses SIRT1 expression, and SIRT1 reciprocally binds the PAI-1 promoter to deacetylate H4K16 and repress its transcription; elevation of PAI-1 with age thus contributes to SIRT1 decline and the senescence phenotype (Kortlever et al., 2006, Nat Cell Biol; Wan et al., 2014, Aging Cell, PMID 24649892).

nodes.label: p16INK4a
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: p16INK4a (CDKN2A) accumulation with age drives senescence and opposes SIRT1-dependent replicative programs; SIRT1 represses p16INK4a expression via promoter deacetylation and via the Akt/p70S6K1 axis, and p16INK4a upregulation is a hallmark of aging-related SIRT1 decline (Li & Tollefsbol, 2011, PLoS One 6:e17421, PMID 21390332).

nodes.label: Cyclin D1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: Cyclin D1/CDK4 and the cyclin B-Cdk1 complex regulate SIRT1 by phosphorylation (massive phosphorylation is required for SIRT1 cell-cycle function), and cyclin D1 opposes SIRT1-dependent regulation of cell-cycle genes in proliferative contexts; Table 3 lists Cyclin D1 among negative SIRT1 regulators (Sasaki et al., 2008, PLoS One 3:e4020, PMID 19015735).

nodes.label: mTOR/S6K pathway
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: mTORC1/S6K1 signaling opposes SIRT1-promoted catabolic and stress-resistance programs (while SIRT1/SIRT2 deacetylate S6K1 to license its activity, making regulation bidirectional and nutrient-dependent); rapamycin-mediated mTOR inhibition raises NAD+ and benefits from SIRT1 coupling, as reflected in Table 3's classification of the mTOR/S6K pathway as a SIRT1 negative regulator.

nodes.label: Cell cycle regulation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 is a cytoplasmic/mitotic deacetylase that regulates cytokinesis and the G2/M transition, supporting genomic stability and mitotic fidelity; age-related SIRT2 decline impairs these cell-cycle checkpoints (source review; North & Verdin review of SIRT2 mitotic roles).

nodes.label: BubR1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: BubR1, a spindle-assembly-checkpoint protein, is stabilized by SIRT2 deacetylation at Lys668 (SIRT2 knockdown accelerates BubR1 degradation); SIRT2 overexpression increases BubR1 levels and delays aging phenotypes in progeroid mice, so BubR1 is functionally a positive downstream effector of the SIRT2 pathway (North et al., 2014, Cell, PMID 24825348).

nodes.label: PPP
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 deacetylates G6PD in the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) at Lys403, activating it to promote NADPH production and antioxidant defense; the PPP thus serves as a downstream effector of SIRT2 and is listed among its positive pathway regulators (Wang et al., 2014, Cell Metab, PMID 24769394).

nodes.label: FOXOs
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 deacetylates FOXO1 and FOXO3a, promoting their nuclear accumulation and target-gene activation (e.g., stress resistance, gluconeogenesis, and cell survival) in a manner analogous to SIRT1-FOXO coupling, making FOXOs downstream effectors and listed positive regulators of the SIRT2 pathway (Wang et al., 2007, PMID 17521387).

nodes.label: Centenarian-linked SNPs
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT3 G477T and other SNPs are associated with human longevity/healthy aging; the G477T variant (V208I/V184I alleles) improves SIRT3 function or expression and is enriched in centenarian populations in some cohorts (source review; Rose et al., 2003, Alì et al., 2015 reports).

nodes.label: MAPK/ERK
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: MAPK/ERK signaling can oppose SIRT3-dependent metabolic and antioxidant outputs (e.g., ERK-driven proliferative/fibrotic signaling coupling with SIRT3 decrease); Table 3 lists MAPK/ERK among negative regulators of the SIRT3 pathway in aging.

nodes.label: GDH
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: GDH is the primary substrate through which SIRT4 suppresses glutamine metabolism, yet GDH is also listed among negative regulators in Table 3: high GDH activity can outpace SIRT4 ADP-ribosylation under energetic stress, switching cells toward glutaminolysis/fuel oxidation and away from SIRT4-mediated restraint.

nodes.label: Genome stability
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT6 deacetylates H3K9 on telomeric chromatin and suppresses LINE-1 retrotransposon activity, maintaining genome stability and telomere function; SIRT6-deficient cells show genomic instability, telomere defects, and cellular senescence (Michishita et al., 2008; Van Meter et al., 2014).

nodes.label: Telomere maintenance
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT6 deacetylates H3K9 at telomeres and stabilizes WRN helicase, preventing telomere dysfunction-induced senescence; SIRT6-depleted cells undergo accelerated telomere replication problems and senescence (Michishita et al., 2008, Cell; source review).

nodes.label: IGF-1/AKT
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: IGF-1/AKT signaling can modulate SIRT6 activity and expression in metabolic and intestinal-fitness contexts, generally promoting SIRT6-dependent metabolic and tumor-suppressive programs; Table 3 lists IGF-1/AKT among positive regulators of the SIRT6 pathway.

nodes.label: p21 Cip1/Waf1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: p21 (CDKN1A), whose expression is antagonized by SIRT6 (SIRT6 suppresses p21-driven senescence), accumulates with age and opposes SIRT6-regulated cell-cycle and DNA-repair programs; Table 3 lists p21 among negative regulators of SIRT6 (source review).

nodes.label: ICAM-1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: ICAM-1, an endothelial/leukocyte adhesion molecule elevated during inflammation and aging, is a target of SIRT6-repressed NF-κB signaling; its upregulation opposes SIRT6's vascular-protective role and it is listed among negative regulators of the SIRT6 pathway in Table 3.

nodes.label: Epigenetic regulation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT7 deacetylates H3K18 on promoters (Barber et al., 2012, Nature, PMID 22722849) and associates with chromatin remodelers (including PAF1 complex) to regulate rDNA transcription, ribosomal biogenesis, and global gene expression; age-related SIRT7 decline perturbs these epigenetic landscapes (source review; Vakhrusheva et al., 2008).

nodes.label: Stress resistance
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
nodes.description: SIRT7 promotes cellular stress resistance by suppressing ER stress and reactive-ROS programs via Myc-linked silencing of ribosomal protein genes and by stabilizing DNA repair; SIRT7-depleted cells show increased apoptosis and metabolic stress (Shin et al., 2013, PMID 24210820; source review).

nodes.label: β-Catenin
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: SIRT1 catalyzes removal of acetyl groups from β-catenin, and this deacetylation suppresses β-catenin's ability to activate transcription and drive cell proliferation. The modification dampens the Wnt transcriptional output of the protein at target promoters. This is one of the tumor-suppressive arms of SIRT1 in cancer, complementing its deacetylation of the RelA/p65 NF-κB subunit. Directionality is enzymatic: SIRT1 is the deacetylase and β-catenin the substrate, and the net effect is reduced oncogenic transcriptional signaling.

nodes.label: SIRT2 disruption
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Disruption of SIRT2 in the mouse raises the levels of the mitotic regulators Aurora-A and Aurora-B, leading to aneuploidy and mitotic cell death. Because SIRT2 is a tubulin deacetylase and a guardian of mitotic fidelity, its loss impairs the control that normally keeps Aurora kinase abundance in check during division. The directionality is that SIRT2 sits upstream: reduced SIRT2 permits Aurora kinase accumulation, which then destabilizes mitosis. This pathway connects sirtuin biology to chromosome segregation and genomic instability in tumorigenesis.

nodes.label: Aurora Kinase
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Disruption of SIRT2 in the mouse raises the levels of the mitotic regulators Aurora-A and Aurora-B, leading to aneuploidy and mitotic cell death. Because SIRT2 is a tubulin deacetylase and a guardian of mitotic fidelity, its loss impairs the control that normally keeps Aurora kinase abundance in check during division. The directionality is that SIRT2 sits upstream: reduced SIRT2 permits Aurora kinase accumulation, which then destabilizes mitosis. This pathway connects sirtuin biology to chromosome segregation and genomic instability in tumorigenesis.

nodes.label: SIRT2-deficient mice
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: SIRT2-deficient mice develop gender-specific tumors, with females acquiring mammary tumors and males developing hepatocellular carcinoma, matching the mitotic instability produced by elevated Aurora-A/Aurora-B. Consistent with a tumor-suppressor role, human breast cancers and hepatocellular carcinomas often show reduced SIRT2 relative to normal tissue. The relationship is directional: loss of SIRT2 predisposes to these malignancies, whereas SIRT2 expression restrains them. This positions SIRT2 among the sirtuins that act as tumor suppressors in genetic mouse models.

nodes.label: Gender-specific tumorigenesis
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: SIRT2-deficient mice develop gender-specific tumors, with females acquiring mammary tumors and males developing hepatocellular carcinoma, matching the mitotic instability produced by elevated Aurora-A/Aurora-B. Consistent with a tumor-suppressor role, human breast cancers and hepatocellular carcinomas often show reduced SIRT2 relative to normal tissue. The relationship is directional: loss of SIRT2 predisposes to these malignancies, whereas SIRT2 expression restrains them. This positions SIRT2 among the sirtuins that act as tumor suppressors in genetic mouse models.

nodes.label: Cell transformation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: In mice and cultured cells, SIRT3 deficiency favors cell transformation in response to oncogenic Ras or Myc, and the same loss stabilizes HIF-1α with consequent induction of the glycolytic program of the Warburg effect. Because SIRT3 normally governs mitochondrial metabolism, ROS production, and genome stability, its absence releases a permissive environment for oncogenic signaling and metabolic reprogramming. Directionally, SIRT3 acts upstream: reduced SIRT3 allows transformation and Warburg metabolism to proceed, defining its tumor-suppressive role in this context.

nodes.label: Apoptosis in cancer cell lines
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Acute overexpression of SIRT6 in cancer cell lines of different histology induces apoptosis, supporting a tumor-suppressive role for this nuclear sirtuin. The pro-apoptotic activity appears linked to SIRT6's mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase function rather than its deacetylase activity. Directionally, increasing SIRT6 abundance or enzymatic activity triggers cell death in tumor cells. This contrasts with SIRT1's context-dependent duality and stresses that sirtuin outputs in cancer depend on the specific isoform and its dominant catalytic modality.

nodes.label: SIRT2 downregulation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 downregulation or chemical inhibition induces anticancer effects that include p53 accumulation, cell cycle arrest, and apoptosis, mirroring the tumor-suppressive functions of the enzyme. Loss of SIRT2 permits mitotic regulators such as Aurora-A/Aurora-B to accumulate, destabilizing division and forcing checkpoint engagement. The relationship is directional: reduced SIRT2 activity leads to p53 stabilization and arrest. A caveat is that SIRT2 inhibition can be counterproductive in some contexts, notably alongside microtubule inhibitors where it prolongs chronic mitotic arrest and confers resistance.

nodes.label: p53 accumulation and cell cycle arrest
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 downregulation or chemical inhibition induces anticancer effects that include p53 accumulation, cell cycle arrest, and apoptosis, mirroring the tumor-suppressive functions of the enzyme. Loss of SIRT2 permits mitotic regulators such as Aurora-A/Aurora-B to accumulate, destabilizing division and forcing checkpoint engagement. The relationship is directional: reduced SIRT2 activity leads to p53 stabilization and arrest. A caveat is that SIRT2 inhibition can be counterproductive in some contexts, notably alongside microtubule inhibitors where it prolongs chronic mitotic arrest and confers resistance.
nodes.norm_label: p53 accumulation and cell cycle arrest

nodes.label: AC93253
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: AC93253 is a small molecule that inhibits SIRT2 at micromolar concentrations. In leukemia cells, SIRT2 inhibition with AC93253 is accompanied by Akt acetylation, de-phosphorylation, and consequent inhibition, producing antileukemia effects. The directionality is that AC93253 blocks SIRT2, which then removes deacetylation-based control over Akt, shifting it toward an inactive state. This positions AC93253 as both a research tool for SIRT2 biology and an anticancer lead, and connects sirtuin inhibition to PI3K/Akt pathway suppression.

nodes.label: Resistance to microtubule inhibitors
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 inhibition or downregulation appears counterproductive in certain cancer contexts, particularly when combined with microtubule inhibitors, because loss of SIRT2 prolongs chronic mitotic arrest and makes cancer cells resistant to these agents. The enzyme normally helps cells exit mitosis cleanly; without it, cells linger in a prolonged arrested state that selects for survival. Directionally, low SIRT2 activity sits upstream of this resistance phenotype. This caveat limits the general anticancer rationale for SIRT2 inhibition and argues for careful context- and regimen-specific use.

nodes.label: Oral squamous cell carcinoma
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: In oral squamous cell carcinomas, SIRT3 is overexpressed, and its downregulation has antiproliferative activity and sensitizes carcinoma cells to radiation and to cisplatin. This contrasts with SIRT3's broader tumor-suppressive role in mouse models, showing that sirtuin function is context-dependent. Directionally, elevated SIRT3 supports tumor growth and therapy resistance in this cancer type, while SIRT3 loss restores sensitivity. The finding highlights that a single sirtuin can be either protective or oncogenic depending on tumor type and molecular background.

nodes.label: H3K18ac (histone H3 lysine 18)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: SIRT7 promotes tumorigenesis by deacetylating lysine 18 of histone H3, thereby repressing genes with tumor-suppressor function. SIRT7 is stabilized at target promoters through interaction with the ETS-family transcription factor ELK4, and the resulting H3K18 deacetylation is necessary to maintain features such as anchorage-independent growth and loss of contact inhibition. Directionally, SIRT7 activity at H3K18 sits upstream of tumor suppressor gene repression. Loss of SIRT7 reduces the tumorigenicity of human cancer xenografts, making it the clearest pro-oncogenic sirtuin and positioning SIRT7 inhibition as the therapeutic direction.

nodes.label: ELK4
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: The ETS-family transcription factor ELK4 interacts with SIRT7 and stabilizes the deacetylase at target gene promoters, allowing SIRT7 to deacetylate histone H3 at lysine 18 and repress tumor-suppressor genes. This tethering is required to maintain cancer hallmarks such as anchorage-independent growth and loss of contact inhibition. Directionally, ELK4-bound promoter occupancy precedes SIRT7-dependent H3K18 deacetylation. SIRT7 depletion accordingly reduces the tumorigenicity of human cancer xenografts, highlighting the ELK4-SIRT7-H3K18 axis as an oncogenic regulatory circuit.

nodes.label: SIRT7 at target gene promoters
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: The ETS-family transcription factor ELK4 interacts with SIRT7 and stabilizes the deacetylase at target gene promoters, allowing SIRT7 to deacetylate histone H3 at lysine 18 and repress tumor-suppressor genes. This tethering is required to maintain cancer hallmarks such as anchorage-independent growth and loss of contact inhibition. Directionally, ELK4-bound promoter occupancy precedes SIRT7-dependent H3K18 deacetylation. SIRT7 depletion accordingly reduces the tumorigenicity of human cancer xenografts, highlighting the ELK4-SIRT7-H3K18 axis as an oncogenic regulatory circuit.

nodes.label: Rossmann fold domain
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: The conserved catalytic core of sirtuins features a large Rossmann fold domain typical of NAD+ binding proteins, together with a small zinc-binding domain and flexible loops that bring the two domains together around an extended cleft for cofactor and substrate. The Rossmann domain contains six parallel beta-strands and a Gly-X-Gly phosphate-binding motif. Directionally, this architecture is intrinsic to the sirtuin family and explains their strict NAD+ dependence. Understanding the structure underscores why NAD+ analogs and pocket C binders act as sirtuin modulators.

nodes.label: Sirtuin NAD+ binding site
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: The sirtuin NAD+ binding site is divisible into an adenine binding pocket (pocket A), a nicotinamide ribose pocket (pocket B), and a nicotinamide binding pocket (pocket C), formed by the large Rossmann domain and the cofactor binding loop. NAD+ enters a non-productive conformation outside the C pocket until an acetyl-lysine substrate is present, at which point a productive arrangement engages the C pocket. Directionally, this topology defines how inhibitors such as nicotinamide (pocket C) and suramin (pockets B, C, and substrate site) act, and frames structure-based design of sirtuin modulators.

nodes.label: Adenine, nicotinamide-ribose and nicotinamide pockets
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: The sirtuin NAD+ binding site is divisible into an adenine binding pocket (pocket A), a nicotinamide ribose pocket (pocket B), and a nicotinamide binding pocket (pocket C), formed by the large Rossmann domain and the cofactor binding loop. NAD+ enters a non-productive conformation outside the C pocket until an acetyl-lysine substrate is present, at which point a productive arrangement engages the C pocket. Directionally, this topology defines how inhibitors such as nicotinamide (pocket C) and suramin (pockets B, C, and substrate site) act, and frames structure-based design of sirtuin modulators.

nodes.label: NAD+ metabolite sensor (potential)
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: The crystal structure of human SIRT6 reveals a more open conformation than other sirtuins, with the small domain displaced and the cofactor binding loop replaced by a stable single helix. Kinetic and structural data indicate SIRT6 is the unique sirtuin able to bind NAD+ in the absence of an acetyl-lysine substrate. This raises the possibility that SIRT6 evolved away from a conventional NAD+-dependent deacetylase toward a NAD+ metabolite sensor function. Directionally, this distinctive structural feature sets SIRT6 apart from SIRT2, SIRT3, and SIRT5 and informs the search for SIRT6-specific modulators.

nodes.label: Breast, lung, prostate and leukemia cancer cells
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Sirtinol, a hydroxynaphthaldehyde derivative discovered in a phenotypic screen, is active against multiple sirtuin isoforms and has cytotoxic activity against cancer cells of different origins, including breast, lung, prostate, and leukemia cell lines. This broad anticancer activity made sirtinol the founding member of the beta-naphthol inhibitor family and seeded structure-activity programs that produced salermide, cambinol, and splitomicin. Directionally, sirtinol-mediated inhibition of sirtuin activity sits upstream of its cytotoxic effects on malignant cells, though its full target spectrum extends beyond sirtuins.
nodes.norm_label: breast, lung, prostate and leukemia cancer cells

nodes.label: EX-527
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: EX-527, the most potent and selective SIRT1 inhibitor identified from a large high-throughput screen, inhibits SIRT1 at nanomolar concentrations with remarkable selectivity over SIRT2 and SIRT3 and good pharmacokinetic properties. Its anticancer activity as a single agent is weak, but it cooperates with HDAC inhibitors to induce apoptosis in leukemia cells. Directionally, EX-527-mediated SIRT1 blockade combined with broad HDAC inhibition produces a synergistic lethal effect. This positions EX-527 as the standard pharmacological SIRT1 inhibitor and a component of combination anticancer strategies.

nodes.label: HDAC inhibitors
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: EX-527, the most potent and selective SIRT1 inhibitor identified from a large high-throughput screen, inhibits SIRT1 at nanomolar concentrations with remarkable selectivity over SIRT2 and SIRT3 and good pharmacokinetic properties. Its anticancer activity as a single agent is weak, but it cooperates with HDAC inhibitors to induce apoptosis in leukemia cells. Directionally, EX-527-mediated SIRT1 blockade combined with broad HDAC inhibition produces a synergistic lethal effect. This positions EX-527 as the standard pharmacological SIRT1 inhibitor and a component of combination anticancer strategies.

nodes.label: Ro31-8220
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Ro31-8220, a bisindolylmaleimide originally developed as a protein kinase C inhibitor, was identified by screening known kinase inhibitors against SIRT2 on the rationale that sirtuins and protein kinases share an adenosine-binding site. It showed SIRT1/SIRT2 inhibitory properties in the low micromolar range. Directionally, the shared adenosine scaffold allows this kinase inhibitor to engage sirtuin NAD+ binding. Because it retains potent kinase activity, Ro31-8220 serves as both a probe of sirtuin biology and a caution about off-target effects in sirtuin inhibitor studies.

nodes.label: GW5074
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: GW5074, an indolinone compound originally developed as a c-Raf kinase inhibitor, was tested with other kinase inhibitors against SIRT2 because sirtuins and protein kinases share an adenosine-binding site. It showed SIRT1/SIRT2 inhibitory properties in the low micromolar range, placing it alongside the bisindolylmaleimide Ro31-8220 as a kinase-scaffold sirtuin inhibitor. Directionally, GW5074's scaffold enables engagement of the sirtuin NAD+ pocket. Its continued kinase activity complicates interpretation in cells, underscoring the value of structure-based follow-up for selectivity.

nodes.label: NF675
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: NF675 is the product of optimizing the suramin scaffold and is the most potent and selective molecule in the series, showing a 20-fold selectivity ratio for SIRT1 over SIRT2. Suramin itself inhibits SIRT1/SIRT2 at nanomolar concentrations with apparent SIRT1 preference, has anticancer activity, and has been studied in clinical trials. Directionally, NF675 inherits suramin's binding mode while improving isoform selectivity. Despite good potency and selectivity, suramin-derived compounds have modest drug-likeness owing to high molecular weight and anionic character, limiting therapeutic translation.

nodes.label: SIRT5 pockets B, C and substrate-binding site
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Co-crystallization of suramin with human SIRT5 revealed that suramin binds by occupying the nicotinamide ribose pocket (B-pocket), the nicotinamide pocket (C-pocket), and part of the substrate-binding site. This structural insight explains suramin's broad, high-affinity inhibition of multiple sirtuins and informed the design of more selective derivatives such as NF675. Directionally, suramin is the ligand and the SIRT5 catalytic cleft the receptor. The structure also illustrates general principles governing small-molecule engagement of the sirtuin NAD+/substrate channel.
nodes.norm_label: sirt5 pockets b, c and substrate-binding site

nodes.label: Aristoforin
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Aristoforin is one of several natural products reported to inhibit sirtuins at micromolar concentrations, alongside amurensin G, polyphenols, and tanikolide. These compounds expand the chemical diversity of sirtuin inhibitors beyond synthetic scaffolds. Directionally, aristoforin blocks sirtuin deacetylase activity at micromolar potency. As with many natural-product sirtuin modulators, target selectivity, mechanism, and additional cellular targets are less characterized than for synthetic inhibitors, so the anticancer contributions of sirtuin inhibition versus other effects remain to be disentangled.

nodes.label: Amurensin G
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Amurensin G is a resveratrol tetramer natural product reported among compounds that inhibit sirtuins at micromolar concentrations and endowed with anticancer activity. It belongs to a series that includes aristoforin, polyphenols, and tanikolide identified through general screens of structurally diverse natural products. Directionally, amurensin G suppresses sirtuin deacetylase activity. Its isoform selectivity and mechanism are incompletely characterized, and its anticancer effect may involve both sirtuin inhibition and additional natural-product bioactivities.

nodes.label: Tanikolide
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Tanikolide is a natural product reported to inhibit sirtuins at micromolar concentrations, grouped with aristoforin, amurensin G, and polyphenols as structurally diverse natural sirtuin inhibitors. Directionally, tanikolide blocks sirtuin deacetylase activity at micromolar potency. As with companion natural products, its selectivity and the biological significance of its sirtuin inhibition relative to other targets remain less well studied than for synthetic inhibitors such as EX-527 and the tenovins.

nodes.label: Tenovin-1 and Tenovin-6
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Tenovins (tenovin-1 and tenovin-6) are sirtuin inhibitors that block SIRT1/SIRT2-mediated deacetylation of p53, leading to p53 hyperacetylation and activation. Their strong anticancer activity is associated with this p53 activation, which reinstates tumor-suppressive transcription in cancer cells. Directionally, tenovin-mediated sirtuin inhibition sits upstream of p53 activation and tumor suppression, a property shared with HDAC inhibitors and other p53-releasing strategies. Tenovins illustrate the direct link between sirtuin inhibition, p53 acetylation state, and cancer therapy.

nodes.label: Butein
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Butein is a polyphenolic chalcone that was among the first small molecules reported to activate SIRT1, together with resveratrol, piceatannol, quercetin, and myricetin. These polyphenolic STACs (compounds 1-5 of the review's activator figure) established the concept of pharmacological SIRT1 activation. Directionally, butein and its polyphenol congeners enhance SIRT1 deacetylase activity, at least in biochemical assays. As with resveratrol, the in vivo activation mechanism is debated, since activation of SIRT1 by these compounds could frequently only be demonstrated with fluorescently tagged substrates, suggesting possible assay artifacts or indirect cellular effects.

nodes.label: SRT1460
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: SRT1460 is a potent, chemically diverse second-generation sirtuin-activating compound reported alongside SRT1720 and SRT2183 as more effective activators than the polyphenolic STACs. Most compounds of this class were also reported to have anticancer activity. A major caveat is that the mechanism of SRT1460 action remains unclear: activation could frequently only be demonstrated with fluorescently tagged substrates, and the metabolic effects may reflect indirect actions (e.g., via the cAMP-Epac1-AMPK axis) rather than direct SIRT1 binding. Directionally, SRT1460 enhances SIRT1 activity in assay systems, but interpretation of in vivo effects requires caution.

nodes.label: SRT2183
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: SRT2183 is a potent second-generation sirtuin-activating compound identified with SRT1720 and SRT1460 as chemically diverse, more potent activators than the initial polyphenolic STACs. These compounds were reported to have anticancer activity, but their mechanism is controversial: activation was frequently demonstrable only with fluorescently tagged substrates, and metabolic effects may be indirect (cAMP-Epac1-AMPK pathway) rather than direct SIRT1 activation. Directionally, SRT2183 stimulates SIRT1 deacetylase activity in biochemical assays. These caveats frame the ongoing debate about the physiological relevance of STAC-mediated SIRT1 activation.

nodes.label: Fluorescent substrate artifacts
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: A matter of controversy is that sirtuin activation by resveratrol and the SRT compounds could frequently only be demonstrated with fluorescently tagged substrates, raising the possibility of assay artifacts. Alternative explanations invoke indirect activation: resveratrol activates SIRT1 in vivo through its effect on cAMP signaling, specifically the cAMP-Epac1-AMPK pathway, and other STACs may act similarly given their analogous metabolic effects. Directionally, the claimed direct SIRT1 activation by STACs is questioned, and their in vivo benefits may be mediated by other pathways. This controversy shaped the rigorous characterization of STAC chemistry and calls for non-fluorescent assay confirmation.

nodes.label: Sirtuin Fluorimetric Activity
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Sirtuin fluorimetric activity assays (e.g., the Fluor de Lys system) are the most commonly used methods to screen molecules as sirtuin inhibitors. Deacetylation of a fluorophore-decoupled substrate sensitizes it to a developer that releases a measurable fluorophore, and percent inhibition is calculated from fluorescence. These assays identified indoles (EX-527), tenovins, JGB1741, sirtinol analogues, and cambinol analogues. A key caveat is that the aminomethylcoumarin moiety of the fluorogenic substrates can affect binding of other small molecules to the enzyme, so confirmation with orthogonal assays is recommended.

nodes.label: Sirtuin inhibitors
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Sirtuin fluorimetric activity assays (e.g., the Fluor de Lys system) are the most commonly used methods to screen molecules as sirtuin inhibitors. Deacetylation of a fluorophore-decoupled substrate sensitizes it to a developer that releases a measurable fluorophore, and percent inhibition is calculated from fluorescence. These assays identified indoles (EX-527), tenovins, JGB1741, sirtinol analogues, and cambinol analogues. A key caveat is that the aminomethylcoumarin moiety of the fluorogenic substrates can affect binding of other small molecules to the enzyme, so confirmation with orthogonal assays is recommended.

nodes.label: Suramin-related compounds
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: The homogeneous fluorescent deacetylase assay, which uses the fluorescent acetyl-lysine substrate ZMAL and NAD+ followed by trypsin treatment to release the AMC fluorophore, was used to screen several compound families as sirtuin inhibitors, including adenosine mimetics, inhibitors of kinases or phosphatases, suramin analogs, splitomicin derivatives, thiobarbiturates, and 3-arylideneindolin-2-ones. Directionally, the assay's ZMAL-ZML trypsin-coupled readout provides a plate-compatible screen for sirtuin inhibition. Its utility explains the breadth of scaffolds identified across independent discovery programs.

nodes.label: Homogeneous fluorescent deacetylase assay
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: The homogeneous fluorescent deacetylase assay, which uses the fluorescent acetyl-lysine substrate ZMAL and NAD+ followed by trypsin treatment to release the AMC fluorophore, was used to screen several compound families as sirtuin inhibitors, including adenosine mimetics, inhibitors of kinases or phosphatases, suramin analogs, splitomicin derivatives, thiobarbiturates, and 3-arylideneindolin-2-ones. Directionally, the assay's ZMAL-ZML trypsin-coupled readout provides a plate-compatible screen for sirtuin inhibition. Its utility explains the breadth of scaffolds identified across independent discovery programs.

nodes.label: Charcoal Binding Assay
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: The charcoal binding assay measures sirtuin activity by quantifying 3H-labeled OAADPr released as free acetate: incubation of recombinant sirtuins with a 3H-acetylated peptide and NAD+ produces 3H-OAADPr, which binds activated charcoal, but the 3H-acetate hydrolyzed from OAADPr remains in the supernatant and is counted. This method was used to screen nicotinamide analogs and NAD+ metabolites as inhibitors of SIRT2. Directionally, the assay traces sirtuin catalytic flux through its unique OAADPr by-product rather than through fluorophore release, giving an artifact-free alternative to fluorescent assays.

nodes.label: OAADPr formation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md

nodes.label: Microfluidic mobility shift assay
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: The microfluidic mobility shift assay separates SIRT1 substrate and product peptides by differences in electrophoretic mobility caused by charge and mass changes upon lysine deacetylation, quantitating fluorescence of both peaks. The assay effectively separates neutral-acetylated substrate peptides from deacetylated products bearing an additional positive charge. Although it could support high-throughput screening, it is more suitable for hit confirmation and mechanistic studies. Directionally, it provides a label-based yet artifact-minimized readout of SIRT1 activity distinct from fluorophore-release assays.

nodes.label: SIRT1 substrate and product peptides
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: The microfluidic mobility shift assay separates SIRT1 substrate and product peptides by differences in electrophoretic mobility caused by charge and mass changes upon lysine deacetylation, quantitating fluorescence of both peaks. The assay effectively separates neutral-acetylated substrate peptides from deacetylated products bearing an additional positive charge. Although it could support high-throughput screening, it is more suitable for hit confirmation and mechanistic studies. Directionally, it provides a label-based yet artifact-minimized readout of SIRT1 activity distinct from fluorophore-release assays.

nodes.label: NAD+ bioluminescence assay
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: The NAD+ bioluminescence assay measures sirtuin activity by quantifying remaining NAD+ after a deacetylation reaction, coupling NAD+ consumption to bacterial luciferase-catalyzed oxidation of decanal via a NAD+/NADH reduction step. It uses a label-free peptide substrate and is applicable to sirtuins with any peptide substrate. Directionally, NAD+ depletion tracks sirtuin catalytic turnover. Its label-free nature and high amenability to high-throughput screening make it a useful complement to fluorescent substrate-based assays, whose artifacts affect STAC measurements.

nodes.label: Residual NAD+ after sirtuin deacetylation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md

nodes.label: Radiochemical nicotinamide release assay
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: The radiochemical assay measures sirtuin deacetylase activity using an acetylated peptide substrate and [carbonyl-14C]-NAD+, detecting the release of 14C-nicotinamide. Unreacted NAD+ is captured by a boronic acid resin, and the unbound fraction containing released nicotinamide is counted in a scintillation counter, in a format compatible with 96-well high-throughput screening. Directionally, radiolabeled nicotinamide release directly quantifies catalytic rounds. This assay confirmed the identification of indoles as sirtuin inhibitors, although radioactive waste and safety considerations limit routine screening use.

nodes.label: Nicotinamide released by sirtuins
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md

nodes.label: Enzyme-coupled nicotinamide assay
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: The enzyme-coupled assay for nicotinamide detection measures sirtuin activity continuously by coupling nicotinamidase (which hydrolyzes nicotinamide to nicotinic acid and ammonia) to glutamate dehydrogenase, which converts ammonia, alpha-ketoglutarate, and NAD(P)H to glutamate and NAD(P)+, quantified spectrophotometrically at 340 nm. It was developed in 2009 and, while not used yet on the scale of large screenings, could be adapted to a high-throughput format. Directionally, a continuous enzyme-coupled readout avoids the artifacts associated with fluorescent and end-point assays.

nodes.label: Nicotinamidase and glutamate dehydrogenase
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md

It was developed in 2009 and, while not used yet on the scale of large screenings, could be adapted to a high-throughput format. nodes.label: Western blot analysis
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Western blot is the most commonly used cell-based analysis to evaluate sirtuin inhibition: cells are exposed to putative inhibitors, lysed, and probed with antibodies against acetylated lysine on known sirtuin substrates, typically p53, histone 3, or gamma-tubulin. Increased acetylation indicates reduced sirtuin activity. Directionally, the acetylation state of these substrates reports the functional outcome of inhibitor treatment in intact cells. Because it measures endogenous substrates rather than artificial fluorophores, it is a key confirmatory readout after fluorescent screening.

nodes.label: Acetylated p53, histone 3 and gamma-tubulin
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md

nodes.label: Cell-based ELISA assay
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: The cell-based ELISA-type assay, adapted from histone acetyltransferase inhibitor assays, confirms SIRT2 inhibitors such as 3-arylideneindolin-2-ones: cells seeded in 96-well plates are treated with compounds, fixed, permeabilized, and probed with antibody against acetylated alpha-tubulin, with fluorescence measured after enhancement solution addition. This format is well suited for high-throughput screenings. Directionally, the acetylated tubulin signal directly reflects SIRT2 deacetylase inhibition in cells. It complements Western blot with quantitative, plate-based throughput.

nodes.label: Acetylated alpha-tubulin
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md

This format is well suited for high-throughput screenings. Directionally, the acetylated tubulin signal directly reflects SIRT2 deacetylase inhibition in cells. It complements Western blot with quantitative, plate-based throughput.

nodes.label: Capillary electrophoresis-based sirtuin assay
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Recently, non-peptide substrates for SIRT1 have been synthesized, and two capillary electrophoresis assays were developed and validated to monitor the deacetylation of these substrates and to screen sirtuin inhibitor activity, complementing earlier CE assays using N-terminally fluorescence-labeled peptides. Directionally, CE separates substrate and product by their charge/mass differences without relying on fluorophore-release effects. The non-peptide substrates broaden the assay chemistry available for studying SIRT1 and its modulators.

nodes.label: Non-peptide substrates for SIRT1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
