nodes.description: Recently, non-peptide substrates for SIRT1 have been synthesized, and two capillary electrophoresis assays were developed and validated to monitor the deacetylation of these substrates and to screen sirtuin inhibitor activity, complementing earlier CE assays using N-terminally fluorescence-labeled peptides. Directionally, CE separates substrate and product by their charge/mass differences without relying on fluorophore-release effects. The non-peptide substrates broaden the assay chemistry available for studying SIRT1 and its modulators.

nodes.label: JGB1741
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: JGB1741 is a small-molecule SIRT1 inhibitor developed on the sirtinol structure and identified with other sirtinol analogues through sirtuin fluorimetric activity assays. As a sirtinol derivative, it is expected to block SIRT1 deacetylase activity, promoting hyperacetylation of substrates such as p53. Directionally, JGB1741 engages the SIRT1 catalytic site to inhibit deacetylation. Its derivation from the sirtinol scaffold places it within the beta-naphthol family of sirtuin inhibitors, whose anticancer activities derive substantially from p53 reactivation.

nodes.label: Tubulin deacetylase
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 is the predominantly cytoplasmic sirtuin that functions as a tubulin deacetylase, removing acetyl groups from alpha-tubulin to regulate microtubule dynamics and mitotic fidelity. Because it deacetylates tubulin and other mitotic regulators, SIRT2 loss impairs the control that normally keeps Aurora-A and Aurora-B in check during division, leading to aneuploidy and mitotic cell death. Directionally, SIRT2's tubulin deacetylase activity is an upstream determinant of normal chromosome segregation, linking sirtuin biology to mitotic stability and tumor suppression.

nodes.label: ETS transcription factor
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: ELK4 (SAP-1) belongs to the ETS-domain ternary complex factor (TCF) subfamily of transcription factors, defined by a conserved ETS DNA-binding domain. Within sirtuin biology, ELK4 is notable for interacting with SIRT7 and stabilizing the deacetylase at target gene promoters, where SIRT7 deacetylates lysine 18 of histone H3 and represses tumor suppressor genes. Directionally, ELK4's identity as an ETS factor underlies its promoter-targeting function. This links the ETS transcription factor family to the pro-oncogenic SIRT7-H3K18ac axis in cancer.

nodes.label: ELK1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: ELK1 is the founding member of the ternary complex factor subfamily of ETS-domain transcription factors, alongside ELK3 and ELK4 (SAP-1), and is a major nuclear target of the RAS-MAPK/ERK cascade that controls immediate-early gene expression. In the context of sirtuin biology it serves as the canonical reference for the ETS-TCF family whose member ELK4 stabilizes SIRT7 at target promoters. Directionally, ELK1's ETS DNA-binding domain and SRF-coupling architecture are shared by the TCF family, informing how ELK4 anchors SIRT7 to chromatin for H3K18 deacetylation.

nodes.label: ETS
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: ETS is a large family of eukaryotic transcription factors sharing a conserved winged helix-turn-helix DNA-binding ETS domain that recognizes purine-rich GGAA/T core motifs and regulates proliferation, differentiation, and oncogenesis. The ETS-family member ELK4 plays a central role in sirtuin biology by stabilizing SIRT7 at target gene promoters, enabling H3K18 deacetylation and repression of tumor suppressor genes. Directionally, the ETS family provides the DNA-binding and promoter-targeting mechanisms that members such as ELK4 use to recruit chromatin-modifying enzymes such as SIRT7.

nodes.label: Transcription factor family
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: ETS is a large family of eukaryotic transcription factors sharing a conserved winged helix-turn-helix DNA-binding ETS domain that recognizes purine-rich GGAA/T core motifs and regulates proliferation, differentiation, and oncogenesis. The ETS-family member ELK4 plays a central role in sirtuin biology by stabilizing SIRT7 at target gene promoters, enabling H3K18 deacetylation and repression of tumor suppressor genes. Directionally, the ETS family provides the DNA-binding and promoter-targeting mechanisms that members such as ELK4 use to recruit chromatin-modifying enzymes such as SIRT7.

nodes.label: Adenosine-binding site with kinases
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Sirtuins and protein kinases both contain an adenosine-binding pocket in their catalytic machinery, an overlap that allowed screening of known kinase inhibitors against SIRT2. This shared scaffold led to the discovery that bisindolylmaleimides such as Ro31-8220 and indolinones such as GW5074 inhibit SIRT1 and SIRT2 in the low micromolar range. Directionally, the shared adenosine site is the molecular basis for cross-inhibition between kinase inhibitors and sirtuins, but it also means these compounds retain kinase activity, complicating the attribution of cellular effects to sirtuin inhibition alone.

nodes.label: Polyphenol STAC
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Butein is a chalcone polyphenol that belongs to the first generation of natural sirtuin-activating compounds (STACs), reported to activate SIRT1 together with resveratrol, piceatannol, quercetin, and myricetin. These polyphenolic activators established the concept of pharmacological SIRT1 activation and served as the basis for later, more potent synthetic STACs such as SRT1460, SRT1720, and SRT2183. Directionally, butein's identification as a polyphenol STAC initiated the activator chemistry that progressed to synthetic scaffolds, though the direct activation mechanism remains controversial due to fluorescent-substrate artifacts.

nodes.label: Synthetic STAC
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: SRT1460 is a second-generation synthetic sirtuin-activating compound (STAC) of the imidazothiazole class, developed with SRT1720 and SRT2183 as chemically diverse and more potent activators than the initial polyphenolic STACs. These compounds were reported to have anticancer activity, but their mechanism is controversial: activation could frequently only be demonstrated with fluorescently tagged substrates, and in vivo effects may be indirect (e.g., via the cAMP-Epac1-AMPK pathway) rather than direct SIRT1 binding. Directionally, SRT1460 belongs to the synthetic STAC class whose biology underlies the ongoing debate about STAC-mediated SIRT1 activation.

nodes.label: Kinase-inhibitor scaffold
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Ro31-8220 is a bisindolylmaleimide compound originally developed as a protein kinase C inhibitor; its adenosine-binding scaffold allowed it to be repurposed as an inhibitor of SIRT1 and SIRT2 in the low micromolar range. It belongs to the kinase-inhibitor scaffolds identified by screening known kinase inhibitors against sirtuins, sharing this property with the indolinone GW5074. Directionally, Ro31-8220's identity as a kinase-inhibitor scaffold underlies its cross-reactivity with sirtuins through the shared adenosine-binding site. Because it retains potent kinase activity, cellular effects cannot be attributed solely to sirtuin inhibition.

nodes.label: SIRT1-selective inhibitor
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: NF675 is a suramin-derived small molecule that is the most potent and selective compound in its scaffold series, showing a 20-fold selectivity ratio for SIRT1 over SIRT2. It was obtained through optimization of the suramin scaffold, which itself is a nanomolar inhibitor of SIRT1/SIRT2. Directionally, NF675's identity as a suramin-derived, SIRT1-selective inhibitor illustrates scaffold engineering for isoform selectivity within the sirtuin inhibitor field. Its modest drug-likeness, stemming from high molecular weight and anionic character, limits therapeutic application despite good potency and selectivity.

nodes.label: Kinase-inhibitor scaffolds
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: SIRT2 is inhibited by kinase-inhibitor scaffolds identified by screening known kinase inhibitors against the enzyme on the rationale that sirtuins and protein kinases share an adenosine-binding site. The bisindolylmaleimide Ro31-8220 and the indolinone GW5074 showed SIRT1/SIRT2 inhibitory properties in the low micromolar range, alongside the general Kinase enzyme family that shares the adenosine pocket. Directionally, the shared adenosine-binding site of SIRT2 and protein kinases underlies this cross-inhibition. Because these scaffolds retain kinase activity, their cellular effects reflect a combination of kinase and sirtuin blockade.

nodes.label: Kinase
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Protein kinases share an adenosine-binding site with sirtuins such as SIRT2, an overlap exploited by screening known kinase inhibitors against sirtuins as a drug-discovery strategy. This shared adenosine pocket allows scaffolds like the bisindolylmaleimide Ro31-8220 and the indolinone GW5074 to engage both families, inhibiting SIRT1 and SIRT2 in the low micromolar range while retaining kinase activity. Directionally, the enzyme superfamily of Kinase proteins and sirtuin deacetylases both rely on an adenosine-binding pocket, explaining the cross-reactivity between kinase-inhibitor scaffolds and sirtuins. This structural convergence frames interpretation of kinase-inhibitor effects in sirtuin biology.

nodes.label: Adenosine-binding site with SIRT2
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
nodes.description: Protein kinases share an adenosine-binding site with sirtuins such as SIRT2, an overlap exploited by screening known kinase inhibitors against sirtuins as a drug-discovery strategy. This shared adenosine pocket allows scaffolds like the bisindolylmaleimide Ro31-8220 and the indolinone GW5074 to engage both families, inhibiting SIRT1 and SIRT2 in the low micromolar range while retaining kinase activity. Directionally, the enzyme superfamily of Kinase proteins and sirtuin deacetylases both rely on an adenosine-binding pocket, explaining the cross-reactivity between kinase-inhibitor scaffolds and sirtuins. This structural convergence frames interpretation of kinase-inhibitor effects in sirtuin biology.

nodes.label: ASAH1
nodes.description: Acid ceramidase (ACase, aCDase) is encoded by ASAH1. It is a lysosomal hydrolase that cleaves ceramide into sphingosine and a free fatty acid.

nodes.label: Carmofur
nodes.description: Carmofur has IC50 29 nM against acid ceramidase, is clinically approved in Japan, crosses the BBB, and is a repurposing candidate for senolytic therapy.

nodes.label: NF-kappaB
nodes.description: AP-1 and NF-κB are co-regulators of inflammatory SASP genes. They share transcriptional targets including IL-6, IL-8, and TNFα.

nodes.label: CXCL5
nodes.description: AP-1 transactivates CXCL5 (a SASP chemokine), which feeds inflammaging. Caloric restriction suppresses inflammaging and activates autophagy via mTOR/AMPK.

nodes.label: Hydroxychloroquine
nodes.description: HCQ blocks cytoprotective autophagy in cancer cells and is combined with chemotherapy in clinical trials. Results have been modest and inconsistent across cancer types.

nodes.label: p62
nodes.description: SQSTM1/p62-mediated selective autophagy directly degrades p16 and p21 (independent of UPS), reversing the senescent phenotype in canine MMVD valve cells.

nodes.label: TRIAD
nodes.description: TRIAD (Test of Rapamycin In Aging Dogs) is a parallel-group, double-masked, randomized, placebo-controlled trial testing rapamycin's effect on lifespan and healthspan in companion dogs.

nodes.label: PAK2
nodes.description: PAK2 directly binds and phosphorylates Caspase-7 at Ser30, Thr173, and Ser239, neutralizing its effector function and promoting survival in breast cancer.

nodes.label: Pin1
nodes.description: Pin1 binding to phosphorylated BAX (Thr167) catalyzes a conformational change that locks Bax in an inactive state, preventing mitochondrial translocation and MOMP.

nodes.label: PTPN5
nodes.description: PTPN5 (STEP), along with PTPN2 and PTPN23, dephosphorylates BAK at Tyr108, licensing it for mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization and apoptosis.

nodes.label: K-RAS
nodes.description: In K-RAS mutated cancers, hyperactive ERK1/2 phosphorylates and inactivates PTPN5, locking BAK in its inactive phosphorylated state and providing resistance to apoptosis.

nodes.label: Geraldol
nodes.description: Fisetin is metabolized by COMT to geraldol (3'-O-methylfisetin). This metabolic activation is concentration-dependent and consumes SAMe, generating SAH.

nodes.label: Cardiolipin
nodes.description: Cardiolipin stimulates DRP1 GTPase activity for fission AND is required for OPA1-mediated fusion — it has dual pro-fusion and pro-fission roles depending on context.

nodes.label: Mice
nodes.description: Male transgenic mice overexpressing SIRT6 show ~30% lifespan extension. SIRT6 KO mice die within ~4 weeks with dramatic progeroid phenotype. [ESTABLISHED: animal data]

nodes.label: PDE4
nodes.description: Resveratrol acts as a competitive inhibitor of cAMP phosphodiesterases (PDE4), leading to cAMP accumulation, Epac1 activation, Ca2+ release, and AMPK activation.

nodes.label: CDK5
nodes.description: CDK5 phosphorylates NOXA at Ser13, causing inactivation in metabolically regulated T-cell leukemia cells.

nodes.label: Trehalose
nodes.description: Trehalose activates TFEB via inhibiting Akt, increasing clearance of proteolipid aggregates in Batten disease and reducing cardiac hypertrophy/fibrosis in chronic MI models.

nodes.label: Celastrol
nodes.description: Celastrol activates TFEB via inhibiting mTORC1, reducing insoluble phosphorylated Tau aggregates and improving memory deficiency in Alzheimer's disease models.

nodes.label: Bleomycin
nodes.description: Bleomycin induces premature senescence via DNA breaks, activating p53-p21 and p16 pathways with SASP secretion.

nodes.label: Sodium Butyrate
nodes.description: Sodium butyrate (HDAC inhibitor) induces senescence-like state via p21 upregulation, which can be both p53-dependent and independent.

nodes.label: Lands cycle
nodes.description: The Lands cycle exchanges fatty acids into the sn-2 position of membrane phospholipids. ACase-liberated fatty acids enter this cycle, enriching PUFA-containing species.

nodes.label: Phospholipid
nodes.description: The Lands cycle exchanges fatty acids into the sn-2 position of membrane phospholipids. ACase-liberated fatty acids enter this cycle, enriching PUFA-containing species.

nodes.label: Sphingosine-1-phosphate
nodes.description: ACase overexpression raises sphingosine/S1P levels, which is classically anti-apoptotic and helps senescent cells resist apoptosis via SCAP pathways.

nodes.label: Huntingtin
nodes.description: Mutant huntingtin (mHTT) uncouples fission from degradation while disrupting autophagic flux. Broad-spectrum autophagy activators like rapamycin may be insufficient if downstream transport remains blocked.

nodes.label: PLK3
nodes.description: PLK3 phosphorylates BCL-XL at Ser49, causing cell cycle G2 arrest in lymphoma cells.

nodes.label: RSK
nodes.description: RSK phosphorylates APAF-1 at Ser268, causing inhibition in prostate cancer cells.

nodes.label: Hepatocellular Carcinoma
nodes.description: SIRT3 expression is lower in HCC tissue than in adjacent tissue. Modulating SIRT3 enhances sorafenib therapy, and SIRT3 downregulates GST-pi1 to enhance chemo- and sorafenib-induced apoptosis. Its loss therefore correlates with tumor aggressiveness and reduced treatment efficacy in hepatocellular carcinoma.

nodes.label: Myocardial Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury
nodes.description: SIRT1 protects against myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury: knockout increases infarct size while overexpression upregulates FoxO1 and MnSOD and downregulates caspase-3 and Bax. Signaling upstream of SIRT1 includes miR-132 inhibition leading to PGC-1alpha/Nrf2, and lncRNA Oip5-as1 acting through the SIRT1/AMPK/PGC-1alpha axis. SIRT1 is thus an endogenous cardioprotective factor against reperfusion damage.

nodes.label: ChREBP
nodes.description: SIRT6 deacetylates ChREBP and SREBP-1c to suppress hepatic lipogenesis, and hepatocyte-specific SIRT6 knockout elevates fibrosis and oxidative stress in NASH mice. SIRT6 also antagonizes liver fibrosis by blocking hepatic stellate cell activation. These actions position SIRT6 as a protective metabolic regulator in NAFLD and NASH.

nodes.label: Liver Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury
nodes.description: SIRT3 protects against liver ischemia-reperfusion injury: systemic GPCR5 knockout suppresses SIRT3, driving proinflammatory macrophages and exacerbated injury. As the dominant mitochondrial sirtuin, SIRT3 sustains mitochondrial function in hepatocytes during reperfusion stress. This protective role parallels SIRT3's cardioprotective function in myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury.

nodes.label: Hepatitis B Virus
nodes.description: SIRT3 is downregulated in HBV-positive patients and inhibits HBV replication via H3K9 deacetylation on cccDNA. This epigenetic silencing of the viral genome at the chromatin level provides a mitochondrial-to-nuclear link in antiviral defense. SIRT6 exerts an analogous H3K9-deacetylation-mediated suppression of HBV on cccDNA.

nodes.label: Peroxiredoxin 3
nodes.description: SIRT3 alleviates mitochondrial oxidative damage and apoptosis in intestinal ischemia-reperfusion injury by deacetylating peroxiredoxin 3. Deacetylation restores peroxiredoxin 3's antioxidant activity within mitochondria, limiting the oxidative burst on reperfusion. This is a canonical example of SIRT3's mitochondrial quality-control function protecting the intestine.

nodes.label: Pancreatitis
nodes.description: SIRT1 is protective in acute pancreatitis via deacetylation of p53 and HSF1, dampening acinar-cell damage. In chronic pancreatitis, however, SIRT1 is upregulated and drives inflammation-induced EMT through the miR-278 axis, illustrating a context-dependent switch from protection to pathogenesis within the same organ.

nodes.label: Huntington's Disease
nodes.description: Brain-specific SIRT1 knockout exacerbates Huntington's disease, while SIRT1 overexpression rescues CREB-CRTC1 interaction to restore BDNF transcription. SIRT1 therefore supports neuronal survival and transcriptional resilience in HD. SIRT2 inhibition also achieves neuroprotection in HD models by mimicking the beneficial effects of sterol-biosynthesis manipulation.

nodes.label: Acute Kidney Injury
nodes.description: SIRT3 has a central protective role in acute kidney injury: deficiency exacerbates sepsis-induced tubular damage and apoptosis with increased Bax and caspase-3 and decreased Bcl-2, and aggravates fatty acid oxidation dysfunction. Honokiol activation increases ATP and reduces ROS and lipid peroxidation, while overexpression attenuates ischemia-reperfusion mitochondrial damage in the kidney.

nodes.label: Kidney Fibrosis
nodes.description: SIRT1 overexpression abolishes TGF-beta1-induced apoptosis and fibrosis through CTGF suppression, and SRT1720 attenuates UUO fibrosis, while SIRT1 represses HIF2alpha. However, SIRT1 downregulation may also inhibit fibroblast activation via EGFR/PDGFR-beta, creating therapeutic ambiguity. The dominant role is renoprotective, opposing tubulointerstitial fibrosis.

nodes.label: Osteoporosis
nodes.description: SIRT1 is protective in osteoporosis: SIRT1 knockout mice have low bone mass, SIRT1 increases osteoblast osteogenesis via FoxO3a, and it deacetylates sclerostin to promote Wnt/beta-catenin signaling. Resveratrol restores alkaline phosphatase and osteocalcin via NF-kB. SIRT1 thus supports bone formation and opposes age-related bone loss.

nodes.label: Tamoxifen
nodes.description: SIRT1 causes tamoxifen resistance in ER-alpha-positive breast cancer by upregulating multidrug resistance protein 2 (MRP2) through FoxO1 deacetylation. SIRT1 inhibition therefore augments paclitaxel and doxorubicin cytotoxicity, while SIRT4 enhances tamoxifen sensitivity via STAT3 inhibition. This makes SIRT1 status a determinant of endocrine-therapy response in breast cancer.

nodes.label: AKR1C1
nodes.description: SIRT2 suppresses NSCLC migration by deacetylating AKR1C1 and inhibiting STAT3. In a counteracting oncogenic axis SIRT2 deacetylates phosphoglycerate mutase at K100 to generate NADPH and accelerate tumor growth, giving SIRT2 a context-dependent dual role in lung cancer.

nodes.label: E-cadherin
nodes.description: SIRT4 upregulates E-cadherin in colorectal cancer while suppressing proliferation, migration, and invasion via glutamine-metabolism inhibition. SIRT4 also increases sensitivity to 5-fluorouracil by inhibiting the cell cycle, cementing its tumor-suppressive role in CRC.

nodes.label: Glutaminolysis
nodes.description: SIRT5 enhances glutaminolysis in colorectal cancer in a deglutarylation-dependent manner to drive colorectal carcinogenesis, and it deacetylates lactate dehydrogenase B to induce hyperactive autophagy and tumorigenesis. SIRT5 overexpression is associated with poor prognosis in CRC, contrasting with protective SIRT6.

nodes.label: Gastric Cancer
nodes.description: SIRT6 is downregulated in gastric cancer where low expression negatively correlates with tumor size and pathological grade and predicts poor prognosis. It inhibits the JAK2/STAT3 pathway to suppress growth, and SIRT6 silencing overcomes sorafenib resistance by promoting ferroptosis.

nodes.label: AIM2
nodes.description: SIRT1 is overexpressed in HPV-infected cervical cancer cells and nullifies AIM2 inflammasome-mediated immunity, correlating with poor clinical outcomes. This immunosuppressive action allows cervical cancer cells to evade inflammasome-driven clearance, positioning SIRT1 as an oncogenic factor in HPV-driven cervical cancer.

nodes.label: Coronary Artery Disease
nodes.description: Genetic SIRT1 polymorphisms are associated with coronary artery disease risk, and SIRT1 expression is reduced in CAD patients where its downregulation is linked to acetylated p53 in CAD monocytes. The lncRNA C2dat1 promotes SIRT1 to suppress miR-34a, driving VSMC proliferation and migration in the vessel wall.

nodes.label: Rspo1
nodes.description: SIRT6 preserves Rspo1 expression to confer intestinal epithelium injury resistance in inflammatory bowel disease, and SIRT6 deletion promotes inflammation via NF-kB. SIRT2 similarly inhibits Wnt/beta-catenin to maintain gut homeostasis, while SIRT3, SIRT5, and SIRT7 knockout mice are susceptible to colitis.

nodes.label: Intestinal Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury
nodes.description: SIRT1 suppresses intestinal epithelial ROS accumulation and apoptosis after ischemia-reperfusion, and resveratrol protects through the SIRT1-NF-kB-iNOS-NO pathway. SIRT3 alleviates mitochondrial oxidative damage and apoptosis via peroxiredoxin 3 deacetylation, while SIRT6 downregulation by miR-351-5p aggravates intestinal IRI injury.

nodes.label: GKRP
nodes.description: SIRT2 promotes glucose-dependent hepatic glucose uptake by deacetylating GKRP at K126, and its downregulation ameliorates reduced Akt activity while increasing insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in insulin-resistant neuro-2a cells. SIRT1 overexpression improves insulin sensitivity, but hepatic SIRT1 knockdown prevents fasting hyperglycemia by increasing hepatic insulin responsiveness, illustrating SIRT1's dual role in diabetes.

nodes.label: Diabetic Retinopathy
nodes.description: SIRT1 overexpression prevents capillary cell apoptosis and degenerative capillary formation in diabetic retinopathy, reduces DM-induced retinal inflammation, and improves visual function. In diabetic cardiomyopathy SIRT1 activation inhibits ROS-induced oxidative stress and fibrosis, while SIRT3 regulates fibrosis, inflammation, apoptosis, and oxidative stress in the diabetic myocardium.

nodes.label: Kidney Stones
nodes.description: SIRT3 is downregulated in kidney stone patients and protects via the Nrf2/heme oxygenase-1 pathway, while suppressing SIRT1 promotes calcium oxalate crystal-cell adhesion and exacerbates injury. SIRT1 also protects against aging-induced kidney injury through HIF-1alpha deacetylation of tubulointerstitial damage.

nodes.label: Vascular Calcification
nodes.description: SIRT6 is markedly downregulated in CKD and vascular calcification patients and suppresses osteogenic transdifferentiation of vascular smooth muscle cells via runt-related transcription factor 2. MSC exosomes inhibit high-phosphate aortic calcification through SIRT6-HMGB1 deacetylation, and soluble epoxide hydrolase destabilizes SIRT3 to accelerate VSMC calcification.

nodes.label: Sclerostin
nodes.description: SIRT1 deacetylates sclerostin to activate Wnt/beta-catenin signaling and increase bone anabolism, and SIRT1 knockout mice have a low bone-mass phenotype while SIRT1 overexpression increases osteoblast osteogenesis via FoxO3a. SIRT6 inhibits age-related bone loss by stabilizing estrogen receptor alpha in preosteoblastic cells.

nodes.label: Intervertebral Disc Degeneration
nodes.description: SIRT1 is reduced in degenerative nucleus pulposus tissues with severity, and inhibits NF-kB transcriptional activity while suppressing c-Fos/c-Jun phosphorylation. SIRT2 reverses IL-1beta action by inhibiting the p53/p21 pathway, SIRT3 maintains nucleus pulposus cell homeostasis, and SIRT6 inhibits inflammatory responses and senescence via NF-kB in IDD.

nodes.label: Melanoma
nodes.description: Oncogene-induced senescence (OIS) is the permanent cell-cycle arrest triggered in cells carrying BRAF/RAS/MYC mutations. The benign melanocytic nevus (mole) is the in-vivo embodiment of OIS and prevents melanoma; bypass of OIS via p53/PTEN loss or TERT activation is required for malignancy. Capped, arrested growth is therefore tumor-suppressive.

nodes.label: Benign Tumor
nodes.description: Benign tumors are dual-natured: OIS-type arrested lesions (nevi) are longevity-positive cancer barriers, whereas growth-signal-driven benign growths such as TSC1/TSC2-loss mTORC1 hamartomas are themselves disease (Tuberous Sclerosis, angiomyolipoma, epilepsy). Arrested growth is good; ongoing growth is bad.

nodes.label: Hamartoma
nodes.description: Benign tumors are dual-natured: OIS-type arrested lesions (nevi) are longevity-positive cancer barriers, whereas growth-signal-driven benign growths such as TSC1/TSC2-loss mTORC1 hamartomas are themselves disease (Tuberous Sclerosis, angiomyolipoma, epilepsy). Arrested growth is good; ongoing growth is bad.

nodes.label: TSC1
nodes.description: Loss of TSC1 or TSC2 removes the GAP that restrains Rheb, causing constitutive mTORC1 hyperactivation that drives benign hamartomas (Tuberous Sclerosis, renal angiomyolipoma, epilepsy, autism). Here benign growth is itself the disease, contrasting with the protective OIS-type benign lesion.

nodes.label: Hyperfunction Theory of Aging
nodes.description: The hyperfunction theory of aging holds that aging is the quasi-programmed continuation of developmental growth signaling; mTOR is the engine of aging and Rapamycin extends lifespan by suppressing mTOR. This frames the key distinction that arrested growth (OIS) is protective while ongoing, unopposed growth signaling is pathogenic.

nodes.label: Ribosome Biogenesis
nodes.description: SIRT7 drives ribosome biogenesis by activating RNA Pol I at rDNA and suppresses p21 via H3K18 deacetylation, fueling the biosynthetic capacity tumors need; it is overexpressed in breast, thyroid, and HCC. This proliferative, biosynthetic driver role makes SIRT7 an oncogenic sirtuin.

nodes.label: Phosphoglycerate Mutase
nodes.description: SIRT2 promotes tumor glycolysis in some settings by deacetylating phosphoglycerate mutase at Lys100, channeling carbon into NADPH production and accelerating tumor growth in lung cancer. This illustrates SIRT2's context-dependent, often harmful, metabolic face versus the protective SIRT1/3/6 axis.

nodes.label: N-Acetylcysteine
nodes.description: In C. elegans, glucose restriction normally raises mitochondrial respiration and ROS, inducing catalase and extending lifespan; NAC pre-treatment completely abolished both the ROS rise and the longevity benefit. NAC is the strongest direct evidence that scavenging the ROS signal blocks mitohormesis.

nodes.label: Prostate Cancer
nodes.description: The SELECT trial (Lippman et al., 2009, JAMA, PMID 19066370) found vitamin E supplementation (400 IU/day) increased prostate cancer risk by 17% in healthy men, cited as a key example of antioxidant supplementation failure. The HOPE trial similarly showed no cardiovascular benefit and a trend to increased heart failure.

nodes.label: Endogenous Antioxidant Upregulation
nodes.description: Exogenous antioxidants prevent the upregulation of endogenous defense enzymes (SOD, GPx) that exercise normally induces via NRF2. The Ristow 2009 study showed antioxidant-supplemented subjects failed to upregulate endogenous SOD/GPx and lost the insulin-sensitizing benefit of exercise.

nodes.label: NF-kB
nodes.description: PAK1 facilitates NF-kB nuclear activation; ivermectin's PAK1 degradation therefore dampens NF-kB signaling. Because NF-kB is the master transcriptional regulator of the SASP, this overlaps with the senomorphic strategy — targeting SASP production without killing senescent cells.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuroprotective Actions of Methylene Blue and Its Derivatives.md
links.context: 2-Chlorophenothiazine, which consists of the phenothiazine nucleus without the amine side chains of methylene blue, acts as a direct free-radical scavenger independent of mitochondria and NADH. In the cell-free mitochondrial lysate oxidation assay it significantly reduced DCF fluorescence both with and without mitochondria/NADH, unlike MB which required both. Despite potent nanomolar neuroprotection against glutamate, IAA, and rotenone toxicity, it had no effect on oxygen consumption, anaerobic glycolysis, or the complex I-III electron shunt, and it did not upregulate complex IV expression, revealing a mechanism distinct from MB.

The conversion of adrenaline to adrenochrome is an oxidation reaction mediated by oxygen radicals (reactive oxygen species). In the adrenochrome pathway, ROS production by stimulated neutrophils stimulated the oxidation of adrenaline, transforming the catecholamine into its pink oxidation product adrenochrome and further into adrenolutin. Because the oxidation step does not require a dedicated enzyme, oxygen radicals can drive it whenever antioxidant defenses are overwhelmed. This ROS-mediated oxidation is the core chemical event of the pathway and is what links inflammatory oxidant production to catecholamine chemistry in the heart. It also explains the classical observation, first made in 1856, that adrenaline exposed to air or oxidizing conditions turns pink as adrenochrome forms, and why scavenging systems normally keep this reaction suppressed.

Reactive oxygen species activate NF-kappaB because oxidants (notably H2O2) modify cysteines on inhibitory proteins and upstream kinases, releasing NF-kappaB for nuclear translocation and target-gene expression. The transcription factor then induces genes that generate more ROS, establishing a feed-forward loop. The directionality is oxidant to transcriptional activation. A caveat is that ROS also activate many other pathways (MAPK, AP-1), and NF-kappaB can be either protective or pathogenic depending on context.

links.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md
links.context: Acetate is converted intracellularly into acetyl-CoA by ACSS2 and is not membrane-permeable acetyl-CoA itself. Acetate supplementation increases global nuclear acetylation including H3K27ac and induces expression of pro-inflammatory genes including IL6, IL8, IL1B and CCL2 without affecting cell cycle regulators p16 and p21. In mitochondria-depleted senescent cells, acetate increases histone acetylation and partially restores a subset of the mitochondrial-dependent SASP programme. However, acetate-induced SASP gene expression is suppressed by the STING inhibitor SN011, showing that chromatin accessibility alone cannot drive SASP transcription without innate immune activation.

links.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md
links.context: Cellular senescence is a key response to various cellular stresses characterized by a permanent cell cycle arrest and the secretion of a pro-inflammatory cocktail of factors known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Senescence serves protective roles in embryonic development, tumour suppression and tissue repair, but persistent SASP activation leads to chronic inflammation contributing to tissue dysfunction, ageing and a broad spectrum of age-related diseases including cancer. This dual nature makes SASP a focal point for understanding both the protective and detrimental effects of senescence.

links.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md
links.context: Many SASP-associated genes are linked to super-enhancer-like regions that are particularly sensitive to changes in histone acetylation, and such loci probably require sustained acetyl-CoA availability to maintain high transcriptional output, rendering them especially vulnerable to interventions that limit acetyl-CoA supply. SLC25A1 inhibition reduces chromatin accessibility at these SASP loci both in vitro and in vivo, selectively suppressing inflammatory gene expression. This positions mitochondrial metabolism as an upstream determinant of chromatin accessibility in senescent cells, aligning with previous reports linking citrate metabolism to SASP regulation.

Senescent stromal cells in the tumor microenvironment secrete soluble SASP factors that confer therapeutic resistance on residual cancer cells, including WNT16B, amphiregulin (AREG) and epiregulin (EREG). Conditioned media from bleomycin-senescent PSC27 stroma elevated viability, migration and invasion of prostate cancer lines (PC3, DU145, M12, LNCaP) and shifted their survival curves against mitoxantrone. Apigenin treatment of the stromal cells diminished this SASP-conferred resistance almost to basal levels and increased cancer cell apoptosis (caspase-3/7 activity).

links.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md
links.context: ChIP-seq analysis of histone H3 acetylation at lysine 27 (H3K27ac) showed that loci gaining acetylation during senescence are markedly reduced following mitochondrial clearance, and these regions are enriched for inflammatory and interleukin signalling pathways central to the SASP. A 51-gene SASP signature induced during senescence is suppressed upon mitochondrial removal, with genes such as IL6 and CCL2 showing coordinated decreases in chromatin acetylation and mRNA expression. Multiple nodes of the mitochondrial citrate-acetyl-CoA axis converge to control H3K27ac at SASP loci, selectively modulating inflammatory gene expression without affecting the senescence-associated cell cycle arrest.

NF-κB is the master transcriptional regulator of the SASP, controlling expression of the bulk of pro-inflammatory interleukins, chemokines, and growth factors. It is activated downstream of multiple senescence inputs including p38 MAPK, GATA4 (via TRAF3IP2), and cGAS-STING, and it cooperates with C/EBPbeta at SASP enhancers. Inhibition of NF-κB robustly suppresses the inflammatory arm of the SASP across many models. A caveat is that NF-κB is necessary but not sufficient -- full SASP establishment requires additional axes such as IL-1α/MyD88 and mTOR.

Chronic SASP secretion from accumulated senescent cells is a principal driver of inflammaging, the sterile, low-grade inflammation that rises with age. By continuously releasing IL-6, IL-1α, TNFalpha, and chemokines, senescent cells maintain a pro-inflammatory tissue milieu that disrupts homeostasis and promotes age-related disease. The relationship is causal and bidirectional with aging: inflammaging further impairs clearance mechanisms. Senolytics and senomorphics both reduce inflammaging by targeting either the source cells or their secretome.

The SASP is a hypersecretory state -- a specialized secretory phenotype -- in which senescent cells upregulate and release hundreds of factors including interleukins, chemokines, growth factors, proteases, and extracellular vesicles. This secreted output contrasts with the quiescent, low-turnover secretome of non-senescent cells and is a defining non-cell-autonomous feature of the senescent state. The composition of the SASP is variable, shaped by the senescence inducer, cell type, and tissue context. Its classification as a secretory phenotype emphasizes that senescence exerts its effects largely through communication with the microenvironment.

The cGAS-STING innate immune pathway is a key driver of the SASP, activated by cytoplasmic nucleic acids including mtDNA released via minority MOMP and chromatin from cytoplasmic chromatin fragments. cGAS senses cytosolic DNA, producing cGAMP that activates STING, which in turn drives type-I interferon and NF-κB signaling to amplify SASP factor production. This linkage connects mitochondrial dysfunction and genomic stress directly to inflammatory senescence output. Importantly, cGAS-STING also enhances immune surveillance, giving the pathway both pro- and anti-tumor consequences.

The mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) promotes SASP production chiefly by enhancing translation of key SASP factors such as IL-1α and by stabilizing SASP mRNAs through the MK2/ZFP36L1 axis. mTOR thereby couples the heightened biosynthetic demand of senescent cells to secretome output. Pharmacologic inhibition with rapamycin suppresses the SASP without necessarily reversing the cell-cycle arrest. This makes mTOR a central node linking metabolic state to the inflammatory phenotype of senescence.

p38 MAPK was the first kinase shown to activate the SASP independently of the canonical DDR, acting upstream of NF-κB to drive pro-inflammatory factor expression. It stabilizes SASP transcripts in the tumor microenvironment and integrates signals from oxidative stress and the ASAP-to-SASP transition. p38 MAPK inhibition suppresses SASP from fibroblasts of older donors, supporting its therapeutic relevance. Its activity is a convergence point for multiple senescence-inducing stresses rather than a single upstream trigger.

The JAK-STAT3 signaling axis promotes a pro-inflammatory SASP by interacting with p38 MAPK and mTOR and by transducing cues from SASP cytokines such as IL-6. STAT3 activation contributes to age-related frailty and to the immune-modulatory and tumor-promoting facets of the secretome. JAK1/2 inhibitors (e.g., ruxolitinib) reduce SASP cytokines IL-6 and IL-8, validating the axis as a senomorphic target. The pathway is especially important for the feed-forward, self-reinforcing inflammation characteristic of chronic senescence.

In most cellular contexts p53 restrains the pro-inflammatory arm of the SASP, limiting expression of cytokines and chemokines; loss or mutation of p53 dramatically amplifies SASP output. This restraint is mechanistically linked to p53's ability to suppress NF-κB-driven inflammation and to its role in DNA-damage-induced senescence. The directionality is suppressive: intact p53 yields a more contained secretome, whereas p53 deficiency yields an exaggerated, tumor-promoting SASP. This nuance explains why p53 status strongly shapes the net effect of senescence in tissues.

p16INK4a can induce a senescence program with a distinctive SASP profile that includes factors such as IGFBP3 and ISG15 and is relatively independent of a classical DNA damage response. This p16-associated secretory phenotype (PASP) is thought to be more p53-dependent for its composition and differs qualitatively from DDR-driven SASP. The relationship highlights that the SASP is not monolithic but varies with the upstream arrest pathway. p16 overexpression thus both enforces arrest and shapes the secretome character.

Cytoplasmic LINE-1 (L1) retrotransposon cDNA, arising from derepression of endogenous retroelements in senescence, triggers interferon signaling through the cGAS-STING pathway. This reinforces SASP factor production, particularly in deeper, more established senescence where retroelement activation is pronounced. The process is restrained by RB1 and SIRT6, whose decline permits L1 derepression. It represents a chromatin-immune feed-forward loop by which genomic destabilization amplifies the inflammatory secretome.

Cytoplasmic chromatin fragments (CCF) -- DNA-SCARS shed into the cytosol in therapy-induced and other senescence -- are sensed by cGAS-STING, activating NF-κB and type-I interferon signaling that induce a robust SASP. CCF formation links persistent DNA damage foci to innate immune activation in the senescent cell. They can also be transmitted to and activate SASP in neighboring recipient cells. The phenomenon is most established in genotoxic-stress-induced senescence, marking a key mechanism bridging damage to secretion.

Rapamycin suppresses the pro-inflammatory SASP by inhibiting mTOR, which reduces translation of SASP factors such as IL-1α and destabilizes SASP mRNAs, and by interfering with the p38 MAPK-IL-1α-NF-κB cascade. As an mTOR inhibitor and autophagy inducer, it also limits inflammasome activation and mitochondrial DAMPs. This senomorphic action reduces the paracrine and systemic consequences of senescence without eliminating the cells. Its broad pleiotropic effects (immunomodulation, metabolic) require careful dosing in therapeutic contexts.

Metformin inhibits NF-κB signaling in fibroblasts, macrophages, and senescent endothelial cells and activates AMPK, which suppresses mTOR-dependent SASP translation. By lowering the inflammatory secretome and improving mitochondrial function, it exerts senomorphic effects relevant to metabolic and vascular aging. Preclinical and epidemiologic data support its anti-inflammatory, potentially anti-aging actions. The magnitude of SASP suppression is context-dependent and generally more modest than dedicated SASP inhibitors.

Resveratrol inhibits pro-inflammatory SASP cytokines primarily through activation of the deacetylase SIRT1, which reduces H3K9 and H4K16 acetylation at SASP gene promoters and interferes with NF-κB. It also acts as an antioxidant, quenching mitochondrial ROS that would otherwise sustain SASP signaling. Evidence for SASP suppression is strong in several cell models but largely preclinical, and bioavailability in vivo is limited. Thus its senomorphic effect is well supported mechanistically though translationally uncertain.

Apigenin, a flavonoid, reduces SASP-driven breast cancer aggressiveness by inhibiting NF-κB-dependent SASP factors and the chemokine CXCL10. It also blocks the ASAP-to-SASP transition by disrupting ATM-HSPA8 and HSPA8-p38 MAPK crosstalk, and binds PRDX6 to inhibit its iPLA2 activity. These actions place apigenin at both the early stress-response and the established-secretome levels. Its effects are documented in specific cancer and fibroblast models, supporting a medium-to-high confidence senomorphic role.

Nutlin 3a suppresses the pro-inflammatory SASP by inhibiting MDM2, the E3 ligase that marks p53 for degradation, thereby stabilizing the tumor suppressor; stabilized p53 in turn restrains NF-kB-driven expression of SASP cytokines and chemokines. This mechanism exploits the natural tumor-suppressive rheostat of p53 rather than broadly blocking inflammation, and it is consistent with the observation that loss of p53 dramatically amplifies secretome output. The compound is primarily a research tool with limited clinical development, which constrains its translational confidence, but mechanistically its SASP-suppressive action is well grounded in p53's restraint of the inflammatory secretome.

BRD4, a bromodomain-containing acetyl-lysine reader, is recruited to senescence-activated enhancers and super-enhancers where it promotes transcription of SASP factors. BET bromodomain inhibitors that displace BRD4 suppress enhancer-driven SASP expression, establishing it as a senomorphic target and confirming that the acetylated enhancer landscape licenses the secretome. Its action is downstream of the chromatin remodeling that opens SASP loci and varies in dependence across individual SASP genes, but BRD4 is a consistent, druggable component of the program. The H3K27ac-marked enhancers it engages provide a therapeutic interface for BET inhibitors in senescence-associated inflammation.

KDM4 histone demethylases promote SASP factor expression by removing repressive H3K9me3 and H3K36me3 marks at SASP loci, thereby opening chromatin for transcription. Inhibition of KDM4 reduces the secretome, positioning it as a candidate senomorphic strategy. The effect is mechanistically coherent with the broad chromatin derepression of senescence, though the specificity and in vivo validation of KDM4 inhibitors as senomorphics are still emerging. Confidence is therefore moderate pending more clinical data.

EZH2, the catalytic subunit of the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), represses pro-inflammatory SASP factors including CCL2, CXCL9, and CXCL10 by depositing the H3K27me3 repressive mark at their loci. Loss or inhibition of EZH2 derepresses these chemokines and augments the SASP, placing polycomb-mediated silencing as a counterbalance to the activating transcription factors of the secretome. The relationship is fairly well established in specific contexts but represents one of several layers of SASP control rather than a master switch, and it contrasts with the activating roles of KDM4 and BRD4 at the same loci.

SIRT1, a NAD+-dependent deacetylase, suppresses the SASP by reducing H3K9 and H4K16 acetylation at the promoters of IL-6 and IL-8, limiting their transcriptional activation. Through this chromatin-mediated restraint and via crosstalk with NF-κB, SIRT1 tempers the inflammatory secretome. Its activity is tied to cellular NAD+ availability, which declines with age, potentially loosening SASP control. The repression is well documented but operates as part of a broader sirtuin-mediated anti-inflammatory network.

AP-1 (for example FOS/JUN dimers) acts as a pioneer factor that opens senescence-activated enhancers and cooperates with NF-kB to drive expression of SASP genes. It is required for establishing the senescence-associated enhancer landscape that licenses the secretome, bridging early stress signaling to the durable transcriptional program. Its contribution is integral to SASP induction but operates in concert with NF-kB, C/EBPb, and other factors rather than alone, and the H3K27ac-marked enhancers it helps open become targets for BET inhibitors. This cooperative enhancer logic ensures the secretome is deployed only after committed, multi-factor licensing of the senescence program.

SASP factors such as IL-1α, TGFβ, VEGF, and CCL2 can act in an autocrine and paracrine manner to reinforce the senescent state and induce growth arrest in neighboring healthy cells -- a process termed paracrine (or bystander) senescence. This spreads the arrested phenotype through tissues, amplifying the functional impact of a small senescent fraction. The directionality is outward: the secretome of one cell converts adjacent cells into a senescent state. A caveat is that paracrine senescence requires susceptible recipients and sufficient SASP magnitude, and it can be both tumor-suppressive and pathological.

SASP chemokines including CCL2, CCL5, CXCL1, and CXCL10 act as find-me signals that recruit natural killer (NK) cells to sites of senescence. NK cells then directly kill senescent cells via NKG2D recognition of stress-induced ligands (MICA, MICB, ULBP2), making this recruitment a key arm of senescence surveillance that converts the secretome into an immune-clearance stimulus. Interferon signaling downstream of cGAS-STING in the senescent cell further boosts NK effector activity. The efficiency of recruitment and killing declines with age and immunosenescence, allowing senescent-cell accumulation, whereas enhancing this axis is an active therapeutic strategy to restore surveillance.

SASP factors promote macrophage migration toward senescent cells and can polarize them toward a pro-inflammatory M1-like phenotype, facilitating phagocytosis of the arrested cells. Chemokines such as CCL2 are central to this recruitment, linking the secretome to innate immune clearance. Macrophage engagement is thus both a clearance mechanism and, when chronic, a contributor to tissue inflammation. The net effect depends on whether polarized macrophages resolve or sustain the inflammatory state.

SASP growth factors such as VEGF and VEGF-C stimulate angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels, in the local microenvironment by acting on endothelial VEGFR2 and VEGFR3. This is beneficial during wound healing and tissue repair, where neovascularization supports regeneration, but can also support tumor vascularization and pathological neovascularization when senescence becomes chronic. The pro-angiogenic direction is conveyed to endothelial cells and contributes to paracrine reprogramming of neighboring stroma. The dual nature means SASP-driven angiogenesis is context-dependent, reparative acutely and harmful when persistent.

Chronic SASP promotes fibrosis through TGFb-mediated pro-fibrotic signaling and through matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) that remodel the extracellular matrix, activating resident fibroblasts and myofibroblasts that deposit collagen. This contributes to idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, liver fibrosis, and renal fibrosis in aging and after tissue injury, where persistent senescence shifts tissue toward scar formation rather than regeneration. The fibrotic arm of the secretome is one of its clearest pathological sequelae and is a principal rationale for senolytic and senomorphic trials in fibrotic disease.

Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is a prototypical SASP cytokine and one of the most consistently upregulated and secreted factors in senescent cells. It acts as an essential mediator of paracrine senescence and immune modulation and is widely used as a biomarker of the senescent secretome and of organismal aging. IL-6 signals through the JAK/STAT3 pathway to promote inflammation and, in some contexts, stemness and cancer stem-cell traits, and it contributes to the feed-forward loop that sustains the SASP. Its prominence, reliability, and frequent co-measurement with IL-8 make IL-6 a canonical reference factor for defining and quantifying the senescent secretome.

Interleukin-8 (IL-8/CXCL8) is a prototypical SASP chemokine secreted by senescent cells and essential for their paracrine effects, particularly neutrophil recruitment and, in tumor contexts, cancer stemness through CXCR2 signaling. It is co-induced with IL-6 downstream of NF-kB and IL-1a and is frequently measured alongside IL-6 as a standard SASP readout in cell culture and clinical samples. Its roles in both inflammation and tumor promotion underscore the dual nature of the secretome, supporting wound-healing neutrophil influx acutely while contributing to chronic inflammation and therapy resistance in established disease. This dualism is a recurring theme across SASP chemokines.

IL-1a is an apical SASP amplifier that sits at the top of the inflammatory cascade, and its proteolytic cleavage (by caspase-5 or calpain) is essential for full SASP regulatory function. Cell-surface and secreted IL-1a engage IL-1R on neighboring cells, activating MyD88-dependent NF-kB signaling that both sustains the SASP in the sender and induces paracrine senescence in recipients. As a master initiator rather than a passive component, IL-1a integrates with the noncanonical inflammasome, whose caspase-5 cleavage licenses the secretome. Its centrality makes IL-1a a key mechanistic and therapeutic node.

Transforming growth factor beta (TGFb) is a SASP factor that promotes paracrine senescence, fibrosis, and immune-suppressive conditions via SMAD and non-SMAD signaling. It contributes to the pro-fibrotic and EMT-inducing arm of the secretome, distinct from the purely inflammatory cytokines, and cooperates with IL-6 to drive TH17 differentiation. TGFb also transcriptionally induces CDKN2B/p15INK4b and p21CIP1 in recipient cells, directly enforcing the G1 arrest that spreads senescence. Its pleiotropic roles make TGFb a major effector of both tissue repair and senescence-associated pathology.

Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) is a SASP growth factor that stimulates angiogenesis in the cancer and wound-healing microenvironment by acting on endothelial VEGFR2 to promote new vessel formation. Its inclusion in the secretome links senescence to blood-vessel formation and to the tumor-promoting angiogenic switch, and it contributes to paracrine reprogramming of neighboring stroma. The growth-factor arm of the SASP that VEGF exemplifies extends beyond pure inflammation, mobilizing vascular and tissue-remodeling responses. Together with VEGF-C, MMPs, and chemokines, it illustrates how the secretome coordinates a broad tissue-level response.

Matrix metalloproteinase-3 (MMP-3) is a SASP protease associated with extracellular matrix degradation, tissue remodeling, and, in tumor contexts, cancer cell invasion and metastasis. Its secretion reflects the matrix-remodeling arm of the secretome that supports wound healing acutely but pathological tissue breakdown chronically, and MMP-3 can activate other MMPs in a cascade, amplifying remodeling. This protease component distinguishes the SASP from a purely cytokine profile and contributes to fibrosis and basement-membrane disruption in aging tissues.

CCL2 (MCP-1) is a SASP chemokine regulated by IL-1a and IL-1b that is a potent chemoattractant for monocytes and CCR2+ myeloid precursors, recruiting macrophages and myeloid-derived suppressor cells to sites of senescence. It thereby links the senescent secretome to innate and suppressive immune infiltration and contributes to paracrine senescence and inflammaging. CCL2's recruitment functions make it a central communicator between senescent cells and the immune milieu, and its CCR2-dependent signaling has been targeted to modulate myeloid infiltration in aging and cancer.

Tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFalpha) is a pro-inflammatory SASP cytokine that contributes to immune modulation, NF-kB reinforcement, and inflammaging. It can act in an autocrine loop to amplify the secretome and in a paracrine manner to affect neighboring cells, and it cooperates with IL-1 family cytokines in driving inflammatory gene programs. TNFalpha is less universally dominant than IL-6 in the SASP but is consistently present in many senescence models and is a canonical target of anti-inflammatory biologics. Its pleiotropic actions solidify its status as a canonical SASP component.

GATA4 is a transcriptional regulator that promotes the pro-inflammatory SASP by activating NF-kB, in part through TRAF3IP2 (Act1), and by inhibiting autophagy, which would otherwise clear damaging organelles and dampen inflammatory signals. Its accumulation in senescent cells makes it an upstream driver of the secretome's inflammatory arm, coupling defective organelle turnover directly to cytokine production. Unlike many SASP regulators that act on a single pathway, GATA4 integrates both transcriptional and autophagy-based control. The mechanism is well supported and positions GATA4 as a distinctive senescence-specific SASP regulator.

The METTL3-METTL14 m6A methyltransferase complex promotes SASP factor expression by installing N6-methyladenosine marks on mRNA that facilitate enhancer-promoter looping and stabilize SASP transcripts. This epitranscriptomic layer adds post-transcriptional control to the secretome, coordinating the sustained expression of multiple SASP genes. The relationship is mechanistically plausible and supported by knockout studies showing reduced SASP, but the field is newer and less consolidated than the NF-kB/mTOR axes, so confidence is moderate.

Ruxolitinib, a JAK1/2 inhibitor, reduces SASP cytokines IL-6 and IL-8 in senescent fibroblasts by blocking JAK-STAT3 signaling downstream of SASP cytokines. As a clinically approved drug for myelofibrosis, it is a translatable senomorphic agent whose suppression is targeted to the JAK-STAT arm of the secretome rather than acting on the whole program. The evidence is robust in cellular models and consistent with its established immunomodulatory profile, and the drug also interrupts the feed-forward loop by which IL-6 sustains chronic inflammation. This positions ruxolitinib as one of the most clinically ready senomorphic candidates for dampening senescence-associated inflammation.

Lamivudine (3TC), a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor, suppresses the SASP by inhibiting LINE-1 (L1) reverse transcription, thereby reducing cytosolic retroelement cDNA that would activate cGAS-STING-NF-kB signaling. This repurposes an antiretroviral agent as a senomorphic that targets the retrotransposon arm of SASP induction, complementing drugs that act on transcription factors or chromatin. The mechanism is supported by studies showing reduced SASP upon LINE-1 inhibition and is consistent with the finding that RB1 and SIRT6 normally restrain L1 activity. Clinical relevance is still investigative, keeping confidence moderate.

SASP factors act as paracrine morphogens that push recipient cells toward stemness or altered lineage commitment, exemplifying paracrine reprogramming. This reshapes tissue architecture and can promote cancer stemness or metaplasia in chronic contexts. The relationship positions the SASP as a fate-modulating signal, not merely an inflammatory one, and is supported by studies of chronic SASP exposure in epithelial and stromal cells. Short-term SASP exposure instead supports regeneration by enhancing recipient-cell plasticity.

IL-6, IL-1beta, and TGFbeta together drive naive T-cell differentiation toward the TH17 lineage, linking the SASP to adaptive immune reprogramming. TH17 cells recruited to senescent niches can amplify inflammation and promote autoimmunity-like responses. The relationship connects the secretome to a distinct effector T-cell subset with pro-inflammatory roles and is a well-established cytokine combination in TH17 biology. This illustrates how the SASP shapes not only innate but also adaptive immune responses.
SASP cytokines IL-6 and IL-8 induce ACase upregulation and ferroptotic sensitization in neighboring proliferative cells via paracrine signaling.

links.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md
links.context: Acetyl-CoA is the obligate donor for protein acetylation, including histone acetylation, a modification associated with chromatin relaxation and increased accessibility to transcriptional machinery. In senescent cells, acetyl-CoA availability determines H3K27ac deposition at SASP gene loci: enhancing acetyl-CoA levels promotes SASP gene expression while depleting it limits the programme. Acetate supplementation, converted intracellularly into acetyl-CoA by ACSS2, increases nuclear acetylation and induces pro-inflammatory genes IL6, IL8, IL1B and CCL2 without affecting cell cycle regulators, linking mitochondrial metabolism to the epigenetic regulation of inflammatory genes.

Histone acetylation opens chromatin by neutralizing the positive charge of lysine residues on histone tails, weakening their electrostatic interaction with the negatively charged DNA backbone. This relaxes nucleosome compaction and increases the accessibility of DNA to transcription factors and other regulatory proteins, promoting gene expression. Acetylation is dynamically deposited by histone acetyltransferases and removed by histone deacetylases, and the balance between these activities tunes chromatin structure across the genome.

Acid ceramidase (ACase) inhibition reduces PL-PUFA levels and lipid peroxidation without altering expression of ACSL4, the acyl-CoA synthetase that canonically drives PUFA incorporation into phospholipids during ferroptosis. After ACase knockdown, ACSL4 protein remained high, indicating that the decrease in PL-PUFAs is driven by reduced supply of saturated/monounsaturated fatty acids for Lands-cycle exchange (due to decreased ceramide lipolysis) rather than by changes in ACSL4. Both ACase and ACSL4 knockdown protect senescent cells against RSL3, but through supply-side versus incorporation-side mechanisms respectively.

links.source_file: _document_ - Could this enzyme help remove "zombie" cells from our tissues?.md
links.context: Acid ceramidase sensitizes cells to ferroptosis through an entirely novel pathway independent of the mechanisms usually associated with ferroptosis-induced cell death - it does not involve changes in iron or glutathione levels but instead modulates lipid metabolism. This distinguishes it from canonical ferroptosis, which is suppressed by GPX4 and glutathione. Because the acid-ceramidase axis operates through ceramide hydrolysis and membrane PUFA enrichment rather than through GPX4/GSH regulation, it opens a separate druggable route for triggering ferroptosis in senescent cells. First author David Soriano-Castell highlighted this as an entirely novel, GPX4/GSH-independent mechanism.

Acid ceramidase (ACase) inhibition protects against ferroptosis independently of iron regulation, despite iron being a classic ferroptosis driver via the Fenton reaction. ACase knockdown increased ferritin heavy chain 1 (FTH1), a buffer of ferrous iron, yet the labile iron pool (LIP, reactive Fe2+) was actually increased in senescent cells after ACase knockdown despite the anti-ferroptotic effect. This demonstrates that ACase inhibition acts upstream of both the GPX4/GSH axis and iron/Fe2+ regulation, protecting cells by reducing the lipid peroxidation substrate pool rather than by modulating iron handling.
ACase catalyzes the primary reaction: Ceramide + H2O → Sphingosine + Free fatty acid. It is a cysteine amidase with activity blocked by thiol-reactive agents targeting Cys143.

Acid ceramidase (ACase) over-expression increases the polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) content of membrane phospholipids, promoting a pro-ferroptotic lipid profile. Mechanistically, ACase-mediated ceramide breakdown releases free saturated and monounsaturated fatty acids that, via the Lands cycle, are exchanged into sn-2 PUFA-containing phospholipids (PL-PUFAs) - the substrates of lipid peroxidation. ACase knockdown in senescent cells decreased the most abundant PL-PUFA species (including PC-AA, PG-DHA, PG-DPA), thereby reducing the lipid peroxidation substrate pool and conferring ferroptosis resistance.

links.source_file: _document_ - Could this enzyme help remove "zombie" cells from our tissues?.md
links.context: Acid ceramidase is a druggable, near-term, testable senotherapeutic target for clearing senescent cells. Experimental drugs targeting acid ceramidase have already been developed for other therapeutic purposes, demonstrating that the enzyme is targetable and lighting the way toward future innovation that could extend healthspans. Because elevated acid ceramidase makes senescent cells more susceptible to ferroptosis, inhibitors of the enzyme could selectively eliminate senescent 'zombie' cells while keeping neighboring cells healthy. The Salk team calls this a big milestone in the public health effort to support healthy aging, with the next steps being pathway completion, animal translation, and clinical trials.

links.source_file: _document_ - Could this enzyme help remove "zombie" cells from our tissues?.md
links.context: Senescent cells express progressively higher levels of the enzyme acid ceramidase, and this elevation is mechanistically tied to their heightened vulnerability to ferroptosis. Salk researchers cultured senescent human lung cells, induced ferroptosis, and found they were far more sensitive to this cell death pathway than young, healthy cells, with sensitivity beginning as senescent cells expressed increasingly higher enzyme levels. Removal of acid ceramidase from both senescent and non-senescent cells made them more resilient to induced ferroptosis. The enzyme thus links the two aging-associated cellular programs of senescence and ferroptosis, providing a potential target for removing senescent 'zombie' cells.

Acid ceramidase (ACase) expression is induced in neighboring proliferative cells by paracrine senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) signaling. Proliferative cells co-cultured with senescent cells (without direct contact) showed a significant time-dependent increase in ACase expression, while ACSL4 was unaffected, and the same effect was observed after incubating proliferative cells with recombinant IL-6/IL-8 (2:1 ratio). This ACase induction by the SASP cytokine IL-6 sensitizes bystander proliferative cells to ferroptosis, providing a mechanism for how senescent cells spread ferroptotic vulnerability through tissue.

Acid ceramidase (ACase) expression is induced in proliferative cells by paracrine SASP signaling, specifically mediated by the cytokines IL-6 and IL-8. Incubating proliferative cells with recombinant IL-6/IL-8 (2:1 ratio) reproduced the ACase upregulation seen with senescent-cell co-culture, without changing ACSL4. This SASP-driven ACase induction produces senescent-like features - elevated ACase and exacerbated lipid peroxidation - that sensitize neighboring cells to ferroptosis, illustrating how a few senescent cells can spread both senescence and ferroptotic vulnerability through tissue.

ARN14794 is a specific chemical inhibitor of acid ceramidase (ACase). Treatment with ARN14794 protected proliferative and senescent WI-38 cells, as well as neuronal-derived murine HT22 cells (a well-studied ferroptosis model), against RSL3-induced ferroptosis. Because ACase inhibitors already exist as drug candidates developed for other indications, ACase represents a tractable senolytic/senomorphic target for attenuating the deleterious effects of senescent cells during aging - a potential 'two birds with one stone' strategy that eliminates senescent cells while keeping neighboring cells healthy.

Acid ceramidase (ACase/ASAH1) is strongly over-expressed in replicatively senescent WI-38 human fibroblasts compared with proliferative cells, with Western blot confirming 5- to 20-fold higher expression. Along with the ferroptosis regulator ACSL4, ACase is among the lipid-metabolism enzymes upregulated in senescence. ACase knockdown reduced its levels strongly in senescent cells (though not fully, consistent with increased stability of ACase in senescence), and the senescence phenotype itself - p21 expression, SA-beta-gal activity, and IL-6/IL-8 secretion - remained intact after knockdown.

links.source_file: _document_ - Could this enzyme help remove "zombie" cells from our tissues?.md
links.context: Acid ceramidase catalyzes the breakdown of ceramides into sphingosine and free fatty acids, directly producing sphingosine in the cell. This enzymatic hydrolysis is a key branch point in sphingolipid metabolism, and in senescent cells the resulting reshaping of membrane lipid composition pushes membranes toward a pro-ferroptotic profile rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), the preferred substrates for lipid peroxidation. Because the excess sphingosine and free fatty acids generated by elevated acid ceramidase feed the lipid-peroxidation cascade, the enzyme serves as a mechanistic link between the cellular programs of senescence and ferroptosis, and its removal protects cells from ferroptotic death.
ACase overexpression creates a pro-ferroptotic membrane lipid profile independent of GPX4/GSH and iron axes, sensitizing senescent cells to ferroptotic death.

links.source_file: _document_ - Could this enzyme help remove "zombie" cells from our tissues?.md
links.context: Acid ceramidase promotes lipid peroxidation by enriching membranes with polyunsaturated fatty acids, the preferred substrates for peroxidative damage. The enzyme breaks down ceramides into sphingosine and free fatty acids, reshaping membrane lipid composition toward a pro-ferroptotic profile, and lipid peroxides accumulate to toxic levels, driving ferroptotic cell death. Healthy cells normally keep lipid peroxides at steady levels with the help of glutathione, an antioxidant that can stave off ferroptosis, but the acid-ceramidase-driven lipid remodeling shifts the balance toward oxidation. This novel pathway is independent of the usual ferroptosis mechanisms, involving neither changes in iron nor glutathione levels.
Acid ceramidase (ACase, aCDase) is encoded by ASAH1. It is a lysosomal hydrolase that cleaves ceramide into sphingosine and a free fatty acid.
ACase overexpression raises sphingosine/S1P levels, which is classically anti-apoptotic and helps senescent cells resist apoptosis via SCAP pathways.

GPx4 protects against ferroptosis as the master negative regulator of this iron-dependent, lipid-peroxidation-driven cell death. By reducing phospholipid hydroperoxides in membranes using GSH, GPx4 prevents the lethal accumulation of oxidized phosphatidylethanolamines. The directionality is enzymatic reduction preventing membrane collapse. A caveat is that GPx4 activity is exquisitely GSH-dependent, so anything depleting GSH (e.g., system xc- inhibition by erastin) triggers ferroptosis even with GPx4 present.

Iron binds to Neuromelanin through physicochemical affinity, forming a complex that modulates the local concentration or activity of the bound species. Mechanistically, Iron acts as the ligand or matrix and Neuromelanin as the binding partner, with the interaction often driven by catechol, quinone, or charge complementarity. This binding is significant because it can sequester toxins or metals, buffer neurotransmitters, or localize damage within pigmented neurons. A caveat is that the physiological magnitude, reversibility, and functional sequelae of the binding in vivo are not always fully quantified and may differ between intracellular and extracellular contexts.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuromelanin, aging, and neuronal vulnerability in Parkinson's disease.md
links.context: Iron causes Oxidative Stress by acting as the upstream trigger whose downstream consequence is the second entity's appearance or dysfunction. The mechanism typically involves oxidative, mitochondrial, or proteotoxic injury in the case of neurotoxins and pigments, or receptor blockade and cell loss in pharmacological and degenerative contexts. This causal relationship is clinically significant because it models or explains features of Parkinson's disease pathology and guides therapeutic targeting. A caveat is that in many of these links the causal claim is experimental, partial, or operates within a broader network of cofactors rather than as an isolated linear event.

Iron accumulates in multiple sclerosis lesions, where free Fe2+ catalyzes the Fenton reaction converting H2O2 to hydroxyl radicals and amplifying oxidative damage. Iron deposition is visualized by MRI and correlates with neurodegeneration. The directionality is iron burden to radical formation. A caveat is that iron accumulation can also be a response to demyelination and oligodendrocyte loss, not purely a cause of damage. Susceptibility-weighted MRI can visualize this iron deposition, offering an in vivo readout of the lesion's oxidative environment.

links.source_file: _document_ - Could this enzyme help remove "zombie" cells from our tissues?.md
links.context: Senescent cells are linked to many age-related conditions, including osteoarthritis, poor wound healing, and neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, according to senior author Pam Maher. The harmful factors senescent cells release (the SASP) promote tissue dysfunction and disease development in surrounding tissue. Because senescence and ferroptosis are both independently linked to age-related dysfunction, the discovery that elevated acid ceramidase makes senescent cells more susceptible to ferroptosis offers a two-birds-with-one-stone strategy: eliminating senescent cells while keeping neighboring cells healthy. Clearing senescent cells is considered a promising therapeutic approach for a multitude of age-related diseases and disorders.

links.source_file: _document_ - Could this enzyme help remove "zombie" cells from our tissues?.md
links.context: Senescent cells are linked to many age-related conditions, including osteoarthritis (arthritis), poor wound healing, and neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's or Parkinson's. The pro-inflammatory factors that senescent cells secrete into surrounding tissues promote tissue dysfunction and disease development, contributing to the joint degeneration seen in arthritis. The Salk findings suggest that making senescent cells vulnerable to ferroptosis through acid ceramidase could provide a novel target for therapeutics applicable to a multitude of diseases and disorders, including arthritis. Senescent cells are considered a hallmark of aging, and clearing them is a major goal of senolytic research for extending healthspan.

links.source_file: _document_ - Could this enzyme help remove "zombie" cells from our tissues?.md
links.context: Senescent cells can promote the development of diseases or disorders, including cancer, through the harmful factors they release into surrounding tissues (the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, or SASP). Though sometimes harmless, senescent cells that accumulate with age produce a pro-inflammatory environment that supports tumor development and age-related tissue dysfunction. This is why senescent cells are a hallmark of aging and why strategies to clear them - for example, via the acid ceramidase/ferroptosis axis - are pursued as senolytic approaches. Senescent cells are linked to many age-related conditions including arthritis, poor wound healing, and neurodegenerative diseases.

links.source_file: _document_ - Could this enzyme help remove "zombie" cells from our tissues?.md
links.context: Senescent cells - often called 'zombie' cells - are a hallmark of aging: they do not completely die but also are not quite alive, and while sometimes harmless, they release harmful factors called the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) into surrounding tissues. This secretory phenotype is pro-inflammatory and can promote the development of diseases or disorders, including cancer, and accelerates aging by driving tissue dysfunction. Because senescent cells are linked to many age-related conditions including arthritis, poor wound healing, and neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, clearing them - as proposed through acid ceramidase-mediated ferroptosis sensitization - is a major strategy for extending healthspan.

links.source_file: _document_ - Could this enzyme help remove "zombie" cells from our tissues?.md
links.context: Vulnerable senescent cells are able to pass their ferroptosis vulnerability on to neighboring cells, helping explain why only a few senescent cells can turn into more and ultimately impact a larger tissue over time. This paracrine transmission of ferroptosis sensitivity means that a small number of senescent cells can spread susceptibility to ferroptotic death across a tissue, and it represents one mechanism by which the Salk team found ferroptosis and senescence to be connected during aging. The researchers describe the target as eliminating senescent cells while keeping neighboring cells healthy for longer, and the finding underpins the therapeutic rationale for targeting acid ceramidase.

Senescent cells are characterized by a chronically elevated baseline of reactive oxygen species and a state of apoptotic priming, remaining alive despite high stress through upregulation of senescent cell anti-apoptotic pathways. This chronically oxidized state makes senescence a redox-dependent phenotype. In the senolytic hypothesis the elevated ROS baseline means senescent cells sit closer to the apoptosis threshold, so additional oxidative stress from adrenochrome redox cycling could push them into cell death.

Senescent cells upregulate senescent cell anti-apoptotic pathways (SCAPs), a network of survival mechanisms that keeps them alive despite high oxidative and genotoxic stress. SCAPs raise the threshold for apoptosis, and because these cells are apoptosis-primed, poised at the edge of death, the senolytic strategy is to remove this protection or to add enough stress, for example ROS from aminochrome redox cycling, to tip them over the threshold into apoptosis. Selective killing therefore depends on the gap between senescent and healthy cell defenses.

links.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md
links.context: IL6 is a representative SASP gene whose expression is suppressed upon mitochondrial clearance, with coordinated decreases in chromatin acetylation at its locus and mRNA expression. Acetate supplementation induces expression of IL6 alongside IL8, IL1B and CCL2, while MPC1 deletion or SLC25A1 inhibition reduces these factors. In aged mice, CTPI2 treatment reduces expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines including Il6 and Il1b in skeletal muscle, and their expression negatively correlates with muscle strength, indicating that mitochondrial acetyl-CoA-dependent histone acetylation gates the secretion of IL-6 as part of the senescent inflammatory programme.

IL-6 is a central driver of in vivo reprogramming toward pluripotency and stemness via JAK/STAT3 signaling, promoting a dedifferentiated, stem-like state in recipient cells. This underlies both wound-healing plasticity and, pathologically, cancer stemness, with STAT3 transcriptionally sustaining stemness factors such as OCT4, NANOG, and SOX2. The relationship links a core SASP cytokine to cell-fate reprogramming and is supported by reprogramming and cancer-stemness studies. Blocking IL-6/JAK/STAT3 signaling can interrupt this reprogramming.

Interleukin-8 (IL-8) is one of the best-known cytokines of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), along with IL-6. Secreted by senescent cells, IL-8 reshapes local tissue microenvironments and exerts paracrine effects on neighboring cells.
