links.context: BNIP3 (BCL-2/adenovirus E1B interacting protein 3) is an outer mitochondrial membrane mitophagy receptor that interacts directly with LC3 to promote engulfment of damaged mitochondria, functioning independently of Parkin. NIX/BNIP3-mediated mitophagy is induced through hypoxia and stabilization of HIF-1alpha. BNIP3 also interacts with OPA1 to induce mitochondrial fragmentation and with FUNDC1 under the control of OPA1 and DRP1, and its protein levels are upregulated at early premalignant stages of several human solid cancers but frequently decrease when tumors become invasive.

Mitophagy is a subtype of selective autophagy targeting only damaged/dysfunctional mitochondria. It converges on the same terminal step (autophagosome → lysosome) but differs in selectivity and initiation.

links.source_file: _document_ - The role of mitochondrial dynamics in disease.md
links.context: Aging of the nervous system combined with decreased mitophagy is a hallmark of neurodegeneration, and mitophagy dysregulation is a predominant factor contributing to various neurodegenerative disorders including Alzheimer's disease, Huntington's disease, ALS and mixed dementia. The mitophagy pathway is affected at multiple stages, from cargo recognition to lysosomal fusion. Inducing mitophagy can produce pathological and cognitive outcomes in AD, yet suppressing mitophagy restored mitochondrial density in synapses in some models; in ALS, mitophagy may be neuroprotective initially but prolonged elevation can aggravate neuronal damage, illustrating its context-dependent role.

links.source_file: _document_ - The role of mitochondrial dynamics in disease.md
links.context: Because autophagosomes in mammalian cells are approximately 500-1500 nm, a large interconnected mitochondrial network must be broken up by fission before mitophagy can occur, and the degradation of fusion- or fission-related factors is required for mitophagy. DRP1-mediated fission promotes mitophagy: inhibition of DRP1 reduces Parkin-mediated mitophagy, and asymmetric fission produces a small dysfunctional fragment that is prevented from fusing and subsequently engulfed and degraded. However, DRP1 is not always necessary for mitophagy, since some reports show that cardiac-specific DRP1 knockout mice maintain mitophagy and that FIS1 can mediate mitophagy independently.

High circulating branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) levels - leucine, isoleucine, and valine - are associated with obesity, insulin resistance, and mortality in humans. High-BCAA diets promote obesity, insulin resistance, inflammation, and decreased lifespan in rodents, whereas dietary restriction of BCAAs promotes metabolic health, reduces frailty, and extends lifespan, recapitulating many benefits of protein restriction. BCAA restriction reduces mTORC1 signaling, induces Fgf21, reduces hepatic cellular senescence, and in human studies improves insulin sensitivity and glucose/insulin homeostasis while increasing circulating FGF21. Although BCAAs are often considered as a group, each individual BCAA plays distinct roles in aging.

Caloric restriction (CR) and intermittent fasting extend both lifespan and healthspan in diverse species, but CR is of little benefit when started in old age and fasting inhibits the mTOR pathway in young but not old mice. By contrast, rapamycin strongly inhibits mTORC1 at any age and extends lifespan whether started late or early in life. The beneficial effects of rapamycin and CR may be additive since they are exerted through overlapping but distinct mechanisms, and intermittent rapamycin and CR can be combined, with exercise potentially most beneficial immediately after rapamycin use.

links.source_file: _document_ - Dietary Advanced Glycation End Products and Aging.md
links.context: Caloric restriction increases lifespan in C. elegans and mice, and several centenarian populations studied share a lower caloric intake. It has been postulated that the positive outcomes of caloric restriction in mice could be explained in part by a decrease in the intake of advanced glycation end products and a concomitant decrease in oxidative stress. When mice on a caloric restriction diet were instead given a CR diet high in AGEs, lifespan benefits were lost and survival was even shorter than in regular-fed mice, supporting the hypothesis that reduced dietary AGE intake contributes to the longevity effects of caloric restriction.

links.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
links.context: Calorie restriction (CR) is considered the most effective approach to extend lifespan in eukaryotes, and its life-prolonging effects may partly be mediated via increased sirtuin function, which requires NAD+ as a substrate. A study in mouse models documented that a one-day fast increases NAD+ in the liver, whereas CR elevates NAD+ and reduces nicotinamide in the brain, implying that increased levels of NAD+ mediate several beneficial effects of calorie restriction. As with CR, nicotinamide riboside (NR) can increase NAD+ levels and Sir2 function, and it extends lifespan in yeast without calorie restriction, supporting the life-prolonging effects of NR supplementation.

Caloric restriction and rapamycin are alternative inducers of autophagy that, like spermidine, engage the lysosomal-degradative program to promote healthspan, but each carries translational limitations. Caloric restriction is difficult to sustain long-term in humans and can have adverse metabolic consequences, while rapamycin has immunosuppressive and potential metabolic side effects. Spermidine offers a more tractable, well-tolerated means to mimic these benefits through safe autophagy induction. The existence of multiple inducers provides flexibility in designing anti-aging interventions.

Moderate caloric restriction induces adaptive autophagy—a beneficial, hormetic form of the pathway that enhances cellular clearance and resilience without causing damage. This adaptive response, driven by AMPK activation and mTORC1 inhibition, contributes substantially to the lifespan and healthspan extension observed with CR. Unlike pathological autophagy, adaptive autophagy is precisely regulated and supports rather than threatens cell survival. It represents the mechanistic core of CR's pro-longevity effects.

Prolonged or severe caloric restriction can drive excessive autophagy that crosses into autophagic cell death, particularly when degradative flux outpaces biosynthetic capacity. This maladaptive extreme underscores the biphasic, hormetic nature of autophagy, where too little or too much is detrimental. The balance between adaptive and excessive autophagy determines whether CR is protective or harmful. Understanding this threshold is important for safely translating CR-mimetic strategies.

Caloric restriction increases the sensitivity of tumor cells to chemotherapy by creating a differential stress resistance in which normal cells enter a protective, autophagy-dependent quiescent state while cancer cells remain vulnerable. CR additionally stimulates CD8+ T cell-mediated anti-tumor immunity and enhances apoptotic priming of malignant cells. The improved therapeutic index allows lower effective doses and reduced toxicity. These effects position CR and its mimetics as adjuncts to conventional cancer therapy.

Caloric restriction attenuates epigenetic drift, the progressive divergence of methylation and chromatin marks that accumulates with age. In C. elegans, caloric restriction reverses the age-related decline of microRNAs, and in mammals it slows age-associated changes in DNA methylation, helping to preserve youthful epigenetic patterns. By limiting drift, caloric restriction maintains transcriptional fidelity and cellular identity, contributing to its well-documented effects on healthspan and lifespan.

Caloric restriction, the best-characterized lifespan-extending intervention, has shown measurable reversal of epigenetic clock estimates in some studies. By limiting energy intake, caloric restriction slows age-related changes in DNA methylation and chromatin, reducing the methylation-predicted biological age of tissues relative to chronological age. These findings indicate that biological age is malleable and have made epigenetic clocks standard endpoints in longevity research and intervention trials.

In yeast, the replicative lifespan extension conferred by caloric restriction is abolished when the SIR2 gene is deleted, establishing Sir2 as a required mediator of the CR response. This dependence reflects the fact that CR raises the NAD+/nicotinamide ratio, which relieves nicotinamide feedback inhibition and boosts Sir2 deacetylase activity. The relationship is directional: CR acts upstream and Sir2 is the necessary downstream effector in this genetic pathway. A caveat is that in higher organisms the requirement is distributed across multiple sirtuins and redundant pathways, so SIR2/SIRT1 is necessary but not solely sufficient.

Reducing glucose from 2% to 0.5% in yeast medium extends replicative lifespan by roughly 30%, an effect mediated through elevated NAD+ availability and Sir2 activation. The mechanism hinges on CR lowering the nicotinamide/NAD+ ratio, thereby disinhibiting Sir2 and reinforcing silencing at repetitive rDNA and subtelomeric regions. This intervention is directional: the dietary manipulation is the cause and the lifespan gain the consequence. The finding seeded the broader hypothesis that sirtuin activation underlies longevity benefits of restricted feeding across species.

Dietary restriction in Drosophila extends lifespan and, as in yeast, this benefit requires the dSir2 (Sir2) gene, indicating evolutionary conservation of the sirtuin-mediated CR pathway. The effect is thought to operate through improved protein homeostasis, stress resistance, and metabolic efficiency rather than simple calorie shortage. Directionally, reduced nutrient signaling upstream engages dSir2 to produce the longevity phenotype. Caveats include that the magnitude and requirement vary with sex, genetic background, and the precise restriction paradigm used.

In rodents, caloric restriction raises SIRT1 levels in multiple tissues, and this elevation is linked to reduced inflammatory and oxidative responses. Higher SIRT1 expression translates into enhanced deacetylation of targets such as NF-κB, FOXO, and PGC-1α, promoting stress resistance and metabolic health. The directionality is that CR is the upstream stimulus and increased SIRT1 abundance/activity the downstream mediator. This adaptation is considered a key explanation for the anti-aging and disease-protective effects of CR in mammals.

Caloric restriction elevates the brain NAD+/nicotinamide ratio, which both supplies more co-substrate for sirtuins and relieves nicotinamide-mediated feedback inhibition of SIRT1. The resulting gain in sirtuin activity supports neuronal stress resistance, mitochondrial function, and suppression of neuroinflammatory signaling. The relationship is directional: CR shifts the ratio upward, which then potentiates sirtuin-dependent protective programs. This mechanism is frequently invoked to explain CR's protective effects against age-related cognitive decline and neurodegenerative pathology.

In pancreatic islets of calorically restricted mice, SIRT4 expression is reduced, shifting the mitochondrial sirtuin balance toward the protective, oxidative-phosphorylation-promoting actions of SIRT3. Because SIRT4 normally restrains amino-acid-stimulated insulin secretion and mitochondrial fat oxidation, its downregulation supports improved β-cell metabolic flexibility. The directionality is that CR suppresses SIRT4 transcription, altering the SIRT3/SIRT4 ratio. Aging shows the opposite pattern—rising SIRT4 and falling SIRT3—so CR counters the age-related drift in this ratio.

In mouse models engineered to develop Alzheimer's-like pathology, caloric restriction prevents accumulation of β-amyloid neuropathology, an effect consistent with SIRT1-driven reductions in neuroinflammation and oxidative stress. CR also preserves cognitive function and synaptic integrity in these models. Directionally, caloric restriction sits upstream of reduced amyloid burden. This supports the hypothesis that CR protects the brain through sirtuin-mediated resilience, and is consistent with SIRT1's promotion of the non-amyloidogenic α-secretase ADAM10. Human translation remains uncertain, but the findings motivate lifestyle interventions and NAD+-boosting strategies in neurodegeneration.

Caloric restriction and intermittent fasting elevate BDNF through SIRT1/FoxO-dependent pathways, contributing to cognitive resilience against aging. Directionally, caloric restriction sits upstream of BDNF elevation via SIRT1/FoxO. This neuroprotective adaptation complements CR's systemic benefits, and it motivates CR and fasting for brain health. By raising BDNF through sirtuin-dependent mechanisms, caloric restriction supports synaptic plasticity, neurogenesis, and neuronal survival. These effects contribute to the protection of cognitive function during aging.

Caloric restriction upregulates SIRT3 and downregulates SIRT4, shifting the SIRT3/SIRT4 ratio toward a protective, oxidative-phosphorylation-promoting state. Directionally, caloric restriction sits upstream of the ratio shift. This counters the age-related pattern of declining SIRT3 and rising SIRT4, and it is a core mechanism of CR's metabolic benefits. By biasing the balance toward SIRT3, caloric restriction promotes mitochondrial oxidation, antioxidant defense, and metabolic flexibility. This ratio shift is a key molecular readout of the beneficial effects of dietary restriction.
Longevity interventions including caloric restriction require autophagy — life-extension by CR is abolished when autophagy is blocked in model organisms.
CR induces autophagy via energy deficit — increased AMP/ATP ratio activates AMPK, which phosphorylates and activates ULK1 while inhibiting mTORC1.

Caloric restriction is a canonical mitohormetic stressor: a transient energy deficit activates AMPK, PGC-1alpha, SIRT1, and NRF2, driving mitochondrial biogenesis, mitophagy, and endogenous antioxidant defenses. Glucose restriction and CR are among the best-established triggers of the hormetic longevity response.
CD38 is the primary enzymatic consumer of NAD+ in mammalian tissues during aging. Chronic inflammaging causes CD38 upregulation on neutrophils and macrophages, starving sirtuins.

links.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
links.context: CD38 is an ectoenzyme that consumes NAD+ as a substrate and was found to also degrade nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN). Its levels and activity increase with aging, and this age-related upregulation is required for the NAD+ decline and mitochondrial dysfunction seen in old tissues. Because CD38 breaks down NMN, it alters the pharmacokinetics and bioavailability of both NMN and NR precursors. Consequently CD38 regulates the levels of NAD+, NMN, and SIRT1 activity, making it a candidate molecule for controlling neurodegeneration; in mice, CD38 knockdown suppressed axon degeneration, demyelination, and immune cell infiltration after facial nerve axotomy, and NR injection mimicked this protective effect.

links.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
links.context: CD38 is the primary NADase in mammals, an ectoenzyme that uses NAD+ to produce and hydrolyze cADP-ribose, a Ca2+-mobilizing second messenger. Because CD38 also degrades the NAD+ intermediates nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), its activity further decreases the content of NAD+. CD38 content increases with age, contributing to the age-related decline in NAD+ and mitochondrial dysfunction. In CD38-deficient mice, NAD+ levels remain high, preserving mitochondrial respiration and metabolic function with age, and pharmacological inhibition of CD38 can increase NAD+ levels and improve glucose and lipid metabolism.

links.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
links.context: CD38, the primary NADase in mammals, degrades the NAD+ intermediates nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), in addition to using NAD+ itself to produce and hydrolyze the Ca2+-mobilizing second messenger cADP-ribose. This degradation of NR and NMN further depletes cellular NAD+ content. CD38 expression increases with age and is also overexpressed in CD4+ and CD8+ lymphocytes upon activation of the adaptive immune response, which exaggerates NAD+ depletion. CD38-deficient mice maintain high NAD+ levels that preserve mitochondrial respiration and metabolic function with age, while CD38 inhibition increases NAD+ and improves glucose and lipid metabolism.

links.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
links.context: The content of CD38, the primary NADase in mammals, increases with age, and this enzyme uses NAD+ to produce and hydrolyze the Ca2+-mobilizing second messenger cADP-ribose while also degrading the NAD+ intermediates nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN). This age-related rise in CD38 therefore contributes to the progressive decline of NAD+ content during aging, and its effect was demonstrated in CD38-deficient mice whose NAD+ levels remain high, preserving mitochondrial respiration and metabolic function. Inhibition of CD38 can increase NAD+ levels and improve glucose and lipid metabolism, supporting NAD+ precursor strategies to counter age-associated decline.

By preserving NAD+, CD38 inhibition boosts sirtuin activity, especially the mitochondrial sirtuin SIRT3, which depends on adequate NAD+ to deacetylate metabolic and antioxidant enzymes. Directionally, CD38 inhibition increases NAD+, which heightens SIRT3 function. This indirectly enhances mitochondrial ROS defense and metabolic health, and is consistent with observations that CD38 knockout mice show elevated NAD+ and increased SIRT1 activity with protection from diet-induced obesity. Pharmacologic CD38 blockers such as 78c extend lifespan in aged mice through this axis, making CD38 inhibition a key pharmacological lever on mitochondrial sirtuin biology.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins (overview, CD38 KO risks, cancer therapies).md
links.context: CD38 consumes NAD+ to produce nicotinamide and cyclic ADP-ribose (cADPR), competing with sirtuins for the same NAD+ pool. Directionally, CD38 sits upstream of NAD+ depletion and nicotinamide generation. Because nicotinamide feedback-inhibits sirtuins, CD38 activity doubly suppresses sirtuin function—both by consuming their co-substrate and by generating an inhibitor. Inhibiting CD38 preserves NAD+ and boosts sirtuin activity, which is the basis for CD38-inhibitor strategies in aging. CD38 expression rises with age, accelerating NAD+ decline and compromising sirtuin-dependent maintenance.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins (overview, CD38 KO risks, cancer therapies).md
links.context: CD38 enzymatic activity depletes NAD+ in the tumor microenvironment and generates adenosine, suppressing anti-tumor T-cell and NK-cell responses. Directionally, CD38 sits upstream of NAD+ depletion and immunosuppression. This links CD38 to cancer immune evasion, and anti-CD38 antibodies both target myeloma and reshape the tumor microenvironment. By consuming NAD+ and producing immunosuppressive adenosine, CD38 on tumor and immune cells dampens anti-tumor immunity. This dual role makes CD38 both a therapeutic target and a mechanism of immune escape in cancer.

CD38, the major NADase in many mouse tissues, increases with age and depletes cellular NAD+ pools, thereby compromising sirtuin function. Mice lacking CD38 show elevated NAD+ levels and increased SIRT1 activity, coupled with protection from diet-induced obesity. Directionally, age-related CD38 upregulation sits upstream of NAD+ depletion and reduced sirtuin activity. Because sirtuins depend on NAD+ as a co-substrate, the rising NAD+ consumption by CD38 during aging starves sirtuin enzymes of their fuel. This makes CD38 a key target for NAD+-restoring interventions, and CD38 inhibition is being explored as a way to preserve NAD+ and support sirtuin function during aging.

NAD+ levels decline as C. elegans worms age, and restoration of NAD+ levels extends longevity through a pathway that requires activation of the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt). Overexpression of the NAD-dependent deacetylase sir-2.1 (the worm SIRT1 homolog) likewise extends lifespan in a UPRmt-dependent fashion. Mitochondrial activity centrally determines the levels of metabolic intermediates such as NAD+/NADH and acetyl-CoA, which act as obligate cofactors for the sirtuin, PARP, and histone acetyltransferase enzyme families.

links.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial Drivers Stem Cell Aging Inflammaging Bautista 2026.md
links.context: The progressive decline in NAD+ levels during aging is a central metabolic bottleneck compromising sirtuin-dependent resilience. Reduced NAD+ availability compromises SIRT1 and SIRT3 activity, which regulate PGC-1α, FOXO, and NRF1 transcriptional programs governing antioxidant defenses, mitochondrial biogenesis and stress adaptation. NAD+ decline arises from both reduced biosynthetic capacity and increased degradation via CD38, PARP1 and SARM1. Restoration of NAD+ enhances UPRmt activity, and PARP inhibition can promote mitonuclear communication and UPRmt activation.

links.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
links.context: NAD+ can directly affect the metabolism of intestinal microorganisms. Because NAD+ is an important component in the energy metabolism of all living organisms, mainly as a cofactor for key enzymes involved in cellular ATP production, boosting NAD+ may promote microbial energy production. NAD+ can also indirectly affect gut microbes by regulating the movement of the colon through the key inhibitory neurotransmitter beta-NAD and by affecting the synthesis of host bile acids, which can be antimicrobial when they destroy bacterial cell membranes. These mechanisms complement the ability of NMN and NR to modulate gut microbiota composition, forming a bidirectional NAD+-microbiota axis.

links.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
links.context: NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) is an essential coenzyme that plays central roles in cellular oxidation-reduction reactions, including most catabolic and anabolic processes such as glycolysis, fatty acid beta-oxidation, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and the synthesis of fatty acids, cholesterol, and steroids. Beyond its redox function, NAD+ is consumed by enzymes including sirtuins, poly-ADP-ribose polymerases (PARPs), CD38/CD157 ectoenzymes, and mono-ADP-ribose transferases, whose activity can deplete cellular NAD+ content.

links.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
links.context: Systemic NAD+ levels decline with aging as a result of both lowered rates of biosynthesis and increased consumption of NAD+. The decreased expression of the NAMPT enzyme is one of the major causes of this age-related NAD+ decline, and NAD+-consuming enzymes, including sirtuins, PARPs, and CD38, are induced by stress factors such as DNA damage, oxidative stress, and inflammation. The content of the primary mammalian NADase CD38 also increases with age, further lowering NAD+ availability. NAD+ depletion contributes to age-associated pathophysiology and is considered a major risk factor for Alzheimer's disease, supporting the use of NAD+ precursor supplementation to counter age-related decline.

links.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
links.context: NAD+ is indispensable for glycolysis because it serves as the electron acceptor in the oxidation of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, and it participates in fatty acid beta-oxidation and the tricarboxylic acid cycle as a redox cofactor. This immense metabolic demand, spanning most catabolic and anabolic reactions including the synthesis of fatty acids, cholesterol, and steroids, drives the high turnover of NAD+ that must be met by de novo synthesis from tryptophan or by salvage pathways from nicotinamide (NAM), nicotinic acid (NA), nicotinamide riboside (NR), and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN).

links.source_file: _document_ - The Sirtuin Network Linking NAD+ Metabolism, Mitochondrial Function, and Metabolic Homoeostasis.md
links.context: NAD+ is efficiently regenerated through the salvage pathway, which recycles nicotinamide produced as a byproduct of sirtuin reactions and other NAD+-consuming enzymes. The pathway converts nicotinamide back to NMN via NAMPT and then to NAD+ via NMN adenylyltransferases (NMNATs). Directionally, the salvage pathway sits upstream of the NAD+ pool that sirtuins depend on as obligate co-substrate. Because recycling is far more economical than de novo synthesis, the salvage pathway is the dominant route of NAD+ maintenance in most tissues. This is why NAMPT and the salvage pathway are central to strategies that restore NAD+ and re-engage sirtuin activity during aging.

Osteoarthritis is treated by senolytics in clinical trials (e.g., NCT04210986) aimed at reducing joint pain and improving function by clearing senescent chondrocytes and synovial cells that accumulate in degenerating joints. Preclinical studies show senolytics alleviate osteoarthritis pathology and improve cartilage integrity by reducing SASP-driven cartilage degradation and inflammation. Because senescent cells in joint tissue secrete proteases and inflammatory cytokines that erode cartilage, their elimination is considered a leading musculoskeletal application of senolytic therapy. Results have been promising enough to support continued clinical investigation in osteoarthritis.

links.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md
links.context: mtDNA-cGAS-STING signalling and mitochondrial control of histone acetylation operate as independently regulated pathways: senescent BAX- and BAK-deficient fibroblasts show reduced SASP gene expression from impaired cytosolic mtDNA release yet unchanged H3K27ac at SASP loci, and STING inhibition suppresses SASP without affecting histone acetylation. Despite this independence the pathways functionally cooperate: disruption of either is sufficient to suppress SASP while activation of either alone is not sufficient to fully restore it. Acetyl-CoA enables chromatin accessibility at SASP loci while mtDNA-driven innate immune signalling provides the activation required to engage these regions.

links.source_file: _document_ - The role of the dynamic epigenetic landscape in senescence_orchestrating SASP expression.md
links.context: The cGAS-STING pathway activates NF-kB, the master transcription factor of the inflammatory response and a key regulator of the SASP. After cGAS binds cytosolic DNA and activates STING, downstream signaling converges on TBK1 and IKK complexes to activate NF-kB, which drives the transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines. In senescent cells this cGAS-STING to NF-kB cascade is a principal route by which cytosolic self-DNA, including retrotransposon cDNA, induces SASP expression. This pathway is therefore a central node linking genomic surveillance to the aging inflammatory program.

The cGAS-STING complex promotes the SASP through interferon signaling activated by cytosolic DNA, including mtDNA, cytoplasmic chromatin fragments, and LINE-1 cDNA. cGAS senses the DNA and produces cGAMP, activating STING to drive IRF3 and NF-kB and type-I interferon, which induce SASP factor expression. This innate immune axis connects genomic and mitochondrial stress to inflammation and is a major, well-validated upstream activator of the senescent secretome. It also licenses immune surveillance of the senescent cell.

links.source_file: _document_ - JCI -Expanding roles of cGAS-STING signaling in neuroinflammation.md
links.context: mtDNA released by minority MOMP activates cGAS-STING, driving type-I interferon and NF-kB-dependent SASP without causing full cell death. The cytosolic mtDNA acts as a damage-associated molecular pattern recognized by cGAS, linking mitochondrial dysfunction (SAMD) directly to innate immune activation. This activation is a pivotal bridge between metabolism and senescence inflammation and also enhances immune surveillance of the arrested cell. It is a well-validated mechanism in multiple senescence models.

links.source_file: _document_ - JCI -Expanding roles of cGAS-STING signaling in neuroinflammation.md
links.context: Cytoplasmic chromatin fragments (CCF), which are shed from DNA-SCARS, are sensed by cGAS-STING to drive NF-kB-mediated SASP. CCF carry both DNA and histones into the cytosol, providing a potent innate immune stimulus in senescent cells, particularly in therapy-induced senescence. This mechanism directly couples persistent DNA damage to secretome activation and is a key bridge between genotoxic stress and inflammation. It represents a chromatin-based route to innate immune signaling in senescence.

links.source_file: _document_ - JCI -Expanding roles of cGAS-STING signaling in neuroinflammation.md
links.context: Cytoplasmic LINE-1 cDNA triggers interferon signaling through cGAS-STING, reinforcing the SASP in deep senescence when retroelements are derepressed. LINE-1 reverse-transcription products provide cytosolic nucleic-acid ligands for cGAS, and this activation is restrained by RB1 and SIRT6, whose decline permits L1 mobilization. The mechanism connects transposon activation to innate immune-driven inflammation and represents a late, amplifying loop in established senescence. It is increasingly recognized as a driver of age-related sterile inflammation.

cGAS-STING in senescent cells enhances senescence surveillance by promoting type-I interferon production that boosts NK- and T-cell killing of the arrested cells. The interferons increase immune visibility and effector function against senescent targets, linking innate sensing to adaptive and innate clearance. This enhanced surveillance is the beneficial face of cGAS-STING in senescence, complementing its role in SASP induction. STING pathway activity thus shapes whether senescence is contained or allowed to accumulate.

links.source_file: _document_ - JCI -Expanding roles of cGAS-STING signaling in neuroinflammation.md
links.context: cGAS-STING is indirectly inhibited by lamivudine (3TC), a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor that blocks LINE-1 propagation, thereby reducing cytosolic retroelement cDNA that would otherwise activate the pathway and downstream NF-kB SASP. This repurposes an antiretroviral as a senomorphic targeting the retrotransposon arm of innate immune activation. The inhibition is indirect but mechanistically supported by studies showing reduced SASP and interferon responses upon LINE-1 inhibition. Clinical relevance remains investigational, giving moderate confidence.

links.source_file: _document_ - Neuroprotective Actions of Methylene Blue and Its Derivatives.md
links.context: Chlorpromazine, a phenothiazine carrying an amine side chain on its 10-nitrogen, was the only compound among those tested that failed to protect HT-22 cells in the rotenone neurotoxicity model. The 10-N substitution causes a roughly 1000-fold loss of potency relative to methylene blue in glutamate, IAA, and rotenone assays, and abolishes the complex I-to-cytochrome c electron shunt, oxygen consumption enhancement, and glycolysis suppression. In the lysate oxidation assay chlorpromazine increased DCF fluorescence with or without mitochondria and NADH, behaving as a pro-oxidant and explaining its weak neuroprotection.

Sarcopenia is an age-related condition marked by declining muscle mass, strength, and functional capacity. Creatine supplementation combined with resistance training is an effective countermeasure: studies in older adults (>65 years) taking 5 g/day during heavy resistance training promoted greater gains in muscle mass and isometric strength, and meta-analyses confirm that older individuals doing resistance training gain more muscle mass, strength, and functional capacity when supplementing creatine. Creatine also preserves muscle mass and promotes fat loss during energy-restricted diets, helping manage adult-onset obesity while preventing the muscle loss that commonly accompanies weight loss in older individuals.

Creatine supplementation has been reported to lower plasma homocysteine, an effect that may reduce cardiovascular disease risk. Because homocysteine is methylated back to methionine by enzymes that require the same methyl-donor pool (S-adenosyl methionine) used for creatine synthesis, supplying exogenous creatine spares methyl groups that would otherwise be consumed in endogenous creatine formation, thereby lowering homocysteine production. Studies in individuals adhering to vegan diets (who tend to have elevated homocysteine) reported that creatine supplementation reduced homocysteine levels and improved systemic microvascular endothelial function, supporting creatine's role in cardiovascular health beyond its direct effects on muscle bioenergetics.

Creatine down-regulates the expression of toll-like receptors, including TLR-2, TLR-3, TLR-4, and TLR-7, in a mouse macrophage cell line (RAW 254.7). This downregulation could reduce the ability to sense some infections in immunocompromised individuals, but TLR-4 downregulation may also alter Parkinson's disease pathology and inhibit neuronal death as the disease progresses. Creatine's influence on toll-like receptors is one component of its broader immunomodulatory effects, which also include altering cytokine production, possibly through the NF-kB signaling pathway, thereby affecting cytokines, receptors, and growth factors that shape immune responses and inflammation.

Creatine supplementation increases brain phosphocreatine content by 5-15% and enhances brain bioenergetics, which is thought to underlie its cognitive benefits. Studies report that creatine attenuates mental fatigue and improves cognition, executive function, working memory, and processing speed, especially in older adults and during sleep deprivation. Examples include improved working memory and processing speed after 5 g/day for 6 weeks, better maintenance of mood, balance, and reaction time after sleep deprivation, and improved long-term memory and random number generation in elderly participants. While not all studies show benefit, the evidence supports creatine as a modest cognitive enhancer, particularly under metabolic or cognitive stress.

Creatine supplementation is one of the most studied and effective ergogenic aids for athletes. It increases muscle creatine and phosphocreatine levels, enhances acute exercise capacity, and improves training adaptations, yielding roughly 10-20% improvements in high-intensity exercise tasks across fitness activities, golf, volleyball, soccer, softball, ice hockey, running, and swimming. The International Society of Sports Nutrition concludes creatine is the most effective ergogenic supplement available for increasing high-intensity exercise capacity and lean body mass during training. Ergogenic benefits are seen in men and women across ages from children to the elderly, although most studies have been conducted in men.

Creatine augments the anticancer efficacy of the metabolite methylglyoxal (MG). Creatine content and energy availability are low in several types of malignant cells and in the T cells that mediate immune responses against cancer, and the creatine transporter SLC6A8 is markedly increased in tumor-infiltrating immune cells. Patra et al. reported that MG efficacy is significantly augmented in the presence of creatine, and combined administration of creatine, methylglyoxal, and ascorbic acid provided greater efficacy and eliminated visible signs of tumor growth. Creatine and creatine kinase, very low in sarcoma tissue, were significantly elevated with concomitant regression of tumor cells.

Creatine is reported to exert antioxidant effects, scavenging reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and stabilizing membranes, effects that are proposed to protect tissues from oxidative damage. Some studies suggest creatine supplementation reduces markers of oxidative stress and muscle damage after intense exercise, and experimental work indicates creatine can directly scavenge superoxide and peroxynitrite in vitro. Because oxidative stress contributes to DNA damage and tumor promotion, creatine's antioxidant capacity is cited in the trace as one possible mechanism for an anti-cancer effect, although direct evidence linking creatine's antioxidant action to cancer prevention in humans is lacking.

Creatine supplementation is one of the most effective and best-documented ergogenic aids for improving performance in high-intensity, short-duration activities. By increasing muscle phosphocreatine stores, creatine enhances the capacity to regenerate ATP during repeated bouts of maximal exercise, increasing power output, strength gains during resistance training, and work performed in repeated sprint protocols. Meta-analyses consistently show moderate improvements in measures such as maximal strength, sprint performance, and lean body mass, with benefit most pronounced in activities relying on the phosphocreatine energy system. These well-established performance effects are the context in which the trace asks whether creatine also influences cancer outcomes.

Creatine supplementation supports healthy glucose management by enhancing glucose uptake and insulin sensitivity. Mechanistically, creatine prevents the decline of GLUT4 during muscle disuse, increases GLUT4 during rehabilitation, and co-ingestion with carbohydrate or protein augments muscle creatine and glycogen. In individuals with type 2 diabetes, creatine supplementation during exercise training improved glucose tolerance to a standard meal, increased GLUT4 translocation, and lowered HbA1c, with AMPK signaling implicated in these effects. Creatine uptake into tissue is itself influenced by glucose and insulin, establishing a bidirectional relationship between creatine status and glycemic physiology that supports creatine as an adjunct for metabolic health.

Creatine supplementation influences glucose handling in skeletal muscle, in part by upregulating the GLUT4 glucose transporter. Creatine prevents declines in GLUT4 during immobilization and increases GLUT4 by about 40% during rehabilitation after atrophy, and co-ingestion with carbohydrate and protein enhances creatine uptake and muscle glycogen. In type 2 diabetic patients, 12 weeks of creatine supplementation during training improved glucose tolerance, increased GLUT4 translocation, and significantly reduced HbA1c, with changes in AMPK signaling related to GLUT4 translocation and HbA1c. These findings indicate creatine enhances glucose uptake and supports glucose management, especially when combined with exercise.

Creatine supplementation increases muscle creatine and phosphocreatine stores and, particularly when combined with resistance training, promotes gains in lean tissue mass and strength. Randomized trials in older adults show greater gains in muscle mass and isometric strength with creatine plus heavy resistance training compared to training alone, and meta-analyses confirm larger gains in muscle mass and upper-body strength in older individuals supplementing creatine during resistance exercise. Creatine also decreases protein breakdown and can preserve muscle mass during energy-restricted weight loss, making it a broadly useful strategy for maintaining muscle across the lifespan and in clinical rehabilitation populations.

Creatine is a naturally occurring nitrogen-containing compound that is synthesized endogenously in the liver, kidney, and pancreas and is also obtained from dietary sources, particularly red meat and fish. Around 95 percent of the body's creatine is stored in skeletal muscle, approximately one-third of it in the phosphorylated form creatine phosphate. In the muscle it is converted to creatine phosphate, which donates its high-energy phosphate group to regenerate ATP from ADP, supporting short-duration, high-intensity exercise. Because of its role in ATP regeneration, creatine is one of the most widely used sports supplements and is increasingly examined for additional therapeutic effects, including possible anti-cancer properties.

Dietary creatine is obtained almost exclusively from animal-derived foods, with red meat and fish being the richest sources. Cooking does not destroy creatine, and an omnivorous diet typically supplies one to two grams of creatine per day, which complements the roughly one gram synthesized endogenously per day. Vegetarians have lower muscle creatine stores and show larger increases in response to supplementation than meat-eaters, reflecting the lower baseline intake. This dietary origin is relevant to epidemiologic questions about meat consumption and cancer risk, because creatine is often discussed alongside other meat-derived compounds when considering diet-cancer associations.

Within cells, creatine is phosphorylated by the enzyme creatine kinase to form creatine phosphate (phosphocreatine), which serves as a rapidly mobilizable reserve of high-energy phosphate. The reaction creatine plus ATP yields creatine phosphate plus ADP, and the reverse reaction regenerates ATP during bursts of high energy demand, such as muscle contraction. The phosphocreatine pool is the immediate energy buffer that sustains ATP levels for the first several seconds of maximal effort, before glycolysis and oxidative metabolism fully contribute. This conversion of creatine to creatine phosphate is the mechanistic heart of the creatine-phosphocreatine energy system.

Roughly two-thirds of the body's creatine pool is phosphorylated and stored as phosphocreatine (PCr), with the remainder held as free creatine. The creatine kinase (CK) reaction interconverts creatine and PCr, and the energy liberated by breaking PCr down into phosphate and creatine (about 10.3 kcal) is used to resynthesize ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. This PCr/CK system is the rapid, phosphagen-based buffer that maintains ATP availability during intense exercise, ischemia, hypoxia, and high metabolic demand. Creatine supplementation raises muscle creatine and PCr stores, expanding this reserve and thereby enhancing high-intensity exercise capacity and training adaptations.

Creatine monohydrate is among the most extensively studied dietary supplements and is generally regarded as safe when used at recommended doses over periods of many years. Long-term supplementation studies report no consistent adverse effects on renal, hepatic, or cardiovascular function in healthy individuals, and creatine is approved for use by many sports organizations. Common minor side effects include water retention and occasional gastrointestinal discomfort. This favorable safety profile is noted in the trace as relevant to the potential evaluation of creatine as an adjunct in oncology settings, where tolerability is a central concern.

Approximately 95 percent of the body's creatine is stored in skeletal muscle, where it exists partly as free creatine and partly as creatine phosphate. The muscle creatine pool is maintained by both endogenous synthesis and dietary intake, and it is depleted by high-intensity activity and resynthesized during recovery. Muscle total creatine concentrations can be increased by supplementation, typically by 10-20 percent, and this elevated store extends the time for which high-intensity exercise can be sustained. The predominance of skeletal muscle as a creatine depot explains why most creatine research has focused on muscle function, strength, and performance.

Creatine is synthesized endogenously from the amino acids arginine, glycine, and methionine in a two-step pathway. The first step, catalyzed by arginine:glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT), takes place primarily in the kidney and pancreas and produces guanidinoacetate; the second step, catalyzed by guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase (GAMT), transfers a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to guanidinoacetate in the liver, producing creatine. This biosynthetic origin connects creatine metabolism to the methylation cycle and one-carbon metabolism, a connection relevant to hypotheses linking creatine status to epigenetic regulation and cancer risk.

Creatine is a naturally occurring nitrogen-containing compound synthesized endogenously in the body. The first step of its biosynthesis condenses arginine and glycine into guanidinoacetate (GAA), a reaction catalyzed by arginine glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT), which is expressed in the kidney, pancreas, liver, and certain brain regions. Endogenous synthesis supplies roughly half of the daily creatine requirement; the remainder must come from the diet, primarily red meat and fish, or from supplements. Deficiencies in the enzymes of this pathway (AGAT, GAMT) or the creatine transporter produce creatine synthesis deficiency syndromes marked by low brain creatine and neurodevelopmental impairment.

Glycine serves as the second amino acid substrate for endogenous creatine synthesis. Arginine glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT) condenses arginine with glycine to produce guanidinoacetate (GAA), which is then methylated by guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase (GAMT) using S-adenosyl methionine to yield creatine. Because glycine and arginine are the committed substrates for creatine biosynthesis, their availability influences the rate of endogenous creatine production, which normally covers about half of daily needs. The rest is obtained from dietary red meat, fish, or supplements, and total body creatine stores are typically around 120 mmol/kg of dry muscle mass.

Because endogenous creatine synthesis is the major consumer of methyl groups donated by S-adenosylmethionine, creatine status may influence DNA methylation reactions that govern gene expression, including the expression of oncogenes and tumor suppressors. Supplemental creatine, by reducing the requirement for de novo creatine synthesis, could preserve methyl groups for DNA methyltransferases and thereby modulate global DNA methylation patterns. The trace notes that this is an emerging and largely hypothesis-driven area: creatine's effects on DNA methylation and on one-carbon metabolism have been examined mainly in animal and small human studies, and any causal link to cancer prevention remains to be firmly established.

Creatine and the creatine kinase system are increasingly studied in the context of cancer metabolism. Some cancer types, particularly those with a poor prognosis, upregulate creatine kinase isoenzymes, and creatine metabolism has been reported to support the growth and invasiveness of certain tumors, whereas in other contexts creatine appears to restrain tumor growth, possibly through effects on energy homeostasis and AMPK. The trace explicitly notes that creatine's relationship to cancer is context-dependent and that current evidence is insufficient to recommend creatine as an anti-cancer intervention, underscoring the need for direct experimental studies.

Emerging evidence reviewed in the source trace suggests creatine may exert direct anti-cancer effects, inhibiting tumorigenesis rather than only supporting athletic performance. Mechanistic studies indicate that creatine supplementation can raise cellular phosphocreatine and creatine kinase activity, and the resulting change in the cellular energy state, together with creatine-mediated effects on AMPK and anabolic signaling, may suppress cancer cell proliferation and transformation. Because cancer cells depend on high glycolytic flux and altered energy metabolism, interventions that perturb the creatine-phosphocreatine system are hypothesized to restrain tumor growth, although the trace stresses that much of this evidence is preliminary and requires confirmation in well-powered clinical studies.

Creatine supplementation can alter the cellular energy status in ways that modulate AMPK, the central sensor of cellular energy charge. High phosphocreatine and low AMP levels generally suppress AMPK activation, while creatine depletion or energetic stress activates it. Because AMPK regulates anabolic processes, including protein synthesis and cell growth, and influences pathways relevant to cancer metabolism, creatine-induced changes in AMPK signaling are proposed to be one mechanism by which creatine could affect tumor cell proliferation. The trace presents this as a plausible but incompletely validated mechanistic link, noting that AMPK-dependent effects of creatine have been shown mainly in skeletal muscle and liver.

Creatine supplementation has been investigated for its ability to attenuate muscle wasting in conditions of disuse, catabolism, and disease. In healthy subjects it amplifies the muscle gains from resistance training, and in some clinical populations, including elderly individuals and people with neuromuscular or catabolic diseases, creatine supplementation preserves lean mass and strength. Because cancer and its treatments frequently cause sarcopenia and cachexia, creatine's potential to blunt muscle loss is proposed as a supportive-care role for creatine in oncology, even if any direct anti-tumor effect remains unproven.

Creatine and phosphocreatine play an important role in maintaining myocardial bioenergetics during ischemic events, reducing arrhythmias, ischemia-related damage, and improving heart function. Intravenous phosphocreatine prevented accumulation of arrhythmogenic lysophosphoglycerides in the ischemic zone of canine hearts, and adding phosphocreatine to cardioplegic solutions improved myocardial energy availability and reduced arrhythmias. Creatine supplementation also maintains energy availability during brain ischemia and reduces stroke-related damage. Several studies report benefits of oral creatine in chronic heart failure patients in rehabilitation, and phosphocreatine administration is considered a protective strategy for the heart during acute myocardial ischemia.

Preclinical studies suggest creatine supplementation can reduce the severity of spinal cord injury. Rats fed creatine before and after moderate spinal cord contusion developed less scar tissue and performed better on locomotor function tests than controls, and rats fed a 2% creatine diet before and after injury experienced less loss of gray matter. In humans with cervical spinal cord injury, creatine supplementation enhanced aerobic exercise capacity, ventilatory anaerobic threshold, and, combined with vitamin D and resistance training, improved arm muscle area, strength, and functional capacity. These findings support creatine as an adjunct that may reduce injury severity and enhance rehabilitation outcomes after spinal cord injury.

Creatine supplementation has shown neuroprotective potential in traumatic brain injury. In animal models, providing creatine in the diet for 5 days prior to TBI decreased cortical brain damage by 36% in rats and 50% in mice, an effect attributed to improved energy availability in the injured brain. Creatine also reduces the severity of mild concussions and ischemic brain damage and improves learning and memory during recovery in neonatal mice. While these preclinical studies cannot be replicated in humans, they support the contention that creatine supplementation may reduce the severity of TBI and serve as an adjunctive strategy in individuals at risk of head injury, complementing its established role in muscle and rehabilitation settings.

Creatine supplementation elevates brain creatine and phosphocreatine, improves brain bioenergetics, and has documented neuroprotective benefits, particularly in response to injury and ischemia. Animal studies show creatine feeding reduces cerebral ischemic brain damage volume by 25-40%, decreases infarct size, and attenuates neuronal death, while human studies report increased brain creatine (9.2% after 7 days), improved corticomotor excitability, and preserved attention during hypoxia. These findings suggest prophylactic creatine may reduce the severity of brain ischemia and stroke-related damage, and it has been investigated as a neuroprotective strategy in pregnancy to improve neonatal outcomes following birth asphyxia.

Creatine provides the immediate phosphate group needed to recycle ADP back into ATP, the cellular energy currency, keeping cellular energy pools saturated and reducing metabolic stress, which protects HRV from plunging during hard training. It is recommended daily at 3-5 grams, ideally post-workout or with the largest carbohydrate meal, because creatine uptake is enhanced by insulin. Pairing creatine with carbohydrates and protein helps drive it into muscle and brain cells more efficiently, with consistency mattering more than exact timing.

Creatine has immunomodulatory effects that include reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and other inflammatory markers like TNF-alpha and PGE2. A creatine-induced reduction of these inflammatory mediators may help explain some of the neuroprotective benefits observed in patients with central nervous system diseases and the attenuation of inflammatory and muscle damage markers after intense exercise. Creatine also down-regulates expression of toll-like receptors (TLR-2, TLR-3, TLR-4, TLR-7) in a mouse macrophage cell line and may influence cytokines through the NF-kB signaling pathway, with potential consequences for immune response and, notably, for TLR-4-mediated pathology in Parkinson's disease progression.

Creatine acts as a direct and indirect antioxidant, in part by coupling to oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria. Creatine diffuses into mitochondria and, via mitochondrial creatine kinase, couples with ATP produced by oxidative phosphorylation and the adenine nucleotide translocator, after which phosphocreatine diffuses back into the cytosol. This coupling reduces the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) by keeping the mitochondrial adenine nucleotide pool well-adenylated and stabilizing electron transport. Consequently creatine supplementation is reported to lower oxidative stress markers, which may contribute to its protective effects on muscle, heart, and brain, particularly under ischemic or metabolically stressed conditions.

The primary biochemical function of creatine is to buffer cellular ATP levels through the creatine-phosphocreatine system. Creatine kinase reversibly catalyzes the transfer of a phosphoryl group from phosphocreatine to ADP, regenerating ATP at rates far exceeding mitochondrial or glycolytic ATP production, which is essential for short bursts of intense activity. The creatine kinase reaction therefore acts as a rapid temporal energy buffer, maintaining ATP:ADP ratios during muscle contraction and other energy-demanding processes. This ATP-regenerating capacity is the basis for creatine's ergogenic effects and is also central to hypotheses about its influence on cancer cell metabolism.

The biological actions of creatine are mediated by the creatine kinase enzyme family, which catalyzes the reversible phosphorylation of creatine by ATP. Tissue-specific creatine kinase isoforms are expressed in muscle, brain, and other tissues, and the enzyme couples the phosphocreatine pool to cellular ATP demand. In tissues with high and fluctuating energy requirements, the creatine kinase reaction buffers ATP levels and transports high-energy phosphate between sites of production and consumption. Because creatine kinase is also expressed in several tumors, the enzyme is a candidate interface through which creatine supplementation could influence cancer cell energy metabolism.

Creatine and its related compound cyclocreatine have documented anticancer properties. Creatine is an important energy source for immune cells and supports CD8 T cell antitumor immunity, since creatine uptake via the SLC6A8 transporter regulates CD8 T cell function and creatine levels are low in malignant cells and antitumor T cells. Creatine also augments the efficacy of the anticancer medication methylglyoxal, with combined creatine, methylglyoxal, and ascorbic acid eliminating visible signs of tumor growth in experimental models. Evidence is emerging rather than definitive in humans, and creatine is being studied as an adjunct in cancer cachexia and treatment contexts.

High-dose, long-term creatine supplementation is a nutritional strategy for creatine synthesis deficiencies caused by mutations in AGAT, GAMT, or the creatine transporter (SLC6A8), which reduce endogenous creatine synthesis or cellular uptake and result in low brain creatine and phosphocreatine. Supplementation at 0.3-0.8 g/kg/day increases brain creatine and PCr levels and improves or stabilizes clinical symptoms including intellectual disability, epilepsy, and movement disorders. Patients with GAMT or AGAT deficiency treated early (e.g., starting at four months of age) can experience normal psychomotor development, and such therapy is well tolerated and may also benefit ornithine aminotransferase deficiency causing gyrate atrophy.

Creatine synthesis is the single largest consumer of S-adenosylmethionine-derived methyl groups in the body, using approximately 70 percent of available methyl donor flux. Guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase transfers a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to guanidinoacetate to form creatine, thereby competing with DNA methylation and other methylation reactions for the methyl pool. Because exogenous creatine supplementation reduces the demand for endogenous creatine synthesis, it can spare methyl groups and shift the balance of methylation reactions. This creatine-methionine interaction forms the mechanistic basis for the hypothesis that creatine could influence epigenetic processes relevant to cancer.

Creatine supports COMT function indirectly by supplying phosphocreatine for cellular energy, allowing the methylation cycle to operate efficiently without diverting as many methyl groups toward de novo creatine synthesis. Because endogenous creatine synthesis consumes a large fraction of the body's methyl groups, exogenous creatine supplementation reduces methyl demand and spares SAMe for COMT and other methyltransferases. This nutritional strategy helps maintain catechol methylation capacity and is especially relevant in slow COMT individuals. It represents a methyl-sparing rather than methyl-donating approach to supporting methylation.

links.context: Creatine supports MTHFR function indirectly by lowering the methyl-group demand of endogenous creatine synthesis, which consumes a substantial share of the body's methyl budget, thereby easing reliance on folate-dependent remethylation. For slow MTHFR variants that generate methylfolate less efficiently, supplemental creatine can reduce the metabolic pressure on an already constrained methylation cycle and help preserve SAMe availability. The benefit is supportive rather than direct enzymatic rescue, but it relieves a major competing methyl sink. This makes creatine a useful adjunct in methylation-support protocols.

Exercise causes a transient but significant elevation of resting metabolic rate that outlasts the exercise bout itself. A number of studies show RMR is increased for at least 24-48 hours following vigorous exercise, and residual increases are detectable even up to 3 days after a single session in some protocols. The elevation appears largely independent of the intensity of the exercise, with high-intensity interval exercise providing comparable post-exercise energy expenditure to continuous moderate exercise when matched for work. This post-exercise elevation is one mechanism by which physical activity raises daily energy expenditure beyond the direct cost of the exercise itself.

Exercise raises total daily energy expenditure (TEE) through several mechanisms acting together: the direct metabolic cost of the exercise bout itself, the elevated resting metabolic rate and excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC) that persist after the session, and increases in nonexercise activity thermogenesis and appetite in some individuals. Speakman uses doubly labelled water studies to show that while athletes have high TEE, the contribution of exercise to TEE in moderately active people is modest in magnitude, and that an exercise-induced rise in TEE of 10-15 percent is not necessarily compensated by reduced activity in other parts of the day.

Exercise is defined as planned, structured, and repetitive physical activity performed specifically to improve or maintain physical fitness, and it constitutes a subset of total physical activity, which also includes occupational activity, domestic activity, and non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT). In the energy balance framework of the Speakman review, exercise is the most flexible and controllable component of total daily energy expenditure, and its contribution to daily energy use is quantified through doubly labelled water studies. Because exercise is a voluntary component, it is the primary target of public-health interventions aimed at raising daily energy expenditure.

An important conclusion of the Speakman review is that exercise does not reliably increase appetite, and that in many individuals appetite is suppressed both during and for a period after exercise, an effect that can persist for up to 24 hours in some protocols. This is counter to the common belief that increased exercise necessarily drives increased food intake. When exercise does raise energy intake, the increase is generally smaller than the energy cost of the exercise, so a net negative energy balance is usually achieved. These findings support the view that exercise contributes to weight control by raising expenditure without a fully compensatory increase in intake.

Exercise generates acute ROS bursts that drive mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant upregulation, and metabolic adaptation via NRF2 and PGC-1alpha. Post-workout high-dose synthetic antioxidants (vitamin C/E) blunt this necessary ROS signal, so letting endogenous adaptation occur is the therapeutic goal.

links.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
links.context: Regular physical exercise reduces AGE accumulation in tissues. In rats, 12 weeks of moderate exercise reduced CML and RAGE in aortic vessels, and treadmill exercise from late middle age to 35 months reduced cardiac AGE levels. Life-long trained athletes had 21% lower AGE cross-link content in the patellar tendon than age-matched untrained subjects, and regular exercise prevented renal AGE deposition in D-galactose-induced aging rats. Physical exercise is therefore proposed as a powerful weapon against AGE formation and AGE-related aging processes.

links.source_file: _document_ - The role of glycation in the pathogenesis of aging and its prevention through herbal products and physical exercise.md
links.context: Regular physical exercise has beneficial effects on glycemic control, and because AGE formation is accelerated by hyperglycemia, improved glycemic control attenuates the formation and accumulation of AGEs in tissues. Exercise benefits diabetic patients by improving glycemic control, and physical activity reduces AGE accumulation in diabetic patients and during aging. The higher energy demands of exercise may also reduce the pool of reactive intermediates available for glycation. Together with its antioxidant effects, glycemic control is a major mechanism by which exercise reduces AGE burden.

links.context: Moderate physical exercise induces the expression of antioxidant enzymes, leading to the reduction of oxidative stress. Exercise effectively inhibits ROS generation and improves the activities of antioxidant enzymes, and because the protein glycation reaction is driven and accelerated by ROS, the inhibition of AGE formation by regular exercise is attributed mainly to exercise-associated antioxidant activity. Physical exercise also decreases oxidative stress in rodent models and is reported to improve systemic antioxidant activity in humans. These antioxidant effects link exercise to reduced AGE accumulation and healthier aging.

links.context: Regular physical exercise effectively inhibits reactive oxygen species generation and improves the activities of antioxidant enzymes. Because the protein glycation reaction is driven and accelerated by ROS, the inhibition of AGE formation by regular exercise is considered the main mechanism of exercise-associated antioxidant activity. Exercise also reduces oxidative stress in rodent models and improves glycemic control, both of which limit AGE accumulation. These effects make physical exercise a non-pharmacological strategy for attenuating glycation stress during aging.

links.context: Exercise raises both BDNF and NAD+ levels, and SIRT1 may mediate exercise-induced BDNF upregulation in the hippocampus. Directionally, exercise sits upstream of BDNF and NAD+ elevation. Higher NAD+ fuels SIRT1, which then supports BDNF, and this provides a mechanistic bridge between physical activity, sirtuins, and brain health. By raising NAD+, exercise engages the sirtuin pathway that promotes BDNF expression and mitochondrial function. This axis is central to the well-established cognitive benefits of exercise and to the geroscience concept of exercise as medicine.

DNA methylation is one of the most extensively studied epigenetic mechanisms, operating alongside histone modification and non-coding RNA regulation. It involves the covalent addition of methyl groups to cytosines at CpG dinucleotides, repressing gene expression in promoter CpG islands by recruiting methyl-binding proteins and chromatin remodeling factors. Patterns are established de novo by DNMT3 enzymes and maintained by DNMT1 during replication, while methylation also silences transposable elements. Age-related global hypomethylation with focal hypermethylation defines the aging methylome, and selected CpG sites feed the epigenetic clocks that estimate biological age.

High levels of DNA methylation in promoter regions, often concentrated in CpG islands, are strongly associated with gene silencing. Methylated promoters recruit methyl-CpG-binding domain (MBD) proteins and inhibit the binding of transcription factors, converting active promoters into transcriptionally inert chromatin. This repressive mechanism is used physiologically for imprinting and for silencing transposable elements, and its aberrant targeting of tumor suppressor gene promoters is a hallmark of cancer.

Methylated DNA is recognized by methyl-CpG-binding domain (MBD) proteins that recruit chromatin remodeling factors and histone deacetylases to the site. These recruited complexes remove acetyl groups and deposit repressive histone modifications, promoting condensation of the chromatin into a transcriptionally inactive state. This cross-talk between DNA methylation and histone modification establishes a self-reinforcing repressive loop that maintains stable gene silencing across cell divisions, and it is a major route by which promoter methylation converts active genes into silenced heterochromatin.

Aberrant DNA methylation is a hallmark of many cancers, characterized by global hypomethylation across repetitive elements and gene bodies together with focal hypermethylation of tumor suppressor gene promoters. Global hypomethylation promotes genomic instability and reactivation of transposable elements, while promoter hypermethylation silences genes that protect against transformation. These alterations cooperate with genetic mutations to drive tumorigenesis and provide targets for epigenetic therapies using DNA methyltransferase inhibitors.

Aging is accompanied by global DNA hypomethylation, particularly at repetitive regions and gene bodies, coupled with focal hypermethylation at CpG islands and specific gene promoters. This pattern of age-related methylation change, known as epigenetic drift, erodes cellular identity and can reactivate silenced transposable elements. The loss of methylation is partly attributed to declining DNMT1 activity, and the resultant epigenetic instability contributes to age-associated dysfunction and disease.

Epigenetic clocks are built from DNA methylation measurements at defined sets of CpG sites whose methylation levels change predictably with chronological age. These statistical models convert methylome data into an estimate of biological age, and deviations between predicted and chronological age indicate accelerated or decelerated aging. Because methylation at these sites responds to interventions such as caloric restriction and partial reprogramming, clocks are used to track the effectiveness of rejuvenation strategies.

DNA methylation helps repress potentially harmful repetitive elements and retrotransposons within the genome. Methylation at the promoters and internal sequences of transposable elements such as LINE-1 and Alu elements maintains them in a transcriptionally silent state, preventing their mobilization and the genomic instability they would otherwise cause. Age-related loss of this methylation derepresses these elements, allowing their transcription and reverse transcription, which in turn triggers innate immune signaling and inflammaging.

DNA methylation patterns regulate the senescent transcriptome and SASP: global hypomethylation with focal hypermethylation at specific loci reshapes gene accessibility and contributes to SASP factor expression. Epigenetic remodeling thus licenses the secretome independently of transcription-factor-only models, and CDKN2B silencing by promoter methylation in cancers exemplifies this control. The relationship is supported by epigenomic profiling of senescent cells. Confidence is moderate given the complexity and context-dependence of senescence epigenetics.

links.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
links.context: AMPK is a cellular energy regulator that senses changes in the intracellular AMP/ATP ratio. Under energy limitation, low ATP levels activate AMPK, which switches on catabolic pathways that produce ATP by enhancing oxidative metabolism and mitochondrial biogenesis while switching off ATP-consuming anabolic pathways, thereby altering the NAD+/NADH ratio. By increasing cellular NAD+ levels, AMPK enhances SIRT1 activity, which then deacetylates and modulates energy metabolism-related targets including PGC-1alpha, FOXO1, and FOXO3a. This AMPK-SIRT1-NMNR circuit explains how nutrient and energy status couples to NAD+-dependent regulation, and why NAD+ precursor supplementation can reinforce these energy-sensing pathways.

links.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
links.context: Activation of AMPK promotes fatty acid oxidation and insulin sensitivity while reducing fatty acid synthesis and gluconeogenesis, and it can also increase mitochondrial biogenesis and glycogen synthesis. Through AMPK-dependent signaling, urolithin A improves muscle energy supply and metabolism. AMPK is therefore a central node connecting cellular energy status to muscle metabolic adaptation, endurance, and overall muscle performance, and its activation is a key mechanism underlying the metabolic effects attributed to urolithin A.

links.source_file: _document_ - Pharmacological Effects of Urolithin A and Its Role in Muscle Health and Performance Current Knowledge and Prospects.md
links.context: By activating AMPK, urolithin A can increase mitochondrial biogenesis and enhance fatty acid oxidation and glycogen synthesis, ultimately improving muscle energy supply and metabolism and enhancing muscle performance. AMPK-driven mitochondrial biogenesis is a major mechanism through which energy-sensing interventions expand the mitochondrial network to meet cellular energy demands. It is a key downstream consequence of urolithin A treatment and is closely coupled to the activation of PGC-1α, the master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis.

AMPK is a canonical inducer of autophagy that responds to rising AMP/ATP ratios during metabolic stress by directly phosphorylating and activating ULK1 at sites that promote phagophore formation. Simultaneously, AMPK inhibits mTORC1 by phosphorylating TSC2 and the mTORC1 subunit Raptor, removing the dominant brake on autophagy. AMPK can also phosphorylate TFEB/STBD1 to further enhance autophagic and glycogenolytic responses. Through these parallel actions, AMPK couples cellular energy scarcity to the rapid deployment of autophagic degradation.

AMPK phosphorylates TFEB on a cluster of serine residues (S466, S467, S469) located in its C-terminal regulatory region in response to energy stress. These phosphorylations enhance TFEB transcriptional activity and promote its nuclear accumulation, synergizing with the relief of mTORC1 repression. The modification thereby directly couples low cellular energy status to activation of the autophagy-lysosomal transcriptional program. This AMPK-TFEB axis provides a transcription-level reinforcement of the rapid post-translational induction of autophagy.

AMPK inhibits mTORC1 through at least two parallel mechanisms during cellular energy depletion: it phosphorylates and activates the TSC2 subunit of the TSC complex, and it directly phosphorylates the mTORC1 scaffold Raptor. These actions reduce Rheb-GTP levels and impair mTORC1 substrate engagement, thereby relieving repression of autophagy. AMPK thus couples the AMP/ATP energy charge to suppression of anabolic mTORC1 signaling. This inhibition is a primary route by which exercise, metformin, and caloric restriction induce autophagy.

During caloric restriction, AMPK activates autophagy by sensing the elevated AMP/ATP ratio and directly phosphorylating ULK1 while inhibiting mTORC1 via TSC2 and Raptor phosphorylation. This dual action removes the principal brake on autophagy and simultaneously initiates phagophore formation. AMPK thereby serves as the executive enzyme translating energy scarcity into degradative activation. Its central role explains why CR-mimetics that activate AMPK recapitulate the autophagic benefits of dieting.

AMPK interacts with sirtuins to link cellular energy status to chromatin regulation and aging. AMPK senses declining energy levels, elevates NAD+ to activate sirtuins such as SIRT1, and shares downstream targets including FOXO and PGC-1alpha, connecting nutrient availability to gene expression and metabolism. This AMPK-sirtuin axis mediates many effects of caloric restriction and hormetic stimuli, coordinating mitochondrial function, autophagy, and stress resistance with the epigenetic state. Pharmacological activation of this axis reproduces many benefits of dietary restriction.

Under low-energy conditions, AMPK directly phosphorylates SIRT1 at Ser27 and Thr344, enhancing its deacetylase activity and coupling energy deficit to sirtuin function. Directionally, AMPK sits upstream of SIRT1 activation. This closes the reciprocal loop with SIRT1, and it ensures sirtuin responses track cellular AMP/ATP state. By phosphorylating SIRT1, AMPK links the energy-sensing kinase network to sirtuin-dependent gene regulation. This mechanism explains how fasting, exercise, and caloric restriction, which activate AMPK, also engage SIRT1-dependent programs.

The mitohormetic trigger activates key nutrient-sensing and stress-response pathways including AMPK, PGC-1alpha, SIRT1, and NRF2. AMPK then drives mitochondrial biogenesis and autophagy, leaving a resilient metabolic engine; this is why mild, pulsed stress enhances longevity and metabolic efficiency.

Neuroprotection and Parkinson's Disease are reciprocally linked entities in the neuromelanin knowledge graph, reflecting their frequent co-occurrence and shared relevance to catecholamine biology or Parkinson's disease. Directionally, the graph relation is symmetric, although biologically Neuroprotection and Parkinson's Disease may occupy distinct mechanistic roles. Their association is significant because both contribute to the chemical and pathological network that defines vulnerability of pigmented neurons. A caveat is that a bidirectional link denotes an association rather than a proven direct causal mechanism between the two entities.

A methyl group is a covalent substituent consisting of one carbon atom bonded to three hydrogen atoms (-CH3), the smallest alkyl group and the universal currency of biological methylation. It is transferred by methyltransferases such as COMT from donors like SAMe to acceptors including DNA, proteins, phospholipids, and catechol rings. Methyl group flux is central to epigenetic regulation, neurotransmitter inactivation, and detoxification. Its availability is governed by the folate and methionine cycles, linking diet to methylation capacity.

Creatine kinase (CK) is the enzyme at the core of the creatine/phosphocreatine energy system. It catalyzes the reversible transfer of a phosphate group between creatine and ADP, using the free energy released from phosphocreatine breakdown (approximately 10.3 kcal) to resynthesize ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. This provides a rapid means of replenishing depleted ATP during high-energy-demand states such as intense exercise or conditions where energy production is impaired (ischemia, hypoxia) or insufficient due to increased demand (mental fatigue, disease states). Cytosolic, glycolytic, and mitochondrial CK isoforms cooperate to buffer ATP/ADP ratios and shuttle high-energy phosphate from mitochondria to sites of ATP consumption.

links.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md
links.context: CTPI2, a third-generation SLC25A1 inhibitor, delays the onset of frailty in aged mice as measured by a validated 31-parameter frailty index, alongside improvements in fur condition, coordination, balance and grip strength. In aged tissues, CTPI2 suppresses SASP-associated inflammatory gene expression across skeletal muscle, liver and heart while leaving p16 and p21 unchanged, and circulating inflammatory cytokines are reduced, indicating a systemic attenuation of inflammatory burden. These benefits arise without broad metabolic reprogramming: body weight, composition, metabolic rate, respiratory exchange ratio, activity and lipid metabolic pathways are largely unaffected.

links.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP.md
links.context: Aged (19-month-old) C57BL/6 mice gavaged with CTPI2 (50 mg/kg three times weekly for 3 months) exhibited more lustrous fur, reduced alopecia and greying, and delayed onset of frailty as measured by a 31-parameter frailty index.
