Directionally, DC SIRT1 sits upstream of suppressed Th1 differentiation. This tempers cell-mediated inflammatory responses and promotes regulatory T-cell generation, shaping the balance between immunity and tolerance. It demonstrates SIRT1's immunoregulatory role in antigen presentation and is relevant to autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, where excessive Th1 responses drive pathology. The effect likely reflects SIRT1-dependent control of cytokine and costimulatory molecule expression in dendritic cells.

SIRT1 is highly expressed in the vasculature, including endothelial and smooth-muscle cells, positioning it as a central regulator of vascular homeostasis. Directionally, constitutive vascular abundance enables rapid SIRT1 responses to metabolic and shear stress. This expression pattern underlies its roles in vasodilation, inflammation, and atherosclerosis, and loss of vascular SIRT1 promotes endothelial dysfunction. Because the endothelium is constantly exposed to hemodynamic and metabolic signals, SIRT1's abundance in this tissue allows it to integrate nutrient status with vascular function, making it a key determinant of blood-vessel health and disease.

SIRT1 modulates angiogenic activity during vascular remodeling and growth, influencing endothelial sprouting and vessel stability in a context-dependent manner. Directionally, SIRT1 tunes angiogenic signaling. It can either promote or restrain angiogenesis depending on oxygen and metabolic cues, reflecting SIRT1's integration of stress and metabolic inputs in the vessel wall. In some settings SIRT1 supports the neovascularization needed for tissue repair, while in others it limits the pathological angiogenesis that feeds tumors. This context-dependence makes SIRT1 a nuanced regulator of vessel growth, with implications for both regenerative medicine and oncology.

links.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
links.context: eNOS-derived nitric oxide activates SIRT1, and SIRT1 deacetylates eNOS to maintain its activity, forming a reciprocal endothelial-protective loop that declines with age; this NO/SIRT1 axis supports cardiovascular healthspan (Mattagajasingh et al., 2007; listed as a positive regulator in the source review's Table 3).

SIRT1 downregulates angiotensin II type 1 receptor (AT1R) expression in vascular smooth-muscle cells, reducing angiotensin-II signaling. Directionally, SIRT1 sits upstream of AT1R suppression. Lower AT1R diminishes vasoconstriction and hypertensive signaling, contributing to SIRT1's antihypertensive actions. This is consistent with the observation that resveratrol-driven SIRT1 elevation reduces angiotensin-II-induced hypertension in vivo. By dampening the renin-angiotensin system's most important receptor, SIRT1 provides vascular protection that parallels the effects of AT1R blockers, positioning sirtuin activation as a complementary approach to blood-pressure control.

SIRT1 regulates tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase 3 (TIMP3), an endogenous inhibitor of matrix metalloproteinases that defends against vascular inflammation and remodeling. Directionally, SIRT1 sits upstream of TIMP3 regulation. By preserving TIMP3, SIRT1 limits extracellular-matrix degradation and inflammatory infiltration in vessels, protecting the vessel wall from pathological remodeling. This adds a matrix-protective dimension to SIRT1's vascular role, complementing its effects on eNOS, AT1R, and NF-κB. TIMP3 also regulates TNF-α signaling, so SIRT1-dependent TIMP3 maintenance connects sirtuins to both matrix homeostasis and inflammatory control.

SIRT1 deacetylates Beclin-1 at multiple lysines, promoting its interaction with the class III PI3K Vps34 and enhancing autophagy initiation and flux. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatically licenses Beclin-1. This supports autophagosome formation and cellular clearance, and it is a central SIRT1 autophagy substrate alongside LC3, Atg5, Atg7, and ULK1. By deacetylating Beclin-1, SIRT1 promotes the assembly of the autophagy initiation complex and couples nutrient status to cellular quality control. This mechanism contributes to SIRT1's protection against the accumulation of damaged proteins and organelles during aging.

SIRT1 activates Nrf2 by modifying Keap1 structure, leading to Nrf2 nuclear translocation and expression of antioxidant genes. Directionally, SIRT1 sits upstream of Nrf2 activation. This is a canonical cytoprotective axis against oxidative and electrophilic insult, and it complements SIRT1's direct antioxidant substrate actions through FOXO and PGC-1α. Because Nrf2 coordinates the expression of hundreds of detoxifying and antioxidant enzymes, SIRT1-dependent Nrf2 activation provides broad protection against cellular stress. This pathway is relevant to aging, where declining Nrf2 activity contributes to the accumulation of oxidative damage.

SIRT1 protects against inflammation by deacetylating and attenuating NLRP3 activity via the AMPKα/XBP1 pathway in macrophages. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatically suppresses NLRP3 through XBP1s. This couples endoplasmic-reticulum stress responses to innate immune regulation, and it is a refined mechanistic view of SIRT1's anti-inflammasome action. By deacetylating XBP1s downstream of AMPK, SIRT1 prevents NLRP3 assembly and the subsequent maturation of IL-1β. This pathway is relevant to atherosclerotic and metabolic disease, where inflammasome-driven inflammation contributes to tissue damage and insulin resistance.

SIRT1 deacetylates SERCA2a at Lys492, restoring its activity and improving cardiac contractility in heart failure. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatically rescues SERCA2a function. Better calcium handling opposes the systolic dysfunction of failing hearts, since SERCA2a-mediated calcium reuptake is depressed in heart failure. This is a direct mechanistic rationale for SIRT1 activation in cardiomyopathy, and it complements SIRT1's effects on PPARα, antioxidant genes, and cardiac metabolism. By restoring the molecular pump that controls cardiac relaxation, SIRT1 addresses a fundamental defect in the failing myocardium.

SIRT1 deacetylates mitofusin 2 (MFN2) at Lys655 and Lys662, regulating mitochondrial fusion and quality control; loss of SIRT1 causes defective autophagy linked to impaired MFN2 function. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatically modifies MFN2. This connects sirtuin activity to mitochondrial dynamics and mitophagy, and it is relevant to neurodegenerative and metabolic disease where fusion is perturbed. By modulating MFN2, SIRT1 influences the balance between mitochondrial fusion and fission that determines mitochondrial network health. This regulation links SIRT1's pro-autophagy and mitophagy functions to the machinery that maintains mitochondrial integrity.

SIRT1 deacetylates p53 specifically at Lys379, inhibiting p53-dependent apoptosis and promoting cell survival under genotoxic stress. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatically inactivates p53 at this site. This is one of several lysines, including Lys317 and Lys370, targeted by SIRT1, and the net effect is cytoprotection that can be oncogenic in established tumors. By dampening p53-mediated apoptosis, SIRT1 biases cells toward repair and survival after DNA damage. The p53-SIRT1 axis is thus a double-edged sword, protecting normal tissues but also potentially shielding cancer cells from death signals.

SIRT1 deacetylates ULK1 at multiple lysines, enhancing its kinase activity and initiating autophagy under glucose starvation. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatically activates ULK1. This places SIRT1 upstream of the core autophagy-initiation complex, and it is a key mechanism by which nutrient stress engages autophagic clearance. By deacetylating ULK1, SIRT1 licenses the initiation of autophagosome formation, and this action complements its deacetylation of Beclin-1, LC3, Atg5, and Atg7. SIRT1's coordinated regulation of the autophagy machinery makes it a central node coupling NAD+ status to cellular quality control.

SIRT1 deacetylates TFEB at Lys116, enhancing its nuclear translocation and transcriptional activity to drive the CLEAR autophagic/lysosomal gene program. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatically activates TFEB. This promotes lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux, and it links SIRT1 to the terminal degradative arm of autophagy alongside ULK1 and Beclin-1. By promoting TFEB nuclear translocation, SIRT1 coordinates the expression of lysosomal enzymes and autophagy machinery. This regulation ensures that sirtuin-dependent quality control extends to the final steps of cargo degradation, and its decline with age impairs cellular clearance.

SIRT1 deacetylates BMAL1, a core circadian transcription factor, gating circadian NAD+ oscillations and coupling metabolic state to clock-gene expression. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatically tunes BMAL1. This places sirtuins at the interface of circadian rhythm and metabolism, and it explains how NAD+ rhythms drive daily transcriptional programs. Because BMAL1/CLOCK regulate NAMPT, the circadian system controls NAD+ production, which in turn activates SIRT1, which deacetylates BMAL1 to feed back on the clock. This SIRT1-BMAL1-NAMPT loop couples daily rhythms to cellular energy metabolism.

SIRT1 deacetylates Atg5, enhancing autophagosome formation as part of its autophagy-promoting function. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatically activates Atg5. Atg5 is essential for LC3 lipidation and autophagosome elongation, so this modification supports the core autophagic machinery. SIRT1's deacetylation of Atg5 adds to its coordinated regulation of ULK1, Beclin-1, Atg7, and LC3, placing SIRT1 at multiple steps of the autophagy pathway. This broad control links sirtuin activity to the clearance of damaged organelles and proteins, contributing to SIRT1's cytoprotective and longevity-associated functions.

SIRT1 deacetylates Atg7, promoting autophagy initiation and autophagosome formation. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatically activates Atg7, the E1-like enzyme that conjugates LC3 to phosphatidylethanolamine. This reinforces SIRT1's broad control of the autophagic machinery, and it complements SIRT1 actions on ULK1, Beclin-1, Atg5, and LC3. By enhancing the lipidation of LC3, SIRT1-dependent Atg7 activation supports autophagosome membrane elongation. This coordinated regulation across multiple autophagy components is a hallmark of SIRT1's role in cellular quality control.

links.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
links.context: SIRT1 deacetylates/modulates HIF-1α, limiting hypoxic glycolytic reprogramming.

SIRT1 deacetylates STAT3 as part of its broad anti-inflammatory and metabolic regulatory functions, altering STAT3-driven transcription. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatically tunes STAT3. Because STAT3 drives proliferation and inflammation, its deacetylation influences cytokine signaling and cell growth, and the effect is relevant to both cancer and chronic inflammation. The evidence for this regulation carries moderate confidence, reflecting incomplete characterization. By modifying STAT3, SIRT1 provides another route to restrain inflammatory and growth-promoting transcription, complementing its actions on NF-κB.

SIRT1 deacetylates the liver X receptor (LXR), a nuclear receptor that regulates cholesterol metabolism and efflux. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatically modulates LXR. This influences reverse cholesterol transport and lipid homeostasis, expanding SIRT1's role in cardiovascular and metabolic regulation. By deacetylating LXR, SIRT1 can alter the expression of cholesterol-efflux genes, connecting sirtuin activity to lipid handling. This regulation is relevant to atherosclerosis and metabolic disease, where cholesterol homeostasis is central, and it complements SIRT1's actions on PPARs and other nuclear receptors.

In mouse embryonic fibroblasts, SIRT1 rescues cells from PML-mediated premature senescence by deacetylating and inhibiting p53, relieving the senescence program. Directionally, SIRT1 sits upstream of senescence rescue. This requires the PML-p53-SIRT1 nuclear-body axis, and it shows SIRT1 can oppose proliferative arrest when appropriately engaged. By deacetylating p53 within PML nuclear bodies, SIRT1 dampens the p53-dependent senescence checkpoint. This dual role—promoting survival in normal cells but potentially enabling cancer-cell proliferation—illustrates the context-dependence of SIRT1's functions.

SIRT1 downregulates ROCK1 expression in neurons, which induces α-secretase (ADAM10) activity relevant to amyloid precursor processing and Alzheimer's prevention under caloric restriction. Directionally, SIRT1 suppresses ROCK1, which induces α-secretase. This shifts APP cleavage away from the amyloidogenic β-secretase pathway, reducing β-amyloid production. By promoting the non-amyloidogenic processing of APP through ADAM10, SIRT1 protects against amyloid pathology in Alzheimer's models. This mechanism is induced by caloric restriction and links sirtuin activity to the prevention of Alzheimer's disease.

During DNA repair, SIRT1 relocalizes to double-strand breaks where it deacetylates repair factors, a central mechanism of the Information Theory of Aging (RCM) framework. Directionally, DNA damage sits upstream of SIRT1 relocalization. This consumes NAD+ and redistributes chromatin modifiers, proposed to drive epigenetic drift, and it is a key node in Sinclair's model of aging. By moving to sites of damage, SIRT1 is thought to abandon its normal genomic loci, causing loss of epigenetic information. This redistribution model is the basis for the ICE-Mouse experiments linking DNA repair to epigenetic aging.

SIRT1 deacetylates FOXO3a, which then transcriptionally induces SOD2, catalase, and glutathione-biosynthesis genes, protecting cells against oxidative stress. Directionally, SIRT1 activates FOXO3a, which drives antioxidant enzyme induction. This is a canonical longevity-associated stress-resistance program, and it underlies much of SIRT1's cytoprotective reputation. By biasing FOXO3a target selection toward antioxidant and repair genes, SIRT1 reduces oxidative damage and supports cellular resilience. This axis is central to the beneficial effects of caloric restriction and NAD+ repletion on redox homeostasis.

SIRT1 physically interacts with and deacetylates PCAF (p300/CBP-associated factor), a histone acetyltransferase, within regulatory complexes at muscle-gene promoters. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatically inhibits PCAF. This counterbalances acetylation during myogenic regulation, and it shows SIRT1 tuning acetyltransferase partners, not only substrates. By deacetylating PCAF, SIRT1 reduces its HAT activity and its contribution to muscle-gene activation. This regulation is part of SIRT1's broader control of the acetylation-deacetylation balance that shapes transcriptional programs.

SIRT1 deacetylates MyoD itself, reducing its transcriptional transactivation potential and retarding muscle differentiation. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatically inhibits MyoD. This keeps myoblasts less differentiated under certain conditions, and it complements SIRT1's deacetylation of PCAF in suppressing myogenesis. By removing acetyl marks from MyoD, SIRT1 reduces its ability to activate muscle-gene expression. This regulation is part of the broader balance between histone acetyltransferases and deacetylases that controls myogenic differentiation.

SIRT1 deacetylates FOXO3a, which transcriptionally induces BNIP3, forming the NAD+-SIRT1-FOXO3a-BNIP3 mitophagy axis that clears damaged mitochondria. Directionally, SIRT1 sits upstream of BNIP3-dependent mitophagy. This protects cells from mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS, and it is a refined mitophagic branch of the SIRT1-FOXO3a program. By inducing BNIP3, FOXO3a promotes the selective removal of damaged mitochondria. This axis connects sirtuin-mediated NAD+ sensing to the quality control of the mitochondrial network.

SIRT1 deacetylates HIF-2α, modulating its stability and transcriptional output to influence metabolic adaptation to hypoxia. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatically tunes HIF-2α. This parallels SIRT1's regulation of HIF-1α, and the evidence carries moderate confidence reflecting less-complete characterization of this substrate. By modifying HIF-2α, SIRT1 may influence the balance between the two hypoxia-inducible factors and their distinct target genes. This regulation is relevant to oxygen sensing, erythropoiesis, and the metabolic adaptation of cells to low-oxygen environments.

SIRT1 deacetylates the retinoblastoma protein (Rb) as part of its cell-cycle regulatory functions, influencing Rb's interaction with E2F and cell-cycle control. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatically modifies Rb. This adds a cell-cycle dimension to SIRT1 beyond p53/E2F, and the evidence carries moderate confidence reflecting incomplete mechanistic detail. By deacetylating Rb, SIRT1 may modulate its ability to restrain E2F-dependent transcription and cell-cycle progression. This regulation connects SIRT1 to the G1/S checkpoint and to the control of proliferation in normal and cancer cells.

SIRT1 deacetylates p73, suppressing its transcriptional activity and inhibiting apoptosis, analogous to its regulation of the related p53 family member. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatically inactivates p73. This promotes cell survival under stress but can be tumor-promoting, and it extends SIRT1's control over the p53 family. By deacetylating p73, SIRT1 dampens its ability to activate pro-apoptotic and cell-cycle-checkpoint genes. This regulation is relevant to both normal tissue protection and cancer, where p73 suppression by SIRT1 may reduce tumor-suppressive responses.

Global SIRT1 overexpression does not extend overall mouse longevity, in contrast to the brain-specific BRASTO model, though it does ameliorate several age-sensitive traits. These include improved glucose homeostasis, better wound healing, and reduced incidence of carcinoma and sarcoma. Directionally, the distinction between global and tissue-specific transgenic effects points to both tissue-specificity and dose-dependence in how sirtuins influence lifespan. The finding tempers simple claims that more SIRT1 universally extends life, and it underscores that organ- and level-dependent actions determine whether SIRT1 elevation is protective or neutral for mammalian longevity.

In BRASTO mice, hypothalamic SIRT1 deacetylates the transcription factor NKX2-1, which drives expression of the orexin type 2 receptor (OX2R); increased OX2R in DMH/LH raises neural activity, physical activity, and energy expenditure, underpinning the approximately 11% lifespan extension. This positions the SIRT1-to-NKX2-1-to-OX2R pathway as a hypothalamic longevity axis that mimics calorie restriction. By increasing physical activity and energy expenditure through orexin signaling, SIRT1 promotes a CR-like metabolic state. This brain-centered mechanism demonstrates that sirtuin effects on lifespan can be mediated through neural control of energy balance.

SIRT1 induces expression of ADAM10, the principal alpha-secretase that cleaves APP away from amyloidogenic beta-secretase (BACE1) processing, reducing beta-amyloid production; this underlies SIRT1's protective role in Alzheimer's disease models. Directionally, SIRT1 upregulates ADAM10 to promote non-amyloidogenic APP processing. By shifting APP cleavage away from the amyloidogenic pathway, SIRT1 reduces the production of toxic beta-amyloid peptides. This mechanism, together with SIRT1's anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions, underlies its protection in Alzheimer's models and supports the idea that sirtuin activation could delay amyloid pathology.

links.source_file: _document_ - The Sirtuin Network Linking NAD+ Metabolism, Mitochondrial Function, and Metabolic Homoeostasis.md
links.context: SIRT1 deacetylates insulin receptor substrate-2 (IRS-2), a key adaptor in insulin and insulin-like growth factor signaling. This deacetylation enables efficient tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS-2 and downstream activation of the PI3K-Akt cascade, improving insulin signal transduction in peripheral tissues. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatic activity sits upstream of enhanced insulin signaling. By reinforcing this pathway, SIRT1 helps counter insulin resistance and hyperglycemia in type 2 diabetes. The regulation illustrates how a single sirtuin can tune insulin sensitivity, and it positions SIRT1 activators as potential metabolic therapeutics alongside lifestyle interventions that raise NAD+.

links.source_file: _document_ - The Sirtuin Network Linking NAD+ Metabolism, Mitochondrial Function, and Metabolic Homoeostasis.md
links.context: SIRT1 deacetylates CREB-regulated transcriptional coactivator 2 (CRTC2), an important regulator of hepatic gluconeogenesis. CRTC2 deacetylation occurs as part of SIRT1's dynamic, fasting-coupled control of glucose production in the liver, complementing its actions on FOXO1 and PGC-1alpha. Directionally, SIRT1 sits upstream of CRTC2-dependent transcriptional programs. Together these branches fine-tune when and how much glucose the liver releases, balancing gluconeogenic output against the body's energy needs. The coordination of CRTC2, FOXO1 and PGC-1alpha shows that SIRT1 integrates multiple transcriptional nodes to achieve homeostatic glucose control during fasting and refeeding.

links.source_file: _document_ - The Sirtuin Network Linking NAD+ Metabolism, Mitochondrial Function, and Metabolic Homoeostasis.md
links.context: SIRT1 deacetylates PPARgamma, and this deacetylation promotes expression of FGF21 among a broader set of thermogenic and browning genes. Induction of FGF21, in turn, supports adipose tissue browning and increases energy expenditure, consistent with SIRT1's anti-obesity actions. Directionally, SIRT1 sits upstream of PPARgamma deacetylation and FGF21 induction. FGF21 acts systemically to enhance glucose uptake, lipid oxidation, and adaptive thermogenesis, extending the effects of SIRT1 beyond the adipocyte itself.

links.source_file: _document_ - The Sirtuin Network Linking NAD+ Metabolism, Mitochondrial Function, and Metabolic Homoeostasis.md
links.context: SIRT1 deacetylates PPARgamma at lysine residues K268 and K293, and this modification promotes exchange of cofactors within the PPARgamma transcriptional complex. The resulting change in cofactor recruitment enhances browning of white adipose tissue, increasing thermogenesis, mitochondrial biogenesis, and PGC-1alpha-dependent oxidative programs. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatic modification of PPARgamma sits upstream of beige adipocyte induction. Because PPARgamma is a master regulator of adipocyte biology, its deacetylation by SIRT1 can shift adipose tissue from a fat-storing toward a fat-burning phenotype.

links.source_file: _document_ - SIRT1 Protein roles at the nexus of health, disease, and therapeutics.md
links.context: SIRT1 expression progressively declines with age, coinciding with reduced NAD+ levels and impaired sirtuin function in tissues. This decline is associated with decreased expression of core circadian clock components, disruption of central circadian regulation, and increased susceptibility to metabolic and neurodegenerative diseases. Directionally, aging sits upstream of reduced SIRT1 activity. Because SIRT1 couples cellular energetics to gene regulation, its loss during aging undermines stress resistance, metabolic flexibility, and DNA repair.

links.source_file: _document_ - SIRT1 Protein roles at the nexus of health, disease, and therapeutics.md
links.context: SIRT1 deacetylates histone H3 at lysine 79, and this modification promotes DNA hypomethylation and favors the formation of tightly compacted chromatin associated with gene silencing. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatic modification of H3K79 sits upstream of altered DNA methylation patterns. This connects SIRT1's histone deacetylase activity to the epigenetic regulation of telomeric chromatin and gene expression. By influencing both histone acetylation and DNA methylation, SIRT1 can exert long-lasting effects on chromatin state that are relevant to aging and genomic stability. The interaction between histone and DNA modifications illustrates how a single sirtuin shapes the epigenetic landscape.

links.source_file: _document_ - SIRT1 Protein roles at the nexus of health, disease, and therapeutics.md
links.context: SIRT1's histone deacetylase activity is directly associated with regulation of telomeric chromatin, gene expression, and the dynamic association of DNA repair factors with chromatin. Telomere shortening occurs over the lifespan and has been linked to the concomitant decrease in SIRT1 expression with age. Directionally, SIRT1 sits upstream of telomeric chromatin maintenance. By preserving the integrity of telomere-associated chromatin and facilitating repair factor access, SIRT1 helps stabilize the chromosome ends whose erosion is a hallmark of aging.

links.source_file: _document_ - SIRT1 Protein roles at the nexus of health, disease, and therapeutics.md
links.context: SIRT1 functions as a deacetylase that modulates more than forty known substrates involved in inflammation, stress resistance, mitochondrial biogenesis, fatty acid metabolism, insulin secretion, glucose production, and lipid homeostasis. Directionally, SIRT1 enzymatic activity sits upstream of a broad network of cellular processes. This extraordinary substrate diversity explains why SIRT1 participates in metabolism, stress resistance, inflammation, and longevity across many tissues. The wide substrate range also means SIRT1's effects are highly context-dependent, with outcomes shaped by the tissue, the nutrient state, and the specific substrates engaged.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: SIRT1 causes tamoxifen resistance in ER-alpha-positive breast cancer cells through upregulation of multidrug resistance protein 2 (MDR2), an effect mediated by deacetylation of the transcription factor FoxO1. Inhibition of SIRT1 impairs nuclear FoxO1 accumulation and MDR2 expression and augments the cytotoxic effects of paclitaxel and doxorubicin in tamoxifen-resistant cells. Directionally, SIRT1 sits upstream of FoxO1- and MDR2-mediated chemoresistance. By driving drug-efflux capacity in resistant cells, SIRT1 reduces the efficacy of endocrine therapy and other agents.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: SIRT1 promotes cisplatin resistance in non-small-cell lung cancer cells by elevating expression of vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A). SIRT1 is upregulated in cisplatin-resistant tumor tissues and cells compared with cisplatin-sensitive groups, correlating with the resistant phenotype. Directionally, SIRT1 sits upstream of VEGF-A-mediated chemoresistance. By enhancing VEGF-A, SIRT1 may support tumor survival and adaptive responses that blunt the cytotoxic effects of cisplatin. This identifies SIRT1 as a potential target for overcoming chemotherapy resistance in lung cancer, since inhibiting SIRT1 could lower VEGF-A and re-sensitize resistant tumors to platinum-based treatment.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: Endothelial-cell-specific overexpression of SIRT1 protects against atherosclerosis in apolipoprotein E-deficient mice, and this protection is associated with inhibition of endothelial cell apoptosis through activation of eNOS expression. Directionally, SIRT1 sits upstream of eNOS-dependent vascular protection. By maintaining nitric oxide production and limiting endothelial cell death, SIRT1 preserves endothelial function and resists the progression of atherosclerotic lesions. This positions SIRT1 as an atheroprotective factor in the vasculature and supports efforts to activate SIRT1 as a strategy against cardiovascular disease.

SIRT1 is substantially decreased in COPD and emphysema lungs, contributing to disease pathogenesis through loss of anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, and antioxidant effects that involve NF-kB, FoxO3, and p53. Pharmacologic activation with SRT1720 inhibits LPS-induced cytokine release in COPD peripheral blood mononuclear cells, supporting SIRT1 restoration as a therapeutic strategy in COPD.

SIRT1 interacts with and activates PPARalpha to prevent the metabolic switch from fatty acid oxidation to glycolysis that occurs in cardiac hypertrophy. By promoting fatty acid oxidation gene expression and inactivating NF-kappaB, SIRT1 preserves the adult heart's preferred fuel preference. Directionally, SIRT1 sits upstream of PPARalpha-dependent metabolic preservation. Maintaining fatty acid oxidation prevents the maladaptive glycolytic shift that accompanies hypertrophic growth and heart failure.

links.source_file: _document_ - SIRT1 Protein roles at the nexus of health, disease, and therapeutics.md
links.context: SIRT1 deacetylates PGC-1alpha and amplifies expression of the circadian transcription factors BMAL1 and CLOCK. A key target of the BMAL1-CLOCK complex is NAMPT, establishing a circadian NAD+ biosynthesis cycle that rhythmically activates and deactivates SIRT1 in alignment with the daily cycle. Directionally, the NAMPT-NAD+ cycle sits upstream of rhythmic SIRT1 activity. Because SIRT1 feeds back to regulate clock components, this forms a stable oscillator coupling metabolism to circadian time. Disruption of this loop, as seen with aging and shift work, impairs both circadian function and metabolic health.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: SIRT1 promotes the progression of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia by regulating the phosphorylation and degradation of the cell-cycle inhibitor p27 through deacetylation of cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2). Directionally, SIRT1 sits upstream of CDK2-dependent cell-cycle progression in leukemia. By licensing CDK2 activity, SIRT1 promotes the degradation of p27 and thereby removes a brake on cell-cycle entry, fueling leukemic proliferation. This makes SIRT1 a promoter of T-ALL progression and identifies SIRT1 inhibition as a potential therapeutic strategy to restore p27-mediated cell-cycle control and suppress leukemic growth.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: Overall SIRT1 knockout mice are highly susceptible to sepsis-induced inflammatory lung injury due to activation of the proinflammatory transcription factor NF-kappaB. Directionally, SIRT1 loss sits upstream of heightened inflammatory lung damage. Because SIRT1 normally deacetylates and restrains NF-kappaB, its absence removes a key brake on inflammatory gene expression during sepsis. This unleashes an exaggerated inflammatory response that damages the lung, illustrating SIRT1's protective role in acute inflammatory injury. Restoring SIRT1 activity may therefore help dampen the excessive inflammation that complicates sepsis and contributes to acute respiratory failure.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: SIRT1, when upregulated by the long noncoding RNA SNHG10, suppresses proliferation of non-small-cell lung cancer cells, acting as a tumor suppressor in this context. Directionally, SIRT1 sits upstream of restrained NSCLC growth. This tumor-suppressive role of SIRT1 in lung cancer contrasts with the oncogenic functions SIRT1 displays in other settings, underscoring the strong context dependence of sirtuin biology. The finding implicates SIRT1 as a mediator of SNHG10's anti-proliferative effects and suggests that sustaining SIRT1 expression may limit NSCLC cell expansion.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: SIRT1, upregulated by circ_0001946, promotes cell growth in lung adenocarcinoma by activating the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway. Directionally, SIRT1 sits upstream of β-catenin-driven proliferation in this lung cancer subtype. This oncogenic SIRT1 function contrasts with the tumor-suppressive anti-proliferative effect SIRT1 exerts in non-small-cell lung cancer when induced by SNHG10, demonstrating that SIRT1's role in lung cancer depends on the tumor subtype and the signaling context.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: Overexpression of SIRT1 protects non-small-cell lung cancer cells against osteopontin-induced NF-κB p65 acetylation and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, thereby attenuating osteopontin-driven cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. Directionally, SIRT1 sits upstream of dampened NF-κB signaling and EMT in response to the pro-metastatic cytokine osteopontin. By deacetylating p65 and restraining EMT, SIRT1 limits the invasive and proliferative program that osteopontin triggers in NSCLC cells, supporting a tumor-suppressive role in this context.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: SIRT1 affects colorectal cancer in a dose-dependent manner by regulating glutamine metabolism and apoptotic pathways. Heterozygous deletion of SIRT1 induces c-Myc expression, enhancing glutamine metabolism, proliferation, autophagy, and cancer formation, whereas homozygous deletion triggers apoptosis, increases cell death, diminishes autophagy, and reduces cancer formation. Directionally, SIRT1 expression level sits upstream of opposing metabolic and survival outcomes in CRC, explaining the dual roles of SIRT1 in colorectal tumorigenesis.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: SIRT1 expression suppresses the expression and acetylation of high-mobility group box 1 protein, thereby inhibiting migration, invasion, and angiogenesis of ovarian cancer cells. Directionally, SIRT1 sits upstream of reduced HMGB1-driven metastatic and angiogenic programs. By dampening HMGB1, SIRT1 limits the invasive and blood-supply-supporting behaviors of ovarian cancer cells, supporting a tumor-suppressive role and identifying the SIRT1-HMGB1 axis as a candidate therapeutic target in ovarian cancer.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: SIRT1 promotes the growth and cisplatin resistance of endometrial cancer cells. Directionally, SIRT1 sits upstream of increased tumor-cell survival and reduced sensitivity to cisplatin in endometrial cancer. By supporting proliferative and survival programs, SIRT1 enables endometrial cancer cells to grow and to withstand platinum-based chemotherapy. This identifies SIRT1 as a potential therapeutic target for improving endometrial cancer treatment outcomes.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: SIRT1 enables HPV-infected cervical cancer cells to continue growing by nullifying absent in melanoma 2 inflammasome-mediated immunity. By inactivating the AIM2 inflammasome, SIRT1 helps HPV-infected cervical cancer cells evade innate immune surveillance, supporting their continued growth. This positions the SIRT1-AIM2 axis as a potential immunotherapeutic target in HPV-driven cervical cancer.

This identifies SIRT1 as a potential target to overcome chemoresistance in pancreatic cancer.

SIRT1 also contributes to telomere maintenance and augments global homologous recombination, linking nuclear sirtuin activity to genome stability and longevity.

links.context: SIRT1 has a dual role in cancer (tumor suppressor and promoter): it can act as tumor suppressor (via p53/β-catenin/survivin restraint) or tumor promoter (via p53 deacetylation), depending on context.

links.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
links.context: SIRT1 is a central mediator of healthspan and longevity: its activity declines with age as NAD+ falls, and genetic/pharmacologic (resveratrol, NAD+ precursors) activation extends lifespan in model organisms; SIRT1-dependent deacetylation of p53, FOXOs, and NF-κB underpins these effects (Giblin et al., 2014, Sirtuins: Guardians of Mammalian Healthspan; Satoh et al., 2013 brain-specific SIRT1-overexpression lifespan extension, PMID 24011076).

links.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
links.context: SIRT1 governs cell-cycle checkpoints by deacetylating p53 (reducing its transcriptional activity) and RB, supporting DNA-repair-coupled arrest rather than apoptosis or premature senescence; age-related SIRT1 decline biases G1/S and G2/M responses toward senescence (reviewed in the source review).

links.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
links.context: SIRT1 inhibits cellular senescence and apoptosis in c-Myc- and PML-driven cancers by deacetylating and inactivating p53 and proapoptotic FOXO transcription factors and by sequestering Bax via deacetylated Ku70. These actions blunt the tumor-suppressive programs that would otherwise eliminate premalignant cells. The directionality is that SIRT1 activity is upstream of senescence suppression, protecting cells from growth arrest. Consequently, SIRT1 inhibitors are frequently anticancer on their own and sensitize cancer cells to anticancer agents or oxidative stress.

links.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
links.context: Estrogen receptor β (Erβ) signaling upregulates SIRT1 expression and activity, linking estrogens to SIRT1-mediated metabolic and neuroprotective programs; estrogen-replacement models show increased SIRT1 levels and reduced oxidative damage (source review Table 3 lists Erβ as a positive SIRT1 regulator).

links.context: FOXO3 and SIRT1 form a feed-forward stress-resistance loop: SIRT1 deacetylates FOXO3 to shunt it toward stress-resistance and metabolic genes, while FOXO3 transactivates SIRT1 expression; this mutually reinforcing pair is central to longevity-associated signalling (Brunet et al., 2004, PMID 15066266).

links.context: PAI-1, a senescence-associated secreted factor (SASP), suppresses SIRT1 expression, and SIRT1 reciprocally binds the PAI-1 promoter to deacetylate H4K16 and repress its transcription; elevation of PAI-1 with age thus contributes to SIRT1 decline and the senescence phenotype (Kortlever et al., 2006, Nat Cell Biol; Wan et al., 2014, Aging Cell, PMID 24649892).

links.context: p16INK4a (CDKN2A) accumulation with age drives senescence and opposes SIRT1-dependent replicative programs; SIRT1 represses p16INK4a expression via promoter deacetylation and via the Akt/p70S6K1 axis, and p16INK4a upregulation is a hallmark of aging-related SIRT1 decline (Li & Tollefsbol, 2011, PLoS One 6:e17421, PMID 21390332).

links.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
links.context: Cyclin D1/CDK4 and the cyclin B-Cdk1 complex regulate SIRT1 by phosphorylation (massive phosphorylation is required for SIRT1 cell-cycle function), and cyclin D1 opposes SIRT1-dependent regulation of cell-cycle genes in proliferative contexts; Table 3 lists Cyclin D1 among negative SIRT1 regulators (Sasaki et al., 2008, PLoS One 3:e4020, PMID 19015735).

links.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
links.context: mTORC1/S6K1 signaling opposes SIRT1-promoted catabolic and stress-resistance programs (while SIRT1/SIRT2 deacetylate S6K1 to license its activity, making regulation bidirectional and nutrient-dependent); rapamycin-mediated mTOR inhibition raises NAD+ and benefits from SIRT1 coupling, as reflected in Table 3's classification of the mTOR/S6K pathway as a SIRT1 negative regulator.

links.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
links.context: SIRT1 catalyzes removal of acetyl groups from β-catenin, and this deacetylation suppresses β-catenin's ability to activate transcription and drive cell proliferation. The modification dampens the Wnt transcriptional output of the protein at target promoters. This is one of the tumor-suppressive arms of SIRT1 in cancer, complementing its deacetylation of the RelA/p65 NF-κB subunit. Directionality is enzymatic: SIRT1 is the deacetylase and β-catenin the substrate, and the net effect is reduced oncogenic transcriptional signaling.
SIRT1 deacetylates RelA/p65 at Lys310, inhibiting NF-κB-dependent pro-inflammatory gene expression (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β). This is an established anti-inflammatory mechanism.

SIRT1 is elevated in breast cancer tissue versus adjacent normal tissue and predicts poor prognosis. In triple-negative breast cancer it regulates EMT-associated programming that drives invasion and metastasis, while also repressing ER-alpha-mediated estrogen proliferative responses. It promotes metadherin-driven chemoresistance and causes tamoxifen resistance through MRP2 upregulation via FoxO1 deacetylation, so SIRT1 inhibition augments paclitaxel and doxorubicin cytotoxicity.

SIRT1 protects against atherosclerosis through multiple mechanisms: endothelial SIRT1 overexpression activates eNOS, SRT1720 activation ameliorates endothelial dysfunction, and SIRT1 reduces Lox-1-mediated foam cell formation via NF-kB. It also protects vascular smooth muscle cells from DNA damage via NBS1. Collectively SIRT1 is a consistent anti-atherosclerotic factor in the endothelium and vasculature.

SIRT1 protects against myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury: knockout increases infarct size while overexpression upregulates FoxO1 and MnSOD and downregulates caspase-3 and Bax. Signaling upstream of SIRT1 includes miR-132 inhibition leading to PGC-1alpha/Nrf2, and lncRNA Oip5-as1 acting through the SIRT1/AMPK/PGC-1alpha axis. SIRT1 is thus an endogenous cardioprotective factor against reperfusion damage.

SIRT1 is protective in acute pancreatitis via deacetylation of p53 and HSF1, dampening acinar-cell damage. In chronic pancreatitis, however, SIRT1 is upregulated and drives inflammation-induced EMT through the miR-278 axis, illustrating a context-dependent switch from protection to pathogenesis within the same organ.

SIRT1 ameliorates the autophagic degradation of alpha-synuclein by deacetylating LC3 and improves motor defects in Parkinson's disease. This connects sirtuin activity directly to clearance of the pathological protein aggregate central to PD. SIRT1's pro-autophagy action here contrasts with SIRT2, which mediates exacerbation of alpha-synuclein toxicity.

Brain-specific SIRT1 knockout exacerbates Huntington's disease, while SIRT1 overexpression rescues CREB-CRTC1 interaction to restore BDNF transcription. SIRT1 therefore supports neuronal survival and transcriptional resilience in HD. SIRT2 inhibition also achieves neuroprotection in HD models by mimicking the beneficial effects of sterol-biosynthesis manipulation.

SIRT1 shows an inverse serum and saliva relationship with Alzheimer's disease, giving it diagnostic potential as a peripheral biomarker. Lower peripheral SIRT1 accompanies AD pathology, while brain SIRT1 reduces amyloid-beta-induced senescence and mitochondrial dysfunction. SIRT6 shows the same inverse serum/saliva relationship with AD, suggesting a shared peripheral readout for the protective sirtuins.

SIRT1 has a dual role in diabetes mellitus: overexpression improves insulin sensitivity while hepatic SIRT1 knockdown prevents fasting hyperglycemia by increasing hepatic insulin responsiveness. SIRT1 therefore both enhances systemic insulin action and constrains hepatic glucose output. This context-dependence is characteristic of SIRT1's master-regulator role in metabolic disease.

SIRT1 is protective in diabetic kidney disease by deacetylating p53 and activating FoxO3a and Nrf2, and resveratrol promotes resistance to diabetic renal fibrosis via Nrf2. These antioxidant and anti-apoptotic actions defend podocytes and the renal tubulointerstitium against hyperglycemic damage.

SIRT1 overexpression abolishes TGF-beta1-induced apoptosis and fibrosis through CTGF suppression, and SRT1720 attenuates UUO fibrosis, while SIRT1 represses HIF2alpha. However, SIRT1 downregulation may also inhibit fibroblast activation via EGFR/PDGFR-beta, creating therapeutic ambiguity. The dominant role is renoprotective, opposing tubulointerstitial fibrosis.

SIRT1 is protective in osteoarthritis by reducing chondrocyte apoptosis and ECM degradation via Wnt/beta-catenin signaling, reversing homocysteine-induced changes through the PGC-1alpha/PPAR-gamma cascade, inhibiting EGFR ubiquitination, and inhibiting chondrocyte senescence. SIRT1 therefore maintains cartilage homeostasis on multiple axes.

SIRT1 is protective in osteoporosis: SIRT1 knockout mice have low bone mass, SIRT1 increases osteoblast osteogenesis via FoxO3a, and it deacetylates sclerostin to promote Wnt/beta-catenin signaling. Resveratrol restores alkaline phosphatase and osteocalcin via NF-kB. SIRT1 thus supports bone formation and opposes age-related bone loss.

SIRT1 causes tamoxifen resistance in ER-alpha-positive breast cancer by upregulating multidrug resistance protein 2 (MRP2) through FoxO1 deacetylation. SIRT1 inhibition therefore augments paclitaxel and doxorubicin cytotoxicity, while SIRT4 enhances tamoxifen sensitivity via STAT3 inhibition. This makes SIRT1 status a determinant of endocrine-therapy response in breast cancer.

SIRT1 promotes cisplatin resistance in lung cancer via VEGF-A signaling, whereas SIRT2 upregulation and SIRT3 (via the FoxO3/CDT1 axis) each increase cisplatin sensitivity. SIRT3 also promotes DNA repair and radioresistance through ATM-Chk2. The opposing SIRT1 vs SIRT2/SIRT3 actions define the chemo-resistance balance in NSCLC.

SIRT1 is overexpressed in HPV-infected cervical cancer cells and nullifies AIM2 inflammasome-mediated immunity, correlating with poor clinical outcomes. This immunosuppressive action allows cervical cancer cells to evade inflammasome-driven clearance, positioning SIRT1 as an oncogenic factor in HPV-driven cervical cancer.

SIRT1 promotes T-ALL progression by deacetylating CDK2, which drives p27 phosphorylation and degradation, and SIRT1 knockdown sensitizes AML to tyrosine kinase inhibitor treatment. SIRT2 activation by NAMPT reduces proliferation and induces apoptosis in AML blasts via the Akt/GSK-3beta/beta-catenin axis, showing opposing leukemic roles for the two sirtuins.

Genetic SIRT1 polymorphisms are associated with coronary artery disease risk, and SIRT1 expression is reduced in CAD patients where its downregulation is linked to acetylated p53 in CAD monocytes. The lncRNA C2dat1 promotes SIRT1 to suppress miR-34a, driving VSMC proliferation and migration in the vessel wall.

SIRT1 and SIRT6 both deacetylate the lipogenic transcription factors ChREBP and SREBP-1c to maintain hepatic lipid homeostasis and oppose fatty liver disease. SIRT1 additionally antagonizes liver fibrosis by blocking hepatic stellate cell activation, while hepatocyte-specific SIRT6 knockout elevates fibrosis and oxidative stress in NASH mice.

SIRT1 suppresses intestinal epithelial ROS accumulation and apoptosis after ischemia-reperfusion, and resveratrol protects through the SIRT1-NF-kB-iNOS-NO pathway. SIRT3 alleviates mitochondrial oxidative damage and apoptosis via peroxiredoxin 3 deacetylation, while SIRT6 downregulation by miR-351-5p aggravates intestinal IRI injury.

SIRT1 reduces O-GlcNAcylation of tau via CREB in Alzheimer's disease, and SIRT3 plays a role in tau acetylation as a potential therapy target. SIRT2 affects tau phosphorylation and autophagic flux, and nuclear SIRT2 is hyperactivated in AD where FoxO1 recruits it to Fzd1/Fzd7 promoters to reduce H4K16ac.

SIRT1 overexpression prevents capillary cell apoptosis and degenerative capillary formation in diabetic retinopathy, reduces DM-induced retinal inflammation, and improves visual function. In diabetic cardiomyopathy SIRT1 activation inhibits ROS-induced oxidative stress and fibrosis, while SIRT3 regulates fibrosis, inflammation, apoptosis, and oxidative stress in the diabetic myocardium.

SIRT1 deacetylates sclerostin to activate Wnt/beta-catenin signaling and increase bone anabolism, and SIRT1 knockout mice have a low bone-mass phenotype while SIRT1 overexpression increases osteoblast osteogenesis via FoxO3a. SIRT6 inhibits age-related bone loss by stabilizing estrogen receptor alpha in preosteoblastic cells.

SIRT1 is reduced in degenerative nucleus pulposus tissues with severity, and inhibits NF-kB transcriptional activity while suppressing c-Fos/c-Jun phosphorylation. SIRT2 reverses IL-1beta action by inhibiting the p53/p21 pathway, SIRT3 maintains nucleus pulposus cell homeostasis, and SIRT6 inhibits inflammatory responses and senescence via NF-kB in IDD.

links.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial Drivers Stem Cell Aging Inflammaging Bautista 2026.md
links.context: SIRT3, a mitochondrial sirtuin whose activity depends on NAD+, weakens antioxidant defenses and mitochondrial detoxification when NAD+ is depleted during aging. Reduced SIRT3 activity compromises the deacetylation of mitochondrial antioxidant and metabolic enzymes, leaving cells vulnerable to ROS-driven mitochondrial damage. Together with SIRT1, SIRT3 regulates PGC-1α, FOXO and NRF1 transcriptional programs that coordinate mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant responses. Because NAD+ decline lowers SIRT3 function, NAD+ repletion is a strategy to restore sirtuin-dependent mitochondrial resilience, delay stem cell senescence, and dampen the ROS-NF-κB-inflammaging axis.

links.source_file: _document_ - NAD+ Precursors Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) and Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) Potential Dietary Contribution to Health.md
links.context: SIRT3 is the primary mitochondrial NAD+-dependent deacetylase, and among its targets is SOD2 (manganese superoxide dismutase). When NR raises NAD+ and activates SIRT3, the acetylation of SOD2 is reduced, increasing mitochondrial SOD2 activity and thereby lowering mitochondrial reactive oxygen species. SIRT3 also deacetylates isocitrate dehydrogenase 2, enhancing mitochondrial antioxidant capacity and quality control. This SIRT3-SOD2 axis is central to NR's protective effects against oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and it also mediates the benefit of gut-microbiota-derived NMN in acute pancreatitis, where the SIRT3-PRDX5 pathway is engaged.

SIRT3 attenuates NLRP3 inflammasome activity by lowering mitochondrial ROS production, which is a principal trigger of NLRP3 assembly and activation. Directionally, SIRT3 reduces mitochondrial ROS, which inhibits NLRP3. This connects mitochondrial redox state to innate immune signaling, since ROS and mitochondrial DNA released from damaged organelles prime the inflammasome. Loss of SIRT3 therefore exacerbates inflammasome-driven inflammation, and SIRT3 induction by fasting or pharmacological activation reduces it. This places mitochondrial sirtuins at the interface of metabolism and immunity, with broad implications for metabolic disease and aging.

links.source_file: _document_ - Nicotinamide Riboside—The Current State of Research and Therapeutic Uses.md
links.context: SIRT3 and SIRT5 are both critical for the health of retinal photoreceptors, and SIRT3 activity is sensitive to the reduction of NAD+ content detected in multiple disorders with retinal degeneration, including age-associated dysfunction, diabetic retinopathy, and light-induced degeneration in mice. SIRT3 is a mitochondrial NAD+-dependent deacetylase that supports ATP homeostasis, ROS detoxification, and neuroprotection, and increasing mitochondrial NAD+ to support SIRT3 is one proposed mechanism of nicotinamide riboside's neuroprotective effects. This suggests a potential therapeutic treatment with NR for a variety of disorders that include photoreceptor degeneration.

SIRT3 reduces ROS and lipid peroxidation by deacetylating LKB1 and thereby activating AMPK, linking mitochondrial sirtuin activity to energy sensing. Directionally, SIRT3 deacetylates LKB1, which activates AMPK. This protects cells from oxidative damage via improved mitochondrial function and antioxidant gene expression. It shows convergent sirtuin control of the LKB1/AMPK node, with SIRT1 and SIRT3 both licensing LKB1 to activate AMPK. Because AMPK in turn raises NAD+ and activates PGC-1α, this creates a positive feedback loop that sustains mitochondrial quality and redox balance.

SIRT3 is the principal mitochondrial sirtuin, imported into the matrix where it removes acetyl, succinyl, and other acyl modifications from respiratory-chain and metabolic enzymes. Its activity is governed by the mitochondrial NAD+/NADH ratio, which links the cell's energy state directly to enzyme function, so SIRT3 serves as a metabolic sensor within the organelle. Because of its mitochondrial residence, SIRT3 is positioned to sense and tune local metabolism, driving oxidative phosphorylation, antioxidant defense, and fatty-acid oxidation.

SIRT3 deacetylates and activates acetyl-CoA synthetase 2 (AceCS2) in the mitochondrial matrix, enabling it to convert acetate into acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle and lipogenesis. Deacetylation relieves autoinhibition, increasing AceCS2's catalytic efficiency and allowing mitochondria to use acetate as an alternative carbon source. Directionally, SIRT3 activates AceCS2 to drive mitochondrial acetyl-CoA production. This supports metabolic flexibility during fasting and alcohol metabolism, when acetate is abundant, and parallels SIRT1's activation of the cytoplasmic isoform AceCS1, demonstrating that sirtuins broadly license acetate salvage across both mitochondrial and cytosolic compartments.

SIRT3 lowers mitochondrial ROS by deacetylating and activating antioxidant enzymes such as MnSOD and components of the electron-transport chain, while also reducing mitochondrial membrane potential in a manner that limits superoxide leak. Higher SIRT3 activity therefore shifts the mitochondrial redox balance toward less oxidative damage. The directionality is SIRT3 activity upstream of reduced ROS. This antioxidant function is a major basis for SIRT3's protective roles in heart, liver, and aging.

Cold exposure induces SIRT3 in brown adipose tissue, where it promotes expression of mitochondrial genes and supports thermogenic programs. The induction enhances oxidative metabolism and uncoupled respiration needed for heat production, with SIRT3 acting upstream of UCP1-dependent thermogenesis. Directionally, a cold stimulus triggers SIRT3 upregulation, which in turn drives thermogenic mitochondrial biogenesis. This ties SIRT3 to adaptive thermogenesis and the metabolic benefits of cold exposure, and conversely SIRT3 is reduced in brown adipose tissue of obese mice, linking obesity to impaired thermogenic capacity and blunted cold-induced mitochondrial function.

Honokiol-activated SIRT3 deacetylates MnSOD at Lys68 and Lys122, markedly increasing its superoxide-scavenging activity in the mitochondrial matrix. Directionally, SIRT3 enzymatically activates MnSOD. Enhanced MnSOD lowers mitochondrial ROS and protects against oxidative injury in the heart, kidney, and brain. This is a principal mechanism for honokiol's cardiorenal and neuroprotective effects, and it parallels SIRT3's regulation of the same enzyme during caloric restriction and fasting. Because mitochondrial superoxide is a key trigger of damage and inflammasome activation, MnSOD activation by SIRT3 is central to mitochondrial stress resistance.

Honokiol-activated SIRT3 deacetylates OSCP, a subunit of the mitochondrial F1Fo-ATP synthase, optimizing coupling of proton flux to ATP synthesis. Directionally, SIRT3 enzymatically tunes ATP synthase function. Improved coupling boosts cellular energy output while limiting proton-leak-associated ROS, enhancing mitochondrial efficiency. This contributes to honokiol's metabolic and cardioprotective actions, and it shows that SIRT3 regulates not only antioxidant enzymes but also the core machinery of ATP production. By improving the efficiency and integrity of oxidative phosphorylation, SIRT3 supports the bioenergetic capacity that declines with age and metabolic disease.

SIRT3 reduces mitochondrial ROS by deacetylating and activating MnSOD and other antioxidant enzymes and by optimizing electron-transport-chain function. Directionally, SIRT3 activity sits upstream of lowered mitochondrial oxidant production. This antioxidant action protects tissues from oxidative damage in cardiovascular and metabolic disease, and it is central to SIRT3's longevity and stress-resistance phenotype. By lowering mitochondrial ROS, SIRT3 also reduces inflammasome priming and preserves mitochondrial DNA integrity, coupling redox homeostasis to genome stability and innate immune regulation, and its induction by fasting and caloric restriction reinforces these protective effects.

SIRT3 opposes aerobic glycolysis indirectly through redox: it activates MnSOD/SOD2 and IDH2, lowering ROS, which destabilizes HIF-1alpha and cuts the master glycolytic transcription factor. SIRT3 loss therefore skews cells toward the Warburg effect and supports tumor metabolism.

SIRT3 activates the AMPK/PGC-1α pathway, driving mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming toward oxidative phosphorylation and biogenesis. Directionally, SIRT3 sits upstream of AMPK/PGC-1α activation. This enhances energy production and stress resistance while limiting glycolytic reliance, supporting the bioenergetic capacity of muscle, heart, and liver. It is a core mechanism for SIRT3's metabolic and cardioprotective benefits, and it reinforces the reciprocal relationship between sirtuins and AMPK. By promoting oxidative metabolism, SIRT3 helps maintain metabolic flexibility that declines with age and is impaired in obesity and diabetes.

SIRT3 deacetylates acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 (ACC1), upregulating its activity and promoting de novo lipogenesis that can fuel invasion and metastasis of cervical cancer cells. Directionally, SIRT3 enzymatically activates ACC1, promoting lipid synthesis. This reveals a tumor-promoting facet of SIRT3 in certain cancers, contrasting with its usual protective role in mitochondrial metabolism and ROS suppression. It highlights that SIRT3's metabolic effects are context-dependent: the same enzyme that protects normal tissues by reducing oxidative stress can supply lipids that support aggressive tumor growth. This dual role must be considered in SIRT3-based therapeutic strategies.

SIRT3 promotes autophagy in angiotensin-II-induced myocardial hypertrophy by deacetylating FoxO1, shifting its program toward autophagic and antioxidant genes. Directionally, SIRT3 deacetylates FoxO1, which promotes autophagy. This mitigates pathological hypertrophy via proteostatic and redox control, preventing the accumulation of damaged proteins and mitochondria in stressed cardiomyocytes. It extends SIRT3's cardiac protective mechanisms beyond ROS scavenging, and it is consistent with the broader role of mitophagy in cardiac health. By coupling FoxO1-dependent autophagy to mitochondrial quality control, SIRT3 preserves cardiac function during pathological stress.

SIRT3, together with SIRT1, inhibits the TGF-β/Smad3 pathway to attenuate cardiac fibrosis in vivo. Directionally, SIRT3 sits upstream of TGF-β/Smad3 blockade. This limits fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition and extracellular-matrix accumulation, preserving myocardial architecture. It complements SIRT3's general anti-inflammatory and metabolic cardiac protection, and SIRT3 deficiency promotes fibrotic responses, including in the aging lung. By restraining both oxidative stress and profibrotic signaling, SIRT3 provides multifactorial protection against organ fibrosis, supporting the therapeutic potential of SIRT3 activation in fibrotic disease.

Pyruvate dehydrogenase E1α (PDH E1α) becomes hyperacetylated at Lys385 in tubular epithelial cells after TGF-β1 stimulation and is deacetylated by SIRT3, modulating pyruvate entry into the TCA cycle. Directionally, SIRT3 enzymatically activates PDH. This links mitochondrial metabolism to TGF-β1-driven kidney injury, and loss of SIRT3 leads to PDH hyperacetylation, reduced glucose oxidation, and pyruvate/lactate accumulation. It shows SIRT3 buffering metabolic dysfunction during fibrosis, and connects the metabolic phenotype of injured kidneys to sirtuin-dependent control of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.

links.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
links.context: FOXO3a translocates to mitochondria where it binds the SIRT3 promoter and induces SIRT3 expression, which in turn activates MnSOD to reduce ROS, forming a FOXO3a-SIRT3-PGC-1α mitochondrial-protective loop (source review; Tseng et al., 2013; also PMC2532794).

SIRT3 deacetylates OPA1 at Lys926 and Lys931 within its GTPase domain, raising OPA1 GTPase activity and enhancing mitochondrial fusion during stress. Directionally, SIRT3 enzymatically activates OPA1. This preserves mitochondrial network integrity under damage, and it links SIRT3 to mitochondrial dynamics and quality control. By promoting fusion, SIRT3 helps mitochondria share membrane potential, dilute damage, and maintain respiratory function. This regulation is particularly important in the heart and during oxidative stress, where maintaining a connected mitochondrial network protects against fragmentation and bioenergetic collapse.

Through OPA1 deacetylation, SIRT3 enhances mitochondrial fusion during stress, maintaining a connected, healthy mitochondrial network. Directionally, SIRT3 activates OPA1, which promotes fusion. Fused mitochondria better share membrane potential and dilute damage, and this protects against fragmentation and bioenergetic collapse. By supporting the fusion arm of mitochondrial dynamics, SIRT3 preserves respiratory efficiency and quality control under conditions that would otherwise fragment the network. This is a key mechanism by which SIRT3 maintains mitochondrial health and supports cardiac and neuronal function.

SIRT3 is induced by caloric restriction and intermittent fasting, enhancing mitochondrial metabolism and antioxidant defenses systemically. Directionally, caloric restriction and fasting sit upstream of SIRT3 induction. This raises the SIRT3/SIRT4 ratio toward protection, and it is a conserved metabolic adaptation that counters aging-related mitochondrial decline. By increasing SIRT3, these interventions boost oxidative phosphorylation, fatty-acid oxidation, and mitochondrial antioxidant capacity. The SIRT3 response is a core component of the beneficial metabolic effects of dietary restriction, linking nutrient availability to mitochondrial resilience.

SIRT3 is induced by intermittent fasting, which enhances mitochondrial health and stress resistance, paralleling caloric restriction. Directionally, fasting sits upstream of SIRT3 induction. This raises the protective SIRT3/SIRT4 ratio and counters the age-related decline in mitochondrial function, and it is a translatable lifestyle intervention engaging sirtuin biology. By increasing SIRT3, intermittent fasting promotes oxidative metabolism, antioxidant defense, and mitochondrial quality control. These effects contribute to the metabolic benefits of fasting, including improved insulin sensitivity and resistance to age-related dysfunction.

SIRT3 promotes mitophagy by deacetylating FOXO3a, which induces BNIP3 and triggers clearance of damaged mitochondria to maintain homeostasis. Directionally, SIRT3 activates FOXO3a, which promotes mitophagy. This removes dysfunctional organelles that would otherwise fuel ROS and inflammation, and it is a key quality-control function of SIRT3. By coupling mitochondrial sirtuin activity to the mitophagic program, SIRT3 ensures that damaged mitochondria are selectively eliminated. This regulation is essential for preserving mitochondrial health in tissues with high energy demand, such as heart and muscle.

Brown adipose tissue of obese mice shows reduced SIRT3 protein and decreased mitochondrial protein expression, linking obesity to impaired thermogenic capacity. Directionally, obesity sits upstream of lower SIRT3. This blunts cold-induced and basal mitochondrial function, and it connects metabolic disease to sirtuin attenuation. By reducing SIRT3, obesity impairs the mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative capacity required for thermogenesis. This observation supports the concept that restoring SIRT3, through fasting or pharmacological activation, could improve the metabolic and thermogenic dysfunction associated with obesity.

SIRT3, as a mitochondrial NAD+-dependent deacetylase, activates mitochondrial Complex I of the electron-transport chain, improving respiratory efficiency. Directionally, SIRT3 sits upstream of Complex I activation. This boosts oxidative phosphorylation and reduces proximal electron leak, and it is a direct mechanism for SIRT3's bioenergetic benefits. By deacetylating Complex I subunits, SIRT3 enhances electron flux and ATP production while limiting superoxide generation. This regulation is central to SIRT3's support of cellular energy metabolism and its protection against oxidative stress.

links.source_file: _document_ - Sirtuins and their Biological Relevance in Aging and Age-Related Diseases.md
links.context: SIRT3 activates IDH2 by deacetylation (Lys413), enhancing mitochondrial antioxidant capacity (Yu 2012 PMID 22416140).

An SNP in SIRT3 (rs11555236, in linkage with a putative enhancer) is associated with increased longevity, male-specific in some cohorts and whole-population in the TRELONG study, with homozygotes showing higher SIRT3 expression, supporting a role for SIRT3 variation in human lifespan. Directionally, the genetic variant is associated with longevity through increased SIRT3 expression. By raising SIRT3 levels, the variant may enhance mitochondrial function and stress resistance. These genetic associations complement the animal data linking SIRT3 to healthspan and position SIRT3 as a candidate human longevity gene.

A nonsynonymous SIRT3 SNP reducing recombinant catalytic activity by about 34% is associated with metabolic syndrome in NAFLD patients and the Finnish Metabolic Syndrome in Men cohort, implicating lowered SIRT3 activity in human metabolic disease susceptibility. Directionally, reduced SIRT3 catalytic activity is associated with metabolic syndrome. This genetic evidence connects impaired mitochondrial sirtuin function to human metabolic disease, and it complements the animal studies showing that SIRT3 loss causes metabolic dysfunction. These findings support SIRT3 as a therapeutic target for metabolic syndrome.

links.source_file: _document_ - The Sirtuin Network Linking NAD+ Metabolism, Mitochondrial Function, and Metabolic Homoeostasis.md
links.context: SIRT3 controls thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue by deacetylating regulatory targets upstream of the uncoupling protein UCP1, maintaining the mitochondrial function required for adaptive heat production. Directionally, SIRT3 sits upstream of UCP1-dependent thermogenic capacity. By preserving mitochondrial oxidative function and reducing oxidative stress in brown fat, SIRT3 ensures that mitochondria can sustain the proton leak through UCP1 that generates heat. This makes SIRT3 important for cold-induced thermogenesis and overall energy balance.

links.source_file: _document_ - The Sirtuin Network Linking NAD+ Metabolism, Mitochondrial Function, and Metabolic Homoeostasis.md
links.context: Fasting induces SIRT3 activation, which in turn enhances fatty acid oxidation through deacetylation and activation of long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCAD), a key enzyme of mitochondrial beta-oxidation. Directionally, SIRT3 enzymatic activation of LCAD sits upstream of enhanced lipid catabolism. This promotes the harvest of energy from fat stores during fasting and caloric restriction, when glucose is scarce. By supporting efficient beta-oxidation, SIRT3 helps maintain ATP production while limiting the accumulation of damaging lipid intermediates.

links.source_file: _document_ - The Sirtuin Network Linking NAD+ Metabolism, Mitochondrial Function, and Metabolic Homoeostasis.md
links.context: SIRT3 maintains the activity of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) by preventing its hyperacetylation, thereby coupling glycolysis-derived carbon to mitochondrial oxidation. Loss of SIRT3 leads to PDH hyperacetylation, reduced glucose oxidation, and accumulation of pyruvate and lactate, impairing metabolic flexibility in skeletal muscle. Directionally, SIRT3 sits upstream of PDH-dependent glucose oxidation. By protecting PDH, SIRT3 ensures that glucose can be oxidized in mitochondria rather than being diverted to lactate, preserving energy efficiency during exercise and metabolic stress. This function is central to SIRT3's role in supporting muscle performance and whole-body glucose handling.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: SIRT3 promotes DNA damage repair and radioresistance through the ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM)-Chk2 pathway in non-small-cell lung cancer cells. By supporting this DNA-damage-response branch, SIRT3 enables cancer cells to survive ionizing radiation more effectively. Directionally, SIRT3 sits upstream of enhanced DNA repair and radiation resistance. This has therapeutic implications, because combining SIRT3 inhibition with radiotherapy could impair the repair of radiation-induced damage and thereby improve treatment efficacy.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: SIRT3 downregulates both the mRNA and protein levels of glutathione S-transferase pi 1 (GSTP1), a phase II detoxification enzyme involved in the metabolism of chemotherapeutic agents. SIRT3 overexpression promotes sorafenib-induced apoptosis and thereby enhances the drug sensitivity of hepatocellular carcinoma cells. Directionally, SIRT3 sits upstream of reduced GSTP1 and enhanced drug responsiveness. By lowering the capacity of cancer cells to detoxify sorafenib, SIRT3 restores sensitivity to this agent. This suggests that SIRT3 expression status could predict sorafenib response in liver cancer, and that boosting SIRT3 may help overcome drug resistance in this malignancy.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: SIRT3 inhibits mitochondrial oxidative stress in airway epithelial cells, and this action contributes to attenuating the progression of COPD. Directionally, SIRT3 sits upstream of reduced airway epithelial oxidative stress. By curbing mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, SIRT3 protects airway cells from the damage inflicted by cigarette smoke and chronic inflammation. Activating the SIRT3 signaling pathway is therefore proposed as a novel therapeutic strategy to slow or prevent COPD pathogenesis. This highlights mitochondrial sirtuins as potential drug targets in chronic lung disease, where oxidative stress is a central driver of tissue injury.

SIRT3 protects against cardiac hypertrophy by inducing expression of the antioxidant proteins SOD2 and catalase. The SIRT3-mediated reduction in reactive oxygen species inhibits AKT signaling and the downstream gene expression associated with hypertrophy induction. Directionally, SIRT3 sits upstream of antioxidant defense and hypertrophy suppression, since by lowering mitochondrial oxidative stress it removes a key stimulus for the growth signaling that drives pathological cardiac enlargement. This places mitochondrial sirtuin activity at the center of the redox control governing cardiac stress responses.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: SIRT3 overexpression dramatically suppresses the metastatic capability of ovarian cancer cells by inhibiting epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition through downregulation of Twist, a key EMT transcription factor. Directionally, SIRT3 sits upstream of Twist suppression and maintenance of an epithelial phenotype. By reducing Twist, SIRT3 blocks the switch that confers migratory and invasive behavior on tumor cells. This restrains the metastatic spread that is the main cause of ovarian cancer mortality. The finding positions SIRT3 as a suppressor of ovarian cancer metastasis and suggests that maintaining SIRT3 activity could help limit disease dissemination.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: SIRT3 stabilizes the interaction between Ku70 and Bax to enhance the viability of glioma cells, representing an oncogenic function in this cancer type that contrasts with its tumor-suppressive roles elsewhere. Directionally, SIRT3 sits upstream of enhanced glioma cell survival. By keeping Bax sequestered by Ku70, SIRT3 prevents the pro-apoptotic protein from triggering mitochondrial cell death, allowing glioma cells to evade apoptosis. This oncogenic facet complicates the picture of SIRT3 as a universal tumor suppressor and underscores that its net effect depends on cellular context. In gliomas, SIRT3 inhibition might be a strategy to promote tumor cell death.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: SIRT3 promotes the expression of manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), and this regulation is crucial for the protective effect of SIRT3 on hyperoxia-induced acute lung injury. Directionally, SIRT3 sits upstream of MnSOD-dependent lung protection. By maintaining MnSOD, SIRT3 supports mitochondrial antioxidant defense against the oxidative stress generated by high oxygen exposure. This shields lung tissue from the reactive oxygen species that drive injury during hyperoxia. The finding highlights SIRT3 as a mitochondrial antioxidant guardian in the lung and suggests that strategies to enhance SIRT3 or MnSOD could protect against oxygen-induced lung damage in clinical settings.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: SIRT3 reduces cisplatin resistance in lung cancer by modulating the FoxO3/Cdc10-dependent transcript 1 protein axis. Directionally, SIRT3 sits upstream of restored platinum sensitivity in drug-resistant lung cancer cells. By acting through the FoxO3/CDT1 pathway, SIRT3 counteracts the survival adaptations that underlie cisplatin resistance, making SIRT3 activation a candidate strategy to re-sensitize resistant lung tumors to platinum-based chemotherapy.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: Overexpression of SIRT3 improves the resistance of colorectal cancer cells to anticancer drugs through regulation of superoxide dismutase 2 and PGC-1α. Directionally, SIRT3 sits upstream of SOD2- and PGC-1α-dependent protective responses in CRC. By enhancing antioxidant and mitochondrial programs, SIRT3 reduces the vulnerability of CRC cells to chemotherapeutic agents, contributing to drug resistance. This resistance-promoting role should be weighed when considering SIRT3-targeted cancer therapy.

links.source_file: _document_ - sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8.md
links.context: SIRT3 contributes to the reprogramming of fatty acid synthesis by upregulating acetyl-coA carboxylase 1 to promote de novo lipogenesis through SIRT3 deacetylation, thereby promoting the invasion and metastasis of cervical cancer cells. Directionally, SIRT3 sits upstream of ACC1-driven de novo lipogenesis and metastatic behavior in cervical cancer. By enhancing lipid synthesis, SIRT3 supports the invasive and metastatic capabilities of cervical cancer cells, identifying SIRT3-ACC1 lipogenesis as a potential therapeutic target.

links.context: The full-length SIRT3 protein is enzymatically inactive and contains a mitochondrial targeting domain at its N-terminus. Mitochondrial matrix processing peptidase cleaves the N-terminal 101 residues, which then activates the enzyme. Directionally, proteolytic processing sits upstream of SIRT3 catalytic activity within the mitochondrial matrix. This maturation step ensures that SIRT3 functions only after import into mitochondria, where it deacetylates metabolic enzymes.

links.context: Through the p53 pathway, SIRT3 prevents dysfunction and senescence caused by high glucose levels in endothelial cells by partially abrogating p53 activity. Directionally, SIRT3 sits upstream of dampened p53 signalling and thereby of protection against glucose-induced endothelial senescence. This links mitochondrial sirtuin activity to vascular health and identifies SIRT3 as a potential target for preventing diabetic endothelial dysfunction.

links.context: SIRT3 could also be used as a marker for colon cancer. In colon cancer, SIRT3 deficiency reduces cell proliferation, invasion, and migration while increasing apoptosis. Directionally, SIRT3 expression levels sit upstream of colon cancer behaviour, with loss of SIRT3 restraining tumour aggressiveness. SIRT3 therefore has potential diagnostic and prognostic utility in colorectal cancer.

links.source_file: _document_ - Rejuvenating Sirtuins The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets.md
links.context: In oral squamous cell carcinomas, SIRT3 is overexpressed, and its downregulation has antiproliferative activity and sensitizes carcinoma cells to radiation and to cisplatin. This contrasts with SIRT3's broader tumor-suppressive role in mouse models, showing that sirtuin function is context-dependent. Directionally, elevated SIRT3 supports tumor growth and therapy resistance in this cancer type, while SIRT3 loss restores sensitivity. The finding highlights that a single sirtuin can be either protective or oncogenic depending on tumor type and molecular background.
SIRT3 deacetylates OPA1 at Lys926/Lys931 to activate mitochondrial fusion. The mechanism of mtSIRTs on autophagy is still unclear.

Serum SIRT3 distinguishes lung cancer patients from healthy controls with an AUC of 0.918, sensitivity of 86.4%, and specificity of 94%. High SIRT1-3 expression correlates with poor survival in NSCLC. In the tumor SIRT3 reduces cisplatin resistance through the FoxO3/CDT1 axis and promotes DNA repair and radioresistance via ATM-Chk2, illustrating how a single sirtuin affects both diagnosis and therapy response.

SIRT3 expression is lower in HCC tissue than in adjacent tissue. Modulating SIRT3 enhances sorafenib therapy, and SIRT3 downregulates GST-pi1 to enhance chemo- and sorafenib-induced apoptosis. Its loss therefore correlates with tumor aggressiveness and reduced treatment efficacy in hepatocellular carcinoma.

SIRT3 deficiency exacerbates myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury, and SIRT3 protects the heart through mitochondrial quality control and oxidative-stress defense. As the primary mitochondrial deacetylase it sustains OXPHOS and antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2, so its loss amplifies reperfusion damage. This makes SIRT3 a key mitochondrial cardioprotective factor.

Serum SIRT3 levels are associated with clinical outcome and prognosis in COVID-19, being markedly lower in severe patients. This positions serum SIRT3 as a potential prognostic biomarker that reflects mitochondrial health and antioxidant reserve during systemic viral inflammation, analogous to its diagnostic value in lung cancer.
